oa:W7161834801.title: Apples and Oranges: Exaggerated Multiple Religious Belief in East Asia
oa:W7161834801.venue: Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion
oa:W7161834801.abstract: ABSTRACT Recent scholarship proposes that East Asians commonly hold multiple religious beliefs simultaneously, even when they report a single religious identity or none at all. This note argues that this claim is substantially exaggerated due to a measurement mismatch: What Global East Survey (GES)‐based studies operationalize as religious belief is better understood as ambient cultural familiarity. Using probability sample data from the 2023 Pew Research Center Survey of Religion and Spirituality in East Asian Societies across Taiwan, Hong Kong, South Korea, and Japan, I test whether the multiple religious belief pattern holds under more precise operationalization. When replicating the GES approach using cultural attachment items, the familiar pattern reproduces. When instead examining active devotion to specific deities, prevalence drops substantially, most sharply among Christians and religious nones, though the extent varies across societies. Comparing cultural attachment to religious belief is comparing apples to oranges.

oa:W7161944451.title: Calvin's "Theodicy" in his «Sermons on Job» and the hiddenness of God
oa:W7161944451.venue: Library and Archives Canada (Government of Canada)
oa:W7161944451.abstract: Calvin's "Theodicy" has been substantially ignored or simply negated until now on the assumption that the issues raised by the modern problem of evil and Calvin's discussion of providence and evil are different. The unspoken premise underlying this conviction is that theodicy would be a modern problem, since earlier formulations in no way attempted to justify God's actions. The goal of the present research decisively goes in the opposite direction. It aims to demonstrate that one of the most important reasons that prompted Calvin to preach for almost 2 years 159 Sermons on the Book of Job was to give an answer to the anguishing problem of human suffering and to "vindicate" God's justice. As if he were installed in a tribunal and with the enthusiasm of a lawyer Calvin made recourse to all the possible formal exceptions and substantive arguments, trying to persuade, convince, and exhort his contemporaries that God, in spite of all the charges made against Him, was not only blameless, but also just. The theologian, the minister, and the God's lawyer were merging within Calvin's person to the extent that very often it is not easy to understand who wrote: the theologian equipped with the instruments of law, or the lawyer armed with the instruments of biblical exegesis. His attempt found its more appropriate expression, when in the Sermons on Job he resorted to the concept of "double justice." The distinction between the "revealed" and the "hidden" justice of God enabled him to try to give a provisional answer to all those cases in which the divine justice was challenged. Nevertheless, Calvin's defence of God's justice reached its apex, when he conveyed the attention of the church to the definitive revelation of God's justice that wi

oa:W7162192314.title: Seder Cognitivo And The Universe Of Instants: Why The Asymmetry Of Memory Is Not A Physical Problem But A Problem Of The Mind
oa:W7162192314.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7162192314.abstract: This preprint introduces the concept of Cognitive Seder (from Hebrew seder, meaning order) as an active principle of the mind that scans and organizes static instants (Nows) into meaningful temporal sequences. Building on Julian Barbour's timeless universe of configurations, the paper argues that the asymmetry of memory — we remember the past but not the future — is not a physical problem but a cognitive one. The mind, acting as a scanner, reduces Sederic entropy (informational disorder) by imposing a coherent narrative order on otherwise ambiguous configurations. A concrete example with four tree states illustrates how the same set of Nows can be ordered differently, and only the ordering that produces sense (B → C → A → D) constitutes genuine temporal experience. The model offers an original critique of physicalism, situates itself within objective idealist theism, and provides a philosophical foundation that addresses the weaknesses often attributed to Barbour's metaphysics. This work is part of a broader research program exploring consciousness, time, and the active role of the mind in constituting reality.

oa:W7162460444.title: Divine Hiddenness: Evidence and Transcendence
oa:W7162460444.abstract: In recent work, Charity Anderson and Jeffrey Sanford Russell have provided important clarifications for evidential versions of the divine hiddenness argument.However, Anderson and Russell don't adequately motivate a shift in this debate from the argument's original deductive formulation.This is conspicuous, given J. L. Schellenberg's claims on the topic.I locate support for such a shift in Michael Rea's recent work on transcendence.Interestingly, Anderson and Russell say of this work that Rea's appeal to transcendence is out of place.I argue they miss something important: in fact, transcendence moves like Rea's are appropriate; and because of this, evidential arguments like those explored by Anderson and Russell are hiddenness's best route forward.

oa:W7162678315.title: God, justice, and accountability
oa:W7162678315.abstract: Abstract This paper argues for the non-existence of God conceived as a perfectly just Supreme Lawgiver who holds all rational agents accountable for commands attributed through revelation. Unlike divine hiddenness arguments that appeal to God’s love, this argument examines the procedural requirements of perfect justice: just accountability requires that agents recognise the existence of the authority to which they are subject. If God justly holds all blameless, non-resistant agents accountable to revealed commands, such agents must believe they have adequate evidence that the Commander exists. Yet many conscientious agents, including canonised saints and sincere seekers, report lacking adequate evidence despite sustained, non-resistant effort. The resulting epistemic situation is incompatible with just accountability since no-one can be justly obligated to obey commands from an authority whose existence they cannot recognise. The argument concludes that no recognisably perfectly just Supreme Lawgiver exists who holds all accountable to revealed commands. The conclusion leaves open the possibility that a non-commanding deistic God exists, but argues that God as the revealed Commander whose justice is recognisably exercised does not exist. Abrahamic conceptions of revealed divine legislation, moral obligation, punishment, and forgiveness cannot be grounded in recognisably just divine authority.

oa:W7162679506.title: The Silent Apophasis
oa:W7162679506.abstract: Abstract This article argues that the contemporary existential and intellectual problem of divine hiddenness ( Deus absconditus ) must be reframed through the intersecting lenses of trauma theory and the sociocultural conditions of a secular age. Moving beyond the analytical philosophical problem of non-belief and classical apophatic (negative) theology, it posits that the perceived silence of God is most acutely experienced as a hermeneutical rupture within contexts of profound suffering and within a secular “immanent frame.” The article constructs a “trauma-informed apophatic theology.” This model reconceives divine hiddenness not primarily as an epistemological puzzle or a mystical ascent, but as a potential mode of kenotic solidarity – a divine participation in godforsakenness that calls for an ethical, narrative, and communal theological response. This approach seeks to reground theological possibility in a responsibility to the traumatised other and in a humble, reflective practice that holds open the space of silence without premature resolution.

oa:W7162698959.title: Belief, No-Fault Unbelief and Medieval Christian Thought
oa:W7162698959.abstract: Traditionally, Christians have viewed unbelief as resulting from moral and/or cognitive shortcomings. However, a recent proposal such as John Schellenberg's 'divine hiddenness argument' for atheism has supported the idea that there is no-fault unbelief. In this Element, the author draws on important insights from medieval Christian thought to argue that both believers and non-believers should stop blaming each other based on mere evidence. Believers may recognise that no-fault unbelief can, in a sense, apply to them, too. They may find it perplexing that they neither believe nor achieve communion with God as much as they would like. Proponents of no-fault unbelief might focus on achieving communion with God rather than solely worrying about absolving themselves of blame. Ultimately, believers and non-believers alike might promote spiritual progress by setting aside the primacy of evidence and committing themselves to God and the good.

oa:W7162756513.title: The Exhaustion of the Grounding Space: A Structural Proof of Agápēic Relational Metaphysics
oa:W7162756513.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7162756513.abstract: This paper argues that the history of systematic metaphysics has produced three canonical responses to the grounding problem — non-relational pure actuality (Thomas Aquinas), internal self-differentiating dialectic (G.W.F. Hegel), and processual relational ground (Alfred North Whitehead and Charles Hartshorne) — and that a fourth family, Dualism, completes the logical space of non-agápēic alternatives. Through a unified structural analysis organized around two diagnostic axes — the unity of the ground and the mode of causation — the paper demonstrates that the resulting four collapse families (Monism, Dualism, Emptiness, and Determinism) are exhaustive: every possible metaphysical first principle either occupies one of these four positions or fails the minimal adequacy conditions for a ground. Agápēic Relational Metaphysics (ARM) is a first-philosophy project deriving the structure of the ultimate ground from transcendental-structural analysis. The term agápē functions throughout as a structural designator — non-coercive, distinction-preserving, self-giving relational actuality — and carries no theological loading in the premises. Under ARM's criterion of constitutive relationality, Aquinas structurally trends toward Monism at the intra-divine level. Hegel exhibits the same structural tendency because creaturely distinction is the Absolute's self-differentiation rather than genuine otherness. Whitehead and Hartshorne collapse into Emptiness because the consequent nature of God is contingent and posterior, inverting the grounding relation. Thomas Nagel's contemporary impasse is formally diagnosed as a structurally necessary consequence of these exhausted options. This paper employs the same two-argument architecture as Paper 6 of this series. The primary argument is a po

oa:W7162958149.title: From Lament to Resistance: Theopolitical Mourning in Shia Islam and Biblical Traditions
oa:W7162958149.abstract: This article compares mourning and lamentation in Biblical religiosity and Shia Islam within this essay. This study moves away from the tendency of academics to see grief as a mere psychological reaction to death. Instead, as a practice, it sees grief as theological, social and political. Based on ritual theory and the continuing bonds approach, the present article builds on earlier work in arguing for mourning and memorialization as a tool to preserve memory and to protest ethically. Biblical mourning is examined as a form of moral protest and theological questioning through a conceptual analysis of sacred texts and ritual performances. In addition, Shia mourning a collective act of ritualized ethical and political devotion through, for example, ta’ziyeh and matam, positions the sacred suffering of Imam Hussein as a source of justice. A discussion of Biblical and Shia Mourning indicates that both practices of lamentation negotiate divine silence and political exile; further, both practices allow believers to strengthen their ties with the dead and collective identity. This paper adds to our understanding of mourning by regarding grief as an affective performative. Ritualized mourning practices in both traditions, therefore, are counter-discursive responses against the dominant power. In other words, in both Biblical and Shia mourning, the use of grief must definitely be considered as an instrument of political and ethical unpacking of death and suffering in the margins ascertaining the dignity of the victim. The article further argues that the transmission and ritualization of mourning contribute to the formation of a shared ethical grammar across historical contexts and sectarian differences.

oa:W7163155753.title: Divine Hiddenness
oa:W7163155753.abstract: Why is God hidden? How might God be pointed out? In this timely study, Chad Engelland provides an original and compelling account of why God the creator is naturally hidden and how God can be intended. Drawing on phenomenology, philosophy of language, and medieval thought, he explores these questions, arguing that if the God in question is the ultimate source of all things, then hiddenness is necessary. Only a creature, rather than the creator, can appear directly in experience. Nonetheless, God the creator can be named as the ultimate source of all through a deferred ostension, which is a way of establishing the reference to a hidden cause through some manifest effect. Moreover, the deferred ostension can be clarified not only through the phenomenology of absent authors, which is a special case of the problem of other minds, but also via the fulfillment of desire in giving thanks for all.

oa:W7163175110.title: Divine Hiddenness and Phenomenology
oa:W7163175110.abstract: Phenomenology is necessary if the phenomenon in question is hidden. But, as Schellenberg and Nietzsche before him observe, God is hidden; therefore, a phenomenology of God is necessary. This phenomenology of God is called “aletheism” from the Greek word for truth, which, with its alpha-privative, implies that the condition for the possibility of truth is hiddenness; aletheism explores the way God, just to be the creator, would have to be hidden to creation.

oa:W7163263126.title: Conclusion
oa:W7163263126.abstract: As a basic phenomenological constraint, God is hidden to creation in virtue of being the creator. The conclusion identifies implications for the typical atheistic and the theistic responses to the problem of divine hiddenness. Against the atheist who holds than an all-loving God would always want to be in a relation with us, the conclusion argues that if God is in fact the hidden creator, our ultimate source, he would be uniquely the sort of thing we were implicitly always in relation to even if we were unaware of it. Against the theist who wants to explain divine hiddenness in terms of a moral defect of the one seeking, the conclusion argues that such resistance would only be detectable after the fact, in light of faith, and so would be an issue for theological, not philosophical explication.

oa:W7163865523.title: Editorial: Advancing sports cardiology: new frontiers in athlete screening and recovery
oa:W7163865523.abstract: Sports cardiology is a rapidly evolving field at the intersection of maximizing athletic performance and safeguarding cardiovascular health [1]. With the continuous advancement of diagnostic technologies and the growing diversity of athletic populations, understanding the cardiac impacts of intense physical activity has become increasingly complex [2,3]. This Research Topic was conceived to explore the latest challenges and innovations, emphasizing a balanced approach that integrates technological advancements with athletes' diverse physiological needs [4][5][6][7]. The five original articles collected herein contribute to shaping new cardiovascular screening methods, exploring the central role of artificial intelligence (AI), defining updated recovery guidelines, and assessing the impact of explosive training.Preventive cardiovascular evaluation is a fundamental tool for mitigating the risk of sudden cardiac death in athletes, which can be triggered by hidden genetic conditions or coronary abnormalities [8,9]. However, differentiating normal physiological adaptations resulting from intensive training from early pathological alterations remains a major clinical challenge [10,11]. In this context, Banerjee analyzes the evolution of screening protocols, highlighting how integrating digital tools and machine learning-including AIenhanced stethoscopes and predictive software for ECG and cardiac magnetic resonance-can revolutionize sports cardiology by optimizing diagnostic accuracy and preventing adverse events.Addressing the intrinsic complexity related to ethnic differences and varying degrees of remodeling in athletic populations [12], Guo and Wu propose an innovative multimodal AI-driven framework. Their system utilizes CardioSpectra and Risk-Stratified Exertional Embed

oa:W7164193909.title: Introduction
oa:W7164193909.abstract: This chapter establishes the foundations for a novel approach to the problem of evil—the Exemplarist Theodicy. After examining the historical development of the problem and evaluating traditional theodicies, including the free will defence, soul-making theodicy, and sceptical theism, it identifies their critical limitations. The chapter introduces the Exemplarist Theodicy as a comprehensive alternative that demonstrates how suffering functions as a logical necessity for transforming individuals into exemplars of moral goodness through a four-stage process: participation in basic goods, exercise of self-formation, acquisition of virtues, and undergoing transformative experiences. This theodicy provides a unified explanation for both human and animal suffering, addresses the uneven distribution of adversity, and responds to anti-theodicy critiques. By beginning with the specific phenomenon of suffering before addressing more abstract formulations, this approach maintains both philosophical rigour and moral sensitivity. The chapter concludes by previewing the book&s;s structure, which develops this theodicy&s;s metaphysical and normative foundations before applying it to major philosophical formulations of the problems of suffering, evil, and divine hiddenness.

oa:W7164197413.title: The Exemplarist Theodicy (iii)
oa:W7164197413.abstract: This chapter examines four major formulations of the problem of divine hiddenness (PH) and demonstrates how the Exemplarist Theodicy provides a comprehensive solution to each. Beginning with J.L. Schellenberg&s;s argument from non-resistant non-belief, which contends that a perfectly loving God would ensure no one capable of relationship with him would fail to believe, the chapter shows how the Exemplarist Theodicy resolves this challenge by articulating a richer conception of divine love and demonstrating that the goods achievable under primary hiddenness differ in kind from those achievable within belief, blocking Schellenberg&s;s objection that any good associated with hiddenness could be achieved through relationship-compatible means. The chapter then addresses Theodore Drange&s;s argument focusing on the non-belief in the gospel message, demonstrating how the Exemplarist Theodicy explains why the current distribution of belief creates optimal conditions for exemplar formation by identifying exemplar transformation as the specific divine desire that overrides God&s;s desire for universal belief, directly meeting Drange&s;s challenge to opponents and demonstrating consistency with the biblical evidence he cites. Next, it examines Stephen Maitzen&s;s formulation centred on the geographic distribution of belief, showing how this distribution enables distinctive exemplar types to develop across different cultural contexts, with the exemplarist framework predicting the geographic clustering with greater specificity than naturalism&s;s explanatorily shallow account of cultural transmission. Finally, the chapter analyses Jason Marsh&s;s argument from natural non-belief throughout evolutionary history, establishing how the Exemplarist Theodicy accounts for the gradual devel

oa:W7164304833.title: The Teleology of Divine Separation
oa:W7164304833.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7164304833.abstract: This study explores the teleological implications of divine separation in Gauḍīya Vedānta, focusing on Śrī Kṛṣṇa's reflection in the *Caitanya-caritāmṛta*, Ādi-līlā 3.14, where He laments the absence of prema-bhakti in the material world. The paper argues that this absence renders the world 'useless,' despite its existing spiritual frameworks of karma, dharma, and liberation. The distinction between restoration and fulfillment is central to the thesis: while liberation restores the jīva's constitutional standing, prema fulfills the purpose for which that standing exists. The material world is thus seen as a veiled field where agency, longing, and relational capacity are matured, culminating in Śrī Caitanya Mahāprabhu's descent to distribute prema-bhakti. The paper employs a three-tiered methodological approach: direct śāstric evidence, inference to the best explanation, and original constructive proposals. It posits that divine hiddenness, or viraha, serves a teleological function, preparing the jīva for the ultimate fulfillment in loving devotion. The study invites a reevaluation of the material world's purpose, suggesting that its highest meaning is unveiled through the distribution of prema-bhakti, which transcends mere liberation and religious adherence. oa:W7164481491.title: The Role of Private Evidence in Avoiding Epistemic Suspension of Judgment (Agnosticism) Regarding the Existence of God
oa:W7164481491.venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
oa:W7164481491.abstract: According to the evidentialist approach, one’s final position on a proposition emerges from the balance between supporting and opposing evidence, and justifying that proposition requires considering (or weighing) all available evidence. Unlike theists and atheists—who interpret evidence to favor their own beliefs — the agnostic regards the evidence as neutral, whether due to ambiguity about what counts as evidence, the failure of individual items to establish the claim, or the equal weight of opposing evidence. In this context, “evidence” typically refers to public evidence accessible to all. Occasionally, however, private and non-shareable evidence may arise in favor of one side. The key question is whether such private evidence can challenge or outweigh public evidence and thereby lift the suspension of judgment. Based on this study’s findings, private evidence can be valid and effective in epistemic dilemmas that incline toward agnosticism, provided two conditions are met: it possesses independent epistemic grounding (evidence supporting evidence), and the opposing public evidence is not so overwhelmingly strong as to create a perfect symmetry. Keywords: Private Evidence; Agnosticism; Suspension of Epistemic Judgment; Theism; Atheism; Religious Experience. IntroductionThe dominant approach in religious epistemology holds that evidence ultimately determines the outcome of debates, with justification resting on the evidence one possesses while rejecting contrary evidence. Theists and atheists both claim that evidence conclusively supports their own stance. In contrast, the epistemic agnostic suspends judgment—often because of uncertainty about what qualifies as evidence, flaws in individual evidential items, or balanced weights among conflicting evidence. oa:W7164503739.title: A Qualitative Approach to Understanding Religion in the Thought of Mohammad Taqi Mesbah Yazdi and Mostafa Malekian
oa:W7164503739.venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
oa:W7164503739.abstract: Religion has always been regarded as one of the fundamental pillars of legitimacy and governance in post-revolutionary Iran. Consequently, various theoretical and discursive efforts have emerged to understand, interpret, and reexamine religion, among which two major currents—“traditional Islam” and “religious intellectualism”—hold a prominent place. This study focuses on the ideas of two influential thinkers, Ayatollah Mohammad-Taqi Mesbah Yazdi and Mostafa Malekian, as key representatives of these two intellectual streams, aiming to explore and analyze the components and mechanisms underlying their understanding of religion. The research adopts a qualitative methodology based on Attride-Stirling’s three-stage thematic analysis, using excerpts from speeches and written works by these two figures to extract the core themes. The findings reveal that Malekian’s thought emphasizes three overarching themes: “the variability of religious knowledge,” “the rationalization of religious beliefs,” and “ethics and spirituality as the foundation of religiosity.” In contrast, Ayatollah Mesbah highlights three central components: “the necessity of explaining religious beliefs,” “the comprehensiveness of religion,” and “faith-based obligation.” This divergence reflects a fundamental difference in the epistemological, methodological, and teleological foundations of their respective approaches to understanding religion. Keywords: Understanding Religion, Religious Intellectualism, Traditional Islam, Misbah Yazdi, Malekian, Qualitative Approach. IntroductionIn contemporary Iranian intellectual discourse, religion continues to serve as a foundational pillar for social legitimacy and governance, shaping both normative frameworks and individual ethical conduct. oa:W7164863935.title: Sceptical theism and fine-tuning: relocating rather than resolving the tension
oa:W7164863935.abstract: Abstract Sceptical theism is commonly deployed as a response to evidential arguments from evil by challenging our entitlement to infer, from the evils we observe, what God would or would not be likely to permit. Standard fine-tuning arguments, however, appear to require precisely the sort of expectation-guided reasoning that sceptical theism places under pressure: namely, the claim that a life-permitting universe is not too improbable given theism. Recent discussion has sharpened this tension: Donahue argues that sceptical-theist considerations undercut standard fine-tuning arguments, while Boyce argues that sceptical theists can nevertheless endorse a suitably revised version. I argue that Boyce’s proposal is philosophically important but dialectically costly. Boyce does not replace generic theism with a more specific hypothesis; rather, he keeps generic theism as the target hypothesis while allowing historically mediated background information, D, to generate the relevant theistic expectations. My objection is that once D is admitted for that positive purpose, it cannot be quarantined from adverse evidential assessment. The result is not merely that the problem of evil is formally reopened. Rather, enriched versions of evil, suffering, and divine hiddenness become serious enough to require independent theistic response. Boyce’s strategy therefore preserves coherence only by narrowing sceptical theism’s traditional broad anti-evil role.

oa:W7165041387.title: Morality, Power, and the Problem of a Self-Sufficient God
oa:W7165041387.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7165041387.abstract: A structured synthesis arguing that human moral and religious authority remains historically entangled with power and has never been authenticated in a way that distinguishes revelation from human assertion — so obedience cannot be justified by claiming divine warrant alone. The case runs in two independent movements that converge. The first (Sections 1–6) is metaphysical: whether a self-sufficient, omniscient God could have any coherent, non-self-referential reason to create a world and command its creatures — engaging the actus purus defense (Davies, with Stump's narrative theodicy as a distinct Thomist alternative), accommodation, Molinism, and the punitive structure of the biblical text. The second (Sections 7–10) is historical and behavioral: the observed conduct of moral-religious systems — how they bind and mobilize groups and serve as the contested lever of power — is fully explained without appeal to a divine author. Sections 11–14 clear the metaethical ground (burden of proof, moral variation, "evil" as a moving designation). The conclusion rests on a final pair of moves (Sections 15–19): no claimed revelation has been authenticated — the public-revelation counter (Sinai; Paul's five hundred) is answered directly — and since authentication fails, the diagnostic question that replaces obedience is cui bono: who benefits if the claim is believed? The diagnostic is scoped against its own misuse and is finally turned on the essay's own recommendation. An appendix states the argument's honest limits. A condensed, general-audience version of the same case is available as a separate essay, "Who Told You That Was God?" oa:W7165813132.title: Only God Knows Best
oa:W7165813132.venue: TheoLogica An International Journal for Philosophy of Religion and Philosophical Theology
oa:W7165813132.abstract: This paper develops an epistemic argument for aspirational theism, the view that for agents who regard theism as a live epistemic possibility, there exist defeasible reasons to rationally hope that God exists. The argument begins from the fact that finite epistemic agents must economize their cognitive resources, and thus should seek sources of substantive, rather than trivial, epistemic goods. If God exists, He would be uniquely well-positioned—given His omniscience and moral perfection—to deliver epistemic goods that are personally fitting and epistemically valuable. The paper distinguishes aspirational theism from pro- and anti-theism and aspirational atheism, situating the favored view within broader debates concerning rational hope, epistemic value, and the ethics of belief. And it engages with several objections from divine hiddenness, privacy, and pessimistic meta-induction, concluding that even under skeptical theist constraints, theistic hope remains epistemically appropriate for many.

oa:W7165859494.title: General Theory of Discrepancy: Pathology, Logos, and Regenerative Recursion
oa:W7165859494.abstract: This project develops the General Theory of Discrepancy (GTD), a conceptual framework proposing that discrepancy is a fundamental condition of human existence rather than pathology itself. The project integrates relational pathology, collective violence, religion, divine silence, and logos into a unified theoretical architecture. Subsequent papers will develop each domain individually while remaining grounded in this overarching framework.

oa:W7166042781.title: Islamic Theodicy Vs Existential Absurdity: A Literary-Discursive Study of Suffering and Divine Silence in Contemporary Fiction
oa:W7166042781.abstract: The question of suffering and the divine silence has long been perceived as a central concern in both theological and modern literature. This study aims to explore the abiding connection of both Islamic theodicy, which highlights suffering within a divine moral order, and existential absurdity that views suffering as primary evidence of an indifferent universe. Thus, this research incorporates a literary-discursive approach to examine how contemporary fiction in modern literature negotiates with the contrasting paradigms of human suffering, silence, and faith. Furthermore, this article draws upon the Islamic theological perspectives of suffering, patience (sabr), and divine wisdom that juxtapose with existentialist interpretations and absurdity as the divine perceived intervention. Through close textual analysis of selected contemporary fiction, the research investigates how characters confront trauma, silence, suffering, and injustice while grappling with questions of divine justice and silence. The study further argues that modern literature is a discursive space where modern and theological frameworks intersect, presenting a mutually inclusive space for characters that reimagined divine justice and existential absurdity. They not only offered a nuanced insight into human research for meaning through suffering and hardships, but they also redefined faith, skepticism, and moral resilience.

oa:W7167343076.title: The Science of Letters
oa:W7167343076.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7167343076.abstract: Shams al-Ma'arif of al-Buni, Volume II: The Letters That Were Said to Build the World Shams al-Ma'arif is what happened when the Muslim love of the divine Names reached for a lever, and reading it with the lights on, as history of ideas and not as practice, shows the exact seam where remembering God's Names tips over into trying to operate them, and why the line matters more than the alphabet. Al-Buni (d. 1225), remembered in some chains as a pious Sufi, compiled the most famous manual of letter-and-Name magic in Islam. Read closely from the public-domain Arabic and honest scholarship, Shams al-Ma'arif is not secret power for sale; it is a document of one human wish, to make the sacred alphabet do work, standing on the seam the shariah draws between worship and transgression. The problem was never the alphabet; it is the claim of command. Audiences: Young Muslim readers who have seen Shams al-Ma'arif sold as a book of power — The book reaches them as frightening magic or hidden purchasable power, never as a text to understand. Readers of the history of ideas and comparative esotericism — The science of letters is either romanticized or sneered at, never read as serious history of thought. Believers uneasy about the line between worship and magic — The pull to treat the divine Names as instruments, prayer as technique, God as a system to operate. Note: written from Indonesian operator context. Frameworks apply broadly to other emerging-market and SME settings.

oa:W7168017544.title: Safavid Epigraphy in Bavanat County, Iran: Architectural and Funerary Inscriptions
oa:W7168017544.abstract: One of the most important achievements of humankind is the invention of writing systems that have enabled the recording of information and the transmission of knowledge. Inscriptions and other written materials are important sources for historical and archaeological studies. They provide information about beliefs, ideas, and historical events and are used in the dating of monuments and the study of calligraphic traditions. During the archaeological survey conducted in 2015 in Bavanat County, a collection of inscriptions from the Safavid period was identified. The aim of this paper is to document these inscriptions and analyze their content in order to understand religious beliefs, cultural characteristics of the region, and assist in dating monuments and cemeteries. These inscriptions are classified into two main groups: architectural inscriptions and gravestone inscriptions, and are written in three scripts: Thuluth, Naskh, and Nasta’liq. The Imamzadeh Seyyed Shah Mirhamzeh inscriptions contain information about the construction date, the name of the architect, and Qur’anic verses. In addition to the Qur’anic verses, the gravestones also contain the names of the deceased and the date of death, which can be used in dating cemeteries and studying the historical developments of the region. The results of this study show that the Safavid inscriptions of Bavanat, in addition to their artistic and calligraphic value, are an important source for understanding the religious, social, and historical dimensions of this region during the Safavid period.

oa:W7168246909.title: Kierkegaard’s Existential Apophaticism
oa:W7168246909.abstract: Abstract This study begins by providing a survey of the scholarly literature on Kierkegaard’s apophaticism and identifying the two main approaches that have been taken. The first approach considers Kierkegaard’s apophaticism to have developed independently of classical apophatic theology, whereas the second approach locates Kierkegaard in the “Neoplatonist-Eckhartian” tradition. The present article argues for the first approach by providing a survey of the apophatic motifs of Kierkegaard’s authorship organized around the notions of “objective apophaticism” and “subjective apophaticism.” “Objective apophaticism” denotes those passages in Kierkegaard’s works where God is considered to be hidden in and of himself. Apophaticism of this kind appears in Kierkegaard’s emphasis on God’s transcendence of existence, reason, and language by virtue of his “infinite qualitative difference” from humankind. “Subjective apophaticism” refers to the hiddenness of God that arises from human beings’ failure to relate to God properly. It is not only God’s transcendent nature that conceals God from human beings but also the “existential misalignment” of human beings. Such existential misalignment comes about through human beings misconceiving God and the kind of relationship they should sustain towards God. Much of the apophaticism of Kierkegaard’s authorship stems from exploring and attempting to correct this existential misalignment, for which reason the article concludes with the claim that the apophatic strand in Kierkegaard’s authorship is best categorized as “existential apophaticism.”

oa:W7168335277.title: La Nuit. Entre la tentative d’animalisation, la memoire et l’intertexte biblique chez Elie Wiesel
oa:W7168335277.venue: CINECA IRIS Institutial research information system (University of Pisa)
oa:W7168335277.abstract: This paper examines La Nuit (Night) by Elie Wiesel through the combined lenses of animalization, memory, and biblical intertextuality, with particular attention to the work’s palimpsestic formation and its theological and ethical implications. Beginning with the complex editorial history of the text – from its original Yiddish version ...Un di velt hot geshvign to the French La Nuit – the study highlights how successive rewritings transform anangry testimonial narrative into a refined literary work addressed to a broader non-Jewish audience. Drawing on Gérard Genette’s theory of transtextuality, the paper argues that La Nuit functions simultaneously as memoir, anti-biblical narrative, and hypertext, especially as an “anti-Exodus” marked by divine absence. The analysis focuses on the systematic dehumanization of the deportees, interpreted as a process of forced animalization, and on Wiesel’s use of Jewish biblical, Talmudic, and kabbalistic references to reframe the Shoah within a symbolic and theological discourse. Central to this reading is the role of memory as an ethical act that preserves humanity in the face of radical evil and divine silence (hester panim). Ultimately, the paper positions La Nuit as an “anti-Tanakh” that denies redemption while affirming testimony as a moral responsibility toward the victims and the future.

oa:W7168366306.title: Asymmetry in Divine Love
oa:W7168366306.abstract: I argue that J. L. Schellenberg’s argument from divine hiddenness, among other hiddenness arguments, rests upon an inadequate conception of perfect love—namely, the assumption that perfect love requires openness to conscious, reciprocal relationship. Through an analysis of paradigmatic human relationships, informed by an Aristotelian understanding of relational reciprocity, patristic articulations of the Trinity, and perfect being theology, I show that genuine loving relationships can exist without conscious reciprocity from one party and that this asymmetry reflects rather than contradicts the nature of divine love. Ultimately, I demonstrate that a Christian account of perfect love in the tradition of classical theism does not necessitate the kind of conscious reciprocal relationship that Schellenberg, among others, demands from the God-creature relationship.

oa:W7169786232.title: God and Love: Divine Nature in Philosophical, Theological, and Feminist Perspective
oa:W7169786232.abstract: This dissertation draws on philosophical, theological, and feminist resources to offer a novel account of divine love, which renders a transformed view of God, where the divine nature is primarily characterized by love. I begin by arguing for the need of a feminist intervention in contemporary theorizing about the divine nature in Christian analytic philosophy of religion, contending that if we take feminist insights seriously, we ought to carve out a more substantial role for love in the divine nature. Doing so, I argue, requires offering a robust account of divine love and that, to offer such an account, we must first inquire into the nature of love, as such. Regarding love’s nature, I argue for two theses: love is a unified notion with several subtypes (including divine love) and love is primarily a matter of robust care for the beloved, which I further specify in terms of attention, investment, and nurturance. Relating this to the divine nature, I argue that divine love can be understood as a subtype of this account of love, with the stipulation that it involves expression of care fitting to divine perfection. Additionally, I argue for a view of the divine traits on which love plays an enlarged shaping role in the divine nature and show how this view finds solid footing in both Christian scripture and doctrine. Overall, on the proposed account, God is the ideal exemplar of personal love, and divine love is a matter of God’s robust care for creation. To deepen and concretize the account, I address potential objections rooted in concrete experience (i.e., suffering and differences in divine and human love) and draw on scripture to identify expressions, or forms, of divine love and relate these to the account. oa:W7170295759.title: عميت عين لا تراك
oa:W7170295759.abstract: Blind Is the Eye That Does Not See You is a philosophical and theological y. It embarks on an intellectual journey into one of humanity's most profound questions: Is the evidence for the existence of the Creator absent, or is it human insight that fails to perceive it? From this central question, the book seeks to reconstruct the discourse on faith in God through an approach that integrates rational argument, scientific evidence, and reflective contemplation, presenting a perspective that respects reason while awakening the innate human disposition toward truth. The book does not proceed from the assumption that evidence for God's existence must be discovered; rather, it argues that such evidence permeates the entire universe—in the harmony of its laws, the precision of its design, the complexity of life, and the remarkable nature of the human disposition. The title, Blind Is the Eye That Does Not See You, symbolizes the idea that true blindness is not the blindness of sight, but the blindness of insight that overlooks the countless signs manifested throughout the universe and within the human soul, failing to recognize the testimony of creation to its Creator. The author guides the reader through an intellectual exploration that spans the principles of causality and cosmic order, the genetic code and the life sciences, as well as human nature, morality, and the meaning of existence. Drawing upon rigorous philosophical discussions, scientific evidence, and contemplative reflections, the book presents a vision in which sound reason, authentic science, and the uncorrupted human disposition converge upon a single conclusion: that this universe has a Wise Creator. Rather than appealing to emotion alone or engaging in philosophical argument for the sake of intellectual victo

oa:W7170496919.title: The Book of Every Talisman
oa:W7170496919.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7170496919.abstract: A World Survey of the Charmed Object, Reproduced in Full from the Sources, with a Tawhid Conscience Gather every talisman the literate world ever made — Babylonian, Egyptian, Jewish, Greek, Islamic, Hermetic, Indic, Sinitic, Nusantaran, African, Norse — reproduce each faithfully from its public-domain source with the theology still attached, and the exhaustiveness itself disenchants: seen whole, the "forbidden secret" turns out to be a public, repetitive, cross-copied human habit, and the surest cure for wanting a charm is to see all ten thousand of them at once. Amelia Febriany did not want to write this book, and says so. It is the exhaustive twin of her Shams al-Ma'arif reading: where that series withholds the working apparatus and reads the wish behind it, this one gathers the apparatus of the whole literate world — beginning with the taweez of Islam and widening to Babylon and Egypt, the Hebrew and late-antique books, the Western grimoires, and the Indic, Sinitic, Nusantaran, African, and Norse traditions — and reproduces each talisman faithfully from its public-domain source, with the theology and the shariah line still attached. Nothing is invented; every square, every letter-chain, every seal resolves to a cited original, and where no clean public-domain scan exists the entry is described, not fabricated. The argument is not that any of it works. The argument is tawhid, made by completeness: when the reader sees the Cairene and the Copt and the Kabbalist and the Javanese dukun and the Icelandic farmer all reach for the same moves with the same wish, the "secret power" reading collapses, and what remains is the archive of a very old human longing to make the sacred obey — and the exact seam, running through the reader's own hands, where remembering God tips over

oa:W7171006084.title: Sincere Seeking and Divine Hiddenness — 50
oa:W7171006084.abstract: A promise that God will be found by all sincere seekers is empirically and epistemically vulnerable. Sincere seekers across cultures report incompatible religious discoveries, while many apparently sincere seekers report no clear divine encounter at all. If a perfectly loving God intended reliable self-disclosure, we would expect clearer, more consistent, and less culture-bound outcomes than the world displays.

oa:W7171758201.title: Person-country Fit and Subjective Well-Being: The Roles of Religious Beliefs
oa:W7171758201.abstract: While previous studies have extensively examined the relationship between religion and subjective well-being (SWB), findings remain mixed, and ongoing debates persist regarding the nature and strength of this association. Moreover, less is known about specific dimensions of religiosity, such as the importance of God in individuals’ lives and its relationship with SWB. Building on the person-country fit literature, this study analyzes the implications of (a) the fit between personal importance of God and country-level religiosity norms for SWB, and (b) the fit between personal importance of God and societal freedom of religion for SWB. Utilizing data from 78 countries and regions ( N = 114,441), the findings reveal that cultural fit—specifically, alignment between individual-level and country-level importance of God—is significantly associated with higher SWB, with this association being particularly strong among older adults. These results provide valuable empirical and theoretical insights, offering important implications for research on religion, person-country fit in religiosity, and SWB.

oa:W7172110107.title: Mekanisme Kognitif Niat Beli Produk Kosmetik Halal: Peran Mediasi Halal Awareness pada Pengaruh Religious Belief dan Sertifikasi Halal
oa:W7172110107.abstract: This study aims to examine the effect of religious belief and halal certification on purchase intention of Safi halal cosmetic products, with halal awareness as a mediating variable. A quantitative approach was employed using a survey method involving 170 potential consumers in Malang City who were aware of Safi products but had never made a purchase. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Square–Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 3 software. The results indicate that religious belief and halal certification have a positive and significant effect on halal awareness and purchase intention. Furthermore, halal awareness is proven to have a positive and significant influence on purchase intention and partially mediates the relationship between religious belief and halal certification on purchase intention. These findings suggest that stronger religious values and clear halal certification enhance consumers’ halal awareness, which subsequently increases their intention to purchase halal cosmetic products.

oa:W7172120504.title: The Inversion of Greatness
oa:W7172120504.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172120504.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is a work of analytic metaphysics and philosophy of religion that reopens the classical question of what, if anything, exists necessarily. Where the cosmological and ontological traditions locate that necessity in a maximally great being — a God standing outside time, space, and matter as the source of all that is possible — this book argues the tradition asked the right question and misplaced the answer. oa:W7172129351.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is a work of analytic metaphysics and philosophy of religion that reopens the classical question of what, if anything, exists necessarily. Where the cosmological and ontological traditions locate that necessity in a maximally great being—a God standing outside time, space, and matter as the source of all that is possible—this book argues the tradition asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Rather than assuming modal logic to get the argument off the ground, the book builds that ground first: it derives the claim that whatever is possible is necessarily possible, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility, rather than taking it as a starting axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change requires temporality, spatiality, and physicality, borne by time, space, and substance, and that these three are necessarily instantiated. oa:W7172135924.title: God as a Unified Categorical Ground: Microphysical Fundamentality, Consciousness, and Panpsychism
oa:W7172135924.abstract: Abstract Contemporary fundamental physics and classical theistic metaphysics appear to exert opposing pressures on our conception of ultimate reality. Microphysical fundamentalism holds that the structure of the physical world is grounded in microphysical entities and their properties, whereas classical theism is committed to a single, unified ultimate ground that is explanatorily prior to all finite reality. Although not formally inconsistent, these commitments generate a substantive metaphysical tension once questions of categorical underwriting are made explicit. Existing theologically sympathetic responses address this tension only at a cost: micropsychist panpsychism preserves microphysical fundamentality but fragments ultimate grounding in a way that sits uneasily with monotheism, while cosmopsychism secures metaphysical unity at the expense of the bottom-up motivations of microphysical fundamentalism. This paper develops a third option, Unified Categorical Basis Panpsychism (UCBP), which preserves the fundamentality of microphysical entities with respect to physical structure and composition while locating ultimate unity at the level of categorical grounding. The view openly posits a novel primitive: a single, irreducibly mental, internally differentiated categorical basis—identified with God—in virtue of which physical properties have the dispositional profiles they have and conscious experience is metaphysically possible. The paper argues that this posit is theoretically motivated, internally coherent, and explanatorily principled, and that UCBP thereby avoids both the combination problem facing micropsychism and the decomposition problem facing cosmopsychism.

oa:W7172202748.title: Relational Emergence Theory： A Hierarchical Emergent Cosmological Model Based on Relational Ontology
oa:W7172202748.abstract: This paper proposes "Relational Emergence Theory," which asserts that the essence of the universe is neither matter, nor energy, nor information, but "relation." Relations continuously derive across different scales, and the process of derivation itself constitutes spacetime. Humans, along with their perception, logic, science, philosophy, and religion, are all localized self-observational phenomena within this relational network. This paper demonstrates the compatibility of this framework with physics, mathematics, biology, cognitive science, philosophy, and religion, and responds to challenges from Gödel's incompleteness theorems, quantum entanglement, Yogācāra Buddhism, the God hypothesis, and nihilism. The paper concludes that although this framework does not provide new observable predictions, it offers a meta-theory capable of delineating boundaries for existing disciplines and indicating ways in which they interconnect, while simultaneously providing a naturalistic foundation for questions of human meaning.

oa:W7172203113.title: The Science of Letters
oa:W7172203113.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172203113.abstract: Shams al-Ma'arif of al-Buni, Volume II: The Letters That Were Said to Build the World Shams al-Ma'arif is what happened when the Muslim love of the divine Names reached for a lever, and reading it with the lights on, as history of ideas and not as practice, shows the exact seam where remembering God's Names tips over into trying to operate them, and why the line matters more than the alphabet. Al-Buni (d. 1225), remembered in some chains as a pious Sufi, compiled the most famous manual of letter-and-Name magic in Islam. Read closely from the public-domain Arabic and honest scholarship, Shams al-Ma'arif is not secret power for sale; it is a document of one human wish, to make the sacred alphabet do work, standing on the seam the shariah draws between worship and transgression. The problem was never the alphabet; it is the claim of command. Audiences: Young Muslim readers who have seen Shams al-Ma'arif sold as a book of power — The book reaches them as frightening magic or hidden purchasable power, never as a text to understand. Readers of the history of ideas and comparative esotericism — The science of letters is either romanticized or sneered at, never read as serious history of thought. Believers uneasy about the line between worship and magic — The pull to treat the divine Names as instruments, prayer as technique, God as a system to operate. Note: written from Indonesian operator context. Frameworks apply broadly to other emerging-market and SME settings.

oa:W7172251218.title: Beyond Western Feminism: Islamic Feminist Ideologies And Muslim Women's Agency In A Woman Is No Man
oa:W7172251218.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172251218.abstract: This paper aims to analyse how Muslim women and patriarchal societies are represented in A Woman Is No Man using the theory of Islamic feminism. Feminist ideology has been dominated by the West and has ignored the role and experience of women who are deeply embedded in religious culture and traditions. Islamic feminism acts as a counter discourse to Western feminism that advocates gender justice by reinterpreting scriptures and challenging patriarchal interpretations of religion. This study is based on the works of various scholars such as Amina Wadud, Asma Barlas, Fatima Mernissi, and others. A close reading of the novel exposes themes such as trauma, diasporic identity, patriarchal power, and the resistance of women. Through the characters of Isra, Deya, and Fareeda, the paper examines how silence and tradition affect the lives of women. However, the paper also argues how women can resist oppression through education, self-reflection, and a new understanding of their religious beliefs. By contextualizing the novel within the debate surrounding Orientalism and Western perceptions of Muslim women, the paper examines the role of literature in subverting stereotypes and representations of Muslim women’s agency. Ultimately, the paper aims to show that Islamic feminism offers a different perspective of the agency of Muslim women in literature.

oa:W7172274175.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/ea6df646-03a8-47e2-b9e6-4cb308ffa567?authuser=1 The Body Is Built to Navigate: Quantum-Governed Embodiment, Relational Mapping, and a Catholic Invariant Grammar of Convergence presents a general theory of human navigation across physical, conceptual, social, moral, scientific, and religious domains. Its governing distinction is that a navigation system does not directly measure its destination. It estimates the traveler’s changing relation to signals, history, landmarks, uncertainty, and possible paths, then corrects movement over time. The paper traces this architecture across quantum-governed molecular processes, biological signal transduction, multisensory integration, neural oscillation, cognitive mapping, predictive modeling, memory, social coordination, and embodied action. It argues that the same general capacities used to move through physical environments also support navigation through ideas, relationships, values, traditions, rituals, and represented futures. A central distinction is drawn between navigational capacity, destination, and criterion. The body supplies the capacity to receive, remember, estimate, map, and correct, but biology alone does not determine which destination is true or good. Philosophies and religions therefore provide differing maps, authorities, practices, standards of error, and accounts of fulfillment. The interpretive method is Catholic Invariant Grammar, a relational framework that preserves distinctions such as source and manifestation, destination and path, sign and thing signified, participation and identity, nature and grace, observer and observed, sender and sent, and unity and distinction. oa:W7172289331.title: An opportunity to ‘be someone else’: the perceptions and experiences of male and female peer support workers in two US state prisons
oa:W7172289331.abstract: PURPOSE: In response to the increasing numbers of older, frail and dying persons in Western prisons and associated healthcare costs, awareness of the need of high-quality peer care in correctional facilities is growing. This paper aims to describe perceptions and experiences of male and female peer caregivers in two US prisons regarding their roles. DESIGN/METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: Data were collected via focus groups with peer caregivers (n = 15) incarcerated in two US state prisons and examined using thematic analysis. FINDINGS: Three themes were identified: "motivation and benefits", "challenges and costs" and "learning" associated with caregiving. The findings point to differences between male and female caregivers' motivation to perform the roles. While male peer caregivers in the sample appeared to be motivated by issues related to identity, masculinity and religious beliefs, female peer caregivers cited the value of meaningful relationships. However, there were several similarities between male and female's daily experiences and learning needs, and both groups enjoyed intrinsic and extrinsic rewards associated with their roles. ORIGINALITY/VALUE: To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first paper to conjointly describe male and female peer caregiver views and experiences of caring for older persons or persons with life-limiting illness. Findings underscore the need for more research aimed at making explicit the varying benefits of peer caregiving behind bars, as well as policies ensuring increased training for peer caregivers and correctional staff.

oa:W7172295569.title: Input Variability in Foreign Language Verb–Argument Construction Learning: A Primary School Intervention
oa:W7172295569.abstract: Abstract Input variability (i.e., varied experience with different grammar exemplars; “[talk/think/rant/wonder] about [god/bicycles/dogs]”) can improve generalization (i.e., “[Verb] about [Noun]”) and enhance learning. Controlled experiments show that input variability benefits children's generalization and extension of linguistic information from input structures to novel contexts (Wonnacott et al., 2012). Such findings drove our investigation into extending input variability benefits to classrooms. Following a usage‐based constructionist approach, we present a two‐week quasi‐experimental teaching intervention with two British Year 2 classes learning German (6‐to‐7‐year‐olds; 20 students per class). The intervention featured a variability and no‐variability condition, using 16 German “approach” event verb–argument constructions (“To the X [verb] the Y”), featuring four separate or just one verb in the verb slot, respectively. Posttests indicated that children exposed to variability generalized better to novel verbs. The findings corroborate controlled experiments. Even in “noisy” classrooms, input variability can benefit students’ construction generalization and extension to novel verbs.

oa:W7172392373.title: Personal Identity Domains among Adolescents in Indonesia: Salience of Religious Beliefs and Purpose in Life
oa:W7172392373.abstract: Research on adolescent identity has largely focused on developmental processes, while the content or domains of personal identity that are salient among adolescents within specific cultural contexts have not been systematically mapped. This gap is important because historically used domain lists may not be relevant for certain populations, including adolescents in Indonesia. This study aims to map the personal identity domains that are most frequently thought about (salience) and most clearly understood (clarity) among adolescents in Indonesia. Participants consisted of 454 adolescents aged 10-18 years (M = 14.49, SD = 2.51) in Indonesia. Data were collected using the Personal Identity Domain Questionnaire, which measures salience and clarity across 30 identity domains. The results indicated that religious beliefs and purpose in life emerged as the domains with the highest levels of salience and clarity among Indonesian adolescents. These findings suggest that certain identity domains are more prominent than others in terms of salience and clarity. Overall, these findings provide a descriptive empirical map of variation across personal identity domains, highlighting the contextual nature of identity content among adolescents in Indonesia.

oa:W7172393732.title: CRITICAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS OF CULTURAL VALUES AND BELIEFS IN SOCIETY THROUGH TEXTBOOKS
oa:W7172393732.abstract: Educational system with its goals and practices is now a dominant part of civilized societies. The purpose of this study is to analyze the ideologies and fundamental values which are working behind the theoretical representation of educational policies in Pakistan. Mixed Method approach has been applied in this study. Fairclough’s 3D model is used to conduct analysis on descriptive level, interpretational level and the explanatory level (Faiclough, 1989). This study has also applied Model of Van Dijk “The socio Cognitive Analysis” for ideological analysis (Dijk, 1989). Teaching content of selected books of Punjab and NWFP Curriculum Board has been analyzed by means of critical approaches. Paper demonstrates the findings which prove that how the textbook knowledge is socially constructed. Analysis has been carried out in various dimensions including textual analysis, analyzing lexical items, indoctrination of cultural social and religious beliefs. Moreover, the awareness of educated class about biasness of text is examined and last section discusses with the results and opinion of researcher. Thus, it has been extracted that course books and textual discourse in Pakistan serves the interests of powerful fraction of society and the interests of learners are kept aside while designing syllabus. This paper is to highlight the fact that books must be designed to transmit knowledge, develop creative skills and to make learners capable, therefore they must not be bias and neither should be mean of manipulating young minds

oa:W7172396774.title: Morality, Power, and the Problem of a Self-Sufficient God
oa:W7172396774.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172396774.abstract: A structured synthesis arguing that human moral and religious authority remains historically entangled with power and has never been authenticated in a way that distinguishes revelation from human assertion — so obedience cannot be justified by claiming divine warrant alone. The case runs in two independent movements that converge. The first (Sections 1–6) is metaphysical: whether a self-sufficient, omniscient God could have any coherent, non-self-referential reason to create a world and command its creatures — engaging the actus purus defense (Davies, with Stump's narrative theodicy as a distinct Thomist alternative), accommodation, Molinism, and the punitive structure of the biblical text. The second (Sections 7–10) is historical and behavioral: the observed conduct of moral-religious systems — how they bind and mobilize groups and serve as the contested lever of power — is fully explained without appeal to a divine author. Sections 11–14 clear the metaethical ground (burden of proof, moral variation, "evil" as a moving designation). The conclusion rests on a final pair of moves (Sections 15–19): no claimed revelation has been authenticated — the public-revelation counter (Sinai; Paul's five hundred) is answered directly — and since authentication fails, the diagnostic question that replaces obedience is cui bono: who benefits if the claim is believed? The diagnostic is scoped against its own misuse and is finally turned on the essay's own recommendation. An appendix states the argument's honest limits. A condensed, general-audience version of the same case is available as a separate essay, "Who Told You That Was God?" oa:W7172402763.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172402763.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/772d39f2-58d6-428e-b830-a72a9a920344?authuser=1 God’s Grammar: Logos, Calibration, and the Invariant Order of Reality argues that intelligibility is not created by human language, scientific theory, religious doctrine, or artificial intelligence. Rather, these are distinct forms of participation in an ordered reality that precedes them. The paper defines grammar as the stable relational structure through which meaning survives changes in vocabulary, medium, discipline, observer, and historical context, and defines calibration as the process by which finite receivers reduce distortion through comparison, correction, preservation, and renewed transmission. Drawing together philosophy, theology, science, mathematics, memory, music, education, communication media, and artificial intelligence, the paper examines how knowledge is discovered, represented, corrected, preserved, reconstructed, and handed forward. Maxwell’s equations serve as a worked example of the distinction between physical reality, its intelligibility, and its historical expression. Isaiah 55:10–11 provides the theological pattern of sending, reception, fruit, and return. Later sections trace the role of oral tradition, writing, print, broadcasting, digital networks, and AI as created mechanisms of dissemination. The paper argues that artificial intelligence does not originate grammar, logic, scientific order, or the realities described in its training materials. It inherits compressed patterns from humanity’s historical engagement with reality and can therefore function as a fallible, calibratable receiver and medium of reconstruction. Its outputs may become more or less faithful to sources, definitions, questions, and reality

The paper defines grammar as the stable relational structure through which meaning survives changes in vocabulary, medium, discipline, observer, and historical context, and defines calibration as the process by which finite receivers reduce distortion through comparison, correction, preservation, and renewed transmission. Drawing together philosophy, theology, science, mathematics, memory, music, education, communication media, and artificial intelligence, the paper examines how knowledge is discovered, represented, corrected, preserved, reconstructed, and handed forward. Maxwell’s equations serve as a worked example of the distinction between physical reality, its intelligibility, and its historical expression. Isaiah 55:10–11 provides the theological pattern of sending, reception, fruit, and return. Later sections trace the role of oral tradition, writing, print, broadcasting, digital networks, and AI as created mechanisms of dissemination. The paper argues that artificial intelligence does not originate grammar, logic, scientific order, or the realities described in its training materials. It inherits compressed patterns from humanity’s historical engagement with reality and can therefore function as a fallible, calibratable receiver and medium of reconstruction. Its outputs may become more or less faithful to sources, definitions, questions, and reality

oa:W7172408418.title: Morality, Power, and the Problem of a Self-Sufficient God
oa:W7172408418.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172408418.abstract: A structured synthesis arguing that human moral and religious authority remains historically entangled with power and has never been authenticated in a way that distinguishes revelation from human assertion — so obedience cannot be justified by claiming divine warrant alone. The case runs in two independent movements that converge. The first (Sections 1–6) is metaphysical: whether a self-sufficient, omniscient God could have any coherent, non-self-referential reason to create a world and command its creatures — engaging the actus purus defense (Davies, with Stump's narrative theodicy as a distinct Thomist alternative), accommodation, Molinism, and the punitive structure of the biblical text. The second (Sections 7–10) is historical and behavioral: the observed conduct of moral-religious systems — how they bind and mobilize groups and serve as the contested lever of power — is fully explained without appeal to a divine author. Sections 11–14 clear the metaethical ground (burden of proof, moral variation, "evil" as a moving designation). The conclusion rests on a final pair of moves (Sections 15–19): no claimed revelation has been authenticated — the public-revelation counter (Sinai; Paul's five hundred) is answered directly — and since authentication fails, the diagnostic question that replaces obedience is cui bono: who benefits if the claim is believed? The diagnostic is scoped against its own misuse and is finally turned on the essay's own recommendation. An appendix states the argument's honest limits. A condensed, general-audience version of the same case is available as a separate essay, "Who Told You That Was God?" oa:W7172409017.title: “It’s your fault!”: Exploring stigma towards lung cancer in a multicultural society
oa:W7172409017.abstract: Stigmatising attitudes towards lung cancer exist across cultures based on societal norms and beliefs. However, there is a notable gap in research on lung cancer stigma within Asian cultures such as Malaysia. Our study explored Malaysian public attitudes towards lung cancer through qualitative semi-structured interviews with 32 participants (11 Malays, 11 Chinese, and 10 Indians). Findings highlighted religious beliefs shaped participants' perceptions, with some seeing cancer as fate or punishment, while gender norms also influenced how lung cancer was perceived, with societal expectations differing for men and women. Participants primarily attributed lung cancer to internal factors such as smoking, leading to moral judgements of personal responsibility, while some acknowledged genetic predispositions and environmental risks. Our study shows how sociocultural factors, including patriarchal and religious values, influence perceptions of lung cancer, underscoring the importance of culturally sensitive approaches to improve public health outcomes of lung cancer.

oa:W7172418972.title: POST-COVID GRIEF AND FAMILY RESILIENCE: A SOCIORELIGIOUS INSIGHTS
oa:W7172418972.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172418972.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic generated unprecedented levels of loss, altering family structures, routines, and emotional stability. Many households continue to grapple with post-COVID grief, characterized by unresolved sorrow, psychological strain, and the long-term effects of disrupted social and economic conditions. This article examines how families navigate the lingering emotional consequences of the pandemic and highlights the socioreligious factors that shape resilience. Drawing on sociological perspectives, the study explores how grief manifests within households, how family roles adjust after loss, and how communities mediate support. It emphasizes the significance of religious beliefs, rituals, and communal practices as coping tools that help families reinterpret trauma, sustain hope, and rebuild social cohesion. Religious narratives, mourning rites, and faith-based support networks provide frameworks for meaning-making and emotional recovery. At the same time, the article acknowledges the limitations of religious coping, particularly when spiritual interpretations intensify guilt, helplessness, or fatalism. The analysis argues that family resilience emerges through the interplay of emotional bonds, adaptive coping strategies, spiritual practices, and supportive social environments. Understanding these socioreligious dynamics is essential for developing culturally sensitive interventions that strengthen family well-being in the post-pandemic era

oa:W7172429242.abstract: Shams al-Ma'arif of al-Buni, Volume VI: Squares, Khalwa, and the Birhatiya Shams al-Ma'arif is what happened when the Muslim love of the divine Names reached for a lever, and reading it with the lights on, as history of ideas and not as practice, shows the exact seam where remembering God's Names tips over into trying to operate them, and why the line matters more than the alphabet. Al-Buni (d. 1225), remembered in some chains as a pious Sufi, compiled the most famous manual of letter-and-Name magic in Islam. Read closely from the public-domain Arabic and honest scholarship, Shams al-Ma'arif is not secret power for sale; it is a document of one human wish, to make the sacred alphabet do work, standing on the seam the shariah draws between worship and transgression. The problem was never the alphabet; it is the claim of command. Audiences: Young Muslim readers who have seen Shams al-Ma'arif sold as a book of power — The book reaches them as frightening magic or hidden purchasable power, never as a text to understand. Readers of the history of ideas and comparative esotericism — The science of letters is either romanticized or sneered at, never read as serious history of thought. Believers uneasy about the line between worship and magic — The pull to treat the divine Names as instruments, prayer as technique, God as a system to operate. oa:W7172432540.title: Genealogies of Race and Religion in Kant
oa:W7172432540.abstract: Immanuel Kant is synonymous with modernity, enlightenment and secularity. This reputation is earned through the incredible influence of his three weighty critiques, which have laid the intellectual, moral and aesthetic foundations for modern philosophical thought. Despite this reputation, many scholars in recent years have argued that Kant’s intellectual contribution to secularism, moral universality and political republicanism ought to be approached more critically. The ‘other’ Kant is also one of the progenitors of the modern concept of race. Kantians have defended Kant against charges that race is essential to his entire critical project. This essay moves beyond the stalemate between race scholars and Kantians by reading his concept of race together with his philosophy of religion. Drawing on critical approaches to religion, race and secularism, this essay argues that race is constitutive of his philosophy. More specifically, it demonstrates how race and religion are deeply entangled in Kant’s construction of Jews and Judaism as the constitutive outsiders of Euro-Christian modernity.
