oa:W7172483276.title: EXPLORING (DIS)CONTINUITIES OF HOMOSEXUALITY AND RELIGION IN NIGERIAN LITERARY DISCOURSE: A STUDY OF CHINELO OKPARANTA'S UNDER THE UDALA TREES AND CHRIS ABANI'S GRACELAND
oa:W7172483276.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172483276.abstract: Abstract: This paper aims at examining the representation and exploration of homosexuality within the context of religion in Nigerian literary space. Nigeria, a country marked by its rich literary tradition and diverse religious landscape, grapples with the intersection of traditional religious beliefs and modern understandings of human sexuality. Prominent in the Nigerian religious space are Christianity, Islam and the Traditional worship. Definitely, the religious beliefs of the people actually map our ‘Africaness’ and African identity. Data gathering and analysis are carried out in Chinelo Okparanta’s Under the Udala Trees and Chris Abani’s Graceland as our methodology employed to examine this topic. The authors navigate the intricacies of religion and sexuality, shedding light on the challenges faced by individuals within religious communities and broader society. There is paucity of researches on homosexuality being explored from the lens of religion. Certainly, beliefs must teach morality, the gap this paper intends to fill. It considers how authors challenge prevailing norms, advocating for greater empathy, inclusivity, and understanding of diverse sexual orientations within religious and cultural contexts. The theories of masculinity, radical feminism and modernism are engaged. The paper concludes by stating the crucial yet ambivalent public role of religion in matters of sexuality, social justice and human rights in contemporary Africa. Keywords: Homosexuality, Religion, (Dis)Continuity, Gender, Morality, Same-sex Marriage, Deprivation, Belief.

oa:W7172487672.title: Do Americans Believe in the Afterlife? A Machine Learning Approach
oa:W7172487672.abstract: Belief in the afterlife has held profound significance for humanity since time immemorial, influencing how individuals contemplate mortality, meaning, and legacy. The current study aimed to identify key factors that predict belief in the afterlife and to examine whether there is a connection between religious identification and such belief. The analysis was based on data from the General Social Survey, spanning 2006 to 2022. A Random Forest model was employed, incorporating multiple imputations and Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique for sampling. Here we show that the key variables associated with belief in the afterlife are the respondent's age, frequency of prayer, and confidence in the existence of God. Notably, the results suggest that belief in the afterlife is more strongly associated with general religiosity than with affiliation to any specific religious tradition. While belief in the afterlife varies across individuals and cultures, it remains crucial for understanding how people cope with mortality and how death and the prospect of an afterlife are perceived within societal contexts.

oa:W7172508465.title: Experiences of patients undergoing general surgery in Somalia: a qualitative study
oa:W7172508465.abstract: This study aimed to investigate patients’ experiences undergoing general surgery in Mogadishu, Somalia. This descriptive phenomenological study, using Colaizzi’s method, was conducted with 30 patients undergoing surgery in the department of general surgery of a training and research hospital in Mogadishu, Somalia. Data were collected between November 2021 and January 2022 through face-to-face, semi-structured, in-depth interviews. All interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using Colaizzi’s descriptive phenomenological method. Three main themes were identified: (1) emotional distress, (2) religious coping, and (3) focus on recovery. These themes included seven sub-themes: fear of death, feeling lonely, feeling the unknown; turning to God, surrender to God; relief from pain, and feeling happy. Participants also reported insufficient preoperative information and a need for psychological support. Many participants relied on religious beliefs and spiritual meaning-making to cope with uncertainty throughout the perioperative experience. Patients undergoing general surgery in Somalia experienced considerable emotional distress while actively constructing hope and meaning through religious beliefs during the perioperative period. The findings highlight the need for structured patient education, integrated psychological support, and culturally sensitive perioperative care.

oa:W7196922436.title: A Unified Definition of Realism The Denial of Fate as the Condition of Explicability and Intervention
oa:W7196922436.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7196922436.abstract: Realism recurs across historiography, political theory, literary criticism, and socialscience methodology, yet no existing account identifies what generates it as anintellectual attitude across these domains. This paper proposes a unified definition:realism is the acceptance of the absence of divine will in the causal explanation ofempirical events. So defined, realism is not a set of claims about the world but atransformation applied to explanatory structures—one that simultaneously producestwo conditions: the explicability of outcomes (because immanent causes can beanalyzed) and the possibility of intervention (because immanent causes can be actedupon). The definition is not atheism; it brackets divine intention from empiricalcausation while leaving the metaphysical question of God's existence untouched. Theverb "acceptance" rather than "exclusion" marks a crucial distinction: the realist doesnot expel the gods but recognizes that they were never present in the causal chain. Thepaper demonstrates this operation across four canonical cases—Thucydides,Machiavelli, Flaubert, and Weber—and derives from the definition a diagnosticreversal test: any explanatory structure that is transcendent, opaque, and foreclosesintervention reinstates fate under a secular name. General equilibrium in economics,the p-value threshold in statistics, and the anthropic principle in cosmology are shownto exhibit this structure. Realism, on this account, is not a doctrine of resignation butthe structural precondition for intervention—a permanent task rather than a completedachievement.

oa:W7196946195.title: SIMILARITAS KONSEP PEMIKIRAN THOMAS AQUINAS DALAM PANDANGAN FILSAFAT JAWA SERAT WIRID HIDAYAT JATI
oa:W7196946195.venue: SOSFILKOM Jurnal Sosial Filsafat dan Komunikasi
oa:W7196946195.abstract: This article discusses the Thomism concept of thought initiated by Thomas Aquinas and the divinity views contained in Serat Wirid Hidayat Jati by Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito as well as the interference of the beliefs or religions held by Thomas Aquinas and Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito. The aim of writing this article is to find out the similarities between the divinity and cosmological concepts of Thomas Aquinas and the concept of divinity in Serat Wirid Hidayat Jati by Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito and the theological views of both. The research method in this study is the literature study method. The result of this research is the finding of similarities between the thoughts of Thomas Aquinas and Ronggowarsito as outlined in Serat Wirid Hidayat Jati and the influence of religion in the perspectives of Thomas Aquinas and Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito. The similarities are in the existence of God, the oneness of God, cosmological arguments and the creation theory of the universe. The religious influence that interferes in Thomas Aqinas' view is Christianity, while in Raden Ngabehi Ronggowarsito's view is Islam.

oa:W7196979514.title: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century
oa:W7196979514.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7196979514.abstract: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century An Agnostic Enlightenment for the Twenty-First Century What remains when inherited certainty begins to fade? For centuries, religious institutions shaped morality, identity, law, and humanity's understanding of existence. Yet the twenty-first century presents an unprecedented reality: scientific progress, democratic institutions, neuroscience, psychology, and universal access to information have profoundly transformed how people approach truth, authority, and belief. In The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century, Northon Salomão de Oliveira offers a bold yet balanced philosophical exploration of this historic transition. Rather than celebrating atheism or defending traditional religion, the book proposes a third path: agnosticism as an intellectual discipline, grounded in evidence, epistemic humility, and the enduring values of the Enlightenment. Drawing inspiration from Voltaire, Denis Diderot, Baron d'Holbach, Karl Popper, Steven Pinker, A. C. Grayling, Martha Nussbaum, Jürgen Habermas, and other influential thinkers, this work examines the decline of religious authority while recognizing the enduring psychological, cultural, and ethical roles that religion has played throughout civilization. Inside, readers will discover: * Why religious dogma is gradually losing its monopoly over truth. * How science, philosophy, and democratic institutions are reshaping moral authority. * The psychological functions religion still fulfills, even in secular societies. * Why agnosticism may represent the most intellectually honest position in an age of uncertainty. * How dogmatic thinking survives beyond religion through ideology, politics, and digital culture. * T

oa:W7197022922.title: Role of Faith and Belief in Healing: A Psychological Review
oa:W7197022922.abstract: People’s techniques for handling illness and their process of healing require their belief systems and religious affiliations and their personal faith. Faith healing refers to the practice of using spiritual or religious beliefs and rituals to restore health and cure ailments, often in the absence of conventional medical treatment. Faith healing practices exist in different religious traditions through their use of prayer and laying on of hands and anointing with oil and their need to call for divine help. The study investigates faith healing through its historical development and cultural practices and religious beliefs across different faith traditions to discover its current use in both religious and secular settings. The authors examine how three psychological and physiological processes which include the placebo effect and faith-driven optimism and community support can lead to people experiencing healing results. Additionally, ethical considerations are examined, particularly the balance between faith-based practices and the need for evidence-based medical care. Through this review, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of faith healing’s place in modern healthcare and its implications for the interplay between belief, health, and well-being.

oa:W7201835736.title: The One Argument at Five Scales: On the Now Held Open at every Magnitude, from the Micro-Gap to the Cosmos
oa:W7201835736.abstract: The One Argument at Five Scales argues that five independently developed essays within the Gaitan Topology are not separate conclusions but one structural argument expressed across five magnitudes: the micro-gap of human freedom, the life of the person, the species, the cosmos, and the inner life of God. Rather than introducing a new premise, the essay demonstrates the architectural unity of the corpus, showing that the same invariant relation between the created Now and its Non-derivative ground survives every increase in scale. The work proposes that coherence across magnitudes is the proper methodological test for structural philosophy and presents the completed framework as a unified metaphysical architecture rather than a collection of independent investigations.

oa:W7201839940.title: The problem of textual variants: Textual criticism undermines religious belief
oa:W7201839940.abstract: Abstract I argue that textual variants pose a problem for religious belief. Specifically, the existence of hundreds of thousands of textual variants in the New Testament's manuscript tradition, many of them large and ideologically motivated, should reduce a believer's confidence in the Bible as a source of information. This problem is different from the problems of evil and divine hiddenness because, whereas those problems entail the falsity of a religious claim, such as theism, this problem poses an epistemic challenge instead.

oa:W7201886218.title: Prevalent Religious and Spiritual Beliefs among College Students in Uasin Gishu County, Kenya
oa:W7201886218.venue: East African Journal of Traditions Culture and Religion
oa:W7201886218.abstract: Higher learning institutions in Kenya are getting to be known for many beliefs, values, and social forces that influence students’ academic and social lives. Among these, religious and spiritual explanations have attracted much attention because they may shape behaviour, motivation, as well as academic attainments. This research extensively examined the prevalence of religious and spiritual beliefs among college students in Uasin Gishu County. The study employed Social Identity Theory (SIT), which provides crucial foundations for understanding how an individual’s beliefs can be internalised to determine learning behaviours, discipline, motivation, and educational attainment. The study adopted a descriptive research design. A combination of stratified and simple random sampling techniques was used. Data was collected using questionnaires, interviews and focus group discussions (FGDs). Data was analysed through descriptive statistics, including frequencies, means, and percentages. The results indicated that numerous students consider their spiritual and religious beliefs crucial to their moral growth and personal connections. The research concluded that common religious and spiritual beliefs among students act as essential resources for emotional support and moral growth. A variety of religious and spiritual beliefs enhances the learning atmosphere by fostering empathy, cooperation, and intellectual development when handled with respect and comprehension. The research recommended that colleges promote student exploration of how their faith can beneficially influence their educational objectives and individual growth.

oa:W7201887217.abstract: This study examines Genesis 32:1–21 (MT 32:2–22) through the lens of Hebrew narrative poetics and concentric (chiastic) analysis, arguing that the pericope is deliberately constructed around a single pivot, X, “Deliver me, I pray” (32:11), embraced by five symmetrical pairs of corresponding panels (A/A′, B/B′, C/C′, D/D′, E/E′). The argument proceeds in three principal movements. Second, a verse-by-verse exegesis first demonstrates the Christ-centeredness of the pivot—“crying out in fear, to God alone”—and then reads the five paired panels under the captions furnished by the structural chart: God draws near first, so let man cease from self-reliance (A/A′); human mediation is finally limited (B/B′); crisis presses in, and fear is real (C/C′); every stratagem is exhausted, yet no assurance follows (D/D′); the promise is the ground, in which prayer takes root (E/E′). oa:W7201968029.title: The Heart Cannot Reach the Spring: A Normative Case for an Irreducible Ayin and Yesh
oa:W7201968029.abstract: Deveykut cannot be defended descriptively. Moshe Idel’s correction of Gershom Scholem established that genuinely unitive and absorptive strands are well attested across Jewish mysticism, which means that any account of deveykut as communion-without-annihilation cannot be presented as a simple report of what Jewish mystics sought or attained. This essay accepts Idel’s finding and draws the consequence: a deveykut that preserves the finite self must be argued for normatively, as a claim about what covenant requires, made in full awareness that the tradition contains the alternative. The argument proceeds in three stages. First, the descriptive route is closed. Second, three normative warrants are advanced for the persistence of the yesh — the conditions of accountability, the structure of ethical summons following Levinas, and the requirement of anti-theodicy after catastrophe — none of which apophasis alone can supply. Third, the resulting model is given a mechanism rather than merely a definition: covenantal asymptoticity, in which distance functions as the medium of relation rather than its deficit, exemplified in Rebbe Nachman’s parable/mashal of the Heart and the Spring. The essay engages Wolfson’s demonstration that Chabad’s own apophatic grammar resists metaphysical closure and concedes the point while identifying what it leaves unaddressed: apophasis destabilizes predication without generating any demand that the finite self-remain finite. An addendum applies the model to the Higher Power of Alcoholics Anonymous, reading Kurtz’s not-God-ness as the practical form of the same normative claim.

oa:W7201978854.title: The Disjunctive Dominance Argument for Catholicism: Epistemic Implications of Divine Transcendence, Access-Maximality Concept, and Implications for Finding the True Religion and True Church
oa:W7201978854.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7201978854.abstract: This paper presents the Disjunctive Dominance Argument for Catholicism, a two-step move beginning with an exhaustive disjunction and a dominance claim followed by a prescriptive wager not unlike Pascal’s. From one premise–the definition of God as transcendent ultimate reality–and the argument’s essential structure, principled grounds are found for the pragmatic dominance of Christian religious affiliation at a macro level followed by Catholicism at a micro-level. The essential argument is that, given the infinite or maximal transcendence of God, we can only know what he allows us to know; hence, the expected value of betting on any hypothesis in which God is maximally willing to be found (“access-maximal”), as reflected through the hypothesis’s own claim about degree and kind of divine activity in the interest of relationality, is always higher than that of any other alternative hypothesis even–or rather especially where–the epistemic landscape is flat as a consequence of divine transcendence. Christianity is argued to be uniquely access-maximal because the Incarnation makes God not merely quantitatively but qualitatively (i.e. infinitely) more accessible than he is other world religions, and Catholicism is likewise argued to be uniquely access-maximal because Papal Infallibility uniquely preserves the possibility of a submission-based true-church-identification principle as opposed to one based on self-reliance, the default represented by all non-Catholic forms of Christianity. This paper introduces and covers such original concepts as the Blind Dart Thrower Thought Experiment, the Aircraft Manual Thought Experiment, the Babel Tower Problem, the DDA-based case for Vatican I’s definition of papal infallibility along with independent theoretical motivation for Vatican I’

oa:W7201983254.title: RELIGIOUS BELIEFS AND CULTURE IN ANCIENT TIMES
oa:W7201983254.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7201983254.abstract: This study analyzes the formation of early religious beliefs using a historical-developmental approach. It examines the emergence of religious concepts in human consciousness, their stages of development, and the characteristics of their origin in different regions from a scientific perspective. The research also explores the worldview of early human societies in adopting religious beliefs, as well as the influence of social and spiritual factors on this process. Furthermore, early forms of belief are considered in terms of their religious, scientific, historical, and modern interpretations, and their role and significance in the development of society are substantiated.

oa:W7202038943.title: Works for 8/9/2026 - Steve Irwin
oa:W7202038943.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202038943.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/651640ef-643f-49e6-be97-2cc908d3bb24?authuser=1 All Roads Lead to Supper: Communion, Divine Hospitality, and the Invariant Act of Eating with God argues that shared eating functions as a persistent embodied relational pattern across changing languages, historical contexts, theological vocabularies, and Abrahamic traditions. Its central claim is not merely that meals recur in religious texts, but that the underlying act itself preserves a recognizable structure: provision, offer, reception, participation, distinction, gratitude, memory, belonging, and relation. The paper develops this argument through Catholic Invariant Grammar, Projection-Induced Ambiguity, and History-Modified Accessibility Systems. These frameworks distinguish the act from its description, preserve unity without identity collapse, and explain how later receivers can access richer meanings in repeated practices without requiring the external act to become a different act. The study traces the table across Abrahamic history. Abrahamic hospitality, Passover, manna, covenant meals, Jesus’ table practices, the Last Supper, Eucharistic participation, Qur’anic divine provision, fasting, hospitality, Paradise, and the heavenly table in Surah al-Ma’idah are compared without collapsing Jewish, Christian, and Islamic theology into doctrinal identity. The paper argues that shared eating repeatedly becomes a site where right relation is enacted, restored, remembered, tested, or anticipated. The theological argument distinguishes supper from the final end. Food is not the destination. Natural theology reasons toward God as the necessary ground of contingent intelligible reality, while revelation concerns right relation to that source.

oa:W7202040139.title: A Reflection on the Relationship Between Literature and Religious Beliefs: A Case Study of Persian Textbooks for the Second Cycle of Secondary Education
oa:W7202040139.venue: Treasury of Persian Language and Literature
oa:W7202040139.abstract: The present study aimed to explain and analyze the intertextual relationships between the fundamental components of religion and literature in Persian-language textbooks used in the second cycle of secondary education. This article is based on the premise that religious and literary texts should not be regarded as two entirely separate domains; rather, because of their shared linguistic, symbolic, and meaning-making functions, they have consistently interacted with and influenced one another. Accordingly, the relationship between religion and literature in Persian textbooks for the second cycle of secondary education was analyzed with particular emphasis on doctrinal components. The study employed a descriptive-analytical research method, based on the assumption that every literary work is, in some way, connected to and indebted to sacred and religious texts. The data-collection instrument was developed according to standardized content-analysis components. Following a review of the theoretical foundations, the instrument was organized around three principal categories: the principles of religion, the subsidiary duties of religion, and ethics. Based on the importance coefficient index, attention to religious components and their relationship with literature was found to be uneven. In Grade 10, the greatest emphasis was placed on the principles of religion, while the subsidiary duties of religion received the least attention. In Grades 11 and 12, the principles of religion similarly received the greatest attention, whereas ethics received the least. Within the category of the principles of religion, monotheism received the greatest emphasis in Grades 10 and 12, while prophethood was mentioned most frequently in Grade 11. oa:W7202046755.title: CHOCOLATE, DESCENDED FROM THE SKY
oa:W7202046755.abstract: CHOCOLATE, DESCENDED FROM THE SKYby Mulualem YakobTaken from the book:“Until God is nullified, and until Michael dies— oh, I wish I would have lived. When Gabriel dozes off, and when Raphael gets tired, the liar, the devil, will repent.”In CHOCOLATE, DESCENDED FROM THE SKY, Mulualem Yakob revives the voice of Aleqa Zeneb, a 19th-century Ethiopian cleric, scholar, and chronicler of Emperor Tewodros II. Drawing from Zeneb’s masterpiece, “Metsehafe Chewata Sigawe We Menfesawe” (The Book of Worldly and Spiritual Conversation), this work reflects on the moral, spiritual, and philosophical lessons hidden in everyday life.Through proverbs, parables, and poetic reflections, the book explores the virtue of humility, the power of knowledge and faith, the balance of creation, the limits of desire, and humanity’s eternal dialogue with God. From bees and kings to storms and scriptures, each image becomes a mirror of divine truth — showing that wisdom is not distant but woven into the rhythm of life itself.Take time with its pages — each reflection holds a wealth of knowledge and a timeless call to live wisely, humbly, and in harmony with creation.“Sharpening is good, for it sharpens iron. oa:W7202063448.title: Personal Gods, Shadows, and Holy Books — 02
oa:W7202063448.abstract: Christianity commonly presents God as perfectly loving, able to communicate, desirous of conscious relationship, and the source of a message meant for human beings across cultures. That claim creates an expected difference: sincere and capable seekers should have some dependable way to identify the divine source rather than merely inherit one local interpretation. The public record does not display that difference. Apparently nonresistant nonbelief occurs; religious identity remains strongly shaped by family and geography; incompatible traditions appeal to similar combinations of scripture, testimony, community, and experience; and no shared corrective reliably separates one claimed revelation from its rivals. This pattern is more expected if religions develop through ordinary human cognition and cultural transmission than if a perfectly capable communicator is providing universally available, source-identifying revelation. The case is cumulative, and four explicit arguments carry it: an expected-difference argument, a symmetry argument, an every-outcome problem for unconstrained replies, and the claim that a book can preserve a message without identifying a divine author. Freedom, soul-making, social dependence, private experience, transcendence, sin, and mystery may explain some ambiguity, but none answers the challenge merely by naming a possible good. The principal limit is important: the evidence does not disprove every god, cancel every person's private justification, or show that sacred texts have no value. It does give reflective inquirers substantial reason to reduce confidence in strong Christian disclosure claims and to suspend allegiance when the alleged source cannot be distinguished from ordinary religious formation.

oa:W7202092194.title: Worship-Worthiness First
oa:W7202092194.abstract: Abstract This paper argues that worship-worthiness should be treated as the foundational question of philosophy of religion. To develop this claim, I divide the philosophy of worship into two branches: the axiology of worship (whether God is worthy of worship) and the deontology of worship (whether we ought to worship God). After developing a tripartite account of worship, I distinguish two broad theological approaches: Worship-Worthiness Theology (WWT), which takes worship-worthiness as its organizing concern, and Non-Worship-Worthiness Theology (NWWT), which begins from other metaphysical or theological priorities. I argue that WWT has axiological, prudential, and methodological priority over NWWT – a thesis I call Worship-Worthiness First. I argue that this thesis can transform existing debates in the philosophy of religion. I develop this thesis through three case studies: perfect being theism, arguments for God’s existence, and the nature of God. Worship-worthiness, this paper argues, is not one topic among others. It is the question that should guide and structure all the others.

oa:W7202118621.title: Works for 8/10/2026 - Bob Ross
oa:W7202118621.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202118621.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/b1bf2b8a-9ce8-440e-ba76-8f8c1e29a6fd?authuser=1 Light from Light: Invariance, Negative Time, and the Relational Structure of Reality develops a cross-disciplinary account of reality organized around a simple question: when representations change across observers, frames, channels, histories, and scales, what remains stable enough to identify one underlying reality? Beginning with Genesis 1 and the narrative priority of light before the luminaries, the paper moves through classical optics, electromagnetism, quantum field theory, special relativity, general relativity, gravitational lensing, astronomy, memory, and the problem of time in quantum gravity. Across these domains it identifies a recurring relational grammar of source, propagation, transformation, local reception, differential accessibility, and invariant constraint. Different representations need not imply different realities; lawful transformations can preserve sufficient structure for one source, event, or system to remain reconstructable across multiple receivers. The paper introduces negative time as a receiver-relative temporal convention in which a later resolved state is assigned coordinate zero and earlier unfinished states receive negative coordinates relative to that completion. This does not imply retrocausation, backward information transfer, or reversal of physical time. Instead, it formalizes the fact that later receiver states can possess more resolved history and therefore interpret earlier states differently without physically altering those earlier events. oa:W7202120629.title: Respiration, Ensoulment, and Personhood of the Human Zygote and Preimplantation Embryo
oa:W7202120629.abstract: Despite the biological reality that new human life begins at fertilization, the concept of embryonic personhood is anathema to the secular medical community. While Christian theologians have never condoned abortion at any stage of development, they have speculated over the timing of ensoulment, with some positing that a baby receives a soul at fertilization, while others postulating delayed ensoulment. Advances in the understanding of how God forms babies in the fallopian tube and in the womb helped the argument for immediate ensoulment to gain support. Furthermore, an appreciation that the zygote and embryo actually breathe adds traction to the argument that they are ensouled, regardless of whether they were formed within the mother or in the laboratory. In contrast to the utilitarian ethos of the secular community, for the Christian, the embryonic baby is a neighbor whom the believer is called to sacrificially love and serve.

oa:W7202161339.title: A Comment on Modal Collapse and Ultrafilters in Gödel's Ontological Argument
oa:W7202161339.abstract: Gödel's ontological argument is modal by design. Possibility and necessity are among its central concerns, and connected interpretation decisions -- extensions or intensions for the positive properties, constant or varying quantifier domains, the choice of modal logic, etc. -- subtly shape the argument and, in particular, whether the modal collapse is implied or not. It is tempting to abstract the modality away and to read the positive properties as merely forming an ultrafilter -- which, however, may replace Gödel's argument with a perhaps more manageable alternative that may have little to do with Gödel's original intention. In this spirit, Odifreddi and Gomes argue that modal collapse is an intrinsic structural feature of any theory that characterises positive properties as an ultrafilter and identifies God as its principal generator. This comment shows, with machine-verified counterexamples, that the structural claim is false: what drives the collapse is primarily not the filter structure but the rigidity of positivity -- itself a thoroughly modal condition. Moreover, two claims of Odifreddi and Gomes are corrected: one on the derivability of Gödel's Theorem IV, one on the extensionality of positivity. All results are machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL.

oa:W7202165013.title: The Role of Biblical-Mythological Topos in Geo Milev’s Poem “September” for the Development of Social-Emotional Competence
oa:W7202165013.venue: Bulgarski Ezik i Literatura-Bulgarian Language and Literature
oa:W7202165013.abstract: Biblical-mythological topos articulate life truths hidden behind images, symbols, and narratives. Geo Milev lives on forever in the poem “September” as a corrective to the problematic search for justice. Life and work become narratives of a suffered human fate on the way to its own Golgotha. Key topos stand out: “The voice of the people is the voice of God”; the biblical warrior Priest Andrey; Chaos and Wrath; the Resurrection and the “New Adam”; sacrifice and the Apocalypse; iconoclasm and the “godless”; the tragic hero and the conflict between personal honor and collective destiny. Through a survey conducted among tenth-grade students, existing opinions and attitudes are identified regarding the resonance that Geo Milev’s narrative leaves in the context of the rebellion against injustice, the motif of a meaningfully lived life, and human will as the engine of change for a better tomorrow. The aim of the article is to establish students‘ attitudes, opinions, and expectations regarding the interpreted meaning of the poem in terms of universal human values. The method used is a group online survey. The subject of the study is the biblical-mythological topos in “September”.

oa:W7202195172.title: Public attitudes and preferences on organ donation and allocation in china: a cross-sectional study
oa:W7202195172.abstract: This cross-sectional study aimed to examine public attitudes toward postmortem organ donation and allocation fairness preferences in China. To this end, an online survey was administered through the Wenjuanxing platform among adults aged ≥ 18 years (N = 895). Only 15.1% of respondents had decided to donate, whereas 74.1% remained undecided; nevertheless, 73.7% would accept a donated organ if needed. Reciprocity (76.0%), first-come-first-served (70.5%), and medical urgency (65.7%) were most frequently endorsed as fair allocation principles. In the full-sample logistic regression (N = 895), positive attitudes (odds ratio [OR] = 5.65, p < 0.001), higher knowledge (OR = 1.56, p < 0.001), and knowing someone who had donated or was considering donating (OR = 1.96, p = 0.013) predicted willingness to donate. Further, a conditional analysis among decision-makers (N = 232) revealed that married status (OR = 0.18, p = 0.007), religious beliefs (OR = 0.22, p = 0.020), and higher education (OR = 1.50, p = 0.024) significantly differentiated donors from non-donors. Collectively, these findings indicate that organ donation willingness in China remains low despite broadly positive attitudes. Knowledge deficits, procedural uncertainty, and family-centered decision-making norms impede commitment, thereby underscoring the need for enhancing public education and institutional transparency.

oa:W7202203146.title: Metaphysical Motifs in Landscape Lyric Poetry of L. I. Milanich
oa:W7202203146.abstract: This article examines the landscape lyric poetry of Khabarovsk-based poet Ludmila Ivanovna Milanich (1934–2018). The study aims to identify the specific modes through which metaphysical motifs are embodied within her pastoral verse. The primary material consists of poems drawn from the collection “Music of a New Day” (Khabarovsk, 2006), with over fifty individual texts subjected to close reading. Employing comparative-typological and motif-oriented approaches to textual analysis, the paper traces the manifestation of key existential ideas and elucidates the nature of imagery characteristic of Milanich's poetic idiom. The argument demonstrates that the poetics of Milanich's landscape lyrics is fundamentally grounded in the notion of cosmic wholeness and ontological unity. Central to her conceptual framework are the notions of GOD, MUSIC, WORD, SUN, and the FEMININE PRINCIPLE, alongside the pervasive idea of an inherent creative impulse animating the world. The present work analyzes the formal strategies employed for the poetic embodiment of these mythologems. Furthermore, the article delineates points of convergence between Milanich's oeuvre and the literary output of the Soviet “Sixtiers” generation. A detailed case study addresses the deployment of the grasshopper narrative. These observations contribute significantly to refining our understanding of the historical-literary trajectory of Russian literature during the second half of the twentieth century.

oa:W7202215322.title: Recovering the Unrecoverable: Documenting and Interpreting a Vanishing Bulgarian National Revival Fresco Cycle
oa:W7202215322.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202215322.abstract: This paper documents and interprets a previously unpublished nineteenth-century fresco cycle from the Church of the Dormition of the Mother of God in the village of Yamborano, Kyustendil province, Bulgaria, photographed by the author in 2005 and, in all likelihood, no longer extant in its recorded state. The cycle, whose painter remains unidentified, depicts four scenes from the Twelve Great Feasts - the Ascension, the Transfiguration, the Entry into Jerusalem, and Pentecost - and survives only in an advanced state of material loss.The paper offers a secure iconographic identification of the four scenes on the basis of their surviving inscriptions, proposes a cautious argument for the presence of Western pictorial influence within an otherwise canonical Orthodox compositional scheme, and situates the fresco within the broader phenomenon of stylistic permeability characteristic of Bulgarian National Revival ecclesiastical painting. A companion computational notebook, described briefly in Section 5 and published separately as an open-access GitHub repository, provides a quantitative map of the extent of surface loss across the cycle. The paper closes by arguing that, where the physical monument itself has in all likelihood ceased to exist, careful documentation is not merely an art-historical convenience but the last remaining form in which the image can continue to resist the passage of the very time it was created to depict.

oa:W7202243752.title: The Problem of Divine Justice: The Logical and Moral Burden of Evil under an Omnipotent and Omniscient God
oa:W7202243752.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202243752.abstract: This paper examines the logical and moral problem of evil under the assumption of an omnipotent and omniscient God. It argues that the simultaneous existence of unlimited divine power and knowledge with intense, apparently gratuitous suffering creates a serious burden of justification for traditional theism. The paper distinguishes between logical contradiction, evidential tension, and moral responsibility, and develops an argument concerning the implications of divine attributes for the problem of evil. The central thesis is that attempts to reconcile omnipotence and omniscience with extensive and apparently unnecessary suffering face a fundamental logical and moral challenge. The paper is presented as an independent philosophical argument and is intended to contribute to contemporary discussions of the problem of evil, divine justice, and the rational foundations of theism.

oa:W7202250561.title: Dialogues Across Differences: Lessons from the Jaina Tradition on Conflict Resolution and Reconciliation
oa:W7202250561.abstract: Contemporary society grapples with diverse values and socio-economic structural differences. These differences extend beyond subtle contextual nuances and strategic considerations, intruding into one’s first-person account and preferences. From its first-order mooring, these divergences ascend to higher-order manifestations, expressing themselves in distinct political perspectives, cultural practices, and religious beliefs. While such differences inevitably give rise to conflicts, a deeper analysis reveals that the core of rising conflict often lies in sectarian differences. Although various conflict resolution mechanisms have been employed to settle disputes, they often fail to yield enduring results. In this regard, the paper proposes interfaith dialogue as a promising approach for conflict resolution and reconciliation. The paper argues that interfaith dialogue is neither a debate nor a negotiation, but a sustained endeavour to break down the walls of difference. Furthermore, to ensure substantive outcomes, the dialogue must be firmly grounded in philosophical foundations that are value-laden and universally acknowledged. Against this backdrop, the paper introduces the Jaina philosophical tradition, specifically the principle of ‘non-absolutism’ (anekāntavāda) and the doctrine of ‘qualified assertion’ (syādvāda), as a coherent framework for dialogical engagements. Focusing on epistemic decentring, conditional articulation, and non-violent involvement, the Jaina framework pushes interfaith dialogue beyond conflict resolution towards conflict transformation.

oa:W7202263772.title: Counter-Inductive Ideational Immunity and the Maintenance of Religious Belief: Introducing the CICI Project
oa:W7202263772.abstract: Sincere, thoughtful, and etiologically similar people persist in mutually contrary religious commitments across generations, without converging and without obvious irrationality. In Problems of Religious Luck: Assessing the Limits of Reasonable Religious Disagreement (PRL, or Axtell 2020a) I argued that this stability is best understood through Counter-Inductive Ideational Immunity (CICI): a coordinated battery of cognitive and affective strategies that treat recognized disagreement and etiological symmetry not as reasons to reduce confidence or revise beliefs and attitudes but as pressure to be neutralized so that the commitment is preserved. This paper introduces the CICI Project — a program that carries forward that taxonomy of strategies and mechanisms from philosophical description into a measurable model. [Collaborators are sought to help carry through the study or a future iteration of it, collect, analyze and publish the data; contact author]

oa:W7202281502.title: The Origins of R. G. Collingwood's Philosophy of History in his Philosophy of Religion, 1916–1943
oa:W7202281502.abstract: Abstract This article argues that R.G. Collingwood's philosophy of history was deeply rooted in his early philosophy of religion as expounded in Religion and Philosophy (1916). Although scholars have tended to separate Collingwood's early religious ideas from his later writings, this study demonstrates that his theory of history was informed by his endeavour to solve the theological problems raised by what he regarded as the reductionism of two Oxford philosophical schools: realism and idealism. In response, he defended a conception of thought as a qualitatively distinct, irreducible activity, enabling him to reinterpret central Christian doctrines, such as the incarnation and atonement, in historical terms. Christ's omniscience, for example, was reconceived as the knowledge of a perfect historian who understood human motives without predetermining them. This dualist conception of thought prefigured the metaphysical premise of his later theory that history was the re‐enactment of past thoughts. The article traces how these themes, first articulated in theological contexts, informed his later works from Speculum Mentis (1924) to the Essay on Metaphysics (1940). It concludes that the origins of Collingwood's philosophy of history cannot be separated from his philosophy of religion: both emerged from a defence of human freedom, historical meaning, and Christian theism.

oa:W7202344526.title: The Architect's Protocol — A Five-Book Civilizational Audit of Truth, Power, Morality, Authorship, and the Human Future: Institutional Research & Series Framework Edition
oa:W7202344526.abstract: The Architect's Protocol is a five-book philosophical and civilizational series by Syed Raheel Shahzad examining truth, power, moral order, authorship, artificial intelligence, transhumanism, and the human future as connected layers of one architectural problem. Rather than treating post-truth, institutional capture, moral relativism, metaphysical explanation, and the machine age as unrelated controversies, the series follows their dependencies in sequence. Book One, GOD IS BACK: The Resurrection of Reason in a Post-Truth World, begins with truth, reason, secular inheritance, moral capital, and the problem of a civilization that removes the Source while continuing to depend on inherited concepts of dignity, conscience, law, and moral order. Book Two, THE JUNGLE PROTOCOL: Dismantling Might Is Right and the Global Power Mafia, follows the fracture into law, institutions, captured statutes, regulatory capture, resource wars, empire, tyranny, and the question of higher law. Book Three, THE MORAL ANCHOR: Objective Right and Wrong in an Age of Relativism, tests whether conscience, reason, consensus, law, utility, the self, or the wider matrix can provide a final moral standard above the actor. Book Four, AUTHORED: The Mind Behind a Maintained Universe, turns toward fine-tuning, entropy, information, origin of life, consciousness, convergence, and the philosophical inference to authorship. Book Five, THE LAST U-TURN: AI, Transhumanism, and the Choice to Remain Human, brings the argument into the machine age and asks whether technology will remain subordinate to the human being or become a replacement source of identity, authority, and meaning. This Institutional Research & Series Framework Edition presents the complete five-book architecture, the relationship between the volum

oa:W7202344708.title: Choosing by religion: Similarity–attraction and religious beliefs in social media assessments
oa:W7202344708.abstract: Abstract Social media assessments in selection increasingly expose applicants' religious beliefs, yet the implications of growing religious diversity in applicant pools remain underexplored. Leveraging social identity theory and the similarity–attraction paradigm, we examine how recruiters respond when applicants openly share their religious beliefs on social media (e.g., LinkedIn). To this end, U.S. working professionals evaluated an applicant's hireability based on a manipulated LinkedIn profile in a 4 (religious belief: Christian, Muslim, Jewish, control) by 2 (qualification: low vs. high) design. In Study 1 ( N = 372), a religion‐stratified sample screened a mid‐20s female applicant. In Study 2 ( N = 294), participants screened a mid‐60s male applicant. Across both studies, we found that similarity in religious beliefs increased raters' liking of the applicant, which in turn predicted ratings of task performance, organizational citizenship behavior, and overall hireability (e.g., interview invitations), above and beyond the applicant's actual qualifications. This bias was further shaped by both individual (rater religiosity, Study 1) and contextual moderators (news engagement with a religiously charged event, i.e., the Israel–Hamas War). Together, our findings position similarity perceptions as a central mechanism through which religious beliefs and social media assessments can influence hiring decisions.

oa:W7202354429.title: MUSLIM FAMILIES AND RELIGIOUS RESOURCES IN DEVELOPING PARENTAL ACCEPTANCE OF CHILDREN WITH DISABILITIES
oa:W7202354429.abstract: Parental acceptance is a crucial component of family adaptation and psychological well-being in families of children with disabilities. This study aims to examine the role of Muslim family environments and religious attitude (RA) in shaping parental acceptance of children with disabilities within a religiously embedded cultural context. Using a quantitative correlational design, data were collected from 77 parents of children with disabilities in Indonesia. The study focuses on key family-based factors, including parental understanding, social support, and Islamic religious beliefs as significant contributors to parental acceptance. The findings reveal that parental understanding (β = .34), Religious Attitude (RA) (β = .29), and social support (β = .25) significantly predict parental acceptance, jointly explaining 48% of the variance. These results indicate that parental acceptance is not solely determined by cognitive factors but is also shaped by social and faith-based resources within Muslim family environments. Islamic values, such as patience (ṣabr – صَبْر), gratitude (shukr – شُكْر), and trust in God (tawakkul – تَوَكُّل), provide meaningful frameworks that support parents in interpreting and accepting their child’s condition. The study implies that integrating Islamic values, strengthening parental understanding, and enhancing social support systems can contribute to more adaptive family processes and improved well-being among families of children with disabilities.

oa:W7202371170.title: ANALYSIS OF SCIENTIFIC LITERATURE ABOUT ANCIENT BACTRIA: PROBLEMS AND SOLUTIONS
authors: Kamoliddin Nabijon oglu Abdujabbarov                                                                                 Ismailov Ubaydulla
oa:W7202371170.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202371170.abstract: The Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrianism, describes Bactria as one of the most ancient regions. The Avesta describes the religious and cultural practices in Bactria, as well as the religious beliefs of the people living there.This information is found in the works of ancient Greek, Persian, Indian, and Chinese historians. The following is an analysis of information about Bactria in the main written sources. Linguists have noted similarities between the Rigveda, the Avesta, and the languages of some Indo-European peoples. As a result of archaeological research conducted in Eastern Europe, various scientific views have emerged regarding the ethnic origin of the Aryans. The texts of the Rigveda contain some images of the funeral ceremony. According to them, the division of the whole world into three parts is symbolic, and there is information about a chariot drawn by three horses. There are ideas that, during the burial process, the body of the deceased was divided into three parts (head, body, feet). Analyses reveal the presence of Indo-Aryan populations in the region at the end of the Bronze Age, their migration to northern India, and their traces in southern Uzbekistan. Herder migration was also present at the beginning of the Bronze Age. The appearance of ethnocultural elements in archaeological finds is reflected in changes that occurred in Northern Bactria, beginning with the Kozali stage of the Sopolli culture.The Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrianism, describes Bactria as one of the most ancient regions. The Avesta describes the religious and cultural practices in Bactria, as well as the religious beliefs of the people living there.

oa:W7202379167.title: Shiba's Truth Ladder: A Structured Method for Testing God, Worldviews, and Christianity One Rung at a Time
oa:W7202379167.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202379167.abstract: Shiba's Truth Ladder is a structured method for pursuing truth and improving debate by requiring participants to establish the foundational questions of a subject before moving to higher-level conclusions. Many debates become circular because people begin from different assumptions, skip unresolved questions, or argue advanced points without first establishing the background needed to evaluate them. The Truth Ladder creates a more even playing field by requiring both sides to begin from common ground, proceed one rung at a time, clearly identify what is established, qualified, rejected, or unresolved, and carry those conclusions forward consistently. If a later argument contradicts an earlier established rung, the participants must return to that rung, resolve the conflict, and rebuild from there. This first working edition applies the method primarily to questions concerning God, competing worldviews, religion, and Christianity, while proposing the Ladder as a broader framework for disciplined inquiry and debate.

oa:W7202384486.title: Analysis of the Religious Symbolism Behind the Pantheon’s Dome
oa:W7202384486.abstract: Hadrian's Pantheon is among the most architecturally significant buildings of the ancient world.No floorplan survives from the Pantheon's construction at the end of the 1 st century BC or from its renovation in the early 2 nd century AD, so the meaning behind many of its architectural features remains a mystery.Scholars have interpreted that some aspects of the building reflect Roman religious beliefs and have proposed connections between elements of the building's architecture and elements of Roman religion.The question remains whether Hadrian and his architects intended for these connections or whether the structure's design was meant to allow for multiple interpretations.This paper aims to investigate the religious significance of the Pantheon's dome.I will argue that it serves as a direct link for the viewer between the heavens and the earth.

oa:W7203442027.title: Semantic Appraisal of Blessing and the Sacred in Contemporary Philosophy of Language and Religion
oa:W7203442027.venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)
oa:W7203442027.abstract: This paper examines the semantic status of blessing and the sacred from the perspectives of contemporary philosophy of language and philosophy of religion. It considers four approaches to these concepts and distinguishes between theories that understand meaning primarily through reference and those that understand meaning through relations within broader linguistic and conceptual networks. Drawing on debates concerning referentialism, semantic holism, contextualism, and religious language, the analysis asks whether blessing and the sacred can be understood without assuming independently existing referents. It also considers the role of belief attribution and the wider importance of semantics for the study of religion. The paper argues that non-referential and holistic approaches provide useful resources for interpreting religious concepts while allowing questions concerning their ontological referents to remain open.

oa:W7203449342.title: ‘I Crossed an Invisible Line’ Introduction
oa:W7203449342.abstract: • Dhaka, Bangladesh – 13 February 2013: Secular activist Ahmed Rajib Haider is stabbed, allegedly in retaliation for his outspoken criticism of religion. His death becomes a turning point in the public contestation of atheism, secularism and Islam in Bangladesh. • Multan, Pakistan – 13 March 2013: University lecturer Junaid Hafeez is accused of blasphemy by Islamist students for allegedly defiling the Prophet's name on social media. A year later, his lawyer is shot dead. In 2019, Hafeez is sentenced to death. Appeal remains ongoing. • Pune, India – 20 August 2013: Rationalist leader Dr Narendra Dabholkar is assassinated while on his morning walk. Right-wing Hindu nationalists, with reported links to the hardline group Sanatan Sanstha, are suspected of orchestrating the attack. • Sylhet, Bangladesh – 12 May 2015: Writer and activist Ananta Bijoy Das is killed after being denied a temporary visa that would have allowed him to seek asylum in Sweden. His murder has significant repercussions for the Swedish asylum system, creating a brief period in which a growing number of atheists and secular activists from Bangladesh gain protection. International humanist and rationalist organisations intensify their lobbying around asylum and protection in response to the killings. In 2013 and the years that followed, a series of targeted attacks unfolded across South Asia, attributed to both militant Islamist and Hindu nationalist actors. While many were decentralised acts by radicalised individuals, others bore the imprint of state actors or proceeded with forms of tacit state involvement.

oa:W7203485685.title: God and the View From Nowhere: De Se Knowledge and Divine Omniscience
oa:W7203485685.abstract: Abstract I argue that classical non-indexical models of divine omniscience are insufficient to account for divine agency conceived as both libertarian and morally responsible. Drawing on work on essential indexicality, I formulate a Self-Location Constraint (SLC): an omniscient agent capable of robust contrastive responsibility must not only know all truths, but also know de se that it is the agent actualising a particular world rather than relevant alternatives. I argue that volitional contrast, actualisation asymmetry, and responsibility across alternatives generate explanatory demands that purely third-personal models of omniscience cannot satisfy. These demands are best explained by irreducibly de se content. I then assess three responses: reductionism about de se cognition, semantic stratification designed to preserve divine simplicity, and necessitarianism, which rejects genuine modal alternatives. I conclude that, given libertarianism and robust contrastive responsibility, theism requires a form of omniscience that includes self-locating knowledge. Although developed within a theistic framework, the structure of SLC generalises to any necessarily unique agent with libertarian powers and exclusively non-indexical cognition.

oa:W7203486397.title: ‘The Blogger Issue Is Over’ Bangladesh (Sylhet)
oa:W7203486397.abstract: Prologue: Ahmed Rajib Haider, 15 February 2013, Dhaka It was on this date that blogger and activist Ahmed Rajib Haider, known by his pen name Thaba Baba, was hacked to death just outside his home. A leading voice in the Shahbag protests and a sharp critic of Islamist politics, Haider had used his blog to advocate for secular justice and to condemn religious fundamentalism. His murder – not the first attack, but the first in what would become a series of brutal killings – marked a turning point in the public visibility and vulnerability of non-religious dissent. The next day, his coffin was carried in a vast public procession to Shahbag Square, draped in the national flag and accompanied by over 100,000 mourners. However, the act of public grieving became a political flashpoint. Islamist groups seized upon Haider's known atheism to brand the entire movement as nāstik – heretical and immoral. What began as a protest for justice swiftly became a referendum on the legitimacy of atheism in public life, setting in motion a period of heightened risk for secular activists. This chapter returns to the enduring reverberations of that moment – to the quieter and more lasting traces left behind after the spectacle receded. Introduction When I revisited Sylhet for a research stint in February and March 2022, I was warmly welcomed by my former research interlocutors and friends.1 Seeing me again after a long time, some of my atheist interlocutors emphasised, ‘Things are very different from when you came before.’

oa:W7203488844.title: ‘From Then on, to Feel Fear Was Normal for Us’ India (Punjab)

oa:W7203492266.title: ‘I Call Being an Atheist a Convert’ Europe (Sweden and the Netherlands)
oa:W7203492266.abstract: Prologue: Ananta Bijoy Das, April–May 2015, Embassy of Sweden, Dhaka and Sylhet Ananta Bijoy Das was a science writer and editor based in Sylhet, in northeastern Bangladesh. He edited Jukti (Logic), a quarterly science magazine, and founded the Sylhet Science and Rationalist Council. Through his writing and public engagement, he sought to popularise scientific thinking and secular humanist ideas in a social context where such positions were marginal and increasingly dangerous. He also contributed regularly to Mukto-Mona (Free Mind), a Bengali-language online platform associated with free thought, atheism and rationalist critique. Much of his work focused on biological evolution and on challenging religious orthodoxies, including aspects of both Islam and Hinduism. By 2013, Das's name had begun to circulate on assassination lists linked to Islamist extremist groups. He received repeated threats, and the risk to his safety was well known within international writer and human rights networks. In early 2015, he was accepted for a placement through the International Cities of Refuge Network (ICORN) and invited by Swedish PEN to travel to Sweden to speak publicly about the escalating violence against secular writers in Bangladesh. Despite this, and despite the documented threats against him, the Swedish embassy in Dhaka refused his visa application in April 2015. The decision stated that he belonged to a category of applicants considered likely not to leave the Schengen area, and that the purpose of his visit was not sufficiently urgent.

oa:W7203500674.title: Numerical Code of Culture: The Symbolism of Numbers 3, 7, and 40 in the Proverbs and Folklore Formulas of Kyrgyz and English Cultures
oa:W7203500674.abstract: The article examines the symbolism of the numbers 3, 7, and 40, which are traditionally regarded as sacred in many world cultures. The study aims to identify and compare the symbolic meanings of these numbers in Kyrgyz and English linguocultural traditions. The research material comprises proverbs, folklore formulas, and set expressions documented in authoritative lexicographic sources of both languages. The goal of the work is to determine the extent to which numerical symbolism reflects the cultural and historical characteristics of a people, including their way of life, religious beliefs, and tribal traditions. The methodological framework is based on contrastive analysis, linguocultural description, and semantic analysis. The study reveals that the number 3 in both cultures is associated with completeness and sacred wholeness; however, in the Kyrgyz tradition, three people embody grace and communality, whereas in English usage, the "third wheel" often carries a negative connotation. The number 7 in Kyrgyz culture is intimately connected with ancestor veneration and genealogical memory ("zheti ata"), while in English culture, it is primarily linked to biblical symbolism and the notion of cosmic completeness. The most significant differences are found in the semantics of the number 40: in Kyrgyz culture, it permeates all major life rituals from birth to death, whereas in English, it appears rarely and almost exclusively in biblical contexts. The findings confirm that numbers in proverbs and folklore formulas function as cultural codes encoding the worldview of a people.

oa:W7203556966.title: Negotiating Tolerance and Belief Boundaries in Islamic Religious Education: A Case Study of a Plural Public School in Indonesia
oa:W7203556966.venue: EDUSOSHUM Journal of Islamic Education and Social Humanities
oa:W7203556966.abstract: In increasingly diverse school environments, Islamic Religious Education (Pendidikan Agama Islam/PAI) is supposed to foster tolerance while upholding students' religious beliefs. However, tolerance is frequently portrayed as a normative ideal without any pedagogical direction for dealing with actual interreligious interactions. In a multiple public school, this study explores how PAI serves as a pedagogical space for negotiating tolerance and defining the parameters of interreligious participation. A qualitative case study was conducted in class XI-9 at SMAN 1 Babadan, Indonesia. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with a PAI teacher, written reflections from two Muslim students and one non-Muslim student, classroom and school observations, and supporting documents. The findings reveal that students develop tolerance not only through classroom instruction but also through everyday interreligious interaction within the school community. School activities strengthen cooperation and mutual respect, while the teacher plays a central role in distinguishing social respect, epistemic openness, and ritual participation when responding to interreligious issues. The study concludes that tolerance becomes educationally meaningful when translated into contextual pedagogical practices that help students navigate real interreligious experiences without compromising their religious beliefs. These findings contribute to multicultural Islamic education by highlighting belief-boundary negotiation as a key pedagogical dimension of tolerance education in plural schools.

oa:W7203572242.abstract: The “union chain”, the 1877 break, and the asylum relevance – including the “irregularity” argument in relation to anti‑Fraternity states, with careful handling of historical and perceptual risks 1. The “union chain” as an inner sense of unity grounded in faith in one God In the tradition of our Fathers, the “chain of union” denotes an inner, shared sense of unity among members of the Fraternity across all nations, anchored in: - a common faith in one God,- shared moral duties derived from that belief, - the conviction that this theistic core is what makes the Fraternity “universal” and mutually recognisable across borders. From this perspective, the “chain” holds only if every regular Fraternity insists on the same minimal theistic foundation. Remove that foundation, and the inner sense of unity is no longer guaranteed; the chain is, in their eyes, broken rather than widened. This is especially significant in a monotheistic world: belief in one God is a point of convergence for Muslims, Jews, Christians and many other believers. In that sense, the traditional requirement of belief in a supreme being can be seen as a bridge between the major monotheisms. Therefore, "irregular" fraternities might have introduced antinomic fallacies and practices within our Union Chain.

oa:W7203572996.title: COME OUT OF BABYLONTHE CHRISTIAN RESPONSE
oa:W7203572996.abstract: A book about hidden power can end in the wrong place. It can leave the reader angry at institutions, intoxicated with secret knowledge, suspicious of every public explanation, frightened by technology, or convinced that spiritual maturity consists in identifying more conspirators than one's neighbor. None of those outcomes is the Christian purpose of discernment. The final summons of Scripture is not to become an expert in darkness but to belong wholly to Jesus Christ. The command, "Come out of her, my people," in Revelation 18:4 calls God's people away from participation in Babylon's sins and away from the judgment attached to them. Read in the wider biblical canon, this separation is not withdrawal from mission, society, vocation, technology, or ordinary commerce. It is a decisive transfer of allegiance. Christians remain in the world as witnesses while refusing the world's idols, lies, corrupt loves, coercive worship, and claims to ultimate authority.This concluding chapter converts the investigation of secret networks, financial power, propaganda, covert action, institutional capture, technological governance, information control, and prophetic convergence into a theology and practice of Christian faithfulness. It summarizes the book's evidentiary results without repeating the historical case for specific organizations. The investigation has established that secrecy, covert action, elite coordination, financial leverage, propaganda, institutional gatekeeping, public-private governance, surveillance capacity, algorithmic visibility, demographic intervention, and coercive policy have all existed in demonstrable forms. oa:W7203574151.title: Personal Ultimate Ground: An Independently Developed Philosophical-Formal Framework
oa:W7203574151.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203574151.abstract: Abstract This work presents a philosophical and formal model of an ultimate personal foundation of reality. Its central principle states that every real and compatible property of a reality is possessed by its complete foundation. Consciousness therefore belongs to the foundation whenever consciousness is established as a real and compatible property. The model explicitly separates assumptions, definitions, deductions, theorems, countermodels, and unresolved premises, and is compared with Gödel–Scott ontological arguments and their formal verification. The work does not claim an unconditional metaphysical proof of God; instead, it develops an explicit formal framework and identifies precisely which conclusions follow from its fundamental principles. oa:W7203578844.title: Personal Ultimate Ground: An Independently Developed Philosophical-Formal Framework
oa:W7203578844.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203578844.abstract: This dossier presents an independently developed philosophical-formal framework for a Personal Ultimate Ground (PUG). The project separates formally checkable modal consequences from substantive metaphysical premises, constructs an explicit impersonal counter-model, and audits the inferential bridges connecting grounding, normativity, agency, reason-responsiveness, sourcehood and ultimacy. The principal model is presented as an abductive explanatory proposal rather than as a deductive proof of the existence of God. A separate single-premise benchmark assumes U* = ◇□P and shows that, under S5, ◇□P entails □P and hence P. The benchmark is deliberately classified as conditional because U* itself is not established. The dossier therefore makes a narrower and more defensible claim: the Personal Ultimate Ground is proposed as a potentially superior unifying explanation among the models examined, while the decisive metaphysical bridge excluding an adequate impersonal ground remains unproved.

Prayer Lord Jesus Christ, You are the true Wisdom of God, greater than Solomon. Open our ears to Your instruction. Writ

oa:W7203588567.title: Beyond Knowledge: The Concept of Ma’rifa in Sufi Literature
oa:W7203588567.abstract: Understanding the concept of ma’rifa within the framework of Sufi mysticism requires a thorough reading of the spiritual journey in the quest for divine knowledge and unity with the Divine. In the traditional Islamic context, 'ilm (knowledge) implies religious knowledge, whereas in the Quran, the term “ilm” refers to God's own understanding, which includes both the visible and hidden aspects of reality. In its broadest sense, 'ilm can refer to understanding of any specific thing or notion, as well as any type of learning. Subsequently, the phrase came to refer to numerous sorts of sciences. In this paper, an argument for ma’rifa is made, with a focus on the experiential phenomenon of understanding that goes beyond knowledge. This is modelled through a qualitative analysis of famous Sufi texts to give a predominantly literary-angled style. The analysis is exemplified with reference to poetic expressions of Rumi, Attar, Al-Ghazali, and Dhu'l-Nûn Al-Misri, where the notion of ma’rifa is developed through love, spiritual cleansing and sacrifice. The paper concludes that a deeply profound bond is found between the mystic and God, demonstrated by using lyrical language and metaphors. Eventually, the paper positions ma’rifa as a key aspect of Sufi philosophy and practice.

oa:W7203597165.title: GOD IS BACK — The Resurrection of Reason in a Post-Truth World
oa:W7203597165.abstract: GOD IS BACK is Book One of The Architect's Protocol and the opening philosophical audit of the five-book sequence. It begins not by assuming a religious conclusion, but by examining a late-modern contradiction: a civilization can deny any transcendent source of truth while continuing to speak in the language of reason, dignity, rights, conscience and universal moral obligation as though those categories still carry unchanged authority. The book treats post-truth as more than misinformation or media disorder. It asks whether post-truth is a deeper protocol failure that appears when truth is reduced to preference, construction, identity, market incentive or institutional power. From there, the argument examines the homelessness of reason, the continued expenditure of inherited moral capital, the rise of substitute objects of ultimate concern, and what the book calls the Architect-shaped hole left by metaphysical deletion. This research and book framework edition places those claims in conversation with Nietzsche's diagnosis of the death of God, modern debates over secular reason, truth, moral inheritance and public rationality. It does not claim that non-believers cannot reason, live morally or defend truth. Its narrower claim is structural: practices can survive for a time after the metaphysical account that once grounded them is rejected, but inheritance and justification are not the same thing. The dossier therefore asks whether reason is merely an instrument for arranging preferences or whether it requires a reality, and ultimately a Source, that is not produced by the reasoner.

oa:W7203597451.title: The Influence of Religion, Country of Origin, and United States Acculturation on Stress Coping Techniques in a Spanish-Speaking Free Clinic Population
oa:W7203597451.abstract: Introduction Many Spanish-speaking individuals in the United States experience high levels of stress but disproportionately underutilize mental health services due to cultural, socioeconomic, and religious barriers in accessing culturally relevant mental health care. Methods Cross-sectional survey of Spanish-speaking adults to assess demographics, religious beliefs, and stress-coping preferences. Results Of 100 participants, 90% of participants identified as religious, with 75% reporting moderate to high religious influence on daily life. Higher religious influence correlated with a broader range of coping strategies, both faith-based (e.g., prayer, church attendance) and secular (e.g., work-related tasks, nature immersion, creative outlets). Non-religious participants primarily relied on exercise, entertainment, and socialization. Acculturation correlated with religious influence ( r [1, 99] = 0.348, p < 0.001), while country of origin was not significantly associated with particular coping strategies. Conclusion These findings suggest that religiosity is associated with an expanded breadth of coping behaviors among Spanish-speaking patients and may serve as an additional protective factor in managing stress. By defining specific mechanisms that are commonly utilized within this population, these findings inform the development of more culturally and spiritually sensitive mental health interventions. Lastly, this study reiterates the importance of tailoring support to individual levels of religiosity and acculturation.

oa:W7203601300.title: Discourse Issues and Ideology in the English-Based Mottos of Selected Tertiary Institutions in Nigeria
oa:W7203601300.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203601300.abstract: Abstract Mottos are concise statements that express the values and identities of educational organisations. While previous studies (Akoto, 2018; Odusina, 2017; Ekpenyong & Tanyi, 2019) have looked at the stylistic, syntactic, and lexico-semantic analysis of mottos in various contexts, research on the discourse issues and ideological orientations of English-based mottos across Nigerian universities, polytechnics and colleges of education remains limited. This study aims at addressing this gap. The study is anchored in Fairclough’s Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA). Using a qualitative research design, the study analyses a purposively selected sample of 31 English-based mottos of 18 universities, 5 colleges of education or technology, and 8 polytechnics drawn from Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones. Data were purposively selected from official institutional websites and publications. Six discourse issues found in the mottos are technological advancement, knowledge and intellectual empowerment, pursuit of excellence, service to society, ethical development, and future orientation. Seven ideological inclinations found are theism, patriotism, legalism, humanitarianism, pioneerism, conservancy, and individualism. Theism is seen in references made to God while patriotism is expressed in loyalty to Nigeria. Legalism positions knowledge as a right, and humanitarianism shows community engagement. Conservancy focuses on safeguarding standards, while individualism is linked to self-reliance. The study contributes to knowledge by demonstrating that Nigerian tertiary-institution mottos function as ideological discourse. oa:W7203606622.title: RELIGIOUS COPING AND CAREGIVER STRESS: SOCIOLOGICAL INSIGHTS INTO DOMESTIC CARE PRACTICES
oa:W7203606622.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203606622.abstract: Family caregiving is an essential yet demanding responsibility that is often accompanied by emotional, physical, and psychological stress. Religious beliefs and practices play a significant role in shaping how caregivers interpret their experiences and cope with the burdens of care in many households. This study examines the sociological dimensions of religious coping among family caregivers, highlighting the influence of faith-based frameworks on stress perception, caregiving roles, and help-seeking behaviors within domestic care settings. Religious coping may serve as a source of emotional strength, offering meaning, hope, and resilience during periods of strain. Prayer, communal support, and reliance on spiritual interpretations of illness can provide comfort and a sense of shared purpose. However, when caregivers feel spiritually inadequate, religious coping may also reinforce self-sacrifice, limit the pursuit of external support, or contribute to guilt. Through a sociological lens, this study explores the interplay between religion, household dynamics, and caregiving expectations, emphasizing how cultural and spiritual values shape the caregiving experience. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for developing culturally sensitive interventions that support caregiver well-being while respecting religious and social contexts. The analysis underscores the need for holistic approaches in domestic care practices that integrate spiritual resources with practical and psychosocial support systems
