oa:W7203614404.title: AUTHORED — The Mind Behind a Maintained Universe — Institutional Research & Book Framework Edition
oa:W7203614404.abstract: AUTHORED is Book Four of The Architect’s Protocol and moves the series from moral order to the structure of reality itself. Its central question is explanatory rather than merely devotional: what kind of account best fits a universe that is mathematically intelligible, law-governed, life-permitting, information-bearing and capable of producing conscious observers who can understand it? The book builds a cumulative case from fine-tuning, physical order, entropy, biological information, origin-of-life questions, consciousness and the convergence of multiple lines of intelligibility. It explicitly rejects a “God of the gaps” method. A gap-filler inference says authorship is true wherever science has not yet explained something; a bounded authorship inference instead asks whether the character of the evidence, including successful scientific explanation itself, is more expected under mind or under brute fact. This dossier places the argument alongside anthropic reasoning, multiverse proposals, naturalistic emergence, philosophy of information, philosophy of mind and the problem of evil. It does not claim that fine-tuning proves a designer, that biological information is literally language in every relevant scientific sense, or that consciousness is impossible under physicalism. Its conclusion is abductive: authorship is presented as a candidate explanation whose force comes from convergence, not from one disputed datum.

oa:W7203615554.title: Miracle Money and Contemporary Nigerian Pentecostalism: A Philosophical Analysis of Matthew 17:24-27
oa:W7203615554.venue: IRASS Journal of Arts Humanities and Social Sciences
oa:W7203615554.abstract: The contemporary doctrine of miracle money has become a notable feature of some Nigerian Pentecostalism, with Matthew 17:24-27 frequently invoked to justify expectations of supernatural financial provision. Despite its growing influence, the doctrine has received limited philosophical scrutiny, particularly regarding its epistemological justification and hermeneutical legitimacy. This study examines the relationship between the Matthean narrative of the coin in the fish's mouth and the contemporary doctrine of miracle money from the perspective of the philosophy of religion. Employing a qualitative methodology that integrates philosophical analysis with contextual biblical hermeneutics, the study critically evaluates the epistemic basis of miracle claims, the interpretive movement from biblical narrative to doctrine, and the ethical implications of contemporary Pentecostal teaching. The analysis demonstrates that the miraculous coin in the fist’s mouth is primarily a Christological and providential narrative addressing a specific historical circumstance rather than establishing a normative doctrine of supernatural financial provision. It further argues that while belief in divine miracles is rationally defensible within Christian theism, the doctrinal universalization of miracle money exceeds the hermeneutical intention of the Matthean text and lacks sufficient epistemic warrant. The study concludes that responsible theological reflection requires a careful distinction between divine possibility and doctrinal normativity, thereby preserving both the integrity of Scripture and the rational coherence of religious belief. oa:W7203616774.title: The Effect of Religious Conversion on the Preservation of Indigenous Knowledge System in Nepal
oa:W7203616774.venue: Journal of Indigenous Knowledge and Practice
oa:W7203616774.abstract: Since there is a close relationship between religious belief and the indigenous knowledge system, religious conversion plays a significant role in minimizing the indigenous knowledge system (IKS) of Nepal. This study analyses the effects of religious conversion on the indigenous knowledge system. The Objectives of this study are to analyze the effects of religious conversion on preserving the indigenous knowledge system of indigenous people living in the study area. The study followed an interpretive paradigm of qualitative research. An in-depth interview was used as a tool for data collection from the field. Five individuals from four indigenous communities of Chitwan district were selected as participants. Purposive sampling techniques were used to select the participants for this study. Pseudonyms (P1–P5) have been given to ensure the secrecy of the participants. Thematic analysis was applied to interpret participants’ narratives. Conversion disrupts ritual obligations, reduces the authority of elders and ritual specialists, and shifts cultural learning spaces from households and communal gatherings to churches. The study brings awareness to the respected community about how conversion operates as both a spiritual and structural force affecting Indigenous knowledge systems.

oa:W7203619790.title: Reassessing the Orans Pose in Roman Egyptian Funerary Art: Two Unpublished Stelae from Mendes
oa:W7203619790.abstract: This study presents, for the first time, two funerary stelae from ancient Mendes (Dakahlia) while aiming to date and interpret them. It also compares these stelae with similar examples from Kom Abu Bellou and Roman-era sarcophagi, tracing their origins and examining the continuity of their design into the Coptic and Christian artistic contexts. The research explores the intended meaning of the raisedhand gesture of the deceased on these stelae, emphasizing the orans posture and relating it to the prevailing religious beliefs of the time. The analysis indicates that the owners of the two stelae were not necessarily Egyptian; however, they were clearly influenced by ancient Egyptian religious concepts, including the depiction of funerary deities such as Anubis. Furthermore, the study shows that the orans posture served as a visual tool, expressing the moral identity of the deceased and their successful passage through divine judgment, in line with Greco-Roman notions of pietas. This approach reflects a hybrid strategy, preserving Egyptian funerary ideology while visually adapting it to be comprehensible within a multicultural environment. In conclusion, the artistic culture in Mendes during the Roman period maintained the continuity of Egyptian funerary practices through the conscious adaptation of traditional symbols and techniques. This reflects a productive interaction between local heritage and classical influences in shaping the posthumous identity of the deceased.

oa:W7203622140.title: Afterword: Why the Question Became Visible
oa:W7203622140.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203622140.abstract: This afterword accompanies the six papers and the methodological companion (Paper 4.5) of the Conscious Cost Research Program. It gives a retrospective account of why the program's central question — who can finally certify that an answer sufficed — became visible: a career in international taxation spent tracing beneficial ownership through conduit structures; an encounter, outside the institutions, with the off-ledger world of care; and the writing of the six papers as the metabolism of six disillusionments. The essay records how the sixth paper (Conscious Cost and God: The Un-foreclosable Addressee) proved to be the program's foundation rather than its summit; notes that descriptions of a structural vacancy and its function exist independently in at least six traditions (this program, the Kyoto School, Lefort, negative theology, Derrida, Buber) — while leaving open whether these are six different seats or one seat observed through six windows; and announces the next program: a catalogue that lays these descriptions side by side and examines the identity of the seats, with the brackets kept closed, beginning with child-rearing as the first site of observation. The papers of the program are available via the DOIs listed in the document. AI-Use Disclosure The conception and the writing of this afterword are the author’s. The author reviewed all AI-assisted text and bears full responsibility for the content, including any errors.

oa:W7203622400.title: AUTHORED — The Mind Behind a Maintained Universe
oa:W7203622400.abstract: AUTHORED is Book Four of The Architect's Protocol and moves the series from moral order to the structure of reality itself. Its central question is explanatory rather than merely devotional: what kind of account best fits a universe that is mathematically intelligible, law-governed, life-permitting, information-bearing and capable of producing conscious observers who can understand it? The book builds a cumulative case from fine-tuning, physical order, entropy, biological information, origin-of-life questions, consciousness and the convergence of multiple lines of intelligibility. It explicitly rejects a "God of the gaps" method. A gap-filler inference says authorship is true wherever science has not yet explained something; a bounded authorship inference instead asks whether the character of the evidence, including successful scientific explanation itself, is more expected under mind or under brute fact. This dossier places the argument alongside anthropic reasoning, multiverse proposals, naturalistic emergence, philosophy of information, philosophy of mind and the problem of evil. It does not claim that fine-tuning proves a designer, that biological information is literally language in every relevant scientific sense, or that consciousness is impossible under physicalism. Its conclusion is abductive: authorship is presented as a candidate explanation whose force comes from convergence, not from one disputed datum.

oa:W7203624031.title: A quest for a pest: A Historical and Etymological Exploration of Termite-Related Terms in Modern Persian
oa:W7203624031.abstract: This study aims to conduct an etymological and comparative analysis of several terms used to refer to termites in Modern Persian, as well as to explore the naming of this insect and its historical development within Indo-Iranian and Indo-European. Termites have annoyed humans throughout history, primarily due to their role in the destruction of organic materials, particularly wood. Consequently, the terminology associated with this insect not only reflects its biological and behavioral traits but also reveals cultural attitudes embedded in its naming. Employing historical and comparative linguistic methods, this research examines the words used to designate termites in Persian from both structural and semantic perspectives. The data for the study have been sourced from Dehkhoda’s Great Persian Dictionary, historical lexicons, and Indo-European etymological references. The etymological analysis reveals that concepts such as “eating,” “cutting,” and “destruction” are directly inspired by termites’ biological characteristics and are mirrored in their linguistic representation. The findings indicate that some of the terms associated with termites have been shaped by the historical interaction between the Persian language and local dialects. Additionally, the study highlights the influence of ancient religious beliefs on the naming of creatures like termites, which are often perceived as pests. These results illuminate the broader relationship between language and human interaction with nature, contributing to the understanding of historical linguistics and the cultural underpinnings of terminology.

oa:W7203639939.title: GOD IS BACK — The Resurrection of Reason in a Post-Truth World — Institutional Research & Book Framework Edition
oa:W7203639939.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203639939.abstract: GOD IS BACK is Book One of The Architect’s Protocol and the opening philosophical audit of the five-book sequence. It begins not by assuming a religious conclusion, but by examining a late-modern contradiction: a civilization can deny any transcendent source of truth while continuing to speak in the language of reason, dignity, rights, conscience and universal moral obligation as though those categories still carry unchanged authority. The book treats post-truth as more than misinformation or media disorder. It asks whether post-truth is a deeper protocol failure that appears when truth is reduced to preference, construction, identity, market incentive or institutional power. From there, the argument examines the homelessness of reason, the continued expenditure of inherited moral capital, the rise of substitute objects of ultimate concern, and what the book calls the Architect-shaped hole left by metaphysical deletion. This research and book framework edition places those claims in conversation with Nietzsche’s diagnosis of the death of God, modern debates over secular reason, truth, moral inheritance and public rationality. It does not claim that non-believers cannot reason, live morally or defend truth. Its narrower claim is structural: practices can survive for a time after the metaphysical account that once grounded them is rejected, but inheritance and justification are not the same thing. The dossier therefore asks whether reason is merely an instrument for arranging preferences or whether it requires a reality, and ultimately a Source, that is not produced by the reasoner.

oa:W7203644340.title: RELIGIOUS COPING AND CAREGIVER STRESS: SOCIOLOGICAL INSIGHTS INTO DOMESTIC CARE PRACTICES
oa:W7203644340.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203644340.abstract: Family caregiving is an essential yet demanding responsibility that is often accompanied by emotional, physical, and psychological stress. Religious beliefs and practices play a significant role in shaping how caregivers interpret their experiences and cope with the burdens of care in many households. This study examines the sociological dimensions of religious coping among family caregivers, highlighting the influence of faith-based frameworks on stress perception, caregiving roles, and help-seeking behaviors within domestic care settings. Religious coping may serve as a source of emotional strength, offering meaning, hope, and resilience during periods of strain. Prayer, communal support, and reliance on spiritual interpretations of illness can provide comfort and a sense of shared purpose. However, when caregivers feel spiritually inadequate, religious coping may also reinforce self-sacrifice, limit the pursuit of external support, or contribute to guilt. Through a sociological lens, this study explores the interplay between religion, household dynamics, and caregiving expectations, emphasizing how cultural and spiritual values shape the caregiving experience. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for developing culturally sensitive interventions that support caregiver well-being while respecting religious and social contexts. The analysis underscores the need for holistic approaches in domestic care practices that integrate spiritual resources with practical and psychosocial support systems

oa:W7203645010.title: நடடபபற மககளன இறநமபககயல நரததககடன சடஙககள: மனடவயல மறறம இலககயவயல ஆயவறகக
oa:W7203645010.venue: KALANJIYAM - International Journal of Tamil Studies
oa:W7203645010.abstract: The traditional deity worship practices that have prevailed in the Indian cultural landscape since ancient times are deeply intertwined with the daily life and social structure of the people. Conceptualizing the great forces of nature and supernatural elements as deities, folk people surrendered to these gods to protect themselves from fear and diseases. The primary ritualistic method undertaken by people to attain divine grace and to express gratitude for the fulfillment of their prayers is called 'Nertikadan' (votive offering/fulfilling a vow). This research paper comprehensively examines the role of votive offerings in Tamil folk religious beliefs through anthropological, sociological, and folkloric perspectives. Based on ritual intensity, physical effort, and psychological background, this paper classifies vows into two major categories—'Mild Votive Offerings' (Menmai-t-thanmaiyulla Nertikadangal) and 'Severe Votive Offerings' (Vanmai-t-thanmaiyulla Nertikadangal)—and explains their cultural norms. Furthermore, by establishing the historical continuity of this vow-fulfilling tradition through Sangam literature, Silappatikaram, and later ethical texts, it critically analyzes regional ritual variations using field-study data from modern open-access journals.

oa:W7203652598.title: Paths of Faith and Focus? ADHD, Adult Religiosity, and Moderation by Race in the Add Health Study
oa:W7203652598.venue: Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion
oa:W7203652598.abstract: ABSTRACT Despite extensive research on attention‐deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), little is known about how ADHD shapes religious belief and practice across the life course. Using longitudinal data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), this study examines whether childhood ADHD diagnosis is associated with multiple dimensions of adult religiosity—religious service attendance, religious importance, and prayer—and whether these associations vary by race/ethnicity. Ordinal logistic regression models show that an ADHD diagnosis before age 18 is strongly and persistently associated with lower religious attendance in early midlife, even after adjusting for adolescent religiosity, demographics, and health selection. In contrast, associations between ADHD and private religiosity were largely explained by background factors. The negative association between ADHD and attendance is significantly stronger for Black and Asian American adults than Whites. We highlight the importance of integrating neurodiversity into research on disability and religiosity across the life course.

oa:W7203664953.title: Being Non-Religious in a Godly Society—Respect and the Negotiation of Social Relations in Indonesia
oa:W7203664953.abstract: This article examines the life of an atheist Chinese Indonesian living in a society where citizens are expected, both legally and socially, to profess belief in God. Occupying a doubly marginalized position as both a member of a historically stigmatized ethnic minority and a non-believer in a religiously defined nation, he must continually negotiate suspicion, belonging, and social acceptance in everyday life. Drawing on a Goffmanian framework and a biographical study of one individual, the article explores how different forms of stigma generate different strategies of management. While visible ethnic difference requires responses to actual stigmatization, atheism remains a concealable but potentially more consequential source of moral suspicion. The analysis shows how these intersecting stigmas are navigated through practices of adjustment, passing, and anticipatory self-presentation. In particular, it identifies the local practice of hormat (respect) as a key moral orientation through which social relationships are maintained despite difference. Attention to hormat reveals how people may navigate stigma as a deeply social and historically shaped condition through practices that prioritize relational harmony and recognition of others’ agency.

oa:W7203666046.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203666046.abstract: Album 80 - Voice of Wisdom: Songs from the Proverbs (ஞானத்தின் குரல் : நீதிமொழிகளில் இருந்து பாடல்கள்) Album 80 is a 7-song collection drawn from the Book of Proverbs. These anointed Tamil worship songs call the remnant to seek true wisdom, fear the Lord, receive instruction, turn from the path of the wicked, and walk in the ways of righteousness. Every song points beyond Solomon to the One greater than Solomon — the Lord Jesus Christ, the Wisdom of God. Offered freely for the remnant. All glory to Jesus Christ alone! Tamil Tracks நீதிமொழிகளைப் படியுங்கள் கர்த்தருக்குப் பயப்படுதலே ஞானம் என் கையை நீட்டுகின்றேன் என் மகனே நீ உன் செவியை ஞானத்திற்கு சாய் ஞானம் உன் இருதயத்தில் பிரவேசிக்கும் என் போதகத்தை நீ மறவாதே ஞானத்தை கண்டடையும் மனுஷன் பாக்கியவான் English Tracks Read the Proverbs – Worship the Greater Solomon The Fear of the Lord Is the Beginning of Wisdom I Stretch Out My Hand My Son, Incline Your Ear to Wisdom Wisdom Will Enter Your Heart Do Not Forget My Teaching Blessed Is the One Who Finds Wisdom Study note: These songs are rooted in Proverbs 1–3 and related passages. Solomon, son of David, wrote the Proverbs to give wisdom, instruction, understanding, justice, and discretion. Yet Jesus declared, “A greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). He is the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30) in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; rejecting His call leads to destruction, while those who find Wisdom find life, honour, and peace. These songs are a call to the remnant to hear Wisdom’s voice and walk in her ways until the day we see the greater Solomon face to face. Prayer Lord Jesus Christ, You are the true Wisdom of God, greater than Solomon. Open our ears to Your instruction. Writ

oa:W7203667048.title: Widowhood and loneliness in Haulawng community
oa:W7203667048.venue: International Journal of Sociology and Humanities
oa:W7203667048.abstract: Bereavement, the loss of a primary source of social and emotional support, alteration in roles and living arrangements defines the horrendous period of widowhood. This study attempts to explore the levels of loneliness during widowhood and analyzing the relationship between support network, coping mechanism and loneliness among widows and widowers. The study is an exploratory research design. The sample size is 30 in which stratified simple random sampling method is used to collect data. The levels of loneliness, support network and coping mechanism are measured. The result of the study indicates that the mean age is 66.66 among which Christianity is a predominant religious belief where majority practice joint family system. The respondents receive positive support from their significant dear ones, community and government services. The data shows that the level of loneliness falls in high category in which widowers are more. There is a significant difference between widows and widowers with regards to coping styles. The study shows that there is significant correlation between loneliness, coping mechanism, support network, time spent with and gender. The study highlights the need for improved psycho-social support both at the professional and community level for widows and widowers. Future research should continue to explore the immediate effects of bereavement and coping to understand the psycho-social impact.

oa:W7203691406.title: The Exhaustion of the Grounding Space: A Structural Proof of Agápēic Relational Metaphysics
oa:W7203691406.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203691406.abstract: This paper argues that the history of systematic metaphysics has produced three canonical responses to the grounding problem — non-relational pure actuality (Thomas Aquinas), internal self-differentiating dialectic (G.W.F. Hegel), and processual relational ground (Alfred North Whitehead and Charles Hartshorne) — and that a fourth family, Dualism, completes the logical space of non-agápēic alternatives. Through a unified structural analysis organized around two diagnostic axes — the unity of the ground and the mode of causation — the paper demonstrates that the resulting four collapse families (Monism, Dualism, Emptiness, and Determinism) are exhaustive: every possible metaphysical first principle either occupies one of these four positions or fails the minimal adequacy conditions for a ground. Agápēic Relational Metaphysics (ARM) is a first-philosophy project deriving the structure of the ultimate ground from transcendental-structural analysis. The term agápē functions throughout as a structural designator — non-coercive, distinction-preserving, self-giving relational actuality — and carries no theological loading in the premises. Under ARM's criterion of constitutive relationality, Aquinas structurally trends toward Monism at the intra-divine level. Hegel exhibits the same structural tendency because creaturely distinction is the Absolute's self-differentiation rather than genuine otherness. Whitehead and Hartshorne collapse into Emptiness because the consequent nature of God is contingent and posterior, inverting the grounding relation. Thomas Nagel's contemporary impasse is formally diagnosed as a structurally necessary consequence of these exhausted options. oa:W7203710378.title: The Metaphysical Foundations Of The Argument From Origination İn Al-Juwaynī: The Conception Of God, Eternal Attributes, And The Relationship Of Creation
oa:W7203710378.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203710378.abstract: This study examines Imām al-Ḥaramayn al-Juwaynī’s understanding of the argument from temporality in relation to his conception of God, eternal attributes, and creation. In the kalām tradition, the argument from temporality is generally explained through the claim that the world came into existence after non-existence and that every originated being requires an originator. However, when al-Juwaynī’s theological system is considered as a whole, this argument cannot be reduced to a merely cosmological proof. Rather, it is closely connected with the idea of God as eternal, powerful, willing, knowing, and a free agent. This study first examines the ontological basis of the argument from temporality within the framework of substance-accident theory and Ashʿarite atomism. It then evaluates al-Juwaynī’s understanding of divine attributes and creation. The study also compares the philosophers’ doctrines of eternity and emanation with the theologians’ account of voluntary creation. It concludes that, in al-Juwaynī’s thought, the argument from temporality is not only an inference from the world to God, but also a comprehensive theological framework that explains the relation from God to the world through creation.

oa:W7203730014.title: Радянські антирелігійні практики крізь призму вчительських спогадів
oa:W7203730014.abstract: The article analyzes the Soviet public policy of «scientific atheism». The analysis was carried out on the basis of oral historical narratives, archival documents, local history materials. It is noted that in the second half of the 20th century the main way of fighting against religion and the church was mass atheistic propaganda. It was justified by the political doctrine of «scientific atheism» and reinforced by a system of state-administrative pressure. With the help of propaganda, the Soviet intellectual elite created an image of the church as an «internal enemy» in order to use it in the process of forming an imaginary community called the «Soviet people». The territorial boundaries of the publication were delineated by the Lviv, Ternopil and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, on the territories of which the memories were recorded. Attention is given to the textual analysis of memories, which in turn is oriented to the reproduction of the meaning that the teachers placed on their specific life experience today, as well as to the study of the sequence in which the events are arranged in the narrative now, in the present time. It is important in this context to understand the structural difference between what the narrators experienced and what they told, as well as to consider the narrative as containing purely contemporary interpretations and evaluations of the narrators. The article examines how former teachers recall the «struggle against religion», aimed at the atheization of society and their (co)relation to this policy. oa:W7203746687.title: Tiv Indigenous Religion: Doctrine, Rituals, Symbols, and Spiritualities
oa:W7203746687.venue: RESEARCH JOURNAL OF HUMANITIES AND CULTURAL STUDIES
oa:W7203746687.abstract: Tiv Indigenous Religion has played a crucial role in shaping the cultural and spiritual identity of the Tiv people of Nigeria. However, modernisation, globalisation, and the influence of Christianity and Islam have significantly altered traditional religious practices, leading to their gradual decline. Despite these challenges, Tiv indigenous religious beliefs, rituals, symbols, and spiritualities remain integral to the community’s social cohesion, governance, and moral order. This study examined the doctrines, rituals, symbols, and spiritualities in Tiv Indigenous Religion, stressing their significance and contemporary relevance. The study adopted a qualitative research design, relying on ethnographic methods and documentary analysis. Data were collected through in-depth interviews with Tiv elders, spiritual leaders, and traditional healers, as well as a review of historical and anthropological literature. Thematic analysis was employed to identify key patterns in Tiv religious beliefs and practices. Findings revealed that Tiv Indigenous Religion is centred on Aôndo, (the Supreme Being), alongside other spiritual entities such as ujijingi (spirits), Akombo (rituals) and Tsav (witchcraft), which govern various aspects of life. Rituals, including initiation rites, healing ceremonies, and divination, serve to maintain social order and connect the human and spiritual realms. Symbols such as the Swem pot, sacred textiles, and ancestral shrines reinforce cultural identity and ethical conduct. The study also found that syncretism has allowed elements of Tiv religion to persist despite external influences, with traditional practices adapting to accommodate aspects of Christianity and Islam. oa:W7203757823.title: The Intersection of Disability and Religiosity among Elderly Beggars: A Qualitative Inquiry in Galle City, Sri Lanka
authors: D. M. H. N. K. Dissanayake
oa:W7203757823.abstract: Begging persists as a marginalized survival strategy shaped by changing socio-structural systems. In Sri Lanka, the decline of traditional extended families and a rapidly aging population have pushed vulnerable older adults into severe destitution. This qualitative study explores how physical disability and religious beliefs intersect to shape the daily experiences of elderly beggars within the Galle City administrative boundaries. Utilizing a qualitative research design, primary data were gathered through structured in-depth interviews with 15 purposely sampled elderly beggars, supplemented by secondary data for literature contextualization and qualitative descriptive data analysis. The empirical findings indicate that physical disability serves a dual, paradoxical role, it completely bars older individuals from conventional labour markets while functioning as a form of visual capital that increases personal sympathy and material donations from passersby. Concurrently, internal religiosity heavily conditions the participants' psychological coping mechanisms. Entrenched cultural beliefs in past-life karma and destiny provide existential meaning to their current suffering, yet they simultaneously in still a fatalistic framework that restricts their proactive capacity to cope, dampens their courage, and limits their ability to escape chronic street dependency. This study bridges a vital literature gap by demonstrating how structural physical limitations and internal cultural-religious systems interact to reinforce and normalize chronic socioeconomic marginalization among elderly urban populations.

oa:W7203761940.title: DOES GOD EXIST? CAN WE TELL IF WE BASED THIS QUESTION ONLY UPON THE APPARENT RANDOMNESS OF EVERYTHING?
oa:W7203761940.abstract: Excluding scientific, archaeological and other evidence that God exists, I play a ‘what if’ scenario where the existence or non-existence of God rests solely on the apparent random events that took place in all of history. The seemingly random events that happened in our personal lives and so on. It examines the rise and collapse of empires, political regimes, warfare, illness, reported miracles, and the failure of many perpetrators to receive earthly justice. The evidence does not establish that these events are literally random; many have identifiable biological, political, or social causes. Nevertheless, their outcomes frequently appear non-monotonic and morally indiscriminate, with no consistent relationship between moral character and health, longevity, safety, prosperity, or political success. Naturalism interprets this pattern through impersonal causation and probability, whereas biblical theology appeals to human agency, regular natural processes, hidden providence, suffering, and delayed judgment. Apparent randomness therefore creates an evidential difficulty for expectations of continuously visible divine control, but it does not independently prove or disprove God because the same observations remain compatible with competing metaphysical interpretations.

oa:W7203783633.title: The human epiphany of Dionysus and his duality with Pentheus in the tragedy "The Bacchae"
oa:W7203783633.abstract: Euripides's "The Bacchae" is the only complete tragedy in which one of the main characters is the god and patron of the theater, Dionysus. It is therefore unsurprising that numerous studies have been devoted to his portrayal in this work. Most of these studies center on the comparison between Dionysus and Pentheus, another main character and the god's cousin, who rejects his cult. On the contrary, in Russian historiography, research questions devoted to Dionysus in tragedy have rarely been touched upon. The author aims to analyze the god's human epiphany. Human epiphany as a subject of study is particularly interesting because such theophany, given the god's appearance in tragedy seemingly with Dionysus's own permission, can be considered a metatragic element of the second order, as this epiphany is accomplished with the permission and intention of the already "tragedic" deity. In this article, the author employs general scientific methods of analysis and synthesis, a comparative historical method, and terminological and lexical analysis. The author examines the appearance of human theophany and the tradition of its transformation, the main features of the image perceived by other characters, both hidden and intended for the audience, expressed in the chorus's lines, and a comparison of Pentheus and Dionysus. The author concludes that the god's appearance is variable, and his features in the tragedy "The Bacchae" are linked to the motifs of the work itself. The author examines the main themes associated with Dionysus's human epiphany, such as the concept of the god as an outsider, the impossibility of capturing him, and the duality of Pentheus and Dionysus, which receives particular attention in the article. oa:W7203786420.title: Forensic Religious Studies Examination of Information Materials: Issues of Authenticity and Interpretation while Studying Religious Concepts in Internet Communications
oa:W7203786420.venue: Theory and Practice of Forensic Science
oa:W7203786420.abstract: Religious studies examination of information materials is a new expert specialty and a relevant area of forensic expert activity. Unlike the state religious expertise, the history and methodology of which is represented in our country by the names of such authors as I.V. Zagrebina, A.V. Pchelintsev, M. Yu. Smirnov, E.S. Elbakyan and others, forensic religious studies examination, actualized by the increased role of social networks, is at the stage of its development and formation of a special range of tasks. The article focuses on applying the changed range of meanings and beliefs about religion in the context of modern Internet communications. The thesis is expressed about the importance for an expert to take into account certain meanings in religious studies and their changes at the stage of interpreting information materials. The conclusion is made that most of religious beliefs disseminated in Internet communications are stigmatized. The stigmatization of religious concepts is related to the forms of narrative practices functioning in the Internet environment. It is caused by a number of processes and in particular by the specifics of reproducing historical memories of institutional forms of religion in the past and present. As a result, the stigmatization of religious beliefs is associated with replication of simplified binary oppositions in relation to religion as a whole. The article substantiates the need for methodological certainty of the data interpretation stage of the examination. oa:W7203786539.title: Social learning of scientific and religious views: parents as transmission agents and their approaches against dissent
oa:W7203786539.abstract: Focusing on two prominent belief frameworks - science and religion - this study examined adults' retrospective perceptions of the role their parents played in transmitting and maintaining beliefs. We adapted a previous method (McLoughlin, 2021) and asked Australian and Malaysian adults to reflect on whether and how their current scientific and religious beliefs were influenced by their parents. Across both countries, adults indicated that their parents were influential for both science and religion. Participants generally recalled scientific influence positively irrespective of how religious they were. For religion, greater participant religiosity was associated with positive influence for Australian adults only. Approximately three-quarters of Malaysian participants identified their parents as the only source for both religious and scientific beliefs. While the same proportion of Australians indicated so for science, significantly less Australian participants identified their parents as the only source for religious beliefs. When reflecting on how their parents approached conflicting views between themselves and their parents, Australian participants generally reported that their parents employed a supportive approach across both domains. Malaysian participants often reported that their parents, though open to accepting dissenting scientific beliefs with a supportive stance, were more inclined toward a directive approach when faced with conflicts in religious views. This study affords novel insights into the universality and variation of parents' roles in the transmission and maintenance of scientific and religious beliefs across diverse populations.

oa:W7203835172.title: The Influence of Greek, Egyptian, and Hindu Mythology on Human Behaviour and Morality
oa:W7203835172.abstract: Mythology has been used by human cultures throughout history to make sense of death, givedeath moral meaning, and deal with the unknown. People’s stories of death and the afterlifeinfluence individual conduct, systems of ethics, and collective norms across civilisations, notmerely mirror cultural beliefs. This review discusses how three of the world’s most influentialancient mythologies, Greek, Egyptian, and Hindu, present death and the afterlife and how thesepresentations continue to inform human psychology and moral conduct. This paper uses acomparative theoretical analysis of primary mythological narratives and their associatedreligious structures to explore the ways in which beliefs about the afterlife influence deathanxiety, life satisfaction, and moral decision-making. It draws upon the figures, rituals, andcosmological frameworks embedded within each custom, including the tripartite judgment ofthe Greek underworld and the Erinyes, the weighing of the heart against the feather of Ma’at,and the karmic cycle of samsāra and the pursuit of moksha in Hinduism, to understand howdifferent spiritual systems produce distinct moral obligations. Together, these traditions revealthat while religious belief is not the only source of morality, mythological narratives are amongthe most enduring and broad structures that individuals and societies use to make sense of life,death, and the choices in between. Therefore, this paper explores the profound and multifacetedimpact of these ancient mythologies on the ethical frameworks and behavioural norms withinand across societies, examining how foundational narratives shape moral reasoning andsocietal structures.

oa:W7203868139.title: Miedo a la muerte en profesionales de enfermería hospitalaria en el sur de Chile
oa:W7203868139.abstract: Introduction: Fear of death is a relevant topic in nursing due to its impact on professional well-being and the quality of care. Objective: To analyze fear of death among nursing professionals in southern Chile according to their demographic and professional-occupational profiles and beliefs. Methodology: A quantitative, descriptive, and inferential study conducted on a random sample of 56 nursing professionals. The Collett-Lester Fear of Death Scale, adapted for the Chilean population, was administered; it assesses four dimensions, two of which are self-oriented and the other two other-oriented. Cut-off points were used to classify fear into low, moderate, and high levels. Results: 76.8 % of the participants exhibited moderate/high levels of fear of death. The highest scores were observed in the dimensions related to the death of others and the dying process of others, while fear of one’s own death showed the lowest scores. A significant association was identified between fear of death and religious belief (χ² = 6.46; p = 0.03; OR = 2.07). Discussion: The results show a heterogeneous expression of fear of death, with greater sensitivity observed in dimensions related to others. The association with religious beliefs should be interpreted with caution given the small sample size and the bivariate analysis. Conclusions: It is necessary to consider cultural and spiritual factors when designing emotional support interventions for nursing professionals and to explore this phenomenon further through future research.

oa:W7203877062.title: LIFE WITHOUT GOD A Philosophy of Survival, Meaning, Freedom, and Human Flourishing
oa:W7203877062.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7203877062.abstract: Life Without God: A Philosophy of Survival, Meaning, Freedom, and Human Flourishing examines one of the most enduring questions of human existence: how should we live if belief in God is not treated as a necessary foundation for morality, meaning, or purpose? Beginning with the origins of religion and human belief, the book explores evolution, cultural development, social institutions, the philosophical arguments for and against the existence of God, and the possibility of constructing an ethical life without divine command. Rather than presenting atheism as a final answer, the book adopts a naturalistic and self-correcting approach in which conclusions remain open to evidence, criticism, and revision. At the center of the work is Survival Philosophy, a framework built around truth-seeking, corrigibility, contextual judgment, sustainable survival, human flourishing, reciprocal freedom, cooperation, integrity, adaptability, and intentional living. The book argues that survival alone is not enough. A life worth preserving must also contain freedom, knowledge, meaningful relationships, creativity, justice, personal growth, and the possibility of improvement. Rejecting both rigid dogmatism and simplistic moral relativism, Life Without God proposes a philosophy designed for imperfect human beings living under uncertainty. Its central message is that the absence of absolute certainty need not lead to meaninglessness. Instead, it can increase our responsibility to think carefully, cooperate intelligently, revise our mistakes, and build conditions in which worthwhile forms of life can continue. Ultimately, this book is not merely about whether God exists. It is about a deeper question: Given the knowledge available to us, the freedom we can build, and the finite time we possess

The Source of Truth System™ comprises fourteen stages moving through existence, revelation, Tawheed, competing authority, Qadar, life, identity, inner formation, human formation, responsibility and prophetic models. The Architect's Protocol comprises five philosophical and civilizational works examining truth, power, objective morality, authorship of reality, artificial intelligence and transhumanism. The Qur'anic Coherence System is a four-volume structural research programme examining Qur'anic order, naẓm, munāsabah, surah unity, placement logic, macro-architecture, all 114 surahs and the evidentiary basis of coherence claims. Adam and the Answerable Being examines Islam, evolution, consciousness, philosophical anthropology and moral responsibility through the proposition that Adam represents the first answerable human. Tomorrow Became a Country examines the United Arab Emirates through the systems sequence Vision → Law → Execution → Openness → Growth → Global Influence. A recurring philosophical distinction throughout the programme is between information and architecture. I

oa:W7203917366.title: Reasons for the use of traditional bonesetter in fracture care: a systematic review and meta-analysis
oa:W7203917366.abstract: Traditional bonesetter (TBS) is often the primary choice in the treatment of fractures by communities, especially in rural areas, even though modern medical services are readily available. Dependence on TBS is a determinant of treatment success because improper fracture management is associated with increased morbidity and patient mortality. Meanwhile, information about why people prefer TBS is still limited. This systematic literature review aims to identify the reasons why patients prefer TBS in fracture treatment to improve understanding of the use of TBS in fracture cases. This study was systematically compiled in this review based on a literature search using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) method. A total of three electronic databases were used, namely PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Scopus. The article search is arranged with the range of 2014-2024. Four of the 1009 selected articles have met the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Funnel Plots were used to test effect size and heterogeneity with a p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The results of the analysis of 4 articles found that the reasons for choosing TBS in the case of fracture were dominated by economic factors, trust in TBS, religious beliefs, and advice from people closest to them. Therefore, it is recommended to increase educational efforts and integrate traditional medicine with modern medicine to reduce the incidence of morbidity and mortality.

oa:W7203918980.title: Spiritual and Religious Beliefs, Behaviors, and Struggles in Relation to Death Anxiety: Evidence from a U.S. Nationwide Probability Sample
oa:W7203918980.abstract: Death anxiety is associated with adverse psychological and health outcomes, yet findings regarding the role of religiosity and spirituality (R/S) as protective or risk factors remain mixed. Prior research has relied on convenience samples, combined disparate R/S constructs, and rarely tested nonlinear associations. This study examined associations between death anxiety and multiple R/S facets in a nationwide probability sample of 3,010 U.S. adults. Regression models tested associations between R/S predictors and death anxiety and tested moderation by age and chronic illness, controlling for demographics, meaning in life, social support, anxiety, and depression. All belief predictors (afterlife beliefs, R/S centrality, R/S peace, and positive view of God) showed curvilinear inverted U-shaped patterns: strong worldviews, both religious and secular, were linked to lower death anxiety, while ambivalence was associated with the highest death anxiety. Regarding behaviors, Bible reading was linearly protective; however, church attendance and prayer were protective only at threshold levels (multiple times per month and week, respectively). R/S struggles (insecure attachment to God and negative view of God) were consistently detrimental. Age moderated several relationships, with R/S centrality, peace, positive view of God, and prayer becoming increasingly protective in later life, while avoidant attachment to God became more harmful. Chronic illness moderated only positive God views such that benevolent God beliefs became more protective with increasing illness burden. These findings clarify inconsistencies in the existing literature and suggest that clarity in one's worldview may be an important target for intervention.

oa:W7203946028.title: Druidry and Priority Polytheism
oa:W7203946028.abstract: Abstract This paper will focus on conceptions of the divine in Modern Druidry. While acknowledging the diversity among Druids in their beliefs about the divine, this paper will have a particular focus on forms of polytheism that include belief in some form of ultimate divinity in addition to the pantheon of gods and goddesses. I will propose a way of understanding how such views can work through engagement with the priority monist view in metaphysics, using this view to construct a version of polytheism called priority polytheism. Following this, I will anticipate and respond to some objections to priority polytheism. Through this, this paper will show how engagement with Druidry in contemporary philosophy of religion can yield fruitful results.

oa:W7203959139.title: Compassion, Doubt, and Eternal Damnation: An Analysis of Sincere Belief and Doubt Under Religious Diversity — 31
oa:W7203959139.abstract: A perfectly loving and just Christian God-concept cannot coherently allow a nonresistant seeker's evidence-proportionate uncertainty, by itself, to determine irreversible punitive exclusion or everlasting suffering under religious diversity. This paper tests belief-conditioned damnation through a cumulative comparison: what accessible guidance the doctrine supplies, what responsible control the seeker has over the required belief response, and whether the consequence is proportioned to culpability. Mariam, a stipulated sincere inquirer who finds Christian and Islamic claims comparably supported, makes the problem concrete without pretending that a numerical credence profile is measured or uniquely rational. Divine hiddenness and religious diversity do not by themselves disprove theism, but they undercut the claim that every conscientious person receives clear, tradition-specific disclosure. Work on belief control distinguishes direct choice from indirect responsibility for inquiry, while the philosophy of hell exposes a further dilemma. If final fate turns on belief outcome under ambiguity—whether belief is called the trigger of condemnation or the condition of rescue—accessible guidance and responsible control over the required response are missing; if uncertainty itself is treated as guilt, proportionate culpability is missing too. If condemnation turns on informed and culpable rejection, Mariam-like doubt is outside its scope. The result survives the point that everlasting duration need not entail infinitely severe suffering: irreversible punitive exclusion still lacks a proportionate basis in nonculpable uncertainty. oa:W7204018384.title: Family Religious Socialization Index: Development and Preliminary Validation
oa:W7204018384.abstract: A key area of interest for religious scholars is how religious beliefs are passed across generations, or religious socialization. To expand this field of study, a theoretically grounded, validated measure of this construct is needed. This article describes the development and validation of the Family Religious Socialization Index (FRSI), a multi-informant, multidimensional assessment of the processes through which parents socialize religion and faith in their children. Based on Social Cognitive Theory and through a rigorous development and validation process, three subscales were developed to represent the primary processes of religious socialization. The FRSI consists of two parallel scales, a parent and adolescent version, each containing the same three subscales. Each subscale can be completed by a parent-child dyad regarding processes of religious socialization. The scales are designed to be used with either or both members of the dyad. Development of these scales included initial item generation, expert assessments, item reduction analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis. Preliminary evidence for the scales' construct, convergent, and discriminant validity and reliability are presented. The use cases for this measure in research on religion in families are discussed.

oa:W7204028803.title: Performing Church in Dystopia
oa:W7204028803.abstract: Abstract Suzanne Collins’s books about the Hunger Games lack references to religious beliefs or practices. However, in this article I argue that the resistance to oppression in the books can be read theologically, starting from an understanding of the church as a visible social body. Building on the political and liturgical theology of William T. Cavanaugh, I discuss how the scattering effects of torture are challenged in The Hunger Games . I focus on how bodily resistance to the practices of torture is described in Collins’s books and connect this to Cavanaugh’s theology about community, individuality, and the idea of ritual practices as resistance. Finally, I discuss how the anti-liturgy of torture is challenged when the performance of social bodies introduces elements of linearity in the repetitive cycle of isolating rituals. The Hunger Games is often read as an individualistic narrative about an individualistic heroine. Reading it in dialogue with Cavanaugh sheds light on how the formation of a social body is a significant part of Katniss’s resistance, both toward the Capitol and later toward the rebels from District 13.

oa:W7204045678.title: The Hidden Personality: Theology and Iconography of the Holy Spirit
oa:W7204045678.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204045678.abstract: The Holy Spirit is frequently perceived in popular piety as an impersonal force or a divine energy, in contrast to the sharply outlined personalities of God the Father and God the Son in the Scriptures. This essay explores the paradox between the rich theological personality of the Holy Spirit (characterized by intimacy, consolation, and sensitivity) and His historical-artistic representation. Through the analysis of the iconographic transition—from primitive abstract symbols and controversial medieval anthropomorphic representations, to the restrictive decree of Pope Benedict XIV in 1745—it examines how art has shaped, and at times limited, our understanding of the third Trinitarian Person. Finally, it proposes that abstraction in contemporary art offers a renewed path to capture the immanence and subtle personality of the Paraclete.

oa:W7204087453.title: Blame It on God? How Divine Attributions Legitimize Horizontal Inequalities and Shape Redistribution Preferences in Nigeria
oa:W7204087453.venue: Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion
oa:W7204087453.abstract: ABSTRACT While earlier research has analyzed how religious affiliations and practices impact support for group‐based (or "horizontal") redistribution, no study has yet investigated how divine attributions of group‐based or horizontal inequalities affect these redistributive attitudes. In this paper, we show that divine attributions of horizontal inequalities (i.e., the belief that horizontal inequalities were created by a supernatural force) reduce support for redistribution in Nigeria and theorize and empirically test two different mechanisms for explaining this association. Using survey data from over 2000 Nigerian respondents, we find that divine attributions of horizontal inequality are not primarily endorsed by the most religiously devout respondents. Instead, they are more common among individuals with stronger preferences for group‐based hierarchy, as measured by Social Dominance Orientation (SDO). We conclude that divine attributions of horizontal inequalities function less as expressions of personal religious beliefs than as ideological narratives deployed instrumentally to legitimize existing social hierarchies and resistance to redistribution.

oa:W7204099109.title: Ist Existenz eine Eigenschaft? Und existiert also Gott? Eine Analyse von Existenzmodalitäten, Virtualität und Gödels Gottesbeweis.
oa:W7204099109.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204099109.abstract: Dieser Text untersucht die Frage, ob Existenz als Eigenschaft verstanden werden kann und welche Konsequenzen dies für metaphysische und logische Systeme hat. Ausgehend von klassischen Existenzmodalitäten (faktisch, möglich, unmöglich, notwendig) analysiert der Artikel die Rolle von Virtualität, Realität und Konstruktion in Wahrnehmung, Psychologie, Mathematik und Physik. Ein Schwerpunkt liegt auf der Frage, ob Existenz selbst eine Eigenschaft sein kann und ob aus dieser Annahme die Existenz Gottes folgt, wie es Gödel in seinem ontologischen Beweis formalisiert hat. Der Text diskutiert die Struktur von Eigenschaften, die Rolle von Virtualität und Realität, die Emergenz von Objekten und Begriffen sowie die Grenzen logischer Beweise im Bereich metaphysischer Entitäten. Der Artikel verbindet mathematische Logik, Ontologie, Semiotik, Physik und philosophische Anthropologie und bietet eine originäre Perspektive auf die Frage, was es bedeutet, zu existieren. This text examines whether existence can be understood as a property and what consequences this has for metaphysical and logical systems. Beginning with classical modalities of existence (factual, possible, impossible, necessary), the article analyzes the role of virtuality, reality, and construction in perception, psychology, mathematics, and physics. A central focus is the question of whether existence itself can be considered a property and whether this assumption implies the existence of God, as formalized in Gödel’s ontological proof. The text discusses the structure of properties, the interplay between virtuality and reality, the emergence of objects and concepts, and the limits of logical proofs concerning metaphysical entities. The article integrates mathematical logic, ontology, semiotics, physics, and philosophic

oa:W7204146571.title: Tracing the Religious Life Course in an American Baby-Boom Cohort: Parental Influence and Temporal Dynamics
oa:W7204146571.abstract: The development of religiosity originates in earlier phases of the family and individual life course, yet few studies have investigated how early exposure to parental religiosity persists into mid- and later life. This investigation uses multigenerational data from 385 baby boom children, ages 16–26, and their parents in 1971, following children’s religious orientations into midlife and old age. Guided by intergenerational transmission and path dependency perspectives, we find that parents’ religious intensity in 1971 strengthened their children’s cognitive and behavioral religiosity in later life, mediated by children’s early and midlife religiosity. Results demonstrate intergenerational transmission followed by durability in religious beliefs and practices across decades of temporal stability. These findings suggest that parental influence creates cumulative religious momentum that carries from young adulthood through old age.

oa:W7204172584.title: Spirituality and Religiosity in End-of-Life Decision-Making in Intensive Care Units: A Systematic Review of Preferences, Ethical Framing, and Meaning-Making
oa:W7204172584.abstract: End-of-life decision-making in intensive care units (ICUs) is a complex and ethically challenging process shaped not only by clinical factors but also by patients' values, cultural contexts, and spiritual or religious beliefs. Although spirituality and religiosity are increasingly recognized as influential in decisions regarding life-sustaining treatment, their role has not been comprehensively synthesized within ICU settings. This systematic review, conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, examined the influence of spirituality and religiosity on end-of-life decision-making among adult ICU patients, surrogate decision-makers, and healthcare professionals. Electronic searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science identified eligible quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies, and findings were synthesized narratively because of methodological heterogeneity. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Overall, higher levels of religiosity were consistently associated with a stronger preference for aggressive life-prolonging interventions and a lower likelihood of treatment limitation. Spiritual and religious beliefs also influenced clinicians' ethical perspectives, particularly regarding the distinction between withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatments, while playing a central role in surrogate decision-making by shaping interpretations of illness, hope, and acceptable care. At the same time, spirituality demonstrated a multidimensional role, facilitating acceptance of death, promoting support for palliative care in some contexts, and contributing to meaning-making during the end-of-life process. oa:W7204174842.title: “Faith” as a Framework for Understanding Barriers and Enablers to Social and Behaviour Change Using Child Marriage in Mozambique, Nepal, and the Philippines as a Case Study
oa:W7204174842.abstract: This study examines the role of faith in social and behaviour change, using child marriage as a case study across Mozambique, Nepal, and the Philippines. While faith is widely acknowledged as a social force, its role in shaping behaviour remains underexplored in development programming. This research addresses that gap by proposing a multidimensional framework for understanding faith's influence on social norms and behaviour. A mixed-methods approach was employed, including surveys (N = 986), focus group discussions, and key informant interviews conducted between 2020 and 2023. The study identifies five key dimensions through which faith shapes behaviour: spirituality, religious beliefs, religious practices, the authority of religious institutions, and faith communities. Findings reveal that all of these aspects of faith may be deeply embedded in decision-making processes, both reinforcing and challenging norms around child marriage. Faith leaders and religious communities are often influential authorities shaping norms, with religious beliefs and practices reinforcing choices, while personal spirituality acts as an internal motivator for change. This study challenges the common tendency to view faith solely as a tool for promoting externally defined development goals. Instead, it argues for a more nuanced, context-specific approach that acknowledges faith as a dynamic and integral aspect of social change. Faith-sensitive approaches can enhance the effectiveness of social and behaviour change interventions by aligning with deeply held values and beliefs within communities. Future research should explore how these five faith dimensions interact across diverse cultural and religious contexts. oa:W7204193047.title: Married Women’s Perception of Family Planning Techniques and Implications for Population Growth in Nigeria: Study of Lagelu LGA, Oyo State
oa:W7204193047.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SOCIAL SCIENCES AND MANAGEMENT RESEARCH
oa:W7204193047.abstract: This study examined married women’s perception of family planning techniques and the implications for population growth in Nigeria, using Lagelu Local Government Area of Oyo State as a case study. The research adopted a descriptive survey design, employing structured questionnaires and interviews to collect data from 520 married women randomly selected across 13 wards that constitute the Local Government Area. Data were analyzed using tables, cross tabulation, percentages and descriptive methods of data analysis. Findings revealed that awareness of modern family planning methods was high in the study area, but actual utilization was limited by spousal disapproval, religious beliefs, fear of infertility, fear of promiscuity and fear of side effects. The study further established a significant relationship between women’s perception of family planning and their fertility behavior, indicating that negative perceptions contribute to high fertility rates and rapid population growth in the area. However, the recommendations put forward include establishment of more functional family planning clinics, more jingles on radio using local language, consistent supply of contraceptives by governments and NGOs, sensitization programme to make men to see the need for family planning techniques among others.

oa:W7204194676.title: Resistance to In-Vitro Fertilization as A Panacea to the Challenge of Infertility in Nigeria
oa:W7204194676.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RELIGIOUS AND CULTURAL PRACTICE
oa:W7204194676.abstract: In Nigeria society high premium is placed on child bearing. This has made childlessness to become a socio-cultural problem. Couples are unnecessarily put under pressure to bear children so as to secure genealogy. Childlessness, in Nigeria, normally attracts marital crisis, social disorder, stigmatization, emotional stress, isolation and depression in marriage. In-vitro fertilization has been discovered to be one of the ways to addressing infertility challenge. This study examines resistance to in-vitro fertilization as a panacea to the challenge of infertility in Nigeria. The study adopted descriptive research approach. Findings revealed that there are religious, cultural, ethical, economic, psychological/social resistance to in-vitro fertilization as a panacea to the challenge of infertility. The study concluded that in-vitro fertilization gives hope to couples faced with infertility challenges, that infertility is seen through the lenses of traditional and religious beliefs and this has become great obstacle to the acceptance of in-vitro fertilization as a solution to the challenge of infertility. This work recommended that there is the need for reproductive education, encouragement of seminars and conferences involving religious leaders, ethicists and medical personnel in order for in vitro fertilization to be acceptable in Nigeria society.

oa:W7204203650.title: The Topology of Time: On Change, Identity, Presence, and the Ground That Holds
oa:W7204203650.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204203650.abstract: The Topology of Time: An Ontological Treatise on Becoming, Presence, and the Ground That Holds This treatise presents a unified and substantially revised account of temporal being developed through the author's earlier writings on the Now, condensation, identity, presence, the past, the future, and the Ground. Although many of its constituent works were originally written as independent publications, this volume is not a collection or compilation of those texts. They have been reorganized, rewritten, connected, and in several cases conceptually corrected so that they function as parts of a single developing argument. The treatise proceeds in four movements. Part I establishes the ontological ground of the framework: the distinction between the Now and the present, actuality and becoming, condensation and succession, and the relation between the created order and the Ground that sustains it. Part II develops the three modes of temporal being. The past is understood as closed confluence and condensation; the present as actualized constitution at the Now; and the future as open reception and asymptotic horizon. Part III deliberately turns the topology against itself, auditing its assumptions in light of presentism, growing-block theory, branching-time semantics, the problem of truthmakers, and the relativity of simultaneity in special relativity. This audit results in a substantive revision of the earlier notion of a single universal Now: the Now is no longer treated as a shared cosmic temporal slice, but as the objective condition of actualization instantiated along each continuant's own history. oa:W7204207213.title: Navigating Taboos
oa:W7204207213.venue: The Proceedings of the International Conference on Social Sciences in the Modern Era.
oa:W7204207213.abstract: Abortion and pre-marital sex are highly sensitive topics and the decision-making process about these circumstances can be complex and influenced by various factors. This research aims to explore the factors shaping abortion and pre-marital sex decision making among Malaysian undergraduates and provide a deeper understanding of their lived experiences that can help the development of effective interventions, as well as improving access to accurate information and supportive resources. Specifically, the focus is on the influence of cultural and religious beliefs, access to information and resources, social stigma, and individual values. In a landscape like Malaysia, where premarital sex is generally considered unacceptable and the laglities around abortion is unclear, cultural and religious beliefs play a significant role in the decision-making process. Additionally, the research explores the effect of peers and individual values and beliefs on today’s youth while navigating through these decisions. The research findings highlight the need for improved sex education, access to accurate information, and a shift in cultural practices to create a more inclusive and informed society. By understanding the factors influencing decision-making and the challenges faced by Malaysian undergraduates, recommendations can be made for future improvements and support systems related to these sensitive topics.

oa:W7204207553.title: AI Machines vs the Non-Processing Minds of Classical Theism
oa:W7204207553.abstract: In the paper I contrast what I take to be a universal feature of all the AI research – namely focusing on processing information or transitions from one state of a machine to another – with the role assigned to non-processing minds in the classical theism framework. I briefly discuss the latter in epistemological context – the issue of inferential internalism and some problems of transparency, opacity, and trust. In this I show that the contrast between AI and the classical theism outlook is highly relevant for the cluster of issues relating to transparency or opacity, reliabilism, and trust, which is discussed today as the black-box problem. In particular, I identify in this context what I take to be the most serious aspect of the black-box problem; I reject the idea that the problem is a superficial one; and I claim that it poses basic limits on the AI research and cannot be solved along the lines of Explainable Artificial Intelligence.

This audit results in a substantive revision of the earlier notion of a single universal Now: the Now is no longer treated as a shared cosmic temporal slice, but as the objective condition of actualization instantiated along each continuant's own history. oa:W7204221334.title: Baysüngür Philosophical Views: Timeless Divine Knowledge, Human Freedom, and the Experience–Choice Cycle
oa:W7204221334.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204221334.abstract: This paper develops the Baysüngür Philosophical Views (BFG), a metaphysical framework concerning the relationship between divine foreknowledge, temporal human agency, and free will. The framework addresses the apparent tension between the claim that God possesses infallible and timeless knowledge of future events and the claim that human beings nevertheless make genuinely free choices. BFG distinguishes divine knowledge from causal coercion and argues that divine foreknowledge does not, by itself, constitute a causal explanation of human choice. Its central conceptual contribution is the Experience–Choice Cycle, represented as Ht → Dt → St → Ht+1, in which accumulated experience influences deliberation, deliberation leads to choice, and each choice contributes to the agent's subsequent experiential history. The framework further distinguishes decision-space possibility from counterfactual metaphysical possibility and examines the relationship between divine knowledge, causation, temporal ontology, alternative possibilities, and moral responsibility. BFG is compared with Boethian timelessness, classical theism, Islamic philosophical accounts of divine knowledge, compatibilism, incompatibilism, Frankfurt-style theories of responsibility, Molinism, and contemporary theories of time. The paper does not claim to provide a conclusively demonstrated solution to the problem of divine foreknowledge and free will. Rather, it presents BFG as a proposed metaphysical research program whose explanatory adequacy remains open to further analysis.

oa:W7204233254.title: Differences in Cultural Views on AI in Healthcare: A Call for Local Engagement
oa:W7204233254.abstract: The limited real-world adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare is often attributed not to technical performance, but to a poor fit with the cultural, social, and ethical contexts of diverse populations. This study investigates this gap by exploring how cultural determinants shape the acceptance and implementation of AI-driven technologies in healthcare. Using multi-source qualitative design approach that combines a global narrative review with an in-depth case study of the AIMIX project in Kenya, we identify key socio-cultural factors—such as religious beliefs, family structures, and community governance—that are critical for designing trustworthy AI. The findings from extensive stakeholder engagement, including 84 participants through interviews and workshops, demonstrate that local legitimacy, secured through community co-design and ethical partnership, is as crucial as technical accuracy for successful implementation. This research suggests that moving beyond Western-centric models—that prioritize individual autonomy and technocratic ethics—to develop context-aware, culturally grounded frameworks is essential for achieving equitable and effective AI in global healthcare.

oa:W7204233546.title: Moral Vigilance Before Heaven: Sindok and Moral Responsibility in Jeong Yak-yong’s Confucian Thought
oa:W7204233546.abstract: This article examines Jeong Yak-yong’s reinterpretation of sindok 愼獨 as moral responsibility before Heaven. It argues that hidden intention, Heaven’s scrutiny, admonition through the moral mind, human response, sincerity, and conduct form a single structure of responsibility. Comparison with Zhu Xi shows that Jeong does not discover an inward meaning of du 獨 absent from Neo-Confucianism. His distinctiveness lies in the personal and sovereign character given to Heaven and in the way Heaven’s admonition is mediated through the moral mind. Heaven is presented not as an abstract norm but as a spiritually lucid presence that sees hidden intention, commands and cautions, and is served with reverence; yet its demand becomes known within the agent and does not determine the response. This double structure exemplifies inner transcendence: moral authority exceeds the empirical self while becoming inwardly accessible in cultivation. The article thereby distinguishes Jeong’s account from secular moral self-regulation and from a modern notion of conscience. It also acknowledges possible Christian resonances without equating Sangje 上帝 with the Christian God or reducing Jeong’s argument to Catholic influence.

oa:W7204239730.title: RELIGION, LAW AND MORALITY IN PRECOLONIAL SOCIETY: EXAMPLE OF ANCIENT ILE-IFE KINGDOM IN YORUBALAND
oa:W7204239730.venue: AFRICAN JOURNAL OF RELIGION CULTURE AND SOCIETY 3141-4370
oa:W7204239730.abstract: Ile-Ife is one of the ancient towns in Yorubaland, southwestern Nigeria.The town is believed to be the cradle of Yoruba culture, civilisation,religious beliefs, and artistic craftsmanship. The town holds enormoussignificance in the cosmological explanations of Yoruba creation myths,which lend credence to the heroic deeds of Odùduwà, the progenitor ofthe Yoruba people. Evidence from oral traditions and ethnographicaccounts of Yoruba people's religious beliefs, social life, history, politicaldevelopment, and economic growth exemplifies the roles andcontributions of the Ife kingdom as an autonomous empire with distinctpolitical hegemony. However, little attention has been given to theadministration of law and morality in the precolonial milieu of the Ile-Ifekingdom. Utilising descriptive and historical content analysis of libraryresources and secondary sources, the findings revealed that during theprecolonial era, Yoruba culture and indigenous practices establishedstrong social mechanisms for communal morality and strict compliancewith indigenous law through several ritual practices. The paperconcludes that all forms of social problems and acts of indiscipline insociety today are the result of moral dereliction and a flagrant disregardfor native laws.

oa:W7204244375.title: Silence’s Paradox
oa:W7204244375.abstract: The following essay argues that Shūsaku Endō’s 1966 novel Silence, elucidates a corrective to pragmatist deliberative philosophy. First, it begins with the book’s protagonist Rodrigues in his eventual role evaluating banned Christian objects to prevent them from entering seventeenth century Japan. While these actions present a model of a dejected, apostate padre, they also model his silent acknowledgement of suffering. Second, Endō’s narrative does not aim to explain the suffering its characters experience. Instead, it draws its readers into a practical concern for what Ludwig Wittgenstein referred to as their form of life. Film adaptations highlight the challenges of interpreting religious examples by including artworks that defy easy apprehension. Third, throughout Silence the story navigates the gap between Rodrigues’s visceral suffering and divine silence. In so doing, it exemplifies Simone Weil’s notion of embodied affliction. To fully appreciate such experiences, Weil suggests that the scope of affliction must include divine silence. The desire for God arises in response. A similar contrast can be seen between the characters’ different dispositions towards keeping quiet. In sum, the essay contends that when immanent suffering is inevitable, practices of embodied silence can be the only way to speak.

oa:W7204271757.title: I See Nothing . . . Atheism as the Condition of Credible Theological Grammar
oa:W7204271757.abstract: How can theology maintain credibility when belief in God is optional? This article argues that atheism functions as the existential ground for credible theological grammar in post-Christendom contexts. Examining Tomáš Halík’s recuperation of atheism as ‘impatience with God’ and Emmanuel Falque’s phenomenological treatment of ‘seeing nothing’ as the fundamental human condition, I propose that experiential atheism constitutes theology’s methodological imperative. Grounded in incarnational logic, credible theology must begin with shared finitude rather than transcendent certainties.
