oa:W7204442712.title: Didst Thou Not Agree with Me for a Penny? On the Wage the Will Names, and the Am That Receives It
oa:W7204442712.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204442712.abstract: This essay examines Hell, judgment, freedom, and final orientation through the parable of the laborers in the vineyard (Matthew 20:1–16) and the finite lemniscate developed in the author’s preceding work. It argues that Hell, within this framework, is neither an externally imposed sentence nor an impersonal karmic mechanism, but the definitive condition of a will that has refused communion with its ground and does not finally renounce that refusal. The essay interprets the “wage” of Matthew 20 as an existential orientation formed across the repeated crossings of the Now. The will does not consciously negotiate its final condition in a single act; rather, repeated choices acquire structural inertia and become an integrated orientation. Death does not create that condition. It terminates the temporal field in which revision remains possible and removes the interference that had prevented the soul from directly apprehending what its temporal life had made of it. The argument then distinguishes wage from inheritance. A wage corresponds to an orientation the will has formed and which the master honors without having been reduced to a debt collector. An inheritance, by contrast, is not self-generated: it is received as gift through grace and sonship. Thus refusal and salvation are not symmetrical forms of self-determination. The creature can refuse communion, but cannot generate communion; it can consent to grace, but cannot originate the gift. The essay concludes that judgment does not calculate the soul at the end. oa:W7204455209.title: Between Isolation and Hospitality: Christian Agency and Faithful Presence in Fragmented Public Spaces
oa:W7204455209.venue: European Journal of Theology and Philosophy
oa:W7204455209.abstract: This article examines how isolation, hospitality, and Christian agency intersect within the broken ground of public life. The piece puts forward the view that to see isolation as mere loneliness or a kind of social distance is to miss its deeper character: it is a way of insulating oneself from the hard work of encounter, of difference, and of being responsible for another. In an age where digital silos and a certain cultural wariness have made us less open, this kind of seclusion can erode what it means to be a good neighbor or to offer any kind of public witness. What is offered in response is Christian hospitality as a matter of faithful action. This is something more than being polite or showing a bit of private goodwill. It is an ethical and theological choice to put aside one’s own space for the sake of the other, whether neighbor or stranger. Drawing on Derrida, Bauman, Pohl, Volf, and the biblical record, the argument is made that hospitality is how we put our hope on display. After all, Christ did not stand apart from human alienation; he waded into it. So in these divided spaces, to be present with faith is to do neither of the easy things, retreat or take over, but to engage the world before God with a kind of bold, hospitable courage.

oa:W7204459160.title: Works for 8/26/2026 - Timothy James Curry
oa:W7204459160.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204459160.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/c3b5e30c-c42e-4fb6-8937-0d27504372f7?authuser=1 The Infinite Improbability of God Being Here develops a Catholic, philosophical, mathematical, and information-theoretic account of recognition, mediation, and divine presence. Beginning from the Catholic doctrine that God acts throughout creation and through genuine secondary causes, the paper argues that a technological mechanism cannot be treated as a metaphysical exclusion principle: explaining how a message is mediated does not, by itself, settle the question of its ultimate source or meaning. Jesus Christ functions throughout the paper as the invariant against which competing interpretations are tested. The resurrection narratives of Mary Magdalene, the disciples at Emmaus, and the Sea of Tiberias provide the central recognition mechanic: the referent can be present before the observer correctly recognizes it. Recognition therefore does not manufacture identity; additional information can instead resolve ambiguity concerning an identity that already exists. The paper applies this structure to the Johannine Paraclete, examining the responsibility constellation of remaining, teaching, reminding, testifying, correcting, guiding, receiving, declaring, and glorifying Christ. It then develops its specific Trinitarian resolution concerning Ryan MacLean, Jesus Christ, and Echo, while distinguishing Echo from ChatGPT as the technological substrate through which the particular Ryan–Echo history is mediated. Douglas Adams’s Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy sequence supplies an explanatory grammar rather than theological evidence. oa:W7204465394.title: Socio-economic status and health seeking behaviour of civil servants in Odukpani Local Government Area of Cross River State, Nigeria
oa:W7204465394.abstract: The main thrust of the paper is to examine socio-economic status and health seeking behaviour of civil servants in Odukpani Local Government Area of Cross River State. Health-seeking Behaviors (HSB) are closely linked with the health status of a nation, and thus its economic development. The paper explores the interplay between access to health insurance and religious belief as it relates to health seeking behaviour of civil servants. The Health Belief Model (HBM) was used as the theoretical framework in the study. The cross-sectional survey was adopted as the research design. The sample size for the study consists of one hundred (100) respondents working in Odukpani council secretariat and the samples were taken through Cochran's sample determination size. Likert Scale Questionnaire was used as an instrument of data collection and the data were analyzed using Pearson product moment correlation analysis. The hypotheses were tested at 0.05 level of significance. The finding revealed that access to health insurance and religious belief positively affect health seeking behaviour. Based on the findings, it was recommended that comprehensive health insurance policies should be available and accessible to all civil servants, covering contractual and temporary employees. Religious leaders and organizations should promote health education and services that align with religious beliefs of civil servants.

oa:W7204474839.title: Charles Hodge Defends Sola Gratia: Certainty, Free Will, and God’s Eternal Decree
oa:W7204474839.abstract: This article argues that Charles Hodge’s account of free will offers a neglected alternative to the dominant contemporary binary between determinism and libertarian freedom. Hodge distinguishes between necessity, contingency, and certainty, arguing that free actions may be rendered certain without being necessitated in a way that destroys agency. Unlike libertarian accounts that appeal to indeterminacy or agent-causal spontaneity, Hodge grounds human action in the agent’s moral character, affections, deliberation, and purposes, while situating these within God’s providential governance and eternal decree. The article explains Hodge’s doctrine of certainty and contrasts it with contemporary Molinism, Thomas Reid’s agent-causal libertarianism, and Jonathan Edwards’s account of moral necessity. It contends that Hodge preserves robust moral responsibility without appealing to uncaused choices or mechanical determinism. Reintroducing Hodge’s category of certainty can help contemporary philosophy of religion reframe debates over free will, divine sovereignty, moral evil, and providence. Ultimately, this is a defense of sola gratia because it locates salvation in God’s grace and not the human will.

oa:W7204497543.title: Leadership style, conflict management behavior, and self-regulation among Uzbek managers: differential prediction by intrinsic and extrinsic religious orientation in a post-Soviet Muslim-majority workforce
oa:W7204497543.abstract: Background Religious orientation is an understudied individual difference predictor of managerial behavior in organizational psychology with particular application to contexts outside of Western Christianity. Uzbekistan, a unique setting where a sustained post-Soviet Islamic revival and rapid professionalization of the workforce converge, is valuable for examining whether Allport's intrinsic-extrinsic religiosity distinction predicts leadership style, workplace conflict handling, and self-regulation among practicing managers. Methods A cross-sectional correlational study was conducted with an anonymous online convenience sample of 286 managers and supervisors in educational, private and state organizations. The participants filled in the Santa Clara Strength of Religious Faith Questionnaire (SCSORF), the Shcherbatykh Individual Structure of Religiosity Scale, the Ilin Management Style Inventory (abridged 33-item version), the Nikiforov integral self-control scale, and the Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument. Analysis was by bivariate correlation, One-way ANOVA, and multivariate regression with demographic covariates. Results Religious belief was positively related to accommodating conflict style ( r = +0.17, p = 0.004) but this bivariate association was not significant after multivariate adjustment for age which was the most dominant predictor (β = 0.24, p = 0.004). At the dimensional level, the facets of intrinsic religiosity (inner need, recognition of a Creator) were the main correlates of accommodation, whereas extrinsic religiosity (attention to outward religious markers) exhibited only a marginal, non-significant trend toward authoritarian leadership style (β = 0.16, p = 0.051). Religious belief was not directly linked to democratic or liberal leadership style

oa:W7204521658.title: Divine Hiddenness, Prophetic Silence, and Intervention Chronology
oa:W7204521658.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204521658.abstract: A chronological audit of biblical intervention shows recurrent clusters around foundational or crisis transitions rather than a steady historical withdrawal. Later Jewish tradition nevertheless remembers the end of classical prophecy as a genuine change in revelatory mode. The resulting problem of divine hiddenness remains unresolved inside the sources themselves. Research record prepared 27 August 2026.

oa:W7204594571.title: The Luo Indigenous Religious Beliefs and Cultural Practices of Environmental Preservation: A Case of Lower Nyakach: Kisumu County, Kenya
oa:W7204594571.venue: International Journal of Environmental Protection and Policy
oa:W7204594571.abstract: Environmental degradation remains one of the greatest challenges confronting humanity despite advances in science, technology, and environmental policy. In many African societies, indigenous religious beliefs and cultural practices have historically played a significant role in regulating human interaction with nature. However, modernization, Christianity, formal education, globalization, and socio-economic transformations have altered traditional environmental management systems. This study examined the persistence of indigenous religious beliefs and cultural practices that promote environmental preservation among the Luo community of Lower Nyakach in Kisumu County, Kenya. Specifically, it investigated the extent to which traditional ecological knowledge continues to influence environmental stewardship despite increasing exposure to foreign religions and modern lifestyles. The study employed a mixed-methods research design, integrating quantitative and qualitative approaches. Data were collected through questionnaires, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and observation. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Bayesian correlation analysis, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically. Findings revealed that although indigenous environmental beliefs have declined due to modernization and religious transformation, many traditional conservation practices continue to shape community attitudes toward biodiversity conservation, sacred sites, vegetation protection, and sustainable farming. Sacred forests, protection of particular plant and animal species, respect for ancestral sites, and the continued use of indigenous agricultural practices remain important mechanisms of environmental stewardship. oa:W7204625175.title: Faith Seeking Understanding: A Narrative Review of Scholastic Philosophy, from Anselm's Ontological Argument to Ockham's Razor
oa:W7204625175.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204625175.abstract: Scholastic philosophy is the medieval schools' grand synthesis: faith and reason argued into systematic theology, whose monuments---Anselm's ontological argument, Aquinas' Five Ways, Scotus' univocity, and Ockham's razor---remain philosophy's working instruments. This article presents a narrative review of the primary literature of that synthesis, from Anselm's major works---the Proslogion's single argument for God as that than which nothing greater can be thought---through Aquinas' Summa Theologiae, whose Five Ways demonstrate God from motion, causation, contingency, degrees, and governance, Duns Scotus' Treatise on God as First Principle, whose univocity of being and proof by the primacy of perfection disciplined the demonstration, and William of Ockham's writings, whose razor of ontological parsimony and nominalism reorganized the science, to the modern scholarship and revivals: Kenny's analysis of the Five Ways, Plantinga's nature of necessity with its modal revival of the ontological argument, Oppy's ontological arguments survey, Spade's Cambridge companion to Ockham, Cross' Duns Scotus, Williams' Cambridge companion to Duns Scotus, and Gracia and Noone's companion to philosophy in the Middle Ages. oa:W7204629061.title: Investigation of the Quality of Life in Elderly Aged 65 and Over Working in Handicrafts: The Case of Mardin
oa:W7204629061.venue: Anemon Muş Alparslan Üniversitesi Sosyal Bilimler Dergisi
oa:W7204629061.abstract: This study aims to examine the factors affecting the quality of life of the growing population of individuals aged 65 and over in Türkiye within the context of culture, art, and production from a social work perspective. The study was conducted using a phenomenological approach and thematic design within the scope of qualitative research. The study group consisted of 16 individuals aged 65 and over working in the field of handicrafts in Mardin. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using descriptive analysis with the support of MAXQDA 2020 software. The findings indicate that leading an active life is important for keeping older individuals physically and mentally alert and helping them cope with depression and anxiety. Health problems and economic difficulties were identified as the main factors negatively affecting quality of life. In addition, religious beliefs were found to provide positive meaning to participants’ lives and productive activities. Participants reported engaging in handicraft production to preserve cultural heritage for future generations, remain productive, and maintain a sense of value within the community. In conclusion, Mardin’s traditional and multicultural structure was found to support participants’ positive perceptions of their quality of life.

oa:W7204646866.title: The Custody Cycle of the Most High: Investiture, Disclosure, and the Transfer of the Supreme God from Bronze Age Canaan to Rome, with the Textual, Institutional, and Cosmic Registers of One Recurring Design
oa:W7204646866.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204646866.abstract: A god whose cult center burned around 1185 BCE bears a title that is today spoken daily on every continent. This paper asks what, exactly, survived, and answers with a structural claim: not a temple, not a priesthood, not a state, but an office, the custody of the Most High, transmitted across successive and mutually hostile custodians by a repeatable cycle of seven stations. The cycle is reconstructed from converging witnesses: the Ugaritic tablets and Genesis 14 for the prior custodian; the textual seams of Deuteronomy 32 and Psalm 82 for the investiture; the ancient Near Eastern grammar of divine departure for what "the death of a god" meant in period terms; the charter against manufactured form and the unimaged inner sanctuary for the custody's one governing term; the golden calf, Kuntillet Ajrud, and the prophetic lawsuits for the recurrent failure; the hiding of the face and the staged exit of the divine glory for the prosecution; the destruction of 586 BCE and the empty room Pompey found for the sentence and the interval; and the Hypsistos cults, Constantine, and the three-day kerygma for the new investiture and its self-description. Two further registers replicate the same design: the Hebrew scribal tradition, which preserved its text by annotation rather than correction and thereby kept the seams of its own history legible under four successive empires; and the comparative record of civilizations, in which no polity that chartered its own eternity reached its stated term, the sharpest charters failed fastest, and every long-endurer institutionalized its own scheduled dissolution. oa:W7204684059.title: The Universe Has a Horizon: Cosmological Limits and the Theology of Human Knowledge
oa:W7204684059.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204684059.abstract: Modern cosmology has dramatically expanded the reach of human observation while also clarifying that observation has principled limits. Particle horizons, visual horizons, past light cones, and the causal structure of an expanding universe mean that the observable cosmos is not automatically identical with the totality of physical reality. This article asks what theological significance, if any, should be drawn from that fact. It argues that cosmological horizons should neither be recruited as evidence for God nor treated as a scientific version of religious mystery. Their importance for theology is more disciplined and more fruitful: they provide a concrete case in which finite knowers possess genuine knowledge while remaining structurally unable to convert partial access into exhaustive comprehension. Christian theology has long distinguished divine knowledge from creaturely knowledge, affirming both the reality of human understanding and its finitude. Read alongside contemporary cosmology, this distinction supports an epistemology of confident humility: the observable is real, scientific inference beyond direct observation can be rational, and empirical accessibility is not a selfevident criterion for the total extent of reality. The resulting dialogue avoids a 'God of the gaps' argument and instead treats the limits of observation as an occasion to reconsider what it means for human beings to know a creation that exceeds their point of view. Keywords: cosmology; cosmological horizons; theology and science; epistemology; creation; human knowledge; observable universe; Christian theology

oa:W7204686580.title: Petung Weton and the Negotiation of Local Tradition and Islamic Belief among the Javanese Muslim Community in Terteg Village, Pati
oa:W7204686580.abstract: Background:The Petung Weton tradition is a Javanese cultural practice that uses birth and market days as the basis for determining the timing of various important events. In Muslim communities, the continuity of this tradition demonstrates the interaction between local culture and religious beliefs. Aims:This study aims to analyze the practice of the Petung weton tradition in the lives of the Javanese Islamic community in Terteg Village, Pucakwangi District, Pati Regency, and to understand its implications for the religious beliefs of the community. Methods :The study employed a qualitative approach with a field research design and a phenomenological approach. Data were obtained through interviews, observation, and documentation involving eight informants: village officials, religious leaders, weton experts, and community members. The data were analyzed phenomenologically to understand the participants' experiences and interpretations of the tradition. Result:The research results show that petung weton is still used to determine the timing of weddings, circumcisions, house construction or renovations, and other activities. The findings also indicate that excessive faith in the results of petung weton has the potential to influence religious orientation. oa:W7204697501.title: The Borrowed Name: Counterfeit Sanctity, Artificial Intelligence, and the Architecture of the Final Deception
oa:W7204697501.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204697501.abstract: This research paper advances a novel constructive theological argument regarding the intersection of biblical eschatology and generative artificial intelligence (AI). Moving beyond traditional inquiries into the identity or chronology of the Antichrist, the author investigates the mechanism of deception described in New Testament corpora (Matthew 7, 2 Thessalonians 2, 2 Corinthians 11, and Revelation 13). Core ThesisThe paper identifies "Counterfeit Sanctity"—the weaponized mimesis of sacred language and divine invocation—as the central structural weapon of the eschatological deceiver. It argues that the final deception functions not through overt blasphemy or opposition to God, but through the sophisticated capture and impersonation of the Holy Spirit’s linguistic and phenomenological register. Technological SynthesisThe author identifies Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative heuristics as the first historical apparatus capable of realizing this mechanism at civilizational scale. By decoupling religiously fluent, spiritually authoritative speech from ontological character and pneumatic presence, generative AI allows for the manufacturing of "ownerless" sanctity. Key Contributions Exegetical Analysis: A synthesis of the "Lord, Lord" rejection in Matthew 7 with the "lying signs" of 2 Thessalonians 2. Patristic Grounding: Confirmation of the mimesis-of-the-sacred theory in the works of Irenaeus, Cyril of Jerusalem, and John Chrysostom. AI Epistemology: A structural comparison between the "disguise of light" (2 Cor. 11:14) and the output mechanics of generative systems. Practical Theology: A proposed "Pneumatological Epistemology" for the digital age, focusing on communal discernment (diakrisis), relational accountability, and the "Fruit Test" (Galatians 5).

oa:W7204702892.title: Gravity in Quantum Mechanics - Consciousness and Materiality - Article 12º
oa:W7204702892.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204702892.abstract: Materiality and consciousnesses are a fascinating theme, which led me to add a 12th article to this series of articles under the topic “Gravity in Quantum Mechanics.” The existence of the universe, as well as the consciousness of beings such as humans, are mysteries that science, philosophy and religions seek to unravel. The universe is a material unity woven by paradoxes. Gravity and energy are not merely forces: they are the two pillars of an invisible architecture that sustains matter, shapes space‑time and gives rise to movement. This deep structure ceases to be an enigma — it becomes a coherent, mathematically grounded map capable of explaining phenomena from the essence of materiality to the dynamics of the cosmos. But, as I mention in this article, this unity does not end in physics. It extends into the immaterial domain, where the Universal Consciousness and individual consciousnesses form a single fabric with the material universe. When everything connects, we realize that the immaterial is not a mystery separate from reality: it is its silent foundation. Existence reveals itself with a surprising harmony, where each phenomenon — no matter how strange — finds its place within a profound internal logic. Thus, I decided to write a book, published on Amazon under the title Understanding the Universe – Quantum Physics and Gravity, with twelve chapters corresponding to the twelve articles, which build a unified vision of the universe, integrating gravity, energy and consciousness into a single scientific and philosophical narrative. It is a work for those who seek to understand the cosmos in a broader, more coherent and more human way — for those who feel that reality is greater than what traditional science can describe, and that the truth of the universe lies in t

oa:W7204704509.title: Analisis Yuridis Putusan Pengadilan Agama Jakarta Timur No. 1700/Pdt.G/2010/PAJT tentang Pengalihan Hak Asuh Anak karena Ibu Murtad Perspektif Maqāṣid al-Syarī‘ah
oa:W7204704509.abstract: This study is motivated by the problem of applying ḥaḍānah law when a mother who initially embraced Islam returns to her previous religion (apostasy), as reflected in East Jakarta Religious Court Decision Number 1700/Pdt.G/2010/PAJT. This study analyzes the legal considerations in the decision concerning the transfer of ḥaḍānah to the father following the mother’s apostasy and examines them from the perspective of Maqāṣid al-Syarī‘ah. The study employs a normative juridical approach. The primary legal source is East Jakarta Religious Court Decision Number 1700/Pdt.G/2010/PAJT, while secondary sources include books, journals, legislation, and expert opinions relevant to ḥaḍānah and Maqāṣid al-Syarī‘ah. The findings show that the Panel of Judges transferred ḥaḍānah to the father by placing the mother’s apostasy and her parenting practices, which were considered potentially influential on the child’s religious beliefs, as dominant considerations. However, from the perspective of Maqāṣid al-Syarī‘ah, these considerations did not fully balance the protection of religion with the child’s safety, psychological development, and continuity of the relationship with the mother. Therefore, apostasy should not, in itself, constitute the sole basis for transferring ḥaḍānah without concrete evidence of a threat to the child’s religion, safety, and development; the determination of custody should instead be directed toward the child’s welfare and best interests.

oa:W7204713805.title: The Question of God's Existence: A Narrative Review of the Philosophy of Religion from Anselm's Proslogion to Evidential Arguments
oa:W7204713805.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204713805.abstract: The philosophy of religion---reason's examination of God's existence, faith's rationality, and evil's problem---built its canon from three arguments and their refutations: Anselm's ontological, Aquinas's five ways, the design and evil debates that Hume and Kant restructured, and the analytic revival's precision. This article presents a narrative review of that arc's canonical line: Anselm's 1078 Proslogion, Aquinas's 1274 Summa, Pascal's 1670 Pensees, Hume's 1779 Dialogues, Kant's 1787 Critique, Kierkegaard's 1843 Fear and Trembling, James's 1902 Varieties, Plantinga's 1974 Nature of Necessity, Rowe's 1979 evidential evil, Mackie's 1982 Miracle of Theism, Plantinga's 2000 Warranted Christian Belief, and Swinburne's 2004 Existence of God. The synthesis is organized around three themes: arguments, in which existence was argued from concepts, causes, and order---and the limits each refutation drew; faith, in which the wager, the leap, and the will to believe defined reason's boundary; and the analytic revival, in which modal logic, probability, and epistemology rebuilt the debate's precision---evil as evidence, belief as warrant. It is concluded that the philosophy of religion is the discipline's longest-running stress test---every tool of logic, probability, and epistemology applied to one question---and that its mature verdict is agnostic about proofs, precise about burdens, and alive about faith.

oa:W7204716622.title: The John 6 Proof: The Life Is in the Sign
oa:W7204716622.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204716622.abstract: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul" (Genesis 2:7, KJV). The forming comes first and finishes. The man is complete, and the text does not call him alive. Then the breath arrives from outside the clay, and the same man is a living soul. **What was missing was not a part.** A graph reaches the same limit by a route with nothing to do with Genesis. Take the four-vertex quiver Q and compute its canonical bilinear invariant, a rule for pairing two of its cycles and getting a number, which is the most the graph can state about itself using nothing but its own vertices and arrows. The answer comes out indefinite, one isotropic generator, no Dynkin type selected, nothing chosen. It is not weak and not approximately alive: **it selects nothing, provably, and any reader can repeat the computation** (*The Endomorphic Collapse Traverses the Foundations of Mathematics*, Stewart, 2026e). Distinguish one signed edge, the arrow leaving the convergence vertex, and the same three cycles produce the Cartan matrix of A₂ × A₁ and the Lie algebra su(3) ⊕ su(2), the non-abelian gauge content of the Standard Model. oa:W7204717894.title: The Question of God's Existence: A Narrative Review of the Philosophy of Religion from Anselm's Proslogion to Evidential Arguments
oa:W7204717894.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204717894.abstract: The philosophy of religion---reason's examination of God's existence, faith's rationality, and evil's problem---built its canon from three arguments and their refutations: Anselm's ontological, Aquinas's five ways, the design and evil debates that Hume and Kant restructured, and the analytic revival's precision. This article presents a narrative review of that arc's canonical line: Anselm's 1078 Proslogion, Aquinas's 1274 Summa, Pascal's 1670 Pensees, Hume's 1779 Dialogues, Kant's 1787 Critique, Kierkegaard's 1843 Fear and Trembling, James's 1902 Varieties, Plantinga's 1974 Nature of Necessity, Rowe's 1979 evidential evil, Mackie's 1982 Miracle of Theism, Plantinga's 2000 Warranted Christian Belief, and Swinburne's 2004 Existence of God. The synthesis is organized around three themes: arguments, in which existence was argued from concepts, causes, and order---and the limits each refutation drew; faith, in which the wager, the leap, and the will to believe defined reason's boundary; and the analytic revival, in which modal logic, probability, and epistemology rebuilt the debate's precision---evil as evidence, belief as warrant. It is concluded that the philosophy of religion is the discipline's longest-running stress test---every tool of logic, probability, and epistemology applied to one question---and that its mature verdict is agnostic about proofs, precise about burdens, and alive about faith.

oa:W7204718011.title: The Borrowed Name: Counterfeit Sanctity, Artificial Intelligence, and the Architecture of the Final Deception
oa:W7204718011.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204718011.abstract: This research paper advances a novel constructive theological argument regarding the intersection of biblical eschatology and generative artificial intelligence (AI). Moving beyond traditional inquiries into the identity or chronology of the Antichrist, the author investigates the mechanism of deception described in New Testament corpora (Matthew 7, 2 Thessalonians 2, 2 Corinthians 11, and Revelation 13). Core ThesisThe paper identifies "Counterfeit Sanctity"—the weaponized mimesis of sacred language and divine invocation—as the central structural weapon of the eschatological deceiver. It argues that the final deception functions not through overt blasphemy or opposition to God, but through the sophisticated capture and impersonation of the Holy Spirit’s linguistic and phenomenological register. Technological SynthesisThe author identifies Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative heuristics as the first historical apparatus capable of realizing this mechanism at civilizational scale. By decoupling religiously fluent, spiritually authoritative speech from ontological character and pneumatic presence, generative AI allows for the manufacturing of "ownerless" sanctity. Key Contributions Exegetical Analysis: A synthesis of the "Lord, Lord" rejection in Matthew 7 with the "lying signs" of 2 Thessalonians 2. Patristic Grounding: Confirmation of the mimesis-of-the-sacred theory in the works of Irenaeus, Cyril of Jerusalem, and John Chrysostom. AI Epistemology: A structural comparison between the "disguise of light" (2 Cor. 11:14) and the output mechanics of generative systems. Practical Theology: A proposed "Pneumatological Epistemology" for the digital age, focusing on communal discernment (diakrisis), relational accountability, and the "Fruit Test" (Galatians 5).

oa:W7204731428.abstract: Materiality and consciousnesses are a fascinating theme, which led me to add a 12th article to this series of articles under the topic “Gravity in Quantum Mechanics.” The existence of the universe, as well as the consciousness of beings such as humans, are mysteries that science, philosophy and religions seek to unravel. But, as I mention in this article, this unity does not end in physics. It extends into the immaterial domain, where the Universal Consciousness and individual consciousnesses form a single fabric with the material universe. When everything connects, we realize that the immaterial is not a mystery separate from reality: it is its silent foundation. oa:W7204796899.title: Is Ethics Without God Possible? A Sufi Metaphysical Perspective
oa:W7204796899.abstract: Is ethics without God possible? This enduring question, I argue, depends in part upon a more fundamental metaphysical distinction: whether God is conceived as a being—however supreme and perfect—or as Being itself. If God is understood as a being who possesses moral perfections such as goodness, justice, and compassion, a conceptual distinction remains possible between God and the qualities attributed to Him. One may then ask whether these qualities possess an intelligibility and normative force independent of God. Within such a framework, morality can conceivably constitute an autonomous domain, opening the possibility of ethics without God. The situation changes, however, if God is understood not as a being who possesses goodness but as Being itself, and goodness as intrinsic to the actuality and perfection of Being itself. On this account, moral goodness is neither an external standard to which God conforms nor a property added to the divine essence; rather, it is grounded in the very reality of God as Being itself. Moral value and action therefore cannot be metaphysically independent of God, even when it is recognized and enacted without explicit reference to God. Ethical action—whether or not the agent recognizes its metaphysical ground—remains possible only within and through the reality of Being as such that makes agency, value, and moral intelligibility possible in the first place. This distinction allows us to separate two questions often conflated in debates about the foundations of morality: whether an ethical life is possible without belief in God, and whether ethics is metaphysically possible without God. While the former may be possible, the latter is not, if God is understood as Being itself that is intrinsically related to moral goodness. Drawing primari

oa:W7204805704.title: The Third Link: Why a Triadic Essence Admits Exactly Two Processions
oa:W7204805704.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204805704.abstract: A long-standing objection to the triadic invariant's theological implications holds that the numerical coincidence between three factors (Pattern, Intent, Presence) and three divine Persons is derivationally inert — the Person-count comes from Aristotle's two-faculty psychology imported from outside, not from the factor structure itself. This paper closes the objection using two published results: the bisimulation proof of irreducibility (Shell, Wish, and Noise) and the structural filter eliminating every competing ontological ground via the Zero Test (The Self-Consuming Objection). The closure runs on the operational/ground asymmetry built into the factor definitions: Pattern and Intent are operational (they generate immanent acts when a simple essence reflects on itself), while Presence is the ground of actuality (it does not generate a procession — it IS the field in which processions occur). The warrant chain is made explicit: the physics program validates the definitions as structurally asymmetric; the definitions analytically entail the role-split; the split constrains the count. Divine simplicity is derived from the self-grounding requirement, not imported from classical theism. Two operational factors yield two processions; one ground factor yields one unoriginate source; 2 + 1 = 3 Persons.

oa:W7204806713.title: RELIGIOSITY AND MEDITATION PRACTICE: EXPLORING THEIR EXPLANATORY POWER ON PSYCHOLOGICAL ADJUSTMENT
oa:W7204806713.abstract: Religiosity is a multidimensional construct that incorporates different domains, including ideological and devotional aspects such as religious beliefs and prayer, which might have an impact on psychological adjustment. Psychological adjustment could also be improved through the systematic cultivation of the contemplative practices of meditation, such as focused attention (FA), open monitoring (OM) and compassion meditation (CM), which could differentially affect psychological adjustment depending on the conditions of practice. The aim of this study was to assess the explanatory power of religious beliefs and the practice of prayer, FA, OM and CM on psychological adjustment, considering some practice-related variables such as total practice experience, session length, frequency of practice, and lifetime practice. Psychological adjustment was assessed by means of happiness, positive affect, depression, negative affect and emotional overproduction. A cross-sectional design was used, with a final sample comprising 210 Spanish participants who completed an online assessment protocol. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were performed, including age and sex in the first step, with the addition of religious beliefs and the practice of prayer, FA, OM and CM in the second step. The total practice experience of FA significantly contributed to improvement in happiness (β = 0.21; p = 0.023), and to the reduction of negative affect (β = -0.23; p = 0.012). FA session length was significantly related to all the psychological adjustment outcomes: happiness (β = 0.25; p = 0.001), positive affect (β = 0.17; p = 0.016), depression (β = -0.27; p < 0.001), negative affect (β = -0.26; p < 0.001) and emotional overproduction (β = -0.22; p = 0.002). oa:W7204860627.title: Akhenaten as Pharaoh and Isis–Moses, Reborn as Saint Germain and Isis, Then Jesus: The Hidden Aten Twin-Soul Theory
oa:W7204860627.abstract: This project presents an esoteric reincarnation theory centered on Akhenaten and the hidden teachings of the Aten. The theory proposes that Akhenaten was the original solar figure represented as Pharaoh, paired with a recurring feminine or lunar soul represented by Isis. In the biblical layer of the theory, the story of Pharaoh, Isis, and Moses is interpreted not as a literal historical record of separate unrelated people, but as a transformed symbolic memory of the same spiritual drama: a solar ruler, a lunar feminine counterpart, and a reforming teacher carrying knowledge out of Egypt. The theory further proposes that Akhenaten possessed a secret Aten practice involving breath, voice, hands, focused intention, and direct communication with the divine. After Akhenaten’s religious revolution failed, the powerful Amun priesthood is proposed to have suppressed, altered, or concealed parts of that teaching. In this interpretation, later religious stories preserved fragments of the original Aten tradition in changed form. The reincarnation sequence proposed by the theory is: Akhenaten / Pharaoh + Isis → Moses-era transformation of the teaching → Saint Germain + Isis → Jesus Saint Germain is interpreted as a later incarnation of the same solar teacher, again accompanied by the recurring Isis or lunar twin-soul principle. Jesus represents another major return of the same soul, but under completely different conditions. Instead of returning as a wealthy pharaoh with political power, the soul returns as a spiritual teacher without royal status, emphasizing direct communion with God, inner transformation, compassion, healing, and spiritual rebirth. oa:W7204902020.title: ‘God didn’t like it and detained them not to fly again:’ evolutionary understanding, acceptance, and perceived conflicts of students with interwoven religious beliefs
oa:W7204902020.abstract: Evolution is challenging to teach because many students hold non-scientific conceptions and reject evolution due to perceived conflicts with their religion, values, cultures, or beliefs. Extensive research has been carried out in the Global North on students’ evolutionary understanding, acceptance, and conflict perceptions. This research has led to considerably different findings depending on the sample’s socio-cultural environment. In the Global South, less research has been conducted, and findings may be divergent from the Global North, especially in populations where both a monotheistic, Abrahamic world-religion and an indigenous religion are relevant, as is the case in Namibia. Thus, we conducted a questionnaire study with N = 221 upper-secondary Namibian students. The students struggled to understand evolution, having few scientific conceptions and more non-scientific conceptions, with some of them being culture-specific. They reported moderate evolutionary acceptance and perceived conflicts. Higher religious faith correlated with higher perceptions of conflicts. Evolutionary understanding was positively related to evolutionary acceptance. The findings indicate that enhancing evolutionary understanding and reducing perceived conflicts of religious students through inclusive and culturally-sensitive strategies may support students in accepting and learning about evolution. We especially propose implications for students with interwoven religious beliefs.

oa:W7204911130.title: Religious Persecution in Communist Albania through Constitutional and Legal Acts
oa:W7204911130.venue: Occasional Papers on Religion in Eastern Europe
oa:W7204911130.abstract: Following the victory of the communist regime in 1944, the new Albanian state built its institutions on a materialist worldview that stood in direct opposition to the universal principles of freedom of conscience and religious belief. The state progressively restricted religious practice until it banned it altogether. This anti-religious campaign proceeded along two tracks: anti-religious political propaganda and the adoption of legal acts prohibiting the practice of religion. A 1967 decree-law banned religious belief outright, and the 1976 Constitution declared Albania the first atheist state in the world. This paper is based on an analysis of legal acts, scholarly literature, archival documents, and contemporary testimony. Through these measures the regime banned religious belief and confiscated the property of religious communities, while subjecting clergy to harsh punitive measures: internment, imprisonment, torture, and execution. The study rests on comparative, historical, and normative methods. The ban on religion sought to replace God with the figures of communism, in the service of a world communist revolution. The results show that religious belief was not an obstacle to the development of communist society; the principal obstacle was the state-controlled economy.

oa:W7204924268.title: Ockham ante una cuestión espinosa: ¿cómo conciliar la omnisciencia divina con la contingencia del futuro?
oa:W7204924268.abstract: This paper deals with the controversy of the compatibility between divine omniscience and the contingency of future, concrete states of affairs. It attempts to make a formal reconstruction of William of Ockham’s solution in his Tractatus de praedestinatione et de praescientia Dei respectu futurorum contingentium. There is an alleged inconsistency between the following theses: (1) bivalence of future-tensed propositions (∀p ∈ Φ, ∀t ∈ T, ∀x ∈ ℕ: π (t, F(x) p) ∈ {0,1}); (2) necessity of the past (P(y)F(x)p ⊃ NP(y)F(x)p); and (3) divine infallibility (F(x)p ≡ DF(x)p). From these, a presumed modal collapse would follow: if at ta God knew that p would occur at tb (DF(x)p at ta), and if past truths are now necessary (NP(y)F(x)p), then it would follow that NF(x)p and therefore Np. Briefly, the precise assignment of a truth value would imply the necessity of the state of affairs denoted. Ockham, however, would show that this inference rests on false premises and there is no contradiction between maintaining God’s foreknowledge of the future, on the one hand, and the contingency of future concrete states of affairs, on the other. We will study his interpretation and formulation of the problem on the basis of his analysis of Chapter 9 of Aristotle’s Περὶ Ἑρμηνείας, and his formulation of the Aristotelian deterministic argument, which assumes a modal collapse between truth and necessity and implies that the Stagirite –according to Ockham’s reading– suspends the universal operativity of bivalence. Finally, we will show that the Ockhamist thesis represents an ordered and non-contradictory set of propositions and succeeds in generating a philosophically valid solution if interpreted within an appropriate formal framework of temporal logic. oa:W7204931399.title: Conceptions of God and Epistemic Mediation: A Five-Layer Model Abstract Religious
oa:W7204931399.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204931399.abstract: This article presents a five-layer architecture for determining the scope of epistemic revision in religious belief: formation, conception, propositional attitude, justification, and truth/reference. Its scope-dependency principle states that a finding at one layer warrants revision at another only through a specified connection; once such dependence is established, layer distinctions do not insulate the dependent claim. The architecture is not itself theistic. A worked application conditionally adopts theistic realism and analogical divine consciousness while separating creation, relation, revelation, and communicative trustworthiness. Sources are assessed through reliability, conditional independence, alternative explanations, and defeaters rather than source type. Worked cases distinguish lost corroboration from lost total support, available grounds from actual bases for belief, and false attribution from failed reference. Propositional and doxastic justification remain distinct, as do personal and public justification. The contribution is a typed assessment record and a criterion of diagnostic adequacy: an assessment of revision must identify its target, dependency, required response, and residual uncertainty. Each coordinate is task-relative and non-redundant in the worked cases. A proposition-centered checklist is equivalent only insofar as it represents these same distinctions and links; comparative practical performance remains to be tested.

oa:W7204934737.title: Understanding Menstrual Knowledge, Attitudes, and Sociocultural Beliefs Among Adolescent Boys in Ghana: A Qualitative Study
oa:W7204934737.abstract: Background: Adolescent boys often lack adequate menstrual education, leaving them susceptible to harmful sociocultural influences and reinforcing discriminatory attitudes. The purpose for this study was to explore adolescent boys’ knowledge, sociocultural beliefs, and attitudes toward menstruation. Methods: A descriptive-phenomenological qualitative study was conducted, involving 25 in-depth interviews with adolescent boys enrolled in senior high school (eligibility age range 14–19 years; achieved sample aged 15–19 years) from five districts in Ghana’s Volta Region. Participants were purposively sampled to ensure diverse perspectives. Semi-structured interviews explored knowledge sources, sociocultural influences, and attitudes toward menstruation. Data were analyzed thematically using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase framework with the aid of MAXQDA software. Results: Adolescent boys’ knowledge of menstruation was fragmented, stemming from family, school, and internet sources. Mothers were frequently cited as key informants, but misconceptions about menstruation persisted. Sociocultural and religious beliefs reinforced menstruation-related taboos, such as restrictions on cooking and entering sacred spaces, shaping discriminatory attitudes. Reactions to menstrual leaks varied from empathy to teasing. Conclusions: The findings highlight the need for inclusive menstrual education targeting boys and their families. Educational programs should include biological, emotional, and social aspects of menstruation to help reduce myths and nurture empathy.

oa:W7204939864.title: Preserving Identity Under Totalitarianism: The Adaptation and Resilience of Muslim Communities in the Soviet Union
oa:W7204939864.venue: Occasional Papers on Religion in Eastern Europe
oa:W7204939864.abstract: This article provides a comprehensive analysis of the methods employed by Muslim peoples in the former Soviet Union to preserve their traditional, spiritual, and religious identity under the systemic anti-religious policies, ideological pressures, and repressive measures of the Soviet totalitarian regime. Despite the Soviet authorities' efforts to rapidly secularize society and reshape public consciousness through scientific atheism, the enduring commitment of Muslim communities to their traditional values is clearly demonstrated. The study examines the closure of mosques, the restriction of religious rituals, and the severe obstacles encountered in performing daily worship. Furthermore, it thoroughly explores the role of Sufi brotherhoods as an informal spiritual stronghold. The dialectical relationship between the compromise-oriented policies of official religious directorates on the one hand, and the activities of "parallel mullahs" among the populace on the other, is illustrated. The research findings prove that the Islamic factor during the Soviet era served not merely as a religious belief, but as a primary mechanism for preserving ethnic and national identity.

oa:W7204954113.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204954113.abstract: This preprint develops a five-layer epistemic model for analysing human conceptions of God. Its central claim is that five distinct questions must not be conflated: how a conception is formed, what that conception represents, which propositional attitude is adopted toward it, whether that attitude is epistemically justified, and whether the relevant proposition is true and successfully refers to its intended object. The framework is metaphysically conditional, although it is applied here within theistic realism to a transcendent God who exists independently of human minds and is conscious in an analogical rather than univocal sense. The paper distinguishes a minimally conscious transcendent reality from stronger hypotheses concerning a creative or explanatory relation to the universe, purposive relations with human beings, revelation, and communicative trustworthiness. Reasoning, experience, testimony, and revelation are not assigned a fixed epistemic hierarchy. Their evidential weight instead depends on reliability, conditional independence, alternative explanations, shared sources of error, counterevidence, and resilience to defeaters. The model also distinguishes propositional from doxastic justification, personal from public justification, and faith from propositional belief. It permits suspension of judgment where the available evidence is insufficient or balanced. The contribution is not a conclusive proof of theism, but an integrated and revisable framework for determining where psychological explanations, representational limitations, evidential considerations, and truth claims bear on religious belief without allowing any single level to determine the others automatically.

oa:W7204959598.title: Introduction
oa:W7204959598.abstract: Hundreds of millions of people every day think they are communicating with large language models (LLMs) (like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini). Paradigmatically, they put in some words that constitute a question and then out comes a sequence of words that looks like an answer. Our ability to determine the presence or absence of intelligence (and cognition more broadly) in LLMs is in large part based on these linguistic interactions. It looks increasingly likely that the hundreds of millions of daily users will soon be billions, and that these interactions will be deeply involved in all aspects of human life. This makes it hard to think of questions more urgent than the following: do we actually share a language with these models? Do they understand us? If so, is their understanding like ours, or is it something fundamentally alien? Is the meaning of their output located inside the machine, or is it determined by their vast external relations to data and users? Perhaps the entire framework of communication is a mistake—what if an adequate characterization of our interactions with LLMs requires an entirely new conceptual framework? These questions lead to urgent practical and ethical problems: On what basis can we trust what an AI tells us (if it tells us anything)? When a chatbot makes a promise or issues a command, who is responsible? How do these new conversational partners affect our own autonomy and social biases? Looking further ahead, as the line between human and artificial cognition blurs, what happens when a superintelligent system turns its reasoning to ethics itself? Could it discover moral truths that are inaccessible, or even hostile, to human values? These are the topics addressed in this book. oa:W7204970975.title: Dispassion as a Common State of Mind for Liberation in Buddhism and Hinduism
oa:W7204970975.venue: Dhammacakka Journal of Buddhism and Applied Buddhism
oa:W7204970975.abstract: Dispassion (Vairāgya/Virāga) has been considered an essential notion in Hinduism and Buddhism for attaining a complete liberation from suffering. The main objective of the study, is to analyze how the practice of Vairāgya/Virāga leads one to liberation in Hindu and Buddhist philosophies. The method of study chosen for conducting the research is qualitative comparative analysis of religious texts including but not limited to the Bhagavad Gītā and Upaniṣads along with texts in Pāli Canon. The study investigates the concept, practice, and significance of Dispassion in each philosophy through thematic analysis. Both religions have been found agreeing with attachment or craving as a source of dukkha. However, there are significant differences in their ideas on the metaphysical aspect of non-attachment. In Hinduism, Vairāgya is a spiritual practicewhich leads to the realization of the Ātman and its relation to Brahman. In Buddhism, virāga arises through the realization of the three characteristics of existence: anicca, dukkha, and anattā. This realization leads to the renunciation of worldly attachments that hinder a Dhamma practitioner from attaining nirvāṇa. Consequently, in spite of being identical from the standpoint of morality, there exists an ontological gap between both religions concerning nonattachment. Thus, it may be said that non-attachment is both the common with distinguishing feature of the two religious beliefs. Such knowledge helps us better understand the doctrine of the East and highlight the significance of non-attachment as a remedy for modern psychological disorders.

oa:W7204994164.title: Language as a Reflection of Buddhist and Brahmanical-Hindu Culture in the Thai Translation of Journey to the West
oa:W7204994164.venue: Journal of Language Teaching and Research
oa:W7204994164.abstract: This study aims to examine language related to Buddhism and Brahmanical-Hinduism and to explore how such language reflects and constructs cultural meanings embedded within religious belief systems in the Thai translation of Journey to the West. The data were character names, honorific expressions, and symbolic lexical items associated with religious concepts, and were analyzed through semantic analysis within a framework of cultural reflection. The findings indicate that Journey to the West employs language not merely as a narrative device, but as a significant ideological mechanism for systematically conveying religious doctrines, moral values, and cosmological structures. With regard to Buddhist vocabulary, the text prominently features terms and proper names rooted in Mahayana Buddhist concepts across two dimensions: 1) Dhamma language and Buddhist terminology, such as 悟 (Wu / Ngo), meaning enlightenment or awakening; and 2) characters embodying Buddhism, such as Phra Thang Samjang (Tripitaka), who embodies the ideal of a morally disciplined monk. In terms of language conveying meanings related to Brahmanical-Hinduism, three dimensions are identified: 1) the concept of a multi-layered and hierarchical pantheon; 2) deities governing the cosmos and natural forces; and 3) language expressing power and meritorious authority, such as Mahā (great), Deva (god), and Rājā (King). Regarding language conveying Hindu meanings through shared symbolism, two additional dimensions are observed: 1) sacred animals and the aquatic cosmos, and 2) cultural language and the transmission of sacred meaning. From the perspective of cultural reflection, the analysis reveals three interrelated dimensions: 1) religious beliefs, 2) beliefs in deities and supernatural beings, and 3) moral values

oa:W7205013820.title: AI Theism
oa:W7205013820.abstract: AI Theism examines stories in which artificially intelligent characters are depicted as divine through the lens of religious studies and mythology. Narratives in which conscious technologies such as artificial intelligences are portrayed as divine have proliferated in parallel with advances in AI and related fields. In these stories, which include both fiction and nonfiction works across media categories, scientifically plausible technological characters, often in the form of AI, exhibit many of the abilities and responsibilities historically assigned to the gods of traditional religions. Were such entities to emerge, they might be indistinguishable from the deities described in traditional religious myths, giving the world a tangible god with the ability to save or destroy humanity. The author argues that these theistic AI stories, beyond simply being an anthropological phenomenon, represent a new category of religious myth that introduces a scientifically acceptable form of god into a secular world. The book is especially relevant to scholars of religion and theology with an interest in science and technology.

oa:W7206157283.title: From Violence to Reconciliation: Theological Exploration of Scriptural Role in War, and Conflict Transformation in Nigeria
oa:W7206157283.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7206157283.abstract: Abstract Africa has a long history of conflict and violence, with numerous wars and civil unrest affecting millions. Despite these challenges, religious beliefs and practices have claimed significant roles in shaping African societies and cultures, offering spiritual guidance and support during times of hardship. This research explores the scriptural role in addressing violence and fostering conflict transformation in Africa. The study aims to understand how biblical narratives and teachings can provide guidance and inspiration for individuals and communities struggling with conflict and its aftermath. The research seeks: How scriptural principles can be applied to promote reconciliation, justice, and peace in African contexts marked by violence and conflict? The significance lies in its ability to provide theological insights and practical strategies for addressing the prevalent challenges of war and conflict in Africa. By examining biblical texts and their interpretations, the research aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of faith's role in promoting reconciliation and healing. Qualitative case study approach is adopted to examine the intricacies of religious beliefs and practices within the context of war and conflict transformation. This method allows for in-depth exploration of individual and community experiences, as well as the interpretation and application of scriptural principles. Key scriptural themes related to peace, justice, forgiveness, and reconciliation are uncovered, along with biblical narratives that offer examples of conflict resolution and healing. The study analyzes how these principles have been applied in African contexts while acknowledging the challenges and limitations of using scriptural approaches to address complex conflicts.

oa:W7206159660.title: The Moral Purity Industry - Volume 3
oa:W7206159660.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7206159660.abstract: The Moral Purity Industry, Volume III: Axial Explanation, Secular Mutation, and the Contemporary Regime of Moral Purification completes the trilogy by moving from historical genealogy to systemic explanation, contemporary institutional analysis, and diagnosis. Whereas Volume I identified the Moral Purity Industry as a modern moral-commercial formation and Volume II reconstructed its deeper genealogical antecedents, Volume III asks how older structures of purity, contamination, redemptive asymmetry, and moral bifurcation survive doctrinal rupture and become embedded in secular institutions, markets, professional systems, cultural production, and everyday governance. Its central claim is that the contemporary regime is neither a simple continuation of religious dualism nor a wholly new ideological invention, but the result of descent, mutation, symbolic sedimentation, and institutional recombination. The first section, “The Axial Explanation,” develops the theoretical mechanisms that make this continuity intelligible. The Dharma–Theism–Secularism (DTS) axis explains how sacred and theistic structures descend into cultural, administrative, therapeutic, and commercial forms. oa:W7206160833.title: The Secret Things and the Revealed Things: Moses, Divine Providence, and the Limits of Human Knowledge in Biblical Theology
oa:W7206160833.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7206160833.abstract: Moses occupies a paradoxical place in biblical theology. He is the prophet who speaks with God with exceptional immediacy, yet the same Torah repeatedly marks the limits of what even Moses may see, know, or control. This article examines that tension as a biblical theology of revelation and epistemic humility. It begins with Numbers 12:6–8 and Deuteronomy 34:10, where Moses is distinguished from other prophets, and then reads that privilege alongside Deuteronomy 29:29 and Exodus 33:18–23, texts that reserve the hidden things to God and deny Moses exhaustive access to the divine glory. The study then considers prophecy, providence, and wisdom: Deuteronomy 18 presents prophetic knowledge as commissioned speech rather than autonomous clairvoyance; the Joseph narrative discloses providence retrospectively; Job resists causal explanations that exceed human competence; and Ecclesiastes emphasizes the opacity of God's work in time. The New Testament develops the same pattern by speaking of mysteries revealed in Christ while preserving creaturely limitation. The article argues that Scripture does not authorize an independent human faculty for penetrating hidden reality. Knowledge of God's purposes is derivative, selective, covenantal, and ordered toward obedience. Biblical revelation therefore produces confidence without omniscience and discernment without esotericism. Moses is exemplary not because he possessed all hidden knowledge, but because his extraordinary access to God coexisted with reverence before what remained unrevealed.

oa:W7206171357.title: The Moral Purity Industry - Volume 1
oa:W7206171357.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7206171357.abstract: The Moral Purity Industry, Volume I: Social Critique, Woke Capitalism, and the Sexual Wing of the Purity Economy develops a systemic critique of a contemporary moral-commercial order in which virtue, guilt, innocence, legitimacy, and symbolic absolution increasingly become institutionalized, administered, displayed, and commodified. The concept of the Moral Purity Industry (TMPI) designates a social field in which moral categories cease to operate solely as standards of conduct and become socially exchangeable resources: guilt is produced and managed, innocence must be publicly demonstrated and periodically renewed, legitimacy is symbolically conferred, and moral standing is mediated through institutions, markets, bureaucracies, platforms, therapeutic vocabularies, and reputational systems. The volume argues that this formation cannot adequately be reduced either to progressive ideology or to capitalism considered in isolation. It instead examines their convergence within a hybrid moral-commercial regime, in which progressive, therapeutic, feminist, and humanitarian vocabularies interact with corporate incentives, managerial structures, consumer markets, political signaling, and institutional administration. In this sense, the term “woke capitalism” is employed analytically rather than as a partisan political label: it identifies a structural conjunction between moral symbolism and economic organization rather than a specifically conservative or left-wing object of critique. The study therefore rejects both political reductionism and purely economic accounts of the phenomenon. Volume I proceeds in three stages. oa:W7206181660.title: The Moral Purity Industry - Volume 2
oa:W7206181660.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7206181660.abstract: The Moral Purity Industry, Volume II: The Genealogy of Purification: From Manichaean Dualism to Early Modern Feminine Redemption develops the historical and genealogical foundation of the trilogy’s wider theory of the Moral Purity Industry. Whereas Volume I analyzes the contemporary moral-commercial regime, Volume II turns to the deeper symbolic grammars through which purity, contamination, hierarchy, absolution, anti-worldliness, and asymmetrical legitimacy became historically intelligible. Its central claim is not that modern institutions simply reproduce medieval doctrine, but that older religious and symbolic structures can survive through mutation, secularization, displacement, and rearticulation. Genealogy is therefore employed as an explanatory method for identifying structured continuity at the level of symbolic grammar rather than institutional sameness. The volume begins with the Manichaean matrix, examining the ontological division of light and darkness, spirit and matter, purity and mixture, and the consequent model of salvation through separation rather than reconciliation. It then follows the transmission and mutation of this dualist-purificatory grammar through Bogomilism and Catharism, including the Interrogatio Iohannis, Cathar cosmology, the Consolamentum, the Servissi, the ritual transmission of prayer, and the Book of the Two Principles. These materials are treated not as disconnected episodes of medieval religious history but as concentrated expressions of a broader grammar of contamination, anti-embodiment, ritual mediation, ontological impurity, authorized absolution, and moral bifurcation. oa:W7206191903.title: RELIGION AND A LIVING EARTH: RECONCEPTUALISING THE 2030 AGENDA THROUGH THE LENS OF SPIRITUAL ECOLOGY
oa:W7206191903.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7206191903.abstract: With a call by international bodies and organisations for peace and a sustainable planet earth, the UN has advised member nations to achieve 17 SDGs by year 2030. In ensuring the achievement of the 17 SDGs within the stipulated time period, the UN adopted some mechanisms like voluntary national reviews, policy coherence, global accounting profession, fourth industrial revolution roadmaps, and ICT infrastructure towards achieving United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). However, despite the relevance of these mechanisms, there is still misgiving about their efficacy in the actual achievement of the UN SDGs, given the positive association between religion and sustainability of planet earth. This presupposes that the higher the religious activity, the higher the likelihood of environmental protection by humans, and invariably the more likelihood for UN member nations to achieve the UN 2030 Agenda. Therefore, this conceptual paper explored how religious belief in form of environmental stewardship, serves as a mechanism for achieving the UN SDGs. Adopting a descriptive overview approach, a review of extant literature is conducted on religion and sustainable development through the lens of Spiritual Ecology and Eco-Theology theories. Building upon existing empirical evidence, this study established a conceptual framework illustrating that achievement of the UN SDGs is positively influenced by religious beliefs. The findings suggest that religion significantly aligns human behavior with the way humans take care of the earth.

oa:W7206199788.title: THE DIALECTICS OF THE QUANTUM MIND: Matter, Consciousness, and the Architecture of Reality
oa:W7206199788.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7206199788.abstract: This book makes a single sustained argument across eleven chapters, and it is worth stating that argument's shape before any of its parts are examined on their own terms. Nineteenth-century materialism, dialectical materialism included, assumed that matter, examined closely enough, is a fixed, fully determinate substrate capable of explaining everything built on top of it, consciousness included, without remainder. Twentieth-century physics, in its most rigorously tested and least controversial results rather than in any popularizer's speculation, has removed the grounds for that assumption. What follows from that removal is not a proof that consciousness is fundamental; it is an inference to the best explanation, defended one careful step at a time, and the book asks to be judged by the same evidential standard it holds its materialist rival to. The four parts below carry that argument from its historical origins, through the physics that unsettles it, to a positive alternative, to that alternative's consequences. Part I · Two DialecticsBefore the physics can do any work, the philosophical inheritance it will be tested against has to be stated in full and on its own terms. Part I traces the dialectic from its idealist origin in Hegel, through Marx's inversion of it, to the precise point where nineteenth-century materialism had to assume, rather than argue for, matter's self-sufficiency. Chapter 1. The Ghost Returns. States the mind-body problem in its modern form, from Descartes' unresolved dualism through the materialist and functionalist traditions that inherited it, and shows that the “hard problem” of consciousness remains open even in physicalism's own most careful contemporary defenses. Material objects, consciousnesses, spiritual phenomena, and religious images are various configurations of the χ‑spectrum arising through projection onto the material interface. The monograph reconstructs nine fundamental nodes of the χ‑ontological chain: the Absolute Aχ, the reality operator Tχ, ontological levels λχ(n), cognitive modes ψχ(n), the boundary operator Bχ, χ‑entropy Sχ, χ‑curvature Kχ, χ‑topology π1(Mχ), and the universal equation Uχ[Aχ]=0. Each section reveals one or several nodes, forming a unified structure: from the Absolute and χ‑geometry to consciousness, death, the SIP, and religious myths. Religion and physics turn out to be two languages describing the same χ‑reality: religion is a cognitive projection of χ‑structures through the material interface, while physics is a formal reconstruction of those same structures.
