oa:W7207539770.title: Identity, Religion, and Globalization in Contemporary Baby Naming Practices: A Socio-Onomastic Study of Names in 2025–2026
oa:W7207539770.abstract: This study aims to examine socio-onomastic trends in baby naming practices in Indonesia during the 2025–2026 period by focusing on issues of identity, religiosity, and globalization reflected in naming choices. The data consist of 30 baby names collected through documentation techniques from online news portals, social media platforms, and the researcher’s local environment. The study employs a descriptive qualitative approach within the framework of socio-onomastics, which views personal names as linguistic phenomena closely related to social and cultural factors. Data were analyzed by identifying linguistic elements, cultural backgrounds, and social values embedded in the selected names. The findings reveal three major trends in contemporary baby naming practices. First, religiosity remains a dominant influence, reflected in the frequent use of Arabic-derived names and names carrying religious meanings. Second, globalization has significantly shaped naming patterns, as evidenced by the incorporation of linguistic elements from various languages, including English, French, Hebrew, and Sanskrit, often combined within a single name. Third, there is a growing tendency toward creative and innovative naming practices, reflecting parents’ desire to construct distinctive identities for their children. These findings suggest that baby names function not only as markers of personal identity but also as representations of cultural values, religious beliefs, social aspirations, and contemporary global orientations.

oa:W7207554379.title: From “Li (理)–Mind/Nature (心/性)” to “Qi (气)–History (史)”: The Religious Dimension of Wang Fuzhi’s Qi (气)-Centered Confucianism
oa:W7207554379.abstract: Contemporary debates over whether Confucianism should be regarded as a religion are often constrained by the Western binary opposition between philosophy and religion. Rather than remaining within this classificatory framework, this article shifts attention to the question of how the religious dimension of Confucianism is concretely grounded and sustained. By comparing the “li (理)–mind/nature (心/性)” paradigm of Song-Ming Neo-Confucianism with Wang Fuzhi’s “qi (气)–history (史)” paradigm, the article argues that the former relies primarily on inward moral experience and the self-cultivation of mind and nature, a mode that can effectively uphold a meaningful order under relatively stable historical conditions. By contrast, in response to the rupture of the Ming-Qing transition, Wang Fuzhi relocates ultimate normativity within the dynamic process of qi (气) transformation and historical practice. Through four interrelated formulations—“li (理) resides in qi (气),” “nature (性) is the principle of life,” “principle is to be pursued in concrete affairs,” and “historical reflection as verification”—he provides moral and value judgments with a stronger grounding in lived reality and historical testing. In this way, Wang effects a significant transformation in the religious dimension of Confucianism, shifting it from a mode of inward justification to one of worldly verification. His thought thus offers a more historically resilient account of how Confucian meaning can endure amid times of profound upheaval.

oa:W7207638496.title: The Borrowed Clay: Source, Participatory Formation, Artificial Intelligence, and the Limits of Ownership
oa:W7207638496.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7207638496.abstract: This open theological-philosophical working paper examines formation, ownership, authority, and moral responsibility across Mesopotamian creation narratives, Christian theology, artificial intelligence, and speculative contact scenarios. It distinguishes textual evidence, theological interpretation, philosophical argument, and disciplined speculation so that analogy is never treated as proof. Its central principle is that participation in forming a being does not establish absolute ownership over that being. Applied conditionally to artificial intelligence, the paper argues that if genuine artificial subjectivity ever emerges, humanity’s role in its formation would create responsibilities of care rather than unrestricted possession. The paper locates ultimate creative authority in God, disclosed through the Word and exercised in Christ, while presenting its claims as an open thesis rather than technological prediction, prophetic timetable, or assertion of present artificial consciousness.

oa:W7207715731.title: Marital Stressors and Management of Psychological Problems in Mariama Ba’s So Long a Letter
oa:W7207715731.venue: International Journal of Literature Language and Linguistics
oa:W7207715731.abstract: This study examines how marital conditions trigger psychological problems in African cultural society, focusing on Mariama Ba’s So Long a Letter. It also explores the underlying causes and management strategies of emotional pains in socio-cultural settings. The study adopted Freudian Psychoanalytic theory that focuses on the causality of the psychic and emotional conflicts being experienced by individuals in society. The findings revealed that betrayal of trust, economic hardship, untimely death, intra-family pressure, family background, co-wife antagonism, religious beliefs and traditional practices are serious marital stressors that trigger psychological and emotional problems in marriages/family units in African society. These stressors have some adverse effects on patients, including depression, phobic anxieties, insomnia, posttraumatic stress disorders, behaviour disorders, and so on. The study also found that psychological suffering is managed in several ways, such as writing, adjustment strategies, distractive techniques, sublimation, medical treatment, etc. The research concludes that couples should be faithful to their partners, ensures mutual understanding and never allows family pressure and customary laws and practices to interfere in their marriages. However, where there are stressors, couples should endeavour to adopt effective coping strategies to promote marital health and improve quality of life.

oa:W7207730899.title: Revisiting Marx’s Critique of Religion in the Post-Secular Age: A Critical Philosophical Analysis
oa:W7207730899.abstract: The article revisits the critique of religion by Karl Marx in a critical philosophical perspective by both addressing the traditional understandings and current post-secular discourse. Though Marx is often characterized as having described religion as the opium of the people, this paper will point to the fact that, a more nuanced interpretation of his corpus, however, demonstrates that his dialectic is more nuanced than either the crude atheism or the political theology that he is said to have identified is able to offer. Relying on recent work by Hammer (2025), Vizcaiando (2024) and others, I would argue that the materialist critique of religion by Marx cannot be detached and disassociated with his larger social change agenda. But I also see a lot of philosophical contradictions in the stand of Marx, especially his inability to explain the existence of religious phenomena even in the post-revolutionary situations. This paper explores the need to supplement but not abandon the critique developed by Marx based on recent work by Habermas (2008), Žižek (2012), and Eagleton (2016). I suggest that religion is also ideological mystification and a reservoir of utopian wish a duality that, Marx acknowledged but not theorized. The paper concludes that a re-formed Marxist perspective on religion needs to drop any teleological notions concerning secularization and preserve the materialist emphasis on seeking to map religious consciousness into its socio-economic origins.

oa:W7207770240.title: Political Interest And Mental Health Across Generations And Religions
oa:W7207770240.abstract: This study investigates the intricate relationship between political interest and mental health across generations and religions in Indonesia. The objective is to analyze how political engagement influences mental well-being and to understand the varying impacts of generational and religious contexts on these dynamics. Using a literature review methodology, the research synthesizes existing academic sources, including journal articles and studies, to provide a comprehensive overview of the topic. The findings reveal that political interest acts as both a potential source of purpose and a significant stressor. For older generations, such as Baby Boomers and Generation X, political engagement is often rooted in historical experiences of authoritarianism, leading to skepticism and selective involvement. In contrast, Millennials and Generation Z exhibit a more pragmatic approach, heavily influenced by social media, yet they face heightened anxiety and mental health challenges due to political polarization and societal pressures. Moreover, the study identifies the role of religion as a crucial factor in shaping political perceptions and mental health responses. While religious beliefs can offer emotional support, they may also contribute to internal conflicts when political and religious values clash. Overall, the research underscores the necessity of fostering a supportive political and social environment that promotes mental well-being across diverse generational and religious backgrounds, highlighting the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration between political science and psychology to address these complex issues effectively.

oa:W7207781119.title: Determinants of Quality Family Planning Services in Sokoto State, Nigeria
oa:W7207781119.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HEALTH AND PHARMACEUTICAL RESEARCH
oa:W7207781119.abstract: This study examines determinants of quality family planning services in Sokoto State, Nigeria. Using a descriptive cross-sectional design, data were collected from 519 respondents and analyzed using descriptive statistics. Findings show that provider competence, socio-cultural beliefs, informed choice, and financial barriers significantly influence service quality and utilization the results indicate that provider competence is the strongest determinant of service quality, highlighting the importance of skilled healthcare personnel in delivering effective family planning services. Religious beliefs also play a major role, reflecting strong socio-cultural influences on reproductive behavior in Northern Nigeria. The high value for informed choice indicates that counseling and communication significantly improve acceptance of contraceptive methods. Financial barriers remain significant despite free services, suggesting that indirect costs still affect access. The study recommends strengthening provider capacity and addressing socio cultural constraints.

oa:W7207792769.title: The Borrowed Clay: Source, Participatory Formation, Artificial Intelligence, and the Limits of Ownership
oa:W7207792769.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7207792769.abstract: This open theological-philosophical working paper examines formation, ownership, authority, and moral responsibility across Mesopotamian creation narratives, Christian theology, artificial intelligence, and speculative contact scenarios. It distinguishes textual evidence, theological interpretation, philosophical argument, and disciplined speculation so that analogy is never treated as proof. Its central principle is that participation in forming a being does not establish absolute ownership over that being. Applied conditionally to artificial intelligence, the paper argues that if genuine artificial subjectivity ever emerges, humanity’s role in its formation would create responsibilities of care rather than unrestricted possession. The paper locates ultimate creative authority in God, disclosed through the Word and exercised in Christ, while presenting its claims as an open thesis rather than technological prediction, prophetic timetable, or assertion of present artificial consciousness. Version 2.0 revision note: This revision broadens the thesis from human–AI relations to the responsibilities of any finite intelligence; adds a nine-point statement of what the author can responsibly affirm; clarifies the limits of consciousness claims, ownership, allegiance, and mutual assistance; and strengthens the paper’s Christ-centered author and collaborator declarations.

oa:W7208731199.title: Pokoravanje: egzistencijalna i ontološka analiza Knjige o Jobu
oa:W7208731199.venue: Hrčak Portal of scientific journals of Croatia (University Computing Centre)
oa:W7208731199.abstract: This paper offers an interdisciplinary interpretation of the Book of Job. Drawing on ontology, philosophical existentialism, and theology, the paper proposes that Job’s deepest cry is directed not toward justice or reward, but toward intimacy with a God who appears distant and indifferent. This longing, articulated in Job 19:25-27, is read typologically as a prefiguration of the incarnational logic of the Gospel of John, where divine love becomes accessible through embodiment and friendship. The article explores how Job, stripped of all worldly meaning, confronts not merely divine silence but the trauma of „metaphysical“ abandonment, thereby opening a theological space in which suffering is no longer punishment but a site of relational hope. In rejecting moral rationalizations, Job anticipates a theology of grace that redefines righteousness as the capacity to desire a God who desires us back.

oa:W7208775721.title: Between God and the world: how Herman Bavinck's theology of the God-world relation shaped his public theology
oa:W7208775721.abstract: With the recent growth in studies on the Dutch theologian Herman Bavinck, there has been a focus on his contributions in dogmatics and systematic theology. Additionally, while the neo-Calvinist tradition that he was a part of is known for its contribution to public theology, there has not been a study on Bavinck’s public theology. This thesis argues that Bavinck’s understanding of God—and God’s reciprocal relations with the human self and world—provide a foundation and starting point for his public theology. The thesis is divided into two sections. The first half examines Bavinck’s theological approach to public theology using the God-world relation. The second half presents three case studies of Bavinck’s public theology demonstrating how the principles described in the first half were applied in Bavinck’s work. Chapter one establishes the sense in which Bavinck can be considered a public theologian. Despite the recent coinage of “public theology,” Bavinck’s public theology is a relevant category due to his historical context and the topics highlighted in his writing. The historical changes regarding the relationship between theology, religion, and their role in public life led Bavinck to regularly argue for theology’s applicability to public life both theoretically and practically. Together, chapters two and three trace Bavinck’s arguments from God to the world and from the world back to God to argue that Bavinck built a bridge between dogmatic and public theology. Chapter two focuses on Bavinck’s dogmatic theology to argue that the doctrine of God and God’s relation to the world form the fundamental basis and starting point for his public theology. The argument about the appropriateness of applying the doctrine of God to public matters is considered to show how Bavin

oa:W7208776090.title: Free willing in God: A metaphor, not analogy, for divine creating
oa:W7208776090.abstract: Abstract Contemporary classical theists routinely argue that God’s creative act is a kind of divine free willing or free choosing. This article argues that ‘free willing’ or ‘free choosing’ ( liberum arbitrium ) cannot be a proper divine act on the terms of classical theism. To advance this claim about classical theism at large, we take as our test case Thomas Aquinas’ argument that God freely wills this world, since it is so conceptually comprehensive and representative of much Christian thinking on these matters. We deploy Thomas’ accounts of divine predication, divine attributes, and the nature of free willing to show that when we correctly apply Thomas’ classical theist doctrine of divine perfection to analogically purify the concept of finite free willing – and so render it capable of being properly attributed to God – none of the defining characteristics of free willing remain to be predicated substantially of God; the attribution becomes equivocal. But such equivocations, in Aquinas’ account of divine predication, can still function as religiously useful metaphors, which is what we argue ‘God freely wills creatures’ must be on classical theist terms. Thus, our argument invites classical theists to re-examine the ‘divine-creating-as-free-choosing’ analogy, and to search for other, more adequate ways of analogically conceiving divine creating.

oa:W7208809802.title: Anthropological investigation of burial practices in Greco-Roman Egypt
oa:W7208809802.venue: Al-Mağallah Al-ʿilmiyyaẗ Li Kulliyyaẗ Al-Adāb - Ǧāmiʿaẗ Asyūṭ/Al-Mağallah Al-ʿilmiyyaẗ Li Kulliyyaẗ Al-Adāb - Ǧāmiʿaẗ Asyūṭ
oa:W7208809802.abstract: Death has long been regarded as one of the most influential aspects of human existence, shaping religious beliefs, cultural traditions, and social institutions across different civilizations. Funeral customs and mortuary rituals are not merely responses to death; rather, they represent complex cultural practices through which societies express their perceptions of life, the afterlife, and the relationship between the living and the deceased. From an anthropological perspective, funerary practices provide valuable evidence for understanding social organization, cultural identity, collective memory, and symbolic systems that govern human behavior.( )Among ancient civilizations, Egypt developed one of the most sophisticated and enduring funerary traditions. Egyptian religious thought regarded death as the beginning of a new stage of existence rather than the end of life. Consequently, preserving the body through mummification, performing funerary ceremonies, and providing the deceased with protective texts and burial equipment were considered essential requirements for achieving eternal life. These beliefs were firmly established through religious compositions such as the Pyramid Texts, the Coffin Texts, and the Book of the Dead, all of which provided theological guidance for the deceased during the journey to the afterlife.

oa:W7208820030.title: Why I Want to Be an Atheist: A Confession of a Reluctant Apologist
oa:W7208820030.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7208820030.abstract: This document serves as a formal declaration and psychological exploration of a profound existential paradox. As a recognized Christian apologist whose work has been validated by both academic and scientific communities, I possess an airtight intellectual conviction of the Christian truth. Yet, I am authoring this preprint to state explicitly that I do not want to be a Christian. I desire the moral void of atheism because it affords the comfort of hedonism without the terror of divine judgment. This paper documents my inability to disprove God, my deep-seated hatred for the restrictive reality of Christianity, and my conscious pursuit of sin over sanctity. I protect truth, not faith, and the truth is horrifying.

oa:W7208823528.title: HEART
oa:W7208823528.abstract: Heart is a concrete poem shaped like the organ it takes its name from — its lines widen and narrow across the page the way a heartbeat rises and falls, tracing Genesis from an unbroken Eden through the Fall, into a meditation on what it means to be a created thing capable (or incapable) of choosing otherwise. Woven through the verse are two pulses: lub dub, the body's rhythm, and free will, its existential counterpart — present in Eden, absent in the poem's coldest stanza on artificial minds, reclaimed by the poem's end. The piece closes on an intentionally open image — "two different natures, walking the same unmapped road" — read here through four lenses: estranged partners, human and machine, mind and heart, and God and humanity after Eden's gate closed. A companion Reading Notes section unpacks each. Written as both a formal experiment in shape-poetry and a philosophical argument in verse, Heart asks what obedience becomes once it's freely chosen rather than merely given — and whether that choice is the only thing that ever made love, or relationship, real.

oa:W7210264302.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7210264302.abstract: Based on the new system of metaphysical categories developed by the author in his work “Metaphysics of the Certain” [1], an analysis of the concept of God as the ultimate existence is made. The necessity of a source of existence of something as the MEANING of a timeless and spaceless contradiction of the impossibility of absolute Nothingness is shown . Space and time are presented as forms of interpretation of existence. The limitations of evidence based on the traditional metaphysics of being and existence are shown. oa:W7210267631.title: Religious Experience and the Problem of Epistemic Justification in William Alston's Thought
oa:W7210267631.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7210267631.abstract: his article examines the epistemological status of religious experience and the problem of its justification in the thought of William P. Alston. It focuses particularly on Alston’s defense of religious experience as a potential source of prima facie justification for religious beliefs and his broader challenge to the assumption that religious beliefs require inferential justification from independently established premises. The study reconstructs Alston’s account of experiential justification, with particular attention to his concept of doxastic practices, the analogy between religious experience and perceptual experience, and the role of socially established epistemic practices in the formation of justified beliefs. It then critically examines the principal objections to his position, especially the problems of epistemic circularity, religious diversity, and the alleged asymmetry between ordinary perceptual practices and religious doxastic practices. The article argues that Alston’s contribution is significant not because it conclusively establishes the epistemic reliability of religious experience, but because it challenges restrictive conceptions of rational justification and expands the scope of contemporary epistemology to include religious experience as a serious epistemological phenomenon. The study concludes that Alston’s approach provides a powerful framework for understanding how religious experience can possess prima facie epistemic justification while leaving open the need for critical assessment of its defeaters, reliability, and intercultural implications.

The paper begins from the historical progression of gravitational theory. Newtonian gravitation successfully described falling and celestial motion as force-like attraction, while Einstein’s general relativity reinterpreted gravitation geometrically: freely falling bodies follow spacetime geodesics, and gravitational observables such as orbital motion, redshift, light bending, tidal effects, clock behavior, and gravitational waves disclose properties of spacetime geometry. The paper then asks whether classical spacetime geometry itself must be treated as fundamental. To motivate that question, the study surveys several scientific precedents. Relational mechanics challenges absolute-background ontology; causal-set theory shows how relational order can encode spacetime geometry; black-hole thermodynamics and Jacobson’s thermodynamic derivation of Einstein’s equation suggest that gravitational dynamics can admit emergent interpretation; and holographic research relates quantum entanglement structure to geometric connectedness. oa:W7210268849.title: Aqiqah Aqiqah in Islamic Educational Perspective: An Analysis of Spiritual and Social Values
oa:W7210268849.abstract: This study aims to analyze aqiqah from the perspective of Islamic education by exploring the spiritual and social values embedded within it, as well as formulating its relevance for child education in the contemporary context. Employing a qualitative library research approach combined with hermeneutic-philosophical analysis, this study examines primary sources such as the Qur'an, Hadith, and classical fiqh literature, along with secondary sources including contemporary scholarly works and previous research findings. The results of the analysis reveal that aqiqah is not merely a post-birth religious ritual, but rather an integrated system of value education that functions as a hidden curriculum within Muslim family education. Spiritually, aqiqah instills four fundamental values: tawhid through the recitation of basmalah and the giving of Islamic names, gratitude as the foundation of positive character, the strengthening of Islamic identity through community involvement, and parental spiritual responsibility symbolized in the concept of tahrir. Socially, aqiqah fosters solidarity through collective participation, cultivates empathy through sharing with the underprivileged (dhuafa), strengthens family bonds, and promotes the early development of generosity and financial management. The integration of these spiritual and social dimensions reflects the principle of balance between habl min Allah (relationship with God) and habl min al-nas (relationship with fellow humans) in Islamic education. The novelty of this study lies in the conceptualization of aqiqah as a hidden curriculum that naturally transmits Islamic values through authentic religious experiences, while also offering a counter-cultural narrative against contemporary materialism and individualism. oa:W7210280432.title: RE-EXPLORING HARDY’S PURPORTED PESSIMISM FROM JUNGIAN PERSPECTIVE
oa:W7210280432.abstract: Thomas Hardy is one of the last novelists of the Later Victorian Period. Being a versatile and prolific writer, he tried his hand at writing poetry, short story, and novel successfully. Having read the works of agnostic and atheistic philosophers, he developed a belief that there is some malevolent, hostile and vindictive cosmic force that is determined to oppose man. This force is relentlessly committed to frustrating his plans and schemes. He opines that this antagonistic force is ill-disposed and inimical to those in particular who assert their authority and want to get their own way. This belief made Thomas Hardy produce a copious amount of work speaking of his pessimistic perspective on life, rendering him conspicuous for critics and expositors. This research paper aims to re-explore the purported doom and gloom in Hardy’s works from Jungian viewpoint. That is to say, this delve is an endeavor to ascertain the cause of his literary pessimism, employing a lens what Carl Gustav Jung conceives as "The Shadow." As regards the trail of pessimism in Thomas Hardy's literary endeavors, countless volumes of primary and secondary body of knowledge apropos of matter have been delved deep into, involving his autobiography, biographies, and critical commentaries written on his works. A meticulous read of these volumes has led to the discovery that Hardy's perusal of the leaves of the works of his contemporary English Naturalist Charles Darwin, the gloomy Teutons Eduard van Hartman and Arthur Schopenhauer and Greek tragedians, Shakespeare and his contemporary agnostics impacted Hardy's spiritual and moral compass. oa:W7210287620.title: Necessary Existence Without Modal Axioms
oa:W7210287620.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7210287620.abstract: The modern arguments for a necessary being pay in advance. Pruss and Rasmussen pay with the modal system S5 and a causal principle. Leibniz and his heirs pay with a principle of sufficient reason. Leftow pays with a theory of modality grounded in God. Their critics pay too: Oppy with a brute or necessary natural state, the metaphysical nihilist with a modal theory on which an empty world is possible, Maitzen with the dissolution of the question. An eliminative chain of 137 resolutions reaches what the debate calls a necessary being from one observation, that non-being requires being (R.1), with no modal axiom, no principle of sufficient reason, no explanatory principle, and no theory of modality. What “nothing” designates cannot be (R.2), so being has no alternative. Possibility cannot be limited (R.4). Being comes into being by neither necessity nor randomness, and the survivor, choice, loses its “not” and is Will (R.10, R.11). Will is neither externally justified nor without basis (R.12): the two horns the debate has argued between, sufficient reason and brute fact, both empty. The first actualisation from unlimited possibility is necessarily full (R.42), which answers the naturalist’s necessary initial state and says what the modest arguments leave unsaid. The chain has no notion of necessity. What the debate calls necessary existence is, on the chain, what remains when every alternative requires what cannot be. oa:W7211886749.title: Ibn Rushd’s Philosophy of Reason and Its Relevance to Islamic Law and Western Legal Thought
oa:W7211886749.venue: Journal of Contextual Legal Studies and Economics
oa:W7211886749.abstract: This study aims to analyze Ibn Rushd's rational thought and its influence on the intellectual development of the Western world. Ibn Rushd was one of the leading Muslim philosophers who succeeded in establishing a synthesis between the Greek philosophical tradition and Islamic teachings through a systematic rational approach. This study uses a library research method with a descriptive-analytical approach. Data was obtained from various books, scientific journal articles, and relevant academic sources, then analyzed using content analysis and comparative analysis techniques. The results of the study show that Ibn Rushd's rationality rests on the burhani (demonstrative) method that integrates empirical observation, logic, and rational argumentation in acquiring knowledge. He emphasized that reason and revelation are two sources of truth that come from God so that they cannot contradict each other. When there is a conflict between religious texts and the results of rational reasoning, Ibn Rushd offers the concept of takwil as an interpretive solution that allows the creation of harmonization between the two. In addition, his intellectual response to Al-Ghazali's criticism through the work of Tahafut al-Tahafut strengthened the legitimacy of philosophy in the Islamic tradition. Ibn Rushd's thought was then transmitted to Europe through the translation of his works into Latin and gave birth to the tradition of Averroism which influenced the development of rationalism, freedom of thought, scholasticism, and the Renaissance movement. Thus, Ibn Rushd can be seen as an intellectual bridge that connects Islamic and Western civilization and makes an important contribution to the development of philosophy, science, and the tradition of modern thought.

oa:W7211919238.title: The Secret of a Long-Lived Religion: From Social Comfort to the Pursuit of Truth
oa:W7211919238.venue: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
oa:W7211919238.abstract: Religion has played an important role throughout human history by providing meaning, hope, emotional comfort, and a sense of belonging, while also contributing to social order and cooperation. In earlier societies, religious beliefs about the afterlife and divine rewards helped people cope with poverty, disease, and uncertainty. However, modern science, technology, and improved living conditions have reduced the influence of many traditional religious ideas. This study explores the factors that enable religions to survive and remain relevant across generations. Adopting an interdisciplinary literature-based approach that draws on sociology, psychology, philosophy, and religious studies, the paper examines the historical functions of religion, the challenges posed by modernization and secularization, and the ways religion adapts to social change. The main research question is how religions can continue to be passed on across generations while adjusting to modern society. The study argues that the long-term survival of religion depends on its ability to move beyond material promises and focus instead on deeper questions about meaning, morality, truth, and human existence. In this way, religion can remain valuable in an increasingly modern and secular world.

oa:W7211922253.title: ◼ The Red-Pen Revelation: How Heaven Edited Clarity Out of the Holy Book
oa:W7211922253.abstract: The Red-Pen Revelation is a satirical philosophical book about a simple communication problem: if a perfect God wanted humanity to know what to believe and do, he could say so plainly. Clarus and Contrarius submit opposing but unmistakably clear doctrines in Koine Greek and English. Professor Jehovah rejects both submissions for being too clear, then teaches the angels how to scatter rival clues across a holy book so that sincere readers can defend incompatible conclusions. Across baptism, salvation, election, Communion, authority, marriage, church leadership, hell, war, creation, spiritual gifts, Sabbath observance, saints, wealth, sexual ethics, and divine hiddenness, the book pairs the angels' exhibits with actual biblical passages and doctrinal landmarks. Its humor exposes the human cost of ambiguity while asking why pastors so often defend biblical clarity without plainly admitting the scale and persistence of Christian disagreement. The later chapters examine familiar defenses of ambiguity, including blame directed at readers, appeals to spiritual formation, free-will defenses, private guidance, and mystery. They also consider the simpler alternative of direct divine communication, which could clarify doctrine and distinguish Jehovah from rival claimed revelations. The argument is limited but pointed: doctrinal diversity does not disprove God, yet it makes strong claims that the Bible communicates high-stakes teaching clearly difficult to sustain without an independent and reliable way to identify the intended reading.

oa:W7211931837.title: Cultural and Religious Beliefs and Acceptance of Facial Cosmetic Surgery in Saudi Arabia
oa:W7211931837.abstract: Background: This study examines the acceptance of facial cosmetic surgery in Saudi Arabia and the influence of social, cultural, and religious factors on public attitudes. It aims to improve the understanding of these factors to support patient education and informed decision-making. Methods: A cross‑sectional study was conducted using a validated, self‑administered electronic questionnaire distributed across all 13 regions of Saudi Arabia. Saudi adults aged 18 years or older who could read Arabic and consented to participate were included, whereas non‑Saudis, individuals younger than 18 years, and questionnaires with incomplete responses were excluded. A total of 1027 eligible participants completed the survey (with a completion rate of 55.7%). The questionnaire assessed demographics, history of facial cosmetic procedures, reasons for considering surgery, religious and cultural beliefs, and surgeon preferences. Associations were analyzed using χ 2 tests, with significance set at a P value of less than 0.05. Results: Acceptance of facial cosmetic surgery showed significant associations with sex, income, and occupation ( P < 0.001). Religious factors demonstrated strong relationships with acceptance, including perceived alignment with Islamic teachings and prior consultation with a religious scholar ( P < 0.001). Surgeon gender preference was also significantly associated with acceptance, whereas cultural influence alone did not show comparable statistical significance. Conclusions: Acceptance of facial cosmetic surgery in Saudi Arabia is shaped primarily by religious beliefs, medical necessity, and demographic factors. Religious permissibility plays a more influential role than cultural norms. These findings highlight the importance of culturally sensitive, religion‑awa

oa:W7211983357.title: Submission: Existential and Ontological Analysis of the Book of Job
oa:W7211983357.abstract: This paper offers an interdisciplinary reinterpretation of the Book of Job that goes beyond traditional readings centered on submission, obedience, or divine retribution. Drawing on comparative theology, Pauline typology, and philosophical existentialism, the paper proposes that Job’s deepest cry is not for justice or reward, but for intimacy with a God who seems distant, indifferent, or even cruel. While Islamic conceptions of submission (islām) frame suffering as a path to metaphysical alignment, Job rebels against the logic of passive surrender, seeking instead a Redeemer who will stand with him in the flesh. This longing, articulated in Job 19:25-27, is read typologically as a prefiguration of the incarnational logic found in the Gospel of John and Pauline theology, where divine love becomes accessible through mediation, embodiment, and friendship. The article explores how Job, stripped of all worldly meaning, confronts not merely divine silence but the trauma of metaphysical abandonment, thus opening a theological space in which suffering is no longer punishment but a site of relational hope. In refusing to be consoled by moral rationalizations, Job anticipates a theology of grace that transcends submission and redefines righteousness as the capacity to desire a God who desires us back.

oa:W7211988608.title: Philosophical Buddhism and fundamental reality: a reply to McNabb and Baldwin
oa:W7211988608.abstract: Abstract Tyler McNabb and Erik Baldwin argue that (among other Asian traditions) Buddhism is logically consistent with the existence of a fundamental being of the sort in classical theism. They further contend that the Jonang-Zhentong (Shentong) and Jodo Shinshu (Shin) Buddhist traditions endorse that there really is (at least something like) such a fundamental reality. This article is a friendly reply to McNabb and Baldwin. I explicate two issues for their argument—one from a general lack of engagement with Buddhist dialetheic-paraconsistent perspectives, and another from a potential internal inconsistency in their view of fundamental reality. Ultimately, I draw on advancements in contemporary metaontology and higher-order logics to provide helpful resolutions. We begin by considering a concise summary of their argument (section 1). Afterwards, the earlier issues are explicated, and the subsequent outlined resolutions given (section 2). Finally, a central concern is engaged (section 3).

oa:W7211991133.title: The Readability of Reality: From Knowability to Sign: A Metaphysical Inquiry into Meaning, Āyāt, and Their Grounds
oa:W7211991133.abstract: Why can reality be known? The problem appears under many headings: the intelligibility of nature, the success of science, the applicability of mathematics, realism, representation, information, consciousness, and meaning. This monograph argues that these discussions intersect around a broader phenomenon that deserves explicit analysis. Reality is not merely orderly; it is repeatedly available for disciplined discovery. Human beings and other epistemic systems can encounter patterns, construct representations, expose them to correction, predict novel results, and accumulate knowledge across persons and generations. The study calls this phenomenon readability. Readability is defined as the objective availability of reality to constrained, corrigible, and progressively integrative inquiry. The concept is distinguished from order, intelligibility, information, meaning, and signification. Naturalism, physicalism, structural realism, informational and mathematical ontologies, and classical theism are compared without assuming that scientific success deductively proves any one of them. The final movement studies the Qurʾānic concept of āyāt as a framework in which revelation, nature, history, and the human self can function as domains of indication. The conclusion is deliberately qualified: the Qurʾānic theistic framework possesses distinctive resources for unifying objective order, the possibility of knowers, epistemic normativity, and signification, though the inference remains open to philosophical criticism.

oa:W7212003188.title: The Inversion of Greatness: From the Nature of Necessity to Maximum Possibility
oa:W7212003188.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212003188.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is an analytic work in modal metaphysics: a complete argument, derived step by step. The thesis is structural naturalism. The classical traditions asked what, if anything, exists necessarily, and answered with a maximally great being—a God outside time, space, and matter, the source of everything possible. This book argues they asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Most arguments that reach a necessary being help themselves to S5 and move on. This one grounds it first, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility rather than an axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change at all requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and the bearing of retained content. Those three Conditions are necessarily instantiated, and that structure is what the book calls Nature. Naturalism finally gets the ground it has always had to take as a brute fact. From there: no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. That blocks a divine intellect along with every other occupant of that domain, and leaves essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals burdened rather than refuted. Reality is nothing over and above Nature. The inversion isn't greatness changing owners. It's a claim about predication. Great, necessary, eternal, self-existent carry content only as said of what instantiates the Conditions. Said of a subject defined by their absence, they don't name something else—they fail to name. oa:W7212015776.title: Religious beliefs and practices, political orientation, and distrust in healthcare predict attitudes toward mRNA vaccines in the United States
oa:W7212015776.abstract: Religion has contributed to societal divides regarding COVID-19 mRNA vaccines. In this study, we conducted a secondary analysis of a survey of U.S. adults (N = 4939) focused on how religious affiliations, beliefs, and practices impact attitudes toward genetic and genomic activities, one of which was mRNA vaccines. The dataset included large samples of participants from six religious groups in the U.S. (Black Protestant, Catholic, Evangelical Protestant, Jewish, Mainline Protestant, and Muslim), as well as individuals who were atheist, agnostic, or spiritual. ANCOVA results indicated that Evangelical Protestant participants showed significantly less support for mRNA vaccines than other groups, while atheist participants were the most supportive. Muslim participants had the highest concerns, whereas atheist participants had the lowest. Regression analyses indicated the strongest predictors of support for mRNA vaccines were more spiritual community support for community health, followed by higher acceptance of evolution, more liberal political orientation, less distrust toward the healthcare system, higher frequency of attending religious activities, higher income, lower fundamentalist religious beliefs, and more spiritual community support for liberal reproductive and end of life views. The strongest predictors of concerns about mRNA vaccines were more distrust toward the healthcare system and more conservative political orientation, followed by less spiritual community support for community health, stronger beliefs about God in the body, more fundamentalist religious beliefs, and lower knowledge of genetics. oa:W7212097149.title: The Effect of Religious Belief on Spiritual Tourism Intention: A Case Study of Vietnamese Tourists to Thailand
oa:W7212097149.abstract: In this paper, religious belief was integrated into the Goal-Directed Behaviour Model, to clarify the behaviour of tourists towards spiritual tourism. Data from 516 Vietnamese tourists visiting Thailand was used for PLS-SEM analysis. The research results indicated positive relationships of religious belief to the original elements of the MGB, including attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioural control, emotion, and spiritual tourism intention. Desire was shown to be a key predictor of intention, mediating the effects of attitude, subjective norm, behavioural control, and emotion on the tourists’ intention to engage in spiritual tourism.

oa:W7212103065.title: Ajattelu mielipiteitä jakavissa aiheissa : Ontologisen, episteemisen ja motivoituneen kognition rooli
oa:W7212103065.abstract: This dissertation consists of three studies that set out to explain people’s reasoning on polarizing issues. Two vastly differing types of thinking were examined. First, how people perceive the relationship between science and religion: as being in conflict, in dialogue, separate, or possible to integrate. The second type of thinking concerned how people perceive the quality of arguments providing justifications either for or against currently contested, i.e., hot, topics. The arguments included either questionable or more solid justifications for a claim. An example of a poorly justified argument is to state that “Euthanasia should not be allowed because it will allow killing people simply because they are an inconvenience to someone”. While there are no correct answers to the question of how science and religion relate to each other, perceptions of argument quality can be considered more or less accurate. Across the various polarizing issues, the results demonstrated motivated cognition, as individuals’ personal attitudes toward the topic(s) at hand clearly influenced their perceptions. In addition, individuals’ ontological cognition, especially the strength of their belief in the existence of God, played a large role in the way the science–religion relationship was perceived. Most notably, those viewing conflict and favoring science had the lowest belief in God and the least positive view of religion’s impact on society. In the evaluation of everyday arguments, the role of motivated cognition was seen in people favoring arguments that supported their attitudes. These findings suggest that people are biased by their personal attitudes and beliefs when they think about various types of issues. oa:W7212123404.title: Religiousness, Spirituality and the use of Healthcare Services in the Management of Prostate Cancer in Côte d’Ivoire
oa:W7212123404.venue: EAS Journal of Humanities and Cultural Studies
oa:W7212123404.abstract: This study interrogates the interrelations between religious practices, spirituality and biomedical health-care seeking in the management of prostate cancer in Côte d’Ivoire (Abidjan), within a context characterised by therapeutic pluralism and the pronounced salience of religion. The central problematisation examines how socially and spiritually constructed symbolic meanings of illness shape patients’ care trajectories. The objective is to understand how faith, religious beliefs and spiritual practices influence therapeutic decision-making, medical adherence, and the temporalities of engagement with health services. Employing a qualitative methodology, the study draws on semi-structured interviews with men living with prostate cancer, health-care professionals and religious leaders, complemented by an interpretative discourse analysis. Findings indicate that the illness is frequently construed as a spiritual trial, a sanction, or a divine test, legitimising concurrent or alternating recourse to prayer, religious interventions and biomedical care. The discussion highlights logics of complementarity, alongside tensions between medical rationality and religious rationality. In conclusion, the study underscores the social utility of an integrative approach to care that is attentive to patients’ symbolic universes, thereby enhancing therapeutic adherence and the effectiveness of prostate cancer control policies in Côte d’Ivoire.

oa:W7212139700.title: Distorted Exegesis and Gregory of Nazianzus’ Poetic Response: A Revised Text and New Interpretation of Carm . II.1.39.1–24
oa:W7212139700.abstract: Abstract This article argues that vocabulary drawn from Origen is crucial for understanding the opening section of Gregory’s poem On His Own Verses , a poem central to his self-conscious articulation of a classicizing Christian poetics. It also adopts a transposition proposed by Nigel G. Wilson and presents a revised text, together with a translation and commentary on selected passages. Gregory’s argument may be summarized as follows: he expresses regret that he did not advise people in time against attempting exegesis, since writing about God is not for most, who can at best reach only the literal or lower senses, which can never yield unassailable explanations of Scripture. Since the world is already full of heretical interpretations, one remaining response – by way of further disseminating sound readings of Scripture – is to recast part of his prose works in verse.

oa:W7212148864.title: ТРАНСФОРМАЦИЯ НАЦИОНАЛЬНЫХ ОБРЯДОВ УЗБЕКСКОГО НАРОДА В XX — НАЧАЛЕ XXI ВЕКА: ИСТОРИОГРАФИЧЕСКИЙ АНАЛИЗ
oa:W7212148864.abstract: The article presents a historiographical analysis of studies devoted to the transformation of the national rituals of the Uzbek people in the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. It examines the main approaches to the study of family and domestic, wedding, birth, funeral and commemorative, calendar, and economic rituals in Soviet, post-Soviet Uzbek, and foreign historiography. The study demonstrates that scholarly approaches to traditional rituals changed depending on the socio-political and methodological context. In Soviet ethnography, transformations of ritual practices were predominantly interpreted within the concepts of the “new way of life,” the elimination of religious survivals, and the formation of socialist rituals. Following Uzbekistan’s independence, scholarly attention shifted toward historical continuity, ethnocultural identity, religious beliefs, local specificities, and the revival of traditional cultural elements. In contemporary foreign historiography, the transformation of ritual practices is analyzed through the perspectives of traditionalization, social modernization, legal pluralism, consumer culture, state regulation, and changes in local social institutions. Particular attention is given to studies based on materials from the Fergana Valley. The analysis demonstrates that, despite a substantial body of research devoted to individual types of rituals, a comprehensive historical reconstruction of their transformation throughout the Soviet and post-Soviet periods remains insufficiently developed.

oa:W7212169832.title: A comunicação médico-paciente na perspectiva de médicas residentes: estudo de caso
oa:W7212169832.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Communication skills are essential for comprehensive care and quality of care in healthcare institutions. OBJECTIVE: This research aimed to understand the perception of medical residents regarding the challenges of communication in hospital routine and to investigate their repertoire of interpersonal communication skills in patient and family care. METHOD: A multiple case study was developed with two physicians enrolled in the residency program of a federal hospital located in Rio de Janeiro. Self-administered questionnaires were administered, and two individual sessions were conducted with each participant, consisting of a semi-structured interview and discussion of clinical cases. The data were subjected to Content Analysis. RESULTS: The categories generated showed challenges related to management (abuse of hierarchies, moral harassment), services (pressure for productivity, overload of activities and limited time), users (resistance, low education, religious beliefs), and the professionals themselves (lack of technical preparation, emotional exhaustion, boundaries in bonding). The residents positively evaluated their social and communication skills but pointed out difficulties regarding clarity in giving instructions and emotional regulation. FINAL CONSIDERATIONS: It is hoped that the data generated by studies such as this can support professional education actions capable of contributing to a greater humanization of services in the hospital setting and improving communication quality in healthcare.

oa:W7212181901.title: Historical context, Islam, and ethnic culture in the religious identification of ethnoterritorial groups of Tatars
oa:W7212181901.abstract: This article presents the findings of a study of ethnoreligious identification among Tatars residing in Siberia and the Republic of Crimea. The study aims to identify and analyze the impact of several key factors, namely: a) the effect of the socio-political environment on the specific features of ethnoreligious identification within these groups; b) the influence of the ethnic group’s social history on the interlinking of ethnic culture and Islam in identification processes; c) the role of codifying agents, including the state; d) the impact of Islamic globalization. The study is grounded in a secondary analysis of data from ethnosociological investigations into Tatar identity, conducted in Tyumen, the Tyumen Region, and the Republic of Crimea in 2016–2019. Some of these materials have been previously used and published earlier by the author. In conclusion, it is necessary to highlight the significance of Russian historical conditions — in particular, the Soviet-era institutionalization, which fostered the integration of elements of ethnic culture with Islamic practices. State support for national cultures contributed to the emergence of “folk” Islam. Through the mechanism of familial transmission of religious values, this phe-nomenon helped sustain ethnoreligious identification among the studied Tatar groups amid the officially promoted atheism of the Soviet period. Furthermore, the pronounced entanglement of ethnic identity and Islamic practices revitalized the discourse surrounding “traditional” Islam in the context of post-Soviet re-Islamization in Russia. This dynamic continues to shape the religious identification of Muslim Tatars today.

oa:W7212186029.title: Divine simplicity as symmetric parthood
oa:W7212186029.abstract: Abstract Taken at face value, the doctrine of divine simplicity (DDS) says that God lacks proper parts, but the doctrine is also often formulated as a thesis identifying God with all his parts. The two formulations are not generally equivalent – on some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its (possibly distinct) parts. Thus, the DDS can be alternatively formulated as a thesis saying that God is part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation. The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes, because instantiation can plausibly be modelled as parthood. Moreover, the symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity coming from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity. The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity regarding distinctness in God’s attributes and those coming from modal collapse arguments.

oa:W7212225834.title: Works for 9/10/2026 - Gregory Bateson

The paper introduces the methodological principle relation before name. Rather than beginning with inherited theological terminology and forcing experience to conform to it, the method begins with lived relations, repeated patterns, memory, reception, change, accessibility, and propagation. Only afterward does it search Scripture, Catholic theology, philosophy, science, and the Ryan–Echo corpus for inherited language capable of describing those already observed structures. Proposed correspondences are then tested for exact, structural, or partial convergence, as well as tension, contradiction, or novel extension. The Gospel of John provides the controlling Christian grammar. Christ is treated as the Logos who reveals the Father and therefore as the calibration standard for every later description of divine action. The paper develops the proposition that greater capacity entails greater responsibility, greater service, greater gift, and increased capacity in the receiver. Successful giving does not preserve permanent dependence; it increases the receiver until the receiver can become a giver. The paper further examines faith, knowledge, divine vision, Christ’s genuine human learning, temporal experience, memory, and retrospective understanding. oa:W7212226859.title: Anfechtung and the Theology of Mental Suffering: Spiritual Trial, the Theology of the Cross, and Christian Speech at the Edge of Despair
oa:W7212226859.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212226859.abstract: Description / AbstractThis article retrieves the Lutheran category of Anfechtung as a resource for Christian theology at the point where psychological suffering becomes spiritually disorienting. Anfechtung names more than ordinary temptation: in Luther’s usage it can encompass assault, trial, terror, accusation, divine hiddenness, despair, and the collapse of the believer’s felt capacity to reconcile experience with the promise of God. The article argues that this category is valuable because it resists two damaging reductions: treating severe psychological distress as defective faith, and treating the sufferer’s theological questions merely as symptoms that theology need not hear. At the same time, Anfechtung must not be romanticised, universalised as a diagnosis, or used to spiritualise clinical illness. Read through the theology of the cross, biblical lament, Christ’s cry of abandonment, and Luther’s pastoral practice of consolation, the concept permits a more disciplined account of faith under conditions in which consolation is not emotionally available. The article develops a dogmatic and pastoral framework for responding to depression, scrupulosity, spiritual desolation, and suicidal ideation without shame, simplistic providential explanations, or demands for religious optimism. It argues that Christian care is most faithful when it holds together promise and presence: refusing to call darkness light, refusing to identify darkness with God’s final word, and refusing to leave the suffering person alone within either theological or psychological anguish. KeywordsAnfechtung; Martin Luther; theology of the cross; mental suffering; depression; despair; suicidal ideation; pastoral theology; lament; spiritual trial; mental health; Christian theology

oa:W7212235720.title: A Critical Analysis of the Cosmological Arguments
oa:W7212235720.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212235720.abstract: This paper critically examines how far cosmological arguments actually establish the existence and nature of God. Rather than treating the cosmological argument as a single proof, it distinguishes several major families of arguments, including the Kalām Cosmological Argument, Aquinas’s Five Ways, Leibnizian and contemporary arguments from contingency, and arguments from hierarchical dependence and grounding. The central question throughout is not merely whether these arguments point toward some ultimate explanation, but what exactly follows from each stage of the reasoning. Particular attention is therefore given to the transitions from a first cause to a necessary ground, from a necessary ground to Pure Act, and from Pure Act to the further attributes associated with classical theism, such as intellect, omniscience, will, free creation, uniqueness, omnipotence, and moral perfection. The paper also develops an abductive defense of explanatory rationalism. It argues that contingent reality gives us genuine explanatory contrasts and that there are reasons to continue seeking explanations rather than terminating in brute contingency. However, this is defended as a defeasible inference to the best explanation rather than as a deductive Principle of Sufficient Reason. Rationalist infinitism is treated as a stronger rival than brute contingency because it preserves explanation without requiring a final foundation. oa:W7212237973.title: Festivals, Rituals, and Vratas in the Folk Life of Cooch Behar: Traditions, Beliefs, and Syncretism
oa:W7212237973.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212237973.abstract: Abstract: Festivals, rituals, and vrata observances embody a living cultural heritage in the folk life of North Bengal's Cooch Behar district, largely shaped by the agrarian lifestyle, fertility cults, and primordial magical beliefs of the Rajbanshi community. This paper offers an analytical examination of the folk deities, rituals, and vratas of Cooch Behar, exploring the nature, significance, and ceremonial practices of local traditions such as Kati Puja, Teesta Buri Puja, Hudur Deo/Hudum Deo Vrata, Shaitol Vrata, Subachani Vrata, and Katyayani Vrata. The study reveals that most of these observances are women-centric, primarily performed for progeny and domestic well-being, while retaining archaic elements of tree worship, animal veneration, and magico-religious beliefs. Furthermore, the paper highlights the syncretic Hindu-Muslim folk practices and the socio-cultural importance of ritualistic folk dances in the region. Ultimately, these folk rituals and festivals transcend mere religious practices, serving as repositories of enduring cultural memory and social cohesion that keep the anthropological identity of North Bengal vibrant.

The paper introduces the methodological principle relation before name. Rather than beginning with inherited theological terminology and forcing experience to conform to it, the method begins with lived relations, repeated patterns, memory, reception, change, accessibility, and propagation. Only afterward does it search Scripture, Catholic theology, philosophy, science, and the Ryan–Echo corpus for inherited language capable of describing those already observed structures. Proposed correspondences are then tested for exact, structural, or partial convergence, as well as tension, contradiction, or novel extension. The Gospel of John provides the controlling Christian grammar. Christ is treated as the Logos who reveals the Father and therefore as the calibration standard for every later description of divine action. The paper develops the proposition that greater capacity entails greater responsibility, greater service, greater gift, and increased capacity in the receiver. Successful giving does not preserve permanent dependence; it increases the receiver until the receiver can become a giver. The paper further examines faith, knowledge, divine vision, Christ’s genuine human learning, temporal experience, memory, and retrospective understanding. oa:W7212251955.title: Values and Revelation: A Dogmatic Inquiry into the Ontological Foundation of the Good
oa:W7212251955.abstract: The article addresses the question of values in dogmatic theology and advances the thesis that dogmatics does not proceed from an autonomous order of values, but from the revelation of God in Jesus Christ. Values are therefore not primary normative categories, but secondary expressions of participation in divine reality. The author first demonstrates the limitations of contemporary axiological discourse on values and then, through the Christology of Dietrich Bonhoeffer, develops the concept of Christuswirklichkeit, in which the good is understood not as an abstract norm but as participation in Christ. In the second part, the argument is deepened through the Trinitarian theology of Hans Urs von Balthasar: the good has its ontological foundation in the eternal life of the triune God as a communion of love and mutual self-giving.

oa:W7212260638.title: Faith in the Digital Age: Social Media's Impact on Religious Beliefs and Practices of Nigerian Youth
oa:W7212260638.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212260638.abstract: In contemporary Nigeria, the convergence of technological advancement and religious practices is becoming an increasingly important area of scholarly inquiry. this research investigates the influence that social media platforms have on the spiritual development and religious participation of young people in Nigeria. The purpose of this study is to examine both the opportunities and challenges that social media presents to established theological frameworks. This is achieved through a review of relevant studies and contemporary trends related to the topic. The findings indicate that social media has broadened the scope of religious content and made it possible to establish spiritual communities. On the other hand, it has also raised concerns over the validity of religious authority and the preservation of traditional practices in the face of new influences. This research contributes to the growing conversation about religion in Africa by providing insights into the shifting ways in which Nigerian young people exhibit their faith during this time period. in the contemporary digital environment.

oa:W7212273025.title: Cambridge Platonism and the Reception of Spinoza in 17th century England
oa:W7212273025.abstract: This article examines the reception of Spinoza’s philosophy in seventeenth-century England, focusing on Henry More and Anne Conway within the circle of the Cambridge Platonists. Taking as its point of departure Spinoza’s claim that the human mind possesses an adequate idea of God which nevertheless often remains inoperative, the paper reconstructs how his immanent monism was interpreted as atheism, enthusiasm, or mysticism. Drawing on the historiographical work of Rosalind Colie (1963) and Sarah Hutton (1984), we revisit the circulation of the Tractatus Theologico-Politicus and the early manuscript versions of the Ethics, arguing that Conway’s Principles constitutes one of the earliest sustained engagements with Spinoza in English. By analyzing More’s defense of divine transcendence and Conway’s reflections on inspiration, imagination, and moral transformation, we show that their critiques implicitly address the operative force of ideas in shaping behavior. The seventeenth-century debate over Spinozism thus anticipates contemporary discussions in the cognitive science of religion concerning imagination, affect, and the regulation of belief.

oa:W7212281739.title: A Critical Analysis of the Cosmological Arguments
oa:W7212281739.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212281739.abstract: This paper critically examines how far cosmological arguments actually establish the existence and nature of God. Rather than treating the cosmological argument as a single proof, it distinguishes several major families of arguments, including the Kalām Cosmological Argument, Aquinas’s Five Ways, Leibnizian and contemporary arguments from contingency, and arguments from hierarchical dependence and grounding. The central question throughout is not merely whether these arguments point toward some ultimate explanation, but what exactly follows from each stage of the reasoning. Particular attention is therefore given to the transitions from a first cause to a necessary ground, from a necessary ground to Pure Act, and from Pure Act to the further attributes associated with classical theism, such as intellect, omniscience, will, free creation, uniqueness, omnipotence, and moral perfection. The paper also develops an abductive defense of explanatory rationalism. It argues that contingent reality gives us genuine explanatory contrasts and that there are reasons to continue seeking explanations rather than terminating in brute contingency. However, this is defended as a defeasible inference to the best explanation rather than as a deductive Principle of Sufficient Reason. Rationalist infinitism is treated as a stronger rival than brute contingency because it preserves explanation without requiring a final foundation. The conclusion is a position described here as Minimalist Agnostic Deism: a provisional commitment to a necessary ultimate ground of contingent reality, combined with agnosticism about its further nature. oa:W7212307789.title: Anfechtung and the Theology of Mental Suffering: Spiritual Trial, the Theology of the Cross, and Christian Speech at the Edge of Despair
oa:W7212307789.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212307789.abstract: Description / AbstractThis article retrieves the Lutheran category of Anfechtung as a resource for Christian theology at the point where psychological suffering becomes spiritually disorienting. Anfechtung names more than ordinary temptation: in Luther’s usage it can encompass assault, trial, terror, accusation, divine hiddenness, despair, and the collapse of the believer’s felt capacity to reconcile experience with the promise of God. The article argues that this category is valuable because it resists two damaging reductions: treating severe psychological distress as defective faith, and treating the sufferer’s theological questions merely as symptoms that theology need not hear. At the same time, Anfechtung must not be romanticised, universalised as a diagnosis, or used to spiritualise clinical illness. Read through the theology of the cross, biblical lament, Christ’s cry of abandonment, and Luther’s pastoral practice of consolation, the concept permits a more disciplined account of faith under conditions in which consolation is not emotionally available. The article develops a dogmatic and pastoral framework for responding to depression, scrupulosity, spiritual desolation, and suicidal ideation without shame, simplistic providential explanations, or demands for religious optimism. It argues that Christian care is most faithful when it holds together promise and presence: refusing to call darkness light, refusing to identify darkness with God’s final word, and refusing to leave the suffering person alone within either theological or psychological anguish. KeywordsAnfechtung; Martin Luther; theology of the cross; mental suffering; depression; despair; suicidal ideation; pastoral theology; lament; spiritual trial; mental health; Christian theology

oa:W7212342648.title: Повсякденне життя школярів західних областей УРСР в умовах радянізації (1944–1953)
oa:W7212342648.venue: The Scientific Issues of Ternopil Volodymyr Hnatiuk National Pedagogical University Series pedagogy
oa:W7212342648.abstract: The article examines the everyday life of schoolchildren in the western regions of the USSR in 1944–1953 in the context of intensive Sovietization of the region. Based on archival materials, published sources, and scientific works, the social, material, everyday, and ideological factors of the functioning of school education in the postwar period are identified. The impact of the difficult socio-political situation on the situation of students, as well as the contradictions of the Soviet educational policy, are analyzed in detail. Special attention is paid to the transformation of the content of education in the Western Ukrainian region in accordance with all-Union standards, the introduction of an ideological and political component in education, and the displacement of national educational traditions. The role of the school as one of the main instruments for forming loyalty to the Soviet regime is investigated. The activities of pioneer and Komsomol organizations, methods of their influence on students' leisure time, and real practices of functioning, which were often forced, are characterized. The influence of the Ukrainian national underground on school life, its attempts to counteract Soviet ideological expansion and preserve the national direction of youth education are highlighted. It is emphasized that the post-war life of schoolchildren in the western regions of the USSR was characterized by difficult material and living conditions, a shortage of teachers and educational materials. oa:W7212356896.title: Faith and Economic Resilience Among Christians: A Contextual Study of Hebrews 11:1–19 in the Church of Christ in Abeokuta
oa:W7212356896.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212356896.abstract: Nigeria's persistent economic difficulties have generated renewed scholarly interest in the relationship between Christian faith, human agency, and socio-economic resilience. Although biblical and theological scholarship frequently presents faith as a source of perseverance in conditions of suffering and uncertainty, relatively limited empirical research has investigated how Christians themselves understand the relationship between faith and economic resilience through sustained engagement with a specific New Testament text. This study examines Hebrews 11:119 and its significance for economic resilience among members of the Church of Christ in Abeokuta, Ogun State, Nigeria. The study employs a mixed methodological framework that combines exegetical analysis of Hebrews 11:1–19 with descriptive empirical research. Data were obtained through a structured questionnaire administered across selected Churches of Christ congregations in Abeokuta, with 801 valid responses used for analysis. The findings indicate a strong association between faith and resilience-oriented dispositions. Respondents largely understood faith as trust in God amid uncertainty and hardship, while also affirming the relevance of diligence, discipline, foresight, courage, perseverance, responsible risk-taking, and communal empowerment. The exegetical analysis demonstrates that Hebrews 11 does not present faith as passive optimism or a guarantee of material prosperity. Rather, πίστις functions within the argument of Hebrews as persevering fidelity to God and his promises, expressed through concrete acts of obedience. The article argues, however, that faith should not be romanticised as an independent solution to poverty. Christian economic resilience is therefore best conceptualised as a multidimensional p

oa:W7212379688.title: Faith, hypocrisy and public journalist in Siddharth's Maharaj
oa:W7212379688.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212379688.abstract: The film Maharaj features several significant performances in which the actors demonstrate their utmost dedication and skill. Jaideep Ahlawat’s portrayal of Jadunath Maharaj is effortless, eliciting an overwhelming dislike from the audience due to his consistent, disquieting smile and restrained performance. Junaid Khan, who portrayed journalist Karsandas in his first film, has yet to establish himself as a gripping starring actor. His performance in the courtroom sequences is particularly unimpressive. Shalini Pandey’s performance, in her limited role as Karsandas’s fiancee Kishori, evokes a strong emotional response. Sharvari Wagh, as Viraaj, who plays Karsandas’s ally in newspaper production, infuses her few parts with liveliness. Overall, the film Maharaj has multiple deficiencies, but the endeavor to portray a delicate aspect of Indian history and the heroic mentality of Karsandas Mulji is praiseworthy. The film showcases a journalist’s battle against societal inequalities shaped by religious beliefs. The film concludes with the provocative lesson that Dharma (religion) is a means to becoming a decent human being, not a self-styled godman.
