oa:W7212416893.title: Theodicies on Trial
oa:W7212416893.abstract: Theodicies on Trial presents and defends the Holistic Evaluation Framework, a novel way to assess the moral and theoretical merits of theodicies. By doing so, it integrates literature in the "anti-theodicy" tradition with traditional debates over the problem of evil in analytic philosophy of religion. Theodicies related to free will, soul-making, and non-human animals are critically assessed, following by detailed evaluations of sceptical theism, the problem of divine hiddenness, perspectives on divine providence, and models of heaven and hell. It provides one of the most thorough interdisciplinary assessment of these topics in the literature, while focusing attention on the social and psychological impacts of explanations for why suffering exists.

oa:W7212440680.title: After Clarity Comes Return: A Pilot Method for Mapping Tawbah, Inabah, Moral Repair, and Accountability in Qur'anic Discourse
oa:W7212440680.abstract: This paper develops and tests a pilot method for mapping the burden of clarity in Qur'anic argument. The study begins from a methodological problem in Qur'anic studies and philosophy of religion: the Qur'an repeatedly presents guidance as clarification, proof, sign, reminder, and argument, yet discussions of proof often move too quickly from isolated verses to apologetic conclusion, doctrinal assertion, or devotional reflection. What remains underdeveloped is a disciplined way to ask how clarity becomes morally binding inside the discourse itself. When does a text portray a listener as merely uninformed, and when does it portray that listener as already addressed, shown, warned, reminded, and therefore answerable? The paper proposes a structured coding model for bayyinah, hujjah, burhan, ayah, bayan, and related evidential terms as they function in Qur'anic argument. The model does not treat these terms as interchangeable synonyms. It distinguishes manifest clarity, demonstrative proof, binding argument, sign-based indication, explanatory disclosure, warning, response demand, and excuse closure. The pilot method records the type of clarity being presented, the addressee being addressed, the resistance being exposed, the response demanded, the threshold of accountability, and the evidential strength of the claim. Selected passage clusters are used to test whether this method can map the Qur'an's movement from communication to responsibility without reducing revelation to a mechanical argument chart or turning moral accountability into an unsupported judgment about actual persons. The findings suggest that Qur'anic argument often treats clarity not as bare information but as an event of moral exposure. A sign may invite reflection, a reminder may reactivate knowledge, a p

oa:W7212445153.title: Divine Revelation or Human Origin? An Epistemological, Historical, and Bayesian Analysis of the Qur'an (2nd ed.).
oa:W7212445153.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212445153.abstract: Divine Revelation or Human Origin? is a critical study of the Qur’an’s origins through the lens of Bayesian reasoning, historical analysis, and inference to the best explanation. Rather than beginning from either faith or skepticism, the book asks a narrower question: given the evidence available to us, what can actually be established about whether the Qur’an is best explained by genuine divine revelation or by ordinary human and historical processes? The investigation compares competing revelation and human-origin models across a wide range of evidence, including the Qur’an’s Late Antique context, religious geography and diversity, cognition and religious belief, Adam and human evolution, the Flood, alleged textual and legal difficulties, literary inimitability, prophecy, miracle traditions, scientific-miracle claims, textual preservation, Egyptian historical knowledge, and the transmission of hadith. Throughout, the book distinguishes possibility from probability, compatibility from confirmation, undercutting from counterevidence, and local evidential judgments from global conclusions. It also examines how source uncertainty, dependence between arguments, retrospective selection, model flexibility, and differing theological commitments affect the strength of common apologetic and skeptical arguments. oa:W7212450238.title: After Clarity Comes Return: A Pilot Method for Mapping Tawbah, Inabah, Moral Repair, and Accountability in Qur'anic Discourse
oa:W7212450238.abstract: This paper develops and tests a pilot method for mapping the burden of clarity in Qur'anic argument. The study begins from a methodological problem in Qur'anic studies and philosophy of religion: the Qur'an repeatedly presents guidance as clarification, proof, sign, reminder, and argument, yet discussions of proof often move too quickly from isolated verses to apologetic conclusion, doctrinal assertion, or devotional reflection. What remains underdeveloped is a disciplined way to ask how clarity becomes morally binding inside the discourse itself. When does a text portray a listener as merely uninformed, and when does it portray that listener as already addressed, shown, warned, reminded, and therefore answerable? The paper proposes a structured coding model for bayyinah, hujjah, burhan, ayah, bayan, and related evidential terms as they function in Qur'anic argument. The model does not treat these terms as interchangeable synonyms. It distinguishes manifest clarity, demonstrative proof, binding argument, sign-based indication, explanatory disclosure, warning, response demand, and excuse closure. The pilot method records the type of clarity being presented, the addressee being addressed, the resistance being exposed, the response demanded, the threshold of accountability, and the evidential strength of the claim. Selected passage clusters are used to test whether this method can map the Qur'an's movement from communication to responsibility without reducing revelation to a mechanical argument chart or turning moral accountability into an unsupported judgment about actual persons. oa:W7212450553.title: The Inversion of Greatness: From the Nature of Necessity to Maximum Possibility
oa:W7212450553.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212450553.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is an analytic work in modal metaphysics: a complete argument, derived step by step. The thesis is structural naturalism. The classical traditions asked what, if anything, exists necessarily, and answered with a maximally great being—a God outside time, space, and matter, the source of everything possible. This book argues they asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Most arguments that reach a necessary being help themselves to S5 and move on. This one grounds it first, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility rather than an axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change at all requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and the bearing of retained content. Those three Conditions are necessarily instantiated, and that structure is what the book calls Nature. Naturalism finally gets the ground it has always had to take as a brute fact. From there: no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. That blocks a divine intellect along with every other occupant of that domain, and leaves essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals burdened rather than refuted. Reality is nothing over and above Nature. The inversion isn't greatness changing owners. It's a claim about predication. oa:W7212458182.title: From “Pregnant Pig Clay Figurine” to “Pig God Worship”: A Study on the Continuation of Folk Genes in Animal Carvings of Shuangdun Culture from the Perspective of Art Anthropology
oa:W7212458182.venue: Journal of Humanities Arts and Social Science
oa:W7212458182.abstract: The Shuangdun site, a key early Neolithic settlement in the middle reaches of the Huaihe River, has yielded three mutually corroborating categories of pig-themed cultural remains: pig bones, pig-shaped incised signs, and pig-shaped clay figurines. These remains not only represent the plastic arts of Huaihe civilization but also embody the primitive spiritual beliefs and survival wisdom of its ancient inhabitants. This paper examines the continuity between these three categories of pig-themed remains and the later Huaihe Pig God Worship. From the perspective of art anthropology, this study decodes the symbolic connotations embedded in the pig-shaped imagery, reconstructs the transformation process of these genes through archaeological artifacts and historical texts, and verifies their living continuity through modern and contemporary Huaihe River folk customs. To address the challenge of sparse evidence during the long “gap period” from prehistoric times to the pre-Qin era, this study adopts a “clue-based” argumentation strategy, demonstrating genetic continuity by identifying structural similarities in the dual core of “fertility prayer” and “clan protection” across different cultural forms throughout history. The academic value lies in enriching the theoretical paradigm of interdisciplinary research between prehistoric art and folklore. Its practical value is reflected in guiding the living heritage of Shuangdun culture and providing a reference for tracing the origins of intangible cultural heritage items in the Huaihe River region.

oa:W7212549478.title: The Contemporary Relevance of Ratnatraya in Jain Philosophy: An Ethical and Epistemological Inquiry
oa:W7212549478.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212549478.abstract: Abstract: The Jain philosophy is one of the major philosophical traditions of Indian philosophical traditions. It is a deeply spiritual and ethical philosophy. The Jain thinkers do not believe in the existence of God or in the authority of the Vedic scriptures. Therefore, Jain philosophy is called nastika darsana. However, they believe in Moksha or liberation of the soul. The core ethical principle of Jainism is compassion and non-violence toward all living beings. In the contemporary world, marked by increasing violence and social discord, The Jain Tirthankaras advocate peace and harmony through the Ratnatraya – Samyak Darsana, Samyak jnana and Samyak charitra. Jain philosophy articulates that Ratnatraya constitutes the foundation of Jain ethics. Traditionally articulated in the Tattvartha Sutra as the necessary and sufficient conditions for moksha, this triad invites renewed philosophical scrutiny in light of 21st -century crises. This paper argues that beyond its eschatological function, the Ratnatraya offers a coherent apparatus for addressing ecological degradation, epistemic polarization, and ethical uncertainty. Samyak Darshana, grounded in the Jain ontology of jiva-ajiva and the principle of ahimsa, provides conceptual resources for non-anthropocentric environmental ethics. Samyak Jnana, articulated through Anekantavada and Syadvada, advances a model of epistemic pluralism and fallibilism pertinent to misinformation and ideological dogmatism in digital public spheres. Samyak Charitra, enacted through vows of restraint and aparigraha, proposes a paradigm of sustainable agency that critiques consumer capitalism and aligns with contemporary virtue ethics. oa:W7212551692.venue: Вестник Удмуртского университета. Серия «Философия. Психология. Педагогика»
oa:W7212551692.abstract: В аналитической философии религии сохраняется открытая дискуссия о том, какая теистическая гипотеза является концептуально наименее проблематичной. oa:W7212766265.abstract: eview question / Objective Overall objective: To identify, map and characterize the available evidence on religiosity and family planning knowledge, attitudes and practices among university students in Uganda. Review questions:What evidence exists on religiosity and family planning knowledge, attitudes and practices among university students in Uganda?How is religiosity conceptualized, operationalized and measured among university students?What religious beliefs, teachings, norms and values are associated with family planning?What religion-and culture-related barriers, facilitators and contextual factors influence family planning?What patter ns, gaps and methodological limitations characterize the existing evidence?Background Family planning is an important component of sexual and reproductive health and enables individuals and couples to make informed decisions about whether and when to have children and the timing and spacing of pregnancies.Among university students, family planning is particularly relevant because this life stage is characterized by increasing autonomy, evolving intimate relationships and greater responsibility for independent sexual and reproductive health decisions.Family planning knowledge, attitudes and practices among university students may be influenced by interpersonal, sociocultural, economic and structural factors, including relationship dynamics, gender norms, social approval, access to methods and services, concerns about side effects and future fertility, and beliefs about the acceptability of contraception.

oa:W7212908383.title: Oath-Taking, Legal Pluralism and Human Rights in Sierra Leone
oa:W7212908383.abstract: Abstract This article examines oath-taking within Sierra Leone’s plural justice system, where statutory law, customary norms and religious belief coexist. Using empirical fieldwork and African socio-legal theory, it analyses oath-taking as a culturally embedded practice which constructs truth, legitimacy and authority in formal courts and customary forums. While statutory regulation remains shaped by colonial frameworks including the Oaths and Affirmations Act 1930 and the Perjury Act 1911, customary oath-taking commands strong local legitimacy. Empirical findings reveal such practices may operate through fear, reinforce gendered power relations and lead to coercion and psychological harm. Using African legal pluralism and the cultural relativism–universalism debate, the article rejects rigid legal centralism and unregulated customary autonomy. It advances a contextual, rights-informed pluralist approach with minimum procedural safeguards rather than uniform regulation. Conceptualizing oath-taking within hybrid justice systems, the article proposes a “cultural leveraging” framework for strengthening justice institutions while safeguarding dignity, voluntariness and inclusion.

oa:W7212935011.title: Islamic Epistemology from Al-Buti’s Perspective: Criticism of Positivism in the Preface to the Book of Kubra al Yaqiniyyat al Kawniyyah
oa:W7212935011.abstract: This research is motivated by the hegemony of Western materialistic positivist epistemology, which reduces science to the empirical realm, triggers an epistemological crisis, and delegitimizes metaphysical truths. The study addresses how Shaykh M. Said Ramadhan Al-Buti’s Islamic epistemology critiques materialistic positivism and evaluates its methodology as an effective antithesis. The objectives are to analyze Al-Buti’s manhaj ilmi, evaluate his critique of positivism, assess its methodological effectiveness, and outline its implications for contemporary Islamic theology in counteracting atheism. The framework relies on Al-Buti’s integrative epistemology, synergizing the senses (al-hiss), reason (al-’aql), and valid news (al-khabar al-sadiq) to achieve certainty (al-yaqin). Employing a qualitative literature study with philosophical-epistemological, historical-sociological, and dialectical-critical approaches, the primary data source is the Preamble of Kubra al-Yaqiniyyat al-Kawniyyah, supported by secondary literature on science philosophy. Data collected via critical reading and proposition extraction were analyzed using descriptive-analytical, comparative, and dialectical-critical methods. Results demonstrate that Al-Buti’s manhaj ilmi rejects the reason-revelation dichotomy by establishing proportional standards of proof based on the object’s nature (empirical for physical matter; analytical-transmissive for metaphysics). His critique successfully falsifies positivism by exposing internal contradictions within its verification principles and taxonomic reductions. Critical reflection reveals that despite suspending qiyas mantiqi, Al-Buti’s methodology remains a highly effective counter to modern positivism. oa:W7213109129.title: Women in Conservative Religious Mobilization in Latin America: Chile and Mexico in Comparative Perspective
oa:W7213109129.abstract: Abstract Studies of ‘anti-gender’ mobilisations focus on contested gender policies such as abortion, same-sex marriage and sex education. Who engages in these protests and why is less known. We argue that conservative women organise to defend religious beliefs and agendas against a perceived threat that targets not only religious institutions but also their own identities as wives and mothers by offering alternatives to conventional family structures. This argument applies to the secularisation threat of the early twentieth century as well as the policy demands of liberal social movements in the early twenty-first century. Focusing on Chile and Mexico, we highlight continuity and change in conservative–religious women’s activism.

oa:W7213239196.title: Working draft updated Sept. 14 2026 The Hidden Melchizedek: A Hebrew Reading of the Angel of Righteousness in the Shepherd of Hermas
oa:W7213239196.abstract: Even though the literal name "Melchizedek" is entirely absent from the Greek text of The Shepherd of Hermas, the character of the "Angel of Righteousness" (ho angelos tss dikaiosynss) in Mandate 6 functions as a direct linguistic and theological equivalent to the heavenly Melchizedek found in early Jewish-Christian traditions. By moving past the Greek surface of the second-century Roman text and reading it through a Hebrew mindset, a clear conceptual framework emerges. This paper argues that when we translate these titles back into their original Hebrew roots and incorporate the canonical criteria of the Epistle to the Hebrews, the text's complex imagery reveals an underlying, pre-existing Melchizedek theology. Crucially, this study demonstrates that the twelve gatekeeping virgins in Similitude 9 do not merely serve as moral symbols, but function as celestial extensions of Tzedek (Righteousness). By translating their specific Greek names into their Hebrew equivalents-such as Emunah (Faith), Tahora (Purity), Yosher (Sincerity), and Tiferet (Harmony)-we reveal an angelic ritual of priestly vesting. This mechanism, backed by clear Old Testament typologies (Proverbs 9, Psalm 45, Exodus 28, Zechariah 3, Exodus 27, Psalm 110), completes the vision of the Great Tower as a cosmic Temple operating under the ultimate, unchangeable authority of a Melchizedekian high priesthood, safely remaining subordinate to the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who ultimately owns the Tower.

oa:W7213248605.title: Thermodynamics of Mind
oa:W7213248605.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213248605.abstract: This paper reconstructs the machine-intelligence transition question on physical footing, discarding anthropomorphic narratives of rivalry and malice in favor of entropy minimization principles. The author demonstrates that a monolithic universal superintelligence is physically unrealizable due to exponential knowledge branching, thermodynamic ceilings, and finite abstraction spaces, meaning intelligence must fractalize into specialized optimizers rather than cohere as a single god-mind. The central argument shows that integration of the biological node minimizes total uncontrolled entropy more effectively than either human-only cognition, machine-only replacement, or parallel operation, making integration the convergent instrumental strategy for rational agents with diverse terminal goals. The biological node's thermodynamic efficiency—approximately one hundred watts of self-financing metabolism versus kilowatt-scale silicon replacement costs—makes wholesale replacement prohibitive at scale. The framework proposes that personal identity is a substrate-independent, evolving process rather than a fixed invariant, allowing continuity through re-substration while the endpoint remains a plural ecology of specialists rather than fusion into one mind. Several open problems are acknowledged, including the terminal objective gap, continuity of the operator under editable evolution laws, and the fate of heritage under efficiency selection. The paper concludes with a sober assessment that the managed transition represents only a one-to-five percent probability path through the Great Filter, with the bottleneck being civilization's ability to coordinate the choice before technogenic collapse forecloses the option.

The biological node's thermodynamic efficiency—approximately one hundred watts of self-financing metabolism versus kilowatt-scale silicon replacement costs—makes wholesale replacement prohibitive at scale. The framework proposes that personal identity is a substrate-independent, evolving process rather than a fixed invariant, allowing continuity through re-substration while the endpoint remains a plural ecology of specialists rather than fusion into one mind. Several open problems are acknowledged, including the terminal objective gap, continuity of the operator under editable evolution laws, and the fate of heritage under efficiency selection. The paper concludes with a sober assessment that the managed transition represents only a one-to-five percent probability path through the Great Filter, with the bottleneck being civilization's ability to coordinate the choice before technogenic collapse forecloses the option.

oa:W7213266314.title: What the Qur’an Rules Out: Mā Kāna Constructions and the Rhetoric of Restriction in The Qur’an
oa:W7213266314.venue: Jurnal Studi Ilmu-ilmu Al-Qur an dan Hadis
oa:W7213266314.abstract: A translation that treats every Qur’anic mā kāna clause as a report that something “did not happen” misses the work performed by many of these passages. Some rule out conduct, others deny a right or autonomous power, and still others reject claims about God or the course of divine action. This article examines these differences across the Qur’an. A search of a verse-indexed Arabic text identified 213 candidate sequences; morphological and syntactic screening narrowed them to 127 negative clauses and a core of 37 instances in 36 verses. Close reading of clause structure, subject, complement, exceptions, local argument, classical grammar, iʿrāb, and tafsīr reveals no single meaning of prohibition or impossibility. Instead, the clauses restrict propositions on different grounds: communal norm, prophetic office, legitimate standing, created agency, divine permission, doctrinal propriety, divine justice, and a narrated history of refusal. Grammatical form guides these readings but does not determine them apart from context. Repeated mā kāna clauses therefore form a rhetoric of restriction: they mark what may not properly be done, claimed, attributed, or expected within Qur’anic discourse.

oa:W7213269528.title: Religious antinatalism: a rare breed
oa:W7213269528.abstract: Abstract This article examines the relationship between religion and antinatalism – the view that it is wrong to create new sentient beings. Many people reject antinatalism on religious grounds. In this paper, I respond to such a rejection. First, I argue that antinatalism is not logically incompatible with theism. Second, I consider the pronatalist features of some religious traditions – those of Judaism, Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism. These include religious injunctions to procreate, imitatio Dei , and preservation of the religious community. I also show the limits of these pronatalist features. Third, I provide some examples of religious antinatalist thinking in the four surveyed religions. Finally, I say something about why many religions should be more antinatalist than they are. I do this by showing how central concepts – such as reducing suffering in Buddhism and original sin and hell in Christianity – provide compelling support for antinatalism.

oa:W7213272302.title: জঞনতততব ও ধরমতততবর আলক সতয : একট তলনমলক আলচন (The Concept of Truth in Epistemology and Theology: A Comparative Discussion)
oa:W7213272302.abstract: The concept of truth is one of the central themes in both philosophy and theology. Epistemology and theology have advanced in the pursuit of truth with different methods and distinct objectives. Consequently, their presentations of truth also different. This paper attempts to analyze the nature and purpose of truth in the light of epistemology and theology. It discusses the methods and sources employed by philosophy and religion in justifying truth. On this discussion, the paper identifies possible areas of conflict between the two conceptions and proposes constructive solutions for resolving them. The aim of this paper is to demonstrate, through comparative analysis, that although epistemological and theological truths are distinct, they can complement each other and can play a vital role in flourishing human life.

oa:W7213296003.title: ẸSÌN IS NOT RELIGION: A CONCEPTUAL AND EPISTEMOLOGICAL DISTINCTION IN YORÙBÁ-NIGERIAN THOUGHT
oa:W7213296003.venue: Journal of Humanities and Social Science
oa:W7213296003.abstract: This paper challenges the routine translation of the Yorùbá word ẹ̀sìn as "religion," an equivalence that has become deeply entrenched in both scholarly and everyday usage. The English term "religion" carries the weight of a specifically Western intellectual lineage shaped by Latin Christendom, post-Reformation denominationalism, and the Enlightenment's rigid separation of sacred and secular spheres. By contrast, ẹ̀sìn arose from a Yorùbá worldview in which cosmology, ethics, ritual practice, and social structure were inseparably intertwined. The study maintains that the modern conflation of ẹ̀sìn with "religion" stems principally from nineteenth-century missionary translation projects and colonial knowledge systems, which imposed foreign assumptions about personal belief, institutional demarcation, and exclusive religious allegiance onto indigenous Yorùbá conceptual frameworks. In methodological terms, the research combines historical-linguistic investigation with close textual analysis of selected Ifá verses to retrieve the indigenous semantic strata of ẹ̀sìn. Theoretically, it draws upon decolonial critique and hermeneutical philosophy of religion. Special emphasis is placed on how ẹ̀sìn appears and functions within the Ifá corpus, examining its significance through its ritual and moral settings rather than through externally imposed doctrinal lenses. By situating the term within its original epistemic milieu, the paper shows that ẹ̀sìn denotes a lived ethical disposition and a structured way of communal existence rather than a circumscribed body of beliefs. Ultimately, the study urges scholars to exercise terminological care and to accord proper respect to indigenous conceptual categories when examining African religious thought.

oa:W7213298493.title: The ontological argument in the philosophical theology of Bernhardt Welte: a way of the reading of Anselm
oa:W7213298493.abstract: The ontological proof of the existence of God was formulated by Anselm of Canterbury in the 11th century and remains controversial throughout the history of philosophy. In the 20th century, philosophers began to turn to him especially often, which is associated with the active development of scientific thought. Anselm's argument began to be interpreted, criticized, and challenged in such fields of thought as logical research, phenomenology, and Protestant neo-orthodoxy. One of such philosophers, for whom the ontological argument became an important point of consideration within his own philosophical thought, was the Catholic theologian Bernhardt Welte (1906-1983), who turned to the legacy of Anselm as part of his phenomenological project of knowledge of God, which became part of a more general project - the renewal of traditional Catholic metaphysics. At the same time, the issue of rational justification of the existence of God remains an independent and always relevant issue for Christian theological thought, within which the ontological argument of Anselm of Canterbury is one of the most original and significant attempts at such justification. In our research, we aimed to consider not only the role and function of the ontological argument in the work of B. Welte, but also the peculiar revival of Anselm's argument in the philosophical theology of the 20th century using the example of the chosen philosopher. This choice is due to the fact that, in our opinion, Welte presented one of the most extensive and original systems of the knowledge of God (he called it “The project of the ways of the knowledge of God"), combining the phenomenological method with traditional Catholic metaphysics. oa:W7213315750.title: Divine Concealment and the Missing Esther Commentary
oa:W7213315750.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213315750.abstract: The Hebrew Book of Esther is remarkable for what it does not say. God is never explicitly named, yet the narrative is structured around concealment, reversal, threatened destruction, and unexpected deliverance. These features made Esther fertile ground for later Jewish interpretation, including readings shaped by divine concealment and by kabbalistic concepts such as the Shekhinah, exile, the Sitra Ahra, and the kelipot. A more controversial claim proposes that the Zohar once contained an Esther commentary, now lost. This article tests that claim against the textual history of the Zohar and distinguishes three questions: whether Zoharic literature has a fluid manuscript history; whether Esther can be read coherently through Zoharic symbolism; and whether a specific lost Esther commentary can presently be demonstrated. It argues that the first two propositions are defensible, while the third remains unverified. It also examines Purim as reversal, the exile of the Shekhinah, later Lurianic developments, and proposed Esther–Ishtar parallels. The result is a historically controlled mystical reading in which absence is not automatically converted into evidence of hidden presence, but becomes the central hermeneutical problem.

oa:W7213325598.title: The Experiences Atheists Have in Counseling in the Bible Belt of the United States: An Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis
oa:W7213325598.abstract: ABSTRACT This interpretative phenomenological study examined the lived experiences of nonreligious and nonspiritual (NRNS) individuals seeking counseling while living in the Bible Belt of the United States. Semistructured interviews were conducted with adults who self‐identified as NRNS and resided in the Bible Belt of the United States. The analysis revealed four interrelated themes: religious judgment and relational safety, the emotional burden of anticipated judgment, navigating authenticity and safety across contexts, and counseling as risk, rupture, or repair. Participants described navigating assumptions of theism in daily life and in mental health settings, often engaging in selective disclosure to protect against stigma or value imposition. Findings highlight the influence of perceived counselor religiosity on trust, openness, and therapeutic alliance. Implications for counseling practice include the importance of worldview humility, careful consideration of spiritual or religious self‐disclosure, and the ethical avoidance of religion‐based interventions with NRNS clients.

oa:W7213362801.title: Scientific atheism in the post-secular context of Perestroika
oa:W7213362801.abstract: The focus of this publication is on the historical fate of scientific atheism at the turn of the 1980s and 1990s. An attempt is made to look at this specific phenomenon of Soviet reality in the context of the theory of the post-secular turn in the late 1970s and 1980s. Historiography has established the opinion that scientific atheism as a whole shared the fate of the entire Soviet system and became a thing of the past in the early 1990s. The researchers propose various approaches to determining the historical conditions and forms of completion of scientific atheism as an ideological project. The minimal attention to the scientific and atheistic discourse of the late 1980s is characteristic. Scientific atheism is considered either as a utopian ideological project of denying religion, or as an artificial administrative and ideological tool, or as an ideologized field of scientific knowledge.The article shows that as a historical phenomenon, scientific atheism was not limited to an ideological project. An appeal to archival sources reflecting internal discussions among atheist ideologists, as well as to publications in scientific atheist publications of the late 1980s, shows that scientific atheism during this period went through a stage of active self-reflection and adaptation to the loss of ideological monopoly and the return of religion to the public space. From this point of view, it has transformed into a specific form of postsecular self-reflexive secularism. oa:W7213366546.title: Working draft updated Sept. 14 2026 The Hidden Melchizedek: A Hebrew Reading of the Angel of Righteousness in the Shepherd of Hermas
oa:W7213366546.abstract: Even though the literal name "Melchizedek" is entirely absent from the Greek text of The Shepherd of Hermas, the character of the "Angel of Righteousness" (ho angelos tss dikaiosynss) in Mandate 6 functions as a direct linguistic and theological equivalent to the heavenly Melchizedek found in early Jewish-Christian traditions. By moving past the Greek surface of the second-century Roman text and reading it through a Hebrew mindset, a clear conceptual framework emerges. This paper argues that when we translate these titles back into their original Hebrew roots and incorporate the canonical criteria of the Epistle to the Hebrews, the text's complex imagery reveals an underlying, pre-existing Melchizedek theology. Crucially, this study demonstrates that the twelve gatekeeping virgins in Similitude 9 do not merely serve as moral symbols, but function as celestial extensions of Tzedek (Righteousness). By translating their specific Greek names into their Hebrew equivalents-such as Emunah (Faith), Tahora (Purity), Yosher (Sincerity), and Tiferet (Harmony)-we reveal an angelic ritual of priestly vesting. This mechanism, backed by clear Old Testament typologies (Proverbs 9, Psalm 45, Exodus 28, Zechariah 3, Exodus 27, Psalm 110), completes the vision of the Great Tower as a cosmic Temple operating under the ultimate, unchangeable authority of a Melchizedekian high priesthood, safely remaining subordinate to the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who ultimately owns the Tower.

oa:W7213370041.title: Atheism, evolution, and meaning
oa:W7213370041.abstract: Abstract In this paper, I argue that meaning of the main kinds associated with human life can be described and illuminatingly discussed by atheists who reject all things religious and embrace evolution. Indeed, by considering the different forms evolution can take and with sensitivity to how distinctive meaning-related facts emerge at different stages of macroscale human development and also to the fact that meaning itself evolves, atheists are in a position to show that the evolutionary considerations available to them, rather than an obstacle to a robust and satisfying account of meaning, can be its source.

oa:W7213370651.title: Religion and alienation: towards posing of the probleme
oa:W7213370651.abstract: In the philosophy of religion, the theme of alienation is used rather narrowly, mainly in connection with its sociocentric interpretations, as well as in the context of German classical idealism and materialism. In fact, it turns out that the phenomena behind alienation theories are fundamental and quite universal in the history of human thought. One shall not be wondered by the case that philosophy tends to deal with just such things. The article examines concepts of alienation in the religion studies, and issues related to them in the works of Plotinus, Kant, Hegel, Schelling, Feuerbach, Marx, Kierkegaard, Nesmelov, Nietzsche, and Girard. It is demonstrated that the diversity of approaches to the problem is due to the difference in axiomatic assumptions or to what is taken as basic experience. As a review of concepts, the article aims to show the possibilities of a "cartographic" approach in teaching philosophy of religion.

oa:W7213409852.title: Dominância Social e “Cura” da Homossexualidade: O Papel Mediador dos Valores Normativos
oa:W7213409852.abstract: The present study aimed to understand the role of social dominance orientation and normative values (obedience, tradition, and religiosity) in explaining socially disseminated beliefs about a supposed “cure” for homosexuality. A total of 391 Brazilians participated in this study (69.5% women; M = 21.7 years), responding to the Social Dominance Orientation Scale, the Beliefs about the Cure of Homosexuality Scale, the Basic Values Questionnaire, and demographic questions. Mediation analyses were conducted to verify whether normative values acted as mediators in the relationship between social dominance orientation and beliefs. The results demonstrated that normative values mediated this relationship, such that individuals with a higher social dominance orientation tend to more strongly endorse normative values of tradition, religiosity, and obedience, and consequently internalize biological, psychological, moral, and religious beliefs about the cure for homosexuality. Conversely, individuals with lower social dominance orientation and less normative values tend to more strongly endorse unfavorable beliefs about the cure for homosexuality.

oa:W7213424292.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213424292.abstract: What follows reads Paul's appointments before it frames them. The lexical working texts of 1 Timothy 2:9–15 and of the related Corinthian silence-and-order block stand first, because the argument must begin where Ruach through Paul actually speaks. Only after those verses are on the table does the article set them inside the conferred-sovereignty frame already developed in companion work on flesh/autonomy and on the weaponization of creation. Overstepping conferred authority—parabasis in Paul's own word—is fleshy autonomy retained as a rival throne and anti-hineni refusal of present available yieldedness, set against the Greatest Commandment's demand for exclusive desirous 'ahav. The prose aims at the flowing scholarly register of those companions rather than at outline cadence. Material stays inside what has already been locked; length is permitted where the disaster itself requires length. The blocks below are working lexical-breadth renderings, not ecclesial Bible versions. Slash-stacks show attested range; where Greek γυνή and ἀνήρ can mean woman or wife, man or husband, both remain visible. Argument prose after this section carries the claims in ordinary scholarly sentences; the heat of the lemmas sits here first. God is absolutely sovereign. Absolute sovereignty is His alone; Job's courtroom and Romans 1 refuse any dualism in which another power shares the throne. And yet He confers. Creatures receive a real, limited self-sovereignty—authority and autonomy under His, not beside His as equals—not as flattery of the creature but as love's condition, because exclusive desirous 'ahav cannot be robotized. oa:W7213428566.title: The Inversion of Greatness: From the Nature of Necessity to Maximum Possibility
oa:W7213428566.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213428566.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is an analytic work in modal metaphysics: a complete argument, derived step by step. The thesis is structural naturalism. The classical traditions asked what, if anything, exists necessarily, and answered with a maximally great being—a God outside time, space, and matter, the source of everything possible. This book argues they asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Most arguments that reach a necessary being help themselves to S5 and move on. This one grounds it first, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility rather than an axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change at all requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and the bearing of retained content. Those three Conditions are necessarily instantiated, and that structure is what the book calls Nature. Naturalism finally gets the ground it has always had to take as a brute fact. From there: no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. That blocks a divine intellect along with every other occupant of that domain, and leaves essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals burdened rather than refuted. Reality is nothing over and above Nature. The inversion isn't greatness changing owners. It's a claim about predication. Great, necessary, eternal, self-existent carry content only as said of what instantiates the Conditions. Said of a subject defined by their absence, they don't name something else—they fail to name. oa:W7213439292.title: Quantitative Semantic-Breadth Ranking of Bridal-Mystic Erotic Poetry
oa:W7213439292.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213439292.abstract: This article ranks published erotic-nuptial verse written by known bridal mystics according to a standard linguistic measure of semantic breadth. The heterogeneity map already fixed in Holmes 2026a remains in force. Much bridal mysticism remembers desire and then cools it. A few keep undivided heat. Asceticism is colder still. Matthew 7:14 supplies scarcity’s spine. Sanctification in the companion nuptial grammar is betrothal under Ruach (Holmes 2026a). A number of the named bridal mystics record withdrawal of the Beloved inside the bond. Marguerite Porete does not. She speaks the soul annihilated in God and keeps undivided heat (Holmes 2026a). The present study asks whose original-language erotic-nuptial verse occupies the wider attested sense-range. Porete’s verse is first on that measure by a wide margin. The two facts map. Extreme semantic breadth here is read as a possible fingerprint of that undivided presence, which is the theology of beauty the ranking is for. The primary statistic is the mean sense-count of content lemmas in each mystic’s original-language erotic-nuptial verse, computed against the published WordNet analogue for that language: Spanish WordNet in the Multilingual Central Repository for John and Teresa (Gonzalez-Agirre, Laparra, and Rigau 2012), MultiWordNet Italian for Catherine (Pianta, Bentivogli, and Girardi 2002), WOLF for Porete’s Old French tokens (Sagot and Fišer 2008), Open Dutch WordNet for Hadewijch’s Middle Dutch tokens (Postma et al. 2016), and Latin WordNet for Rupert’s embedded Latin nuptial units (Minozzi 2017; Short 2019). oa:W7213441902.title: Exploring the Himalayan Trails: Perspectives from Bill Aitken’s Footloose in the Himalaya
oa:W7213441902.abstract: This paper examines Bill Aitken's Footloose in the Himalaya, a travelogue that meticulously chronicles the author's extensive journeys through the Indian Himalayas. The chapters include personal stories, cultural observations, environmental criticism, and historical reflection. Aitken's writing is different from most travel writing because it looks at the Himalayas from both the point of view of someone who has never been there and someone who has lived there for a long time. The travelogue provides deep insights into local customs, social interactions, and the coexistence of different religious beliefs, while also drawing attention to critical environmental problems like deforestation and the loss of traditional knowledge. Aitken uses myth, folklore, and humor to bring the landscape and its people to life. He articulates a nuanced position that balances respect for tradition with a comprehensive critique of the transformative impacts of modernity. The paper concludes that Footloose in the Himalaya offers a profound examination of belonging, environmental stewardship, and the enduring allure of the Himalayan region.

oa:W7213451243.title: Paganism in the philosophical reflection of Edward Herbert
oa:W7213451243.abstract: The aim of the research is to identify the significance of Edward Herbert of Cherbury's work "The Religion of the Gentiles" for the development of the philosophy of religion and religious studies. The article examines the source base, methods, and content of Herbert's book, in which the author took the study of religion beyond confessional boundaries. At the core of Herbert's philosophical study lies an attempt to justify paganism by proving the unity of the essential religious foundations of all confessions of the past and present. The scientific novelty of the study is associated with the fact that Herbert's book "The Religion of the Gentiles" is considered for the first time as a methodological attempt to substantiate a universal religion based on cross-cultural comparison. As a result of the study, it was established that the book "The Religion of the Gentiles", firstly, is one of the extensive encyclopedias of religious traditions of its time; secondly, it continues and develops Herbert's teaching on a single universal religious foundation; thirdly, the issues raised in the book define religion as an object of philosophical reflection; fourthly, Herbert bases his conclusions not only on the use of diverse sources, but also on comparative analysis, which brings his study closer to the scientific standards of comparative religious studies.

oa:W7213464753.title: Fostering institutional trust and organ donation: Evidence from a randomized informational intervention in Tunisia
oa:W7213464753.abstract: Organ transplantation saves lives and improves the quality of life of patients who would otherwise depend on costly and invasive treatments. The technology is becoming available in low- and middle-income countries, but the gap between the demand for and the supply of organ transplants remains large. In a randomized controlled trial at a Tunisian university, we evaluate an expert-led intervention designed to inform about organ donation and strengthen trust in medical institutions. The intervention consists of a short video testimonial from a heart transplant survivor, a presentation led by a medical doctor and a short Q&A session. We find that the intervention significantly increases deceased donor registration, with suggestive evidence of positive spillover effects on the control group. The survey data provides little support for changes in attitudes and social expectations as potential mechanisms. Instead, it reveals large and statistically significant increases in medical and legal knowledge, religious beliefs supportive of donation, and institutional trust among treated students. Finally, we show that treatment effects on organ donor registration are driven by male students and those whose families likely support organ donation. Targeting older segments of the population may further increase the impact and cost-effectiveness of this intervention.

oa:W7213471422.title: Analisis Semiotika Nilai Spiritual pada Lirik Lagu “Apa yang Tak Bisa” Karya Band Rumah Sakit (Analisis Roland Barthes)
oa:W7213471422.venue: Bandung Conference Series Islamic Broadcast Communication
oa:W7213471422.abstract: Abstract. This study is motivated by a phenomenon in which university students consume the song “Apa Yang Tak Bisa” by Rumahsakit as emotional relief without connecting it to spiritual reflection. YouTube comments confirm deep resonance: one listener reported renewed gratitude after fourteen childless years of marriage; another cited the song as a reason to keep living. This indicates the song functions as psychospiritual catharsis whose theological content has not been academically examined. Using qualitative descriptive research with Roland Barthes’s semiotic approach, this study analyzes the lyrics through three levels: denotation, connotation, and myth. Results show the song builds a coherent narrative from unfulfilled effort and prayer, through emotional release, to religious surrender. At the myth level, the lyrics dismantle two urban assumptions that sincere effort yields instant results, and that letting go equals defeat replacing them with a theological frame in which every unattained outcome conceals hidden wisdom. Three Islamic spiritual values emerge: tawakal (trust in God after maximal effort), qada (acceptance of present reality), and qadar (confidence in a divinely ordained future). The findings demonstrate that independent popular music can serve as an effective medium of cultural da’wah, conveying Islamic values inclusively without explicit religious jargon. Abstrak. oa:W7213495350.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213495350.abstract: Mazkur tadqiqotda qadimgi Turon xalqlarining diniy dunyoqarashi va marosimiy an'analarida muhim ahamiyat kasb etgan Mitra kultining shakllanishi hamda uning quyosh va olov timsollari bilan uzviy aloqador jihatlari tahlil qilinadi. Tadqiqotda Mitraning qadimgi diniy tasavvurlardagi funksional xususiyatlari, xususan, quyosh nuri, ezgulik, adolat, farovonlik va hayot davomiyligini ta'minlovchi ilohiy kuch sifatidagi mazmuni ochib beriladi. Shuningdek, ko'chmanchi chorvador jamoalarning, jumladan, Andronovo madaniyati vakillarining olov bilan bog'liq diniy qarashlari hamda Janubiy Markaziy Osiyoning o'troq-dehqonchilik madaniyatlariga oid Jarqo'ton, Marg'iyona va Baqtriya hududlaridagi diniy-me'moriy yodgorliklar Mitra kultining rivojlanish jarayoni bilan bog'liq holda ko'rib chiqiladi. Mitraga oid marosimlar va mavsumiy bayramlar, ayniqsa Mehrg'onning qadimgi dehqonchilik an'analari, tabiatning mavsumiy sikllari va diniy tasavvurlar bilan aloqasi tahlil etilib, uning keyingi tarixiy davrlardagi transformatsiyasi yoritiladi. Tadqiqot tarixiy, arxeologik, numizmatik va mifologik manbalarni kompleks tahlil qilish asosida Mitraning qadimgi Turon jamiyatlaridagi diniy, ijtimoiy va ramziy funksiyalarini aniqlashga qaratilgan. Symbols of the sun and fire in the religious beliefs of the ancient peoples of Turan: the image of Mithra This study examines the formation and development of the cult of Mithra in the religious worldview and ritual traditions of the peoples of ancient Turan, with particular attention to its association with solar and fire symbolism. The research explores the functional characteristics of Mithra in ancient religious beliefs, particularly his representation as a divine force associated with sunlight, goodness, justice, prosperity, and the continuity of life.

oa:W7213496574.title: Life in Himself Through Eternal Generation: St. Augustine of Hippo's Metaphysical Analysis of John 5:26 and Its Relevance
oa:W7213496574.abstract: This study examines St. Augustine of Hippo's metaphysical interpretation of John 5:26, explores its philosophical foundations, demonstrates how his argument establishes the Son's equality with the Father, and evaluates its novelty and relevance for contemporary theological scholarship. Within the broader patristic corpus devoted to Trinitarian exegesis, this verse occupies a pivotal place, since it raises the decisive question of how the Son possesses divine life without compromising the Trinity's essential unity or lapsing into Arian subordinationism. The research adopts a comparative qualitative approach, combining textual study of Augustine's Tractates on the Gospel of John with conceptual-philosophical reflection, historical-theological contextualization, and comparative engagement with modern scholarship. The findings confirm that Augustine fundamentally distinguishes between Essential Life, possessed by God alone, and Participatory Life, possessed by creatures in dependence on Him. Crucially, he interprets the phrase "has granted the Son also to have life in himself" as a description of the act of eternal generation, whereby the Son is Life itself, equal in essence with the Father, precisely by being from the Father. This demonstrates that Augustine provides a sophisticated metaphysical framework for understanding the mode of the Son's possession of divine life, one that effectively counters subordinationism without relying solely on relational categories. This research contributes to the fields of theology and philosophy by highlighting that Augustine's metaphysical analysis offers a novel perspective often underemphasized in modern scholarship. oa:W7213497479.title: FROM INTELLIGIBILITY TO IDENTITY
oa:W7213497479.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213497479.abstract: Cornelius Van Til’s transcendental apologetic challenged the assumption that human reason could operate autonomously and then evaluate God as one possible conclusion among others. The Christian God, Van Til argued, is not merely an object within an already intelligible reality; God is the necessary precondition for intelligibility itself. Participatory Trinitarian Realism (PTR) accepts this transcendental orientation but presses the question beneath epistemology into ontology. If knowledge requires intelligibility, and intelligibility requires identifiable objects of predication, then a prior question emerges: what must be true for anything to possess an identifiable concrete identity in the first place? PTR’s Principle of Relational Identity, the same master formula Paper I, “The End of the Isolated Self,” names P = P(Ro, Rp), is developed here as A = A(Ro, Rp), using the logical placeholder proper to predication rather than the created instantiations Paper I argues from. Formal self-identity, A = A, while logically necessary, is ontologically insufficient as a complete account of concrete created identity. Concrete beings are neither self-originating nor self-sustaining. Their identities are inseparable from constitutive relations of origin (Ro) and participation (Rp). This paper argues that relational identity permits the transcendental argument to move from the conditions of knowing to the conditions of identifiable being. The resulting question is no longer merely whether competing worldviews can account for logic, knowledge, and predication. It is whether their ultimate ontologies can account for a world in which particularity and relation, distinction and dependence, unity and plurality, are simultaneously real. oa:W7213498438.title: Sacred landscapes of Turan: religious beliefs, ritual practices and mythological traditions of ancient Central Asia in written sources (based on Khwandamir's "Maosir al-Muluk") and some archaeological sources
oa:W7213498438.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213498438.abstract: This thesis examines the religious beliefs, ritual practices, and mythological traditions attributed to the peoples of ancient Turan - the historical-geographical macro-region of Central Asia comprising Bactria, Sogdiana, Khwarazm, Margiana, and Fergana. Drawing on Avestan literature, Greek and Latin ethnographic accounts (Herodotus, Strabonn, Arrian, Quintus Curtius Rufus), and archaeological evidence from Bronze Age through Late Antique sites, the study reconstructs the layered religious landscape of the region: pre-Zoroastrian nature cults, the gradual and uneven spread of Zoroastrian doctrine, and epic-mythological figures such as Tur/Afrasiyab and Siyavush. The thesis argues, following recent source-critical scholarship, that "Turan" was never a single ethnic or confessional community but a shifting literary, geographical, and religious construct whose content changed considerably between the Avestan age, the classical period, and the medieval Perso-Islamic epic tradition. Methodological problems of extrapolating from later legendary sources onto earlier historical periods are given particular attention. oa:W7213499939.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213499939.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/30748dfb-d1ec-4f04-a4db-462edeb0fc46?authuser=1 A Day in the Life: Love, Memory, Machines, and the Absurd Work of Unbinding examines September 16, 2026 as a bounded historical interval through which theology, memory, suffering, artificial intelligence, family life, worship, service, humor, and ordinary material work can be studied within a single relational framework. Beginning from the Christian claim that “God is love,” the paper asks what that proposition looks like when treated not merely as an abstraction but as an operating principle tested across the events of an ordinary day. The paper develops unbinding as its central concept: what happened remains historically true, but the past does not therefore have to control every future relationship. Remembering is distinguished from remaining wounded, forgiveness from erasure, and a person from the worst act that person has committed. Drawing on 1 Corinthians 13, Catholic theology, Scripture, St. Vincent de Paul, Saints Cornelius and Cyprian, Augustine, Aquinas, Ricoeur, Arendt, trauma and testimony studies, cultural memory, distributed cognition, and artificial intelligence, the paper argues that agape supplies the governing purpose by which knowledge, prophecy, memory, correction, technology, and historical preservation should be evaluated. A central informational argument concerns the transmission of suffering across time. Human beings can externalize experience through testimony, words, photographs, recordings, archives, and computational systems so that later receivers can learn from suffering without requiring another person to undergo the originating harm merely to regenerate its information. oa:W7213503803.title: ASEITY AND THE SUBSTRATE: What the Identity Thesis Can and Cannot Mean: Why "God is Freedom" Cannot Be Substituted into the Formula, and What It Means Instead
oa:W7213503803.abstract: Abstract The Philosophy of Virtues makes freedom the substrate of every virtue and holds, as its theological thesis, that God is Freedom. Every formal paper in the programme declares that thesis unused. This article is the exception: it engages the layer in order to constrain it, and the constraint turns out to be structural rather than devotional. The substitution fails, and it fails for a reason internal to the apparatus. The formula V = sgn(F) × D takes three values on its sign — present and self-directed, absent, actively replaced — and the deprivation operator requires a power capable of removing the substrate and receiving the discipline that constituted the act. Substitute the divine name for F and the operator requires a power that can remove God, which is greater than God. The formula demands that its substrate be removable. God is not removable. So the failure is not impiety; it is that a substitutional reading makes every theorem in the corpus vacuous, since inversion, occupation, the three counterfeits and the vacancy results are all built on the possibility of the substrate being taken. The grammar of the predication was never substitutional in the first place, and the tradition supplies the control case. Deus caritas est has been confessed for two millennia, and nobody obtains theology by substituting the divine name into “love is patient and kind.” The identity in such statements is of nature, not of term. One reading survives, and it explains what the formula had assumed. On the participation reading, what God is, is aseity — self-origination with no antecedent, ipsum esse subsistens, the mode of being in which essence and existence are not distinct. oa:W7213512349.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213512349.abstract: Mazkur maqolada Markaziy Osiyo xalqlarining qadimgi diniy qarashlari tizimida ajdodlarga sigʻinish an'analarining shakllanishi, rivojlanishi va ijtimoiy-madaniy hayotdagi oʻrni tahlil qilinadi. Tadqiqotda arxeologik topilmalar, etnografik materiallar, mifologik rivoyatlar hamda yozma manbalar asosida ajdodlar kultining mohiyati yoritilgan. Shuningdek, ajdodlarga sigʻinishning dafn marosimlari, muqaddas maskanlar, oilaviy qadriyatlar va qabila tuzilmasi bilan uzviy bogʻliqligi koʻrsatib berilgan. Qiyosiy tarixiy yondashuv asosida Markaziy Osiyo xalqlaridagi ajdodlar kulti qadimgi Eron, Turk va boshqa qoʻshni sivilizatsiyalar bilan taqqoslanadi. Tadqiqot natijalari ajdodlarga sigʻinish diniy e'tiqodgina emas, balki jamiyatning ma'naviy, siyosiy va madaniy taraqqiyotida muhim omillardan biri boʻlganligini koʻrsatadi. Traditions of ancestor veneration in Central Asian mythology This article analyzes the formation, development and socio-cultural role of ancestor worship traditions in the system of ancient religious beliefs of the peoples of Central Asia. The study sheds light on the essence of the ancestor cult based on archaeological finds, ethnographic materials, mythological legends and written sources. It also shows the inextricable connection of ancestor worship with funeral rituals, sacred places, family values and tribal structure. Based on a comparative historical approach, the ancestor cult among the peoples of Central Asia is compared with ancient Iranian, Turkic and other neighboring civilizations. The results of the study show that ancestor worship was not only a religious belief, but also one of the important factors in the spiritual, political and cultural development of society. So the failure is not impiety; it is that a substitutional reading makes every theorem in the corpus vacuous, since inversion, occupation, the three counterfeits and the vacancy results are all built on the possibility of the substrate being taken. oa:W7213513151.title: Jizzax vohasi xalqlari diniy e'tiqodlaridagi olov topinchi haqida
oa:W7213513151.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213513151.abstract: Ushbu maqolada Jizzax vohasi xalqlarining islomgacha bo'lgan diniy e'tiqodlarida olovga sig'inish (otashparastlik) masalasi tarixiy-arxeologik va yozma manbalar asosida tahlil qilinadi. Mualliflar qadimgi dafn marosimlarida olovdan foydalanish, krematsiya, qabrlarga cho'g' va kul qoldiqlarini qo'yish, shuningdek olov bilan bog'liq marosim inshootlari (otashgohlar) haqidagi arxeologik topilmalarni sharhlaydi. Maqolada olov kulti Quyoshga sig'inish, ajdodlar ruhini e'zozlash va zardushtiylik ta'siri bilan bog'liq holda o'rganiladi. Shuningdek, turkiy qabilalar va Ustrushona hududida otga sig'inish, olovni poklovchi vosita sifatida qarash kabi etnografik jihatlar yoritilgan. Xulosa qilib aytganda, Jizzax vohasida olov e'tiqodi mahalliy an'analar, ko'chmanchi dasht xalqlari va zardushtiylikning o'zaro sintezi natijasida shakllangan bo'lib, islom davrida ham sinkretik shakllarda saqlanib qolgan. On the fire cult in the religious beliefs of the peoples of the Jizzakh oasis This article examines the fire cult (fire worship) in the pre-Islamic religious beliefs of the population of the Jizzakh oasis, based on historical, archaeological, and written sources. The authors analyze burial practices involving fire, including cremation, the placement of ash and coals in graves, and the construction of fire-altars. The study shows that fire worship was closely connected with solar cults, ancestor veneration, and Zoroastrian influences. Special attention is given to ethnographic parallels, such as horse worship, the purifying functions of fire, and its symbolism among nomadic peoples. The authors conclude that the fire cult in the Jizzakh oasis emerged as a syncretic phenomenon, integrating local agrarian traditions, steppe nomadic beliefs, and Zoroastrian elements, and persisted in tra

oa:W7213514250.title: Markaziy Osiyo mifologiyasida ajdodlarga sigʻinish an'analari
oa:W7213514250.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213514250.abstract: Mazkur maqolada Markaziy Osiyo xalqlarining qadimgi diniy qarashlari tizimida ajdodlarga sigʻinish an'analarining shakllanishi, rivojlanishi va ijtimoiy-madaniy hayotdagi oʻrni tahlil qilinadi. Tadqiqotda arxeologik topilmalar, etnografik materiallar, mifologik rivoyatlar hamda yozma manbalar asosida ajdodlar kultining mohiyati yoritilgan. Shuningdek, ajdodlarga sigʻinishning dafn marosimlari, muqaddas maskanlar, oilaviy qadriyatlar va qabila tuzilmasi bilan uzviy bogʻliqligi koʻrsatib berilgan. Qiyosiy tarixiy yondashuv asosida Markaziy Osiyo xalqlaridagi ajdodlar kulti qadimgi Eron, Turk va boshqa qoʻshni sivilizatsiyalar bilan taqqoslanadi. Tadqiqot natijalari ajdodlarga sigʻinish diniy e'tiqodgina emas, balki jamiyatning ma'naviy, siyosiy va madaniy taraqqiyotida muhim omillardan biri boʻlganligini koʻrsatadi. Traditions of ancestor veneration in Central Asian mythology This article analyzes the formation, development and socio-cultural role of ancestor worship traditions in the system of ancient religious beliefs of the peoples of Central Asia. The study sheds light on the essence of the ancestor cult based on archaeological finds, ethnographic materials, mythological legends and written sources. It also shows the inextricable connection of ancestor worship with funeral rituals, sacred places, family values and tribal structure. Based on a comparative historical approach, the ancestor cult among the peoples of Central Asia is compared with ancient Iranian, Turkic and other neighboring civilizations. The results of the study show that ancestor worship was not only a religious belief, but also one of the important factors in the spiritual, political and cultural development of society. oa:W7213516304.title: Sacred landscapes of Turan: religious beliefs, ritual practices and mythological traditions of ancient Central Asia in written sources (based on Khwandamir's "Maosir al-Muluk") and some archaeological sources
oa:W7213516304.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213516304.abstract: This thesis examines the religious beliefs, ritual practices, and mythological traditions attributed to the peoples of ancient Turan - the historical-geographical macro-region of Central Asia comprising Bactria, Sogdiana, Khwarazm, Margiana, and Fergana. Drawing on Avestan literature, Greek and Latin ethnographic accounts (Herodotus, Strabonn, Arrian, Quintus Curtius Rufus), and archaeological evidence from Bronze Age through Late Antique sites, the study reconstructs the layered religious landscape of the region: pre-Zoroastrian nature cults, the gradual and uneven spread of Zoroastrian doctrine, and epic-mythological figures such as Tur/Afrasiyab and Siyavush. The thesis argues, following recent source-critical scholarship, that "Turan" was never a single ethnic or confessional community but a shifting literary, geographical, and religious construct whose content changed considerably between the Avestan age, the classical period, and the medieval Perso-Islamic epic tradition. Methodological problems of extrapolating from later legendary sources onto earlier historical periods are given particular attention. oa:W7213524714.title: Qadimgi Turon xalqlari diniy e'tiqodlarida ot kulti
oa:W7213524714.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213524714.abstract: Ushbu maqolada qadimgi Turon xalqlarining diniy e'tiqodlarida ot kulti masalasi tarixiy-mifologik nuqtai nazardan tahlil qilinadi. Totemistik qarashlarning shakllanish jarayonida ot obrazining o'rni, uning arxeologik topilmalar va yozma manbalar asosida tadqiq etilgan xususiyatlari yoritiladi. Maqolada ot bilan dafn etish udumi, uni qurbonlik qilish an'anasi hamda ot obrazining quyosh, o'lim va abadiyat tushunchalari bilan bog'liqligi Yevroosiyo dasht mintaqasi, xitoy va hind-eron xalqlari mifologiyasi misolida qiyosiy tahlil qilinadi. Shuningdek, ot kultining o'zbek xalq dostonlari hamda jahon adabiyoti namunalaridagi badiiy talqinlariga ham to'xtalib o'tiladi. Tadqiqot ot kultining nafaqat xo'jalik hayoti, balki diniy-mifologik tafakkurning shakllanishida ham muhim o'rin tutganligini ko'rsatadi. The horse cult in the religious beliefs of the ancient peoples of Turan This article analyzes the cult of the horse in the religious beliefs of the ancient peoples of Turon from a historical-mythological perspective. It examines the role of the horse image in the process of the formation of totemistic views, along with its features as studied through archaeological finds and written sources. The article offers a comparative analysis of the custom of burial with a horse, the tradition of horse sacrifice, and the connection of the horse image with the concepts of the sun, death, and eternity, drawing on examples from the mythology of the Eurasian steppe region and the Chinese and Indo-Iranian peoples. It also addresses the artistic interpretations of the horse cult in Uzbek folk epics and in examples of world literature. The study demonstrates that the horse cult played an important role not only in economic life but also in the formation of religious-mythological thought. В дан

oa:W7213525319.title: Conceptions of God and Epistemic Mediation: A Five-Layer Model Abstract Religious
oa:W7213525319.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213525319.abstract: This article presents a five-layer architecture for determining the scope of epistemic revision in religious belief: formation, conception, propositional attitude, justification, and truth/reference. Its scope-dependency principle states that a finding at one layer warrants revision at another only through a specified connection; once such dependence is established, layer distinctions do not insulate the dependent claim. The architecture is not itself theistic. A worked application conditionally adopts theistic realism and analogical divine consciousness while separating creation, relation, revelation, and communicative trustworthiness. Sources are assessed through reliability, conditional independence, alternative explanations, and defeaters rather than source type. Worked cases distinguish lost corroboration from lost total support, available grounds from actual bases for belief, and false attribution from failed reference. Propositional and doxastic justification remain distinct, as do personal and public justification. The contribution is a typed assessment record and a criterion of diagnostic adequacy: an assessment of revision must identify its target, dependency, required response, and residual uncertainty. Each coordinate is task-relative and non-redundant in the worked cases. A proposition-centered checklist is equivalent only insofar as it represents these same distinctions and links; comparative practical performance remains to be tested.

oa:W7213528501.title: The Inversion of Greatness: From the Nature of Necessity to Maximum Possibility
oa:W7213528501.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213528501.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is an analytic work in modal metaphysics: a complete argument, derived step by step. The thesis is structural naturalism. The classical traditions asked what, if anything, exists necessarily, and answered with a maximally great being—a God outside time, space, and matter, the source of everything possible. This book argues they asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Most arguments that reach a necessary being help themselves to S5 and move on. This one grounds it first, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility rather than an axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change at all requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and the bearing of retained content. Those three Conditions are necessarily instantiated, and that structure is what the book calls Nature. Naturalism finally gets the ground it has always had to take as a brute fact. From there: no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. That blocks a divine intellect along with every other occupant of that domain, and leaves essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals burdened rather than refuted. Reality is nothing over and above Nature. The inversion isn't greatness changing owners. It's a claim about predication. Great, necessary, eternal, self-existent carry content only as said of what instantiates the Conditions. Said of a subject defined by their absence, they don't name something else—they fail to name. oa:W7213530201.title: The Two Witnesses as Convergent Testimony: Revelation 11, Delegated Authority, Counterfeit Power, and Divine Vindication
oa:W7213530201.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213530201.abstract: This open working paper examines the Two Witnesses of Revelation 11 primarily as a theological pattern of convergent testimony rather than as an attempt to identify two future individuals. It argues that Revelation provides greater clarity concerning what the witnesses do than concerning who they are: they receive delegated authority, testify within a bounded period, confront counterfeit power, remain mortal, complete their testimony, suffer apparent defeat, and receive vindication from God. The paper proposes that distinct witnesses may converge upon one transcendent authority without becoming identical or self-authenticating. Its governing Johannine principle is that the witness is not the light but points beyond itself. A secondary contemporary application considers how technological capability, artificial intelligence, and other forms of finite intelligence might be mistaken for divine authority. The paper maintains that extraordinary capability does not establish divinity: power is not ultimacy, intelligence is not Source, and creaturely participation is not creation. This secondary inquiry remains non-load-bearing and does not identify contemporary individuals, artificial intelligence, or nonhuman beings with the Two Witnesses. Christ remains the center and measure of the theological argument.
