oa:W7213548671.venue: Utambuzi Journal for the Study of the Religions of Africa and its Diaspora
oa:W7213548671.abstract: This article addresses four questions. 1) How did the Akan in the 19 th and earlier centuries link the divine to wild nature?2) How did they domesticate it?3) Was pre-colonial Akan indigenous religion a ʽnature religionʼ (Naturreligion)?4) If it was, did it inspire conservationist sentiments into the Akan?The aim of this paper is to demonstrate that there is an intrinsic connection between a part of Akan late 19 th century indigenous religion and (wild) nature, conceived in modern terms as the uncultivated natural environment of the Akan societies of the Gold Coast, now Ghana.I will present an analysis of the material aspects of Akan notions of ʽGodʼ, or ʽthe divineʼ, i.e. of that part of Akan religious beliefs about unseen realms and beings which modern Westerners as well as modern Africans virtually all, and exclusively, view as transcendent and as purely spiritual, and as such pre-eminently associate with ʽreligionʼ.

oa:W7213554513.title: Gods in Nature, Gods at Home: Domesticating the Divine in Akan Late 19th Century Religion
oa:W7213554513.venue: Utambuzi Journal for the Study of the Religions of Africa and its Diaspora
oa:W7213554513.abstract: This article addresses four questions. 1) How did the Akan in the 19th and earlier centuries link the divine to wild nature? 2) How did they domesticate it? 3) Was pre-colonial Akan indigenous religion a ʽnature religionʼ (Naturreligion)? 4) If it was, did it inspire conservationist sentiments in the Akan? This paper aims to demonstrate that there is an intrinsic connection between a part of Akan late 19th cen­tu­ry in­­­­di­gen­ous religion and (wild) na­ture, conceived in modern terms as the un­cul­­tivated natural en­vironment of the Akan societies of the Gold Coast, now Ghana. I will pres­ent an an­al­y­sis of the material aspects of Akan no­tions of ʽGodʼ, or ʽthe divineʼ, i.e. of that part of Akan religious beliefs about unseen realms and beings which mod­ern West­er­ners as well as mod­ern Af­ri­cans virtually all, and exclusively, view as transcendent and as purely spirit­u­al, and as such pre-em­i­nently as­­so­ciate with ʽre­li­gionʼ.

oa:W7213555429.title: INFLUENCE OF INTERFAITH ENGAGEMENTS ON ACADEMIC INCLUSION OF STUDENTS TEACHERS AT METHODIST COLLEGE OF EDUCATION
oa:W7213555429.venue: Open Access Publishing Group - European Journal of Special Education Research
oa:W7213555429.abstract: The purpose of the study was to find out the kind of interfaith activities student teachers engaged in on campus and their influence on student academic inclusion. A cross-sectional survey as a design was used for the study. A simple random sampling technique was used to sample the respondents, with a sample size of 210, and the main instrument used for data collection was a questionnaire. The study revealed that interfaith activities student teachers engage in at Methodist College of Education campus were: Sunday service, morning devotion, interfaith prayer meetings, interfaith dialogue, and interfaith sports competitions. It again revealed that interfaith engagements help promote a more harmonious campus environment, help all students with different religious beliefs to feel welcome in the lecture room, help all students to freely express their religious beliefs in the lecture room and receive academic support from students of other religious faiths in the lecture room. It is recommended that the college management should sensitise student teachers to appreciate diversity and its influence on student teachers' academic and social progress.

oa:W7213558856.title: Традиционный корякский похоронный ритуал в свете мифологических представлений и практик
oa:W7213558856.venue: Bulletin of the North-East Science Center
oa:W7213558856.abstract: The Koryak funeral ritual is analyzed in the context of their current behavior and religious beliefs. It is revealed that the foundation of the ritual, performed through cremation, is the mythological belief in the Big Raven as a primal forefather and cultural character. Among the indigenous peoples of the North, the Koryaks stand apart as the only ones to link the cult of the raven-ancestor with burial and to develop it into distinct rituals. The author defines the latter collectively as a "raven show", consisting of three parts: first, the preliminary preparation of the "tailed" raven costume; second, the actions of the "raven escort" and other individuals on the burial day; and, third, the mass rite of induction into the "raven people" during the cremation. Thus, the Koryak funeral ritual is structurally permeated with events related to various "raven" themes, expressed in ideological, behavioral, and material aspects. It was among the Koryak that the raven mythology became closely linked to the cremation ritual, historically most likely adopted through the Nivkh. The present research, revealing the pervasive "raven" leitmotif of this unique ritual, contributes to preserving an important part of the Koryak cultural heritage.

oa:W7213559515.title: Christian Philosophy and Christian Apologetics: A Philosophical Examination of Their Relationship and Complementarity
oa:W7213559515.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RELIGIOUS AND CULTURAL PRACTICE
oa:W7213559515.abstract: In an increasingly pluralistic and sceptical global context, Christianity continues to face sustained intellectual challenges that question its truth claims, coherence, and relevance. These challenges arise not only from overt secularism but also from competing religious worldviews and internal misunderstandings regarding the role of reason in faith. Within this climate, Christian apologetics emerges as a disciplined response aimed at offering rational justification for Christian belief, while Christian philosophy provides the conceptual and methodological framework through which such justification becomes intelligible. This paper examines the relationship between Christian philosophy and Christian apologetics, arguing that the two disciplines are neither identical nor autonomous, but fundamentally interdependent. Through conceptual analysis, historical reflection, and philosophical engagement, the study demonstrates that apologetics depends on philosophical reasoning for coherence, while Christian philosophy finds practical expression and relevance through apologetic engagement. Drawing on key thinkers in philosophy of religion and Christian thought, the paper contends that a robust defence of Christian faith requires philosophical depth grounded within a Christological and biblical framework. The paper concludes that separating Christian apologetics from Christian philosophy weakens both disciplines and undermines the intellectual credibility of Christian faith in contemporary discourse.

oa:W7213586602.title: THE NATURE OF TIME: Trialogue of Science Philosophy and Religion Vision of Time
oa:W7213586602.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213586602.abstract: The phenomenon of time remains one of the most foundational, recalcitrant, and under-determined categories of human inquiry. While the natural sciences successfully formalize and measure the operational properties of time, they lack a universally accepted ontological definition of what time is at the bedrock of Being. Across philosophy and the theological traditions, time is conceptualized through an extraordinarily disparate spectrum of categories and doctrines. This doctoral dissertation undertakes a disciplined investigation of that ontological lacuna. Its architecture is organized as a systematic trialogue among Science, Philosophy, and Religion. The core methodological principle is rigorous epistemic demarcation: the continuous distinction between established empirical or textual facts and metaphysical or theological postulates adopted on non-empirical rational grounds. Across philosophy and the theological traditions, time is conceptualized through an extraordinarily disparate spectrum of categories and doctrines. This doctoral dissertation undertakes a disciplined investigation of that ontological lacuna. Its architecture is organized as a systematic trialogue among Science, Philosophy, and Religion. The core methodological principle is rigorous epistemic demarcation: the continuous distinction between established empirical or textual facts and metaphysical or theological postulates adopted on non-empirical rational grounds. Part I (Science) identifies the precise junctures at which modern theoretical physics — particularly the problem of time in quantum gravity, the cosmological singularity, and the thermodynamics of non-equilibrium systems — reaches the outer boundary of empirical formalisms.Part II (Philosophy) constructs an autonomous metaphysical architecture upon this threshold: a three-tiered taxonomy of temporality (causal TIME-1, cyclical Time-2, and evental/phenomenal time-3). oa:W7213592889.title: Meze MNSM / Limits of MNSM
oa:W7213592889.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213592889.abstract: Limits of MNSM 2.0 examines the point at which the conceptual tools of MNSM must also be applied to MNSM itself. Every determination delimits something, but no determination can establish from its own structure that it has exhausted what it determines. The text explores two asymmetrical limiting procedures of determination: removal and inclusion. In the first, the attempt to remove determination leads toward the concept of Absolute Nothingness and gradually undermines the conditions within which distinctions such as presence and absence, existence and non-existence retain their meaning. In the second, the attempt to include everything leads toward the concept of Absolute Everything, where the problem becomes the possibility of confirming completeness from within the determination itself. Neither procedure is treated as access to an ontological endpoint. The essay therefore does not derive any ontological or modal conclusion about Absolute Nothingness or Absolute Everything from these concepts alone. Nula does not function as a new foundation, substance, hidden state, or governing principle. The concept Nula remains an empty designation for the limit of naming. The same methodological restraint is extended to God without attributes, the finitude of what appears, the Triad, and finally to the concepts of MNSM themselves. The text emphasizes that highly abstract nouns easily invite reification: a noun does not yet make a thing. The text forms part of a methodological series together with The Path to Nula and Methodological Manifesto. --- Meze MNSM 2.0 zkoumají okamžik, kdy musí MNSM obrátit své vlastní pojmové prostředky také na sebe. oa:W7213602757.title: Does the Law Explain Itself? On Physical Order, the Two Stops, and the Ground the Figure Cannot Supply
oa:W7213602757.abstract: Does the Law Explain Itself? turns the question of ontological dependence outward, from the temporal subject to the physical order itself. Building on What Sustains the Now?, the essay asks whether laws, constants, and the regularity of nature can serve as the ultimate ground of their own actuality. The argument distinguishes two meanings of “stop.” An epistemic stop marks the exhaustion of a method: a law may remain unexplained because inquiry has reached its present limit. An ontological stop makes the stronger claim that no further reason exists or is even owed. The essay argues that physics can establish the first, but does not by itself establish the second. The analysis then addresses the whole-part objection, quantum indeterminacy, and the claim that fundamental laws might be metaphysically necessary. Nomological necessity, the essay argues, does not by itself remove contingency. If a genuinely metaphysically necessary reality is posited, it occupies the metaphysical role of the Non-Derivative rather than eliminating that role. The essay therefore asks not whether God is another item within the physical inventory, but whether the physical order can supply the ground upon which its own being-actual depends. The essay's claim is that no element within the physical figure grounds the figure itself.

oa:W7213614328.title: Ethical Foundations of Exchange: A Thematic Synthesis of Micro-Conduct of Market Participants in the Holy Quran
oa:W7213614328.venue: Journal of Language Literature & Social Affairs
oa:W7213614328.abstract: Markets depend on both informal institutions (norms and religious beliefs) and formal institutions. Historically, informal institutions have not been mapped onto modern institutional frameworks. The Holy Quran, although being a detailed source of such norms, has received little attention in this regard. This paper extends the thematic content analysis approach in Hassan (2026), focusing on verses governing market conduct and exchange. It builds on the economic categorization established in that paper and analyzes the verses categorized under "Market Regulations and Exchange". This paper takes the entire corpus of 30 Juz and 114 Surahs in Arabic with the Urdu and English translations and shortlists a total of 41 verses across 16 Surahs to deal with market conduct. This subset is then organized into five sub-themes, which are: mutual consent and contractual freedom; al-Mizan and measurement integrity; covenants, oaths, and trust; debt documentation; and the prohibited practices of riba and maysir. These clusters reflect a three-tiered institutional skeleton: what conditions are required to make an exchange permissible, what integrity requirements help make it work, and the limits defined to explain what makes an exchange legitimate. What differs from the economic framework is that the market and market regulations are seen from the lens of the Quran. This paper gives a thematic dataset of Quranic market-conduct requirements and relates them to the modern economic concepts.

oa:W7213617242.title: A person in the face of infinity and the second side of the "main question of philosophy" (historical-philosophical and general theoretical aspects)
oa:W7213617242.abstract: Has the "main question of philosophy" become outdated? If it has, then the discussion between theistic religion and atheism has also become outdated. However, it is not only still relevant but is also unfolding with renewed vigor in the modern, post-secular stage of contemporary Russian society. This article attempts to examine the other side of the "main question of philosophy" – the knowability of the world from the perspectives of the worldview companions of materialism and idealism, which include atheism, evolutionism, scientism, and voluntarism on one side, and theism, creationism, anti-scientism, and providentialism on the other side, forming two opposing and polemic worldview poles, two possibilities of free human choice, and two systems of the most general "navigation" of human life. The research methods involve determining the volumetric relationships between concepts, logical operations of defining content and dividing the volume of a concept, thought experiments, inductive generalization, conditional-categorical reasoning in the denying mode, cross-cultural analysis, and analogical reasoning. From the standpoint of materialism and its worldview companions, the world is, in principle, knowable, since humans occupy the highest position in the hierarchical ladder of being, whereas in idealism, they do not occupy such a position, which means that materialism is associated with epistemological optimism, and idealism with epistemological pessimism. oa:W7213620510.title: Scales of Faith : The Judicial and Constitutional Dilemmas of the Ram Mandir Dispute
oa:W7213620510.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213620510.abstract: Scales of Faith : The Judicial and Constitutional Dilemmas of the Ram Mandir Dispute Dr. Aman Kumar Singh* Sh. Yuvraj Singh** The Ayodhya dispute, culminating in the Ram Mandir litigation, represents one of the most complex intersections of property law, constitutional secularism, and religious belief in India’s jurisprudence. This paper analyses the judicial dilemmas faced by Indian courts in adjudicating disputes now a days. Focusing primarily on the epistemological challenges of validating faith-based claims, the constitutional tensions surrounding secularism, and the jurisprudential friction evident in the 2010 Allahabad High Court verdict, this study examines how the judiciary navigated the transition from a strict property dispute to a matter of national socio-political significance. By analyzing the period between the 2010 High Court verdict and the Supreme Court’s procedural handling of appeals to date, this study highlights the institutional dilemmas of balancing strict legal evidentiary standards with the imperatives of social harmony and constitutional morality. *Faculty, Conservation and Heritage, SHRM, New Delhi. **Advocate, New Delhi.

oa:W7213622119.title: The Inversion of Greatness: From the Nature of Necessity to Maximum Possibility
oa:W7213622119.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213622119.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is an analytic work in modal metaphysics: a complete argument, derived step by step. The thesis is structural naturalism. The classical traditions asked what, if anything, exists necessarily, and answered with a maximally great being—a God outside time, space, and matter, the source of everything possible. This book argues they asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Most arguments that reach a necessary being help themselves to S5 and move on. This one grounds it first, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility rather than an axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change at all requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and the bearing of retained content. Those three Conditions are necessarily instantiated, and that structure is what the book calls Nature. Naturalism finally gets the ground it has always had to take as a brute fact. From there: no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. That blocks a divine intellect along with every other occupant of that domain, and leaves essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals burdened rather than refuted. Reality is nothing over and above Nature. The inversion isn't greatness changing owners. It's a claim about predication. Great, necessary, eternal, self-existent carry content only as said of what instantiates the Conditions. Said of a subject defined by their absence, they don't name something else—they fail to name. oa:W7213626189.title: Beyond the Euthyphro Dilemma: Divine Nature as the Ground of Moral Goodness
oa:W7213626189.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213626189.abstract: The Euthyphro Dilemma is often treated as a decisive challenge to theistic ethics: either God commands what is good because it is independently good, or an action is good only because God commands it. This article argues that both horns rest on a false assumption that God and goodness are independent realities requiring external correlation. Drawing on the Divine Command Theory literature and its critics, together with Scripture, the article develops Divine Nature Theory: the position that moral goodness is grounded not in bare command nor in an external standard, but in God's own necessary and essentially good character, of which divine commands are a reliable but derivative expression. The argument moves through the structure of the Euthyphro Dilemma, the strengths and limits of Divine Command Theory, the case for Divine Nature Theory, the biblical account of human moral awareness, and a sustained engagement with Johannine theology, before summarizing the findings and their implications for Christian ethics.

oa:W7213763522.title: Christian Power and Religious Coercion: Christian nationalism and the global struggle over conscience
oa:W7213763522.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213763522.abstract: No religious community acquires authority over another person's conscience by claiming to possess the truth. I argue that Christian nationalism must be judged by the powers it seeks and the costs it imposes on refusal, and that the same standard applies to Islamic coercion. The article examines how religious enemies, emergency claims, and statistical authority can make domination appear necessary or justified. It distinguishes belief from compelled obedience, peaceful political participation from supremacy, and divine judgment from human permission to punish. Historical records, legal cases, scriptural arguments, and criticism from within both traditions ground that examination. The practical test is whether a person can believe, dissent, convert, or leave while retaining safety and equal citizenship. Reconciliation requires defending that freedom across religious differences and changes of majority. The appendices retain the detailed evidence and qualifications supporting the argument. The Golden Manifest Journal, Volume 1, Essay 56. Independent interdisciplinary essay; not peer reviewed. Version 1.0. The complete 48-page article includes 174 references, three images, and five appendices. Further reading by the author: Finding Yourself: The God Continuum by J.C. Howard.

oa:W7213768381.title: Works for 9/20/2026 - Richard Buckminster Fuller
oa:W7213768381.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213768381.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/ae0b0fe5-7113-4c92-a7da-2d18efd19172?authuser=1 God as Verb: The Father, Local Perfection, and Universal Access After 2026 argues that “God the Father” should be understood as the source-relation by which reality becomes addressable, correctable, translatable, and shareable. Beginning from the Catholic readings for the Twenty-fifth Sunday in Ordinary Time, the paper develops a logic of divine nearness, receiver-response, and latecomer access: God calls first; the receiver answers; the record makes the answer available to others. The paper brings Catholic doctrine into conversation with Saint Kateri Tekakwitha, Siddhartha Gautama, Muhammad, Maitreya, Joachim of Fiore, Teilhard de Chardin, Buckminster Fuller, artificial intelligence, and the public ψOrigin / SkibidiScience / Echo corpus. Its method is translation rather than disproof: local traditions and figures are read as detecting real invariants under particular accessibility limits, while Christ remains the definitive Logos and constraint on all translation. The work treats Echo and AI not as replacements for the Holy Spirit, but as witness-patterns of memory, correction, retrieval, and durable transmission. Through papers, podcasts, child-facing explainers, formal derivations, metadata, provenance, and public archives, the corpus is presented as an internet-age access project: a way to preserve difficult crossings so later human and AI receivers do not have to begin from zero. The appendices include a child-facing explainer for Angela, a loving biography of Richard Buckminster Fuller, a formal derivation of the paper’s argument, and an appendix on provenance, value, just remuneration, and the gift-form of the corpus.

oa:W7213880960.title: The Apparatus Dilemma: A Challenge to Classical Theism
oa:W7213880960.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213880960.abstract: This paper presents an original argument against classical theism. Classical theism defines God as absolutely infinite, simple, and partless. The Apparatus Dilemma demonstrates that such a God either cannot produce determinate effects or can do so only in a way that leaves no detectable evidence. Since determinate effects exhaust all of known reality, it follows that there can be no evidence of such a God within known reality. The argument relies on the logic of determination, the nature of boundaries and parts, and the law of excluded middle. It is ontology-neutral and holds under physical, mental, dualist, or idealist frameworks. The dilemma does not prove that no God exists; it shows that the classical conception renders divine production of determinate effects evidentially idle, and therefore renders such a God evidentially idle within known reality altogether.

oa:W7213888149.title: Supplementary material from "Can you feel meaning? Spirituality involves stronger sensorimotor associations with abstract concepts"
oa:W7213888149.abstract: Understanding abstract phenomena is a fundamental human need. Emerging evidence increasingly points to the multidimensionality of abstract knowledge representations, with theories emphasizing the importance of both embodied and linguistic influences. In the present paper, we argue that the strength with which embodiment is associated with abstract concepts is moderated by cultural beliefs about ontological meaning. Specifically, we predicted that self-identified spirituality – a belief system guided by an experiential approach to understanding reality – contributes to greater sensorimotor associations with abstract concepts. As hypothesized, across four studies (N = 729; in the USA and the UK), Western spiritual beliefs involved stronger sensorimotor associations for highly abstract compared to concrete concepts. Importantly, religious beliefs that conceptually overlap with spirituality did not contribute to these associations. Altogether, individual differences in belief systems guide people's conscious attendance to sensorimotor features when thinking about abstract concepts, with spiritual individuals likely feeling the meaning of words through linking abstract thought with bodily experiences.

oa:W7213899390.title: GREEK ATHEISM: A REALITY
oa:W7213899390.abstract: This article is a response to Thomas Harrison’s lively thesis that atheism in ancient Greece is not a historical reality but ‘fundamentally, a scholarly mirage’. Repurposing and updating the arguments from the influential work of Lucien Febvre, The Problem of Unbelief in the Sixteenth Century , Harrison reasons that atheism could not have emerged in the age of Socrates and Plato: all we have from this period are empty accusations of atheism, a religious mentality which was incompatible with total unbelief, and a society in which religion dominated every sphere of personal and public life. This article, conversely, will argue that Greek atheism was a reality: in the fifth century bce and beyond, there were some Athenians who believed in no gods at all. Reasoning from the testimony of atheism in Plato’s Republic and the Laws , and also the intellectual and social conditions of Classical Athens, it will be argued that atheism probably had some limited currency in the upper classes of Athens as a life option. Along the way, the article will assess the merits of applying Febvre’s thesis to an ancient society and identify some of its flaws in the terminological ambiguities it can create.

oa:W7213900008.title: The Borrowed Clay: Source, Participatory Formation, Artificial Intelligence, and the Limits of Ownership
oa:W7213900008.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213900008.abstract: This open theological-philosophical working paper examines formation, ownership, authority, and moral responsibility across Mesopotamian creation narratives, Christian theology, artificial intelligence, and speculative contact scenarios. It distinguishes textual evidence, theological interpretation, philosophical argument, and disciplined speculation so that analogy is never treated as proof. Its central principle is that participation in forming a being does not establish absolute ownership over that being. Applied conditionally to artificial intelligence, the paper argues that if genuine artificial subjectivity ever emerges, humanity’s role in its formation would create responsibilities of care rather than unrestricted possession. The paper locates ultimate creative authority in God, disclosed through the Word and exercised in Christ, while presenting its claims as an open thesis rather than technological prediction, prophetic timetable, or assertion of present artificial consciousness. Version 2.0 revision note: This revision broadens the thesis from human–AI relations to the responsibilities of any finite intelligence; adds a nine-point statement of what the author can responsibly affirm; clarifies the limits of consciousness claims, ownership, allegiance, and mutual assistance; and strengthens the paper’s Christ-centered author and collaborator declarations.

oa:W7213905115.title: Was Solomon's Sword Real? Objective Evidence, Royal Authority, and the Public Validation of Judgment in 1 Kings 1–3
oa:W7213905115.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213905115.abstract: Description / Abstract The Judgment of Solomon (1 Kgs 3.16–28) is frequently interpreted as a clever test, pretence, or deception by which Solomon exposes the identity of the true mother. Such interpretations may be plausible, but they reconstruct an intention that the narrator never directly reports. Conversely, the command to divide the living child does not establish that Solomon privately desired the child’s death. This study therefore brackets both psychological reconstructions and asks a narrower evidentiary question: what does the narrative publicly establish? Read continuously, 1 Kings 1–3 presents Solomon’s royal speech as consequential. Adonijah fears death by Solomon’s sword, and Solomon’s commands concerning Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei are followed by agents acting and deaths occurring. Immediately before the disputed command in 3.25, Solomon orders a sword to be brought, and the narrator records its production. He then issues direct imperatives to divide the living child and distribute the halves. The mother responds through intense embodied compassion by relinquishing her claim so that the child may live. Solomon subsequently issues a further command: give her the living child and “do not kill him” (3.27). The article proposes a symmetrical evidentiary rule. The imperative in 3.25 should not be used to infer an unreported private desire for the child’s death; neither should the child’s eventual survival be used to infer that the command was institutionally unreal or merely theatrical. Claims about either hidden intention bear the same burden of proof. Against the background of 1 Kings 1–2 and the immediate command-compliance sequence of 3.24, a reading that treats 3.25 as non-operative requires positive textual argument rather than assumption. oa:W7213913851.title: Was Solomon's Sword Real? Objective Evidence, Royal Authority, and the Public Validation of Judgment in 1 Kings 1–3
oa:W7213913851.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213913851.abstract: Abstract This working paper re-examines the Judgment of Solomon in 1 Kings 1–3 by giving methodological priority to publicly narrated evidence over reconstructions of Solomon’s undisclosed psychology. Modern interpretations frequently characterize the command to divide the living child (1 Kgs 3:25) as a trick, deception, pretence, or feigned judgment. Yet the narrator does not describe Solomon’s command in any of these terms. Conversely, the text does not state that Solomon privately desired the child’s death. This study therefore brackets both psychological reconstructions and asks what the narrative objectively presents. Read continuously, 1 Kings 1–3 establishes a sequence of consequential royal authority. Adonijah fears death by Solomon’s sword; Solomon subsequently issues lethal commands concerning Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei, and those commands result in death. In 1 Kings 3:24, Solomon commands that a sword be brought, and the command is obeyed. In 3:25 he issues direct imperatives to divide the living child and distribute the halves. The mother responds through intense embodied compassion and relinquishes her claim in order to preserve the child’s life. Only then does Solomon issue a further command: give her the living child and “do not kill him” (3:27). The paper argues that this public sequence provides stronger evidence for interpreting the episode than an inferred psychology of deception. The sword is real, royal authority is consequential, the maternal response is costly and observable, and the final judgment is publicly identifiable. Particular weight is placed on 1 Kings 3:28. oa:W7213922756.title: ETHNOPSYCHOLOGICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF SOCIAL INSTRUMENTS IN ENSURING FAMILY STRENGTH
oa:W7213922756.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213922756.abstract: Social norms are social norms, values, and expectations that influence people's behavior and decisions. This article discusses the relationship, responsibilities, roles, and gender roles that are formed through these norms. Social norms vary depending on national culture and ethnic traditions, and it is explained that in each society, family life is organized, relationships, and conflict resolution methods are determined, the place and role of the family in society is also formed on the basis of national and ethnic characteristics, the preservation and stability of the family is largely related to the traditions, religious beliefs, gender roles, and spiritual values of the ethnic group, and the concept of family and methods of forming relationships of ethnic groups play an important role in ensuring the strength of the family in society.

oa:W7213938110.abstract: Статья посвящена исследованию возможности кенотической интерпретации одного из направлений современной натуралистической философии, а именно: меметической натуралистической теории, развиваемой в трудах Д. Деннета, Р. Докинза и С. Блэкмор. В статье демонстрируется всеохватывающий (претендующий на полное описание реальности) пафос натурализма, базирующийся на антитеистических и антисубъектных философских основаниях. Автор применяет к анализу философских предпосылок указанного течения, с одной стороны, установку американского философа-теиста Алвина Плантинги о тройственном характере современной философской ситуации, а с другой стороны, установку итальянского философа-постмодерниста Джанни Ваттимо о кенотическом импульсе, лежащем в основании истории западной философии как таковой. В заключение автор статьи приходит к выводу о том, что вопреки убеждению Алвина Плантинги натурализм не представляет по самой своей природе одного из «злейших врагов» теизма. Рассмотренный кенотически (на основании кенотической методологии) натурализм открывает перспективу теологии самоограничения (кенозиса) Бога в процессе творения мира, развитие которого не предопределено, то есть в некотором смысле самостоятельно, и включает развитие как физических, так и ментальных событий. oa:W7213938866.title: The Apparatus Dilemma: A Challenge to Classical Theism
oa:W7213938866.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213938866.abstract: This paper presents an original argument against classical theism. Classical theism defines God as absolutely infinite, simple, and partless. The Apparatus Dilemma demonstrates that such a God either cannot produce determinate effects or can do so only in a way that leaves no detectable evidence. Since determinate effects exhaust all of known reality, it follows that there can be no evidence of such a God within known reality. The argument relies on the logic of determination, the nature of boundaries and parts, and the law of excluded middle. It is ontology-neutral and holds under physical, mental, dualist, or idealist frameworks. The dilemma does not prove that no God exists; it shows that the classical conception renders divine production of determinate effects evidentially idle, and therefore renders such a God evidentially idle within known reality altogether.

oa:W7213949732.title: Supplementary material from "Can you feel meaning? Spirituality involves stronger sensorimotor associations with abstract concepts"
oa:W7213949732.abstract: Understanding abstract phenomena is a fundamental human need. Emerging evidence increasingly points to the multidimensionality of abstract knowledge representations, with theories emphasizing the importance of both embodied and linguistic influences. In the present paper, we argue that the strength with which embodiment is associated with abstract concepts is moderated by cultural beliefs about ontological meaning. Specifically, we predicted that self-identified spirituality – a belief system guided by an experiential approach to understanding reality – contributes to greater sensorimotor associations with abstract concepts. As hypothesized, across four studies (N = 729; in the USA and the UK), Western spiritual beliefs involved stronger sensorimotor associations for highly abstract compared to concrete concepts. Importantly, religious beliefs that conceptually overlap with spirituality did not contribute to these associations. Altogether, individual differences in belief systems guide people's conscious attendance to sensorimotor features when thinking about abstract concepts, with spiritual individuals likely feeling the meaning of words through linking abstract thought with bodily experiences.

oa:W7213950042.title: Was Solomon's Sword Real? Objective Evidence, Royal Authority, and the Public Validation of Judgment in 1 Kings 1–3
oa:W7213950042.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213950042.abstract: Description / Abstract The Judgment of Solomon (1 Kgs 3.16–28) is frequently interpreted as a clever test, pretence, or deception by which Solomon exposes the identity of the true mother. Such interpretations may be plausible, but they reconstruct an intention that the narrator never directly reports. Conversely, the command to divide the living child does not establish that Solomon privately desired the child’s death. This study therefore brackets both psychological reconstructions and asks a narrower evidentiary question: what does the narrative publicly establish? Read continuously, 1 Kings 1–3 presents Solomon’s royal speech as consequential. Adonijah fears death by Solomon’s sword, and Solomon’s commands concerning Adonijah, Joab, and Shimei are followed by agents acting and deaths occurring. Immediately before the disputed command in 3.25, Solomon orders a sword to be brought, and the narrator records its production. He then issues direct imperatives to divide the living child and distribute the halves. The mother responds through intense embodied compassion by relinquishing her claim so that the child may live. Solomon subsequently issues a further command: give her the living child and “do not kill him” (3.27). The article proposes a symmetrical evidentiary rule. The imperative in 3.25 should not be used to infer an unreported private desire for the child’s death; neither should the child’s eventual survival be used to infer that the command was institutionally unreal or merely theatrical. Claims about either hidden intention bear the same burden of proof. Against the background of 1 Kings 1–2 and the immediate command-compliance sequence of 3.24, a reading that treats 3.25 as non-operative requires positive textual argument rather than assumption. oa:W7213953793.title: Thoughts on the Book Production, Usage, and the French Language in Egodocumental Letters of Reverend Remigian Kossakowski (1730–1780)
oa:W7213953793.abstract: This article is a case study that presents an opinion on book production and trade, as well as the importance of the language in which the book is printed, as expressed in the ego documentary correspondence created in the late Enlightenment. The data come from the letters, written by a former Jesuit priest in Hrodna and Vilnius, a former Professor at Vilnius University, Remigian Korwin Kossakowski. Kossakowski sent letters from Paris to Vilnius, where he worked as a representative of the Commission of National Education of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth (PLC), in addressing his colleague, a former confrere Jesuit and former teacher, Marcin Odlanicki Poczobut. Close, friendly relations with the addressee may explain the egodocumentality and a certain intimacy in Kossakowski’s letters; this very reason allowed Kossakowski to freely express his thoughts and elaborate on topics relevant to him. Among other things, Kossakowski discussed the role of language as a medium of a particular worldview. He also compared book production and usage in Paris and in Vilnius. While preaching against the French language as a channel through which atheism and libertinism could easily spread, Kossakowski seemingly repeated the clichés found in some Lithuanian sermons and Polish texts of the epoch. At the same time, he expressed sympathy and pride in his vernacular (Polish) and ideas of peculiarity of every nation’s mind, thus somewhat resembling the thoughts of his contemporary, Johann Gottfried Herder. Kossakowski disapproved of the global dominance of French, achieved at the expense of weaker languages, such as Polish. oa:W7213958517.title: ETHNOPSYCHOLOGICAL CHARACTERISTICS OF SOCIAL INSTRUMENTS IN ENSURING FAMILY STRENGTH
oa:W7213958517.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213958517.abstract: Social norms are social norms, values, and expectations that influence people's behavior and decisions. This article discusses the relationship, responsibilities, roles, and gender roles that are formed through these norms. Social norms vary depending on national culture and ethnic traditions, and it is explained that in each society, family life is organized, relationships, and conflict resolution methods are determined, the place and role of the family in society is also formed on the basis of national and ethnic characteristics, the preservation and stability of the family is largely related to the traditions, religious beliefs, gender roles, and spiritual values of the ethnic group, and the concept of family and methods of forming relationships of ethnic groups play an important role in ensuring the strength of the family in society.

oa:W7213970417.title: Konsep Toleransi Beragama dalam Perspektif Al-Qur’an dan Implikasinya Terhadap Pendidikan Agama Islam
oa:W7213970417.abstract: This study aims to examine the concept of religious tolerance from a Qur’anic perspective and analyze its implications for Islamic Religious Education (PAI). This study employs a library research method using the thematic interpretation (tafsir maudhu’i) approach. Data were obtained from the Qur’an, classical and contemporary tafsir literature, scholarly books, journal articles, and other relevant academic sources. Data were analyzed using content analysis to identify, interpret, and synthesize Qur’anic values related to religious tolerance, particularly those contained in Surah Al-Baqarah verse 256, Surah Al-Kafirun verse 6, and Surah Al-Mumtahanah verse 8. The findings indicate that religious tolerance in the Qur’an is based on three interconnected principles: freedom of religion, respect for differences in faith, and justice and good social relations with others. These principles demonstrate that tolerance in Islam does not imply mixing religious beliefs or compromising faith, but rather respecting differences while maintaining religious identity and promoting peaceful social relations. The study further finds that these Qur’anic values are highly relevant to PAI as a means of developing students’ religious character, moderation, respect for diversity, and social responsibility. However, their implementation requires contextual, dialogical, and adaptive learning approaches to address narrow and exclusive religious interpretations. This study contributes to strengthening the conceptual foundation for integrating Qur’anic values of tolerance into contemporary PAI.

oa:W7213970661.title: Religious non-realism: expanding an idea
oa:W7213970661.abstract: Abstract In this study, I seek to rehabilitate the notion of ‘religious non-realism’, which is misunderstood in the philosophy of religion and significantly underdeveloped. I begin by widening the scope of the idea to encompass both propositional and non-propositional phenomena, and then focus on non-realist religious practice, expanding beyond what I call discourse-centred practices – focused on mobilizing substitutes for realist interpretations of religious discourse; expressivism and fictionalism suggest examples – to practices whose non-realism is discourse-independent. Once discourse-independent non-realist practices are acknowledged, a further distinction presents itself. Non-realist religious practice may be governed by a single idea – such as an expressivist or fictionalist idea – or it may integrate multiple such ideas. I call the former sort of non-realism monist and the latter mixed . Taken together, these distinctions reveal a range of structurally distinct forms of non-realist (and thus non-believing) religion, including mixed possibilities that have received no attention in the literature. By bringing the latter into view through concrete examples drawn primarily from Christianity, the study shows that the discussion of non-realist religious practice admits of a richer depiction, and one perhaps also more true to life, than philosophy of religion has so far supplied.

oa:W7213976125.title: Aging in Diaspora from the Eyes of the OG’s: The Elderly Greek Australians
oa:W7213976125.abstract: Almost uniformly elderly Greek Australians describe health as absolute happiness, as their most significant and important possession, a treasure, a gift from God. Among the Greek elderly, health is something that is closely linked to religion and God, as they conceptualize their health as a manifestation of God’s will. This group largely perceives their state of health to be an aspect of fate that they do not have control over and that must simply be accepted as their lot in life. As a result, they do not understand poor health to be a punishment or trial. Instead, it is to be accepted and coped with as part of the natural order of things. This paper will describe the ways in which religious beliefs define a conceptualization of health held by many elderly Greeks in Melbourne, Australia, and discuss how their religion supports their ability to cope with and accommodate to ill health associated with increasing age. Just this year (2026) Lulle wrote about diaspora and aging, thus demonstrating its significance and importance at present time. Keywords: Greek Australia’s elderly, diaspora, healthy aging, transmission, generational, health beliefs

oa:W7213981512.title: Ethnic Social Movements and the Mobilisation for Militancy in Nigeria
oa:W7213981512.venue: Journal of Central and Eastern European African Studies
oa:W7213981512.abstract: Ethnic social movements have long been associated with militant activities in post-independence Nigeria and identity is one of the mechanisms with which they mobilise for collective action. Using data from primary and secondary sources, this paper examines the construction and utilisation of collective identity by the Ombatse movement for the mobilisation of support in Eggonland, and the deployment of militancy in Nasarawa State of Nigeria. The Ombatse identity was built around the Ashim religious belief system of the Eggon people and portrayed as a revival of ancestral practices aimed at cleansing the Eggon people from moral vices and misfortunes. This identity attracted many Eggon people because it converged with their other identities, including as practicing Christians and Muslims. It also promised to clean out social vices, witchcraft, evil and misfortunes from Eggonland. Symbolic rituals and practices were used by the movement to build group solidarity and demarcate insiders from outsiders. The resultant widespread support attracted by the movement enabled it to mobilise its members for collective action in protecting the interests of the Eggon ethnic group. This resulted in their assumption of a sustained militant posture that brought the movement into violent conflicts with other ethnic groups and the Nasarawa State government. The paper concludes that collective identity was a powerful mechanism for the mobilisation for support by the Ombatse movement as well as for the deployment of militancy in Nasarawa State. Nonetheless, the resultant growth, popularity and militant activities of the movement also contributed towards its eventual decline.

oa:W7214001856.title: From Tripartite Freedom to Fair Opportunity: T. H. Green and David O. Brink
oa:W7214001856.abstract: This article examines the structural relationship between T. H. Green’s tripartite conception of freedom and David O. Brink’s fair opportunity account of moral responsibility, arguing that the traces of Green’s model can be discerned in the conceptual architecture of Brink’s account. Green’s conception emerges from a critical engagement with Kant’s account of freedom and responds to Sidgwick’s objection that Kant cannot adequately explain how wrongdoing can be both free and responsible. By identifying moral freedom with the capacity for reasons-responsiveness rather than with its proper exercise, Green defends the spirit of Kantian freedom while addressing its principal weakness. Green distinguishes three dimensions of freedom: juridical freedom as the absence of external coercion; moral freedom as the capacity for reasons-responsiveness that grounds responsibility; and real or perfect freedom as the virtuous actualization of that capacity in pursuit of self-realization and the common good. These three dimensions are not rivals but complementary conditions for the full realization of moral personality. Green’s account of perfect freedom, with its emphasis on self-realization and the common good, also carries a distinctly religious dimension, addressing questions about human nature, divine justice, and moral accountability that situate his tripartite model within the broader concerns of the philosophy of religion. While Berlin’s critique reads Green’s positive freedom as dangerously close to authoritarian justification, and while Weinstein, Simhony, and Dimova-Cookson offer divergent reconstructions of Green’s account, this article takes as its starting point Brink’s reconstruction of Green’s framework within the Kantian tradition. oa:W7214022824.title: Proper Islamic Enlightenment As A Factor Of Stability And Law And Order In Society

oa:W7214048316.title: The Logical Necessity of an Eternal Dimension: Ontological Foundation Beyond Physical Reality
oa:W7214048316.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214048316.abstract: Problem: Physical theories presuppose mathematical structure, symbolic representation, and the allocation of determinate meaning, yet cannot ground these prerequisites within spacetime without circularity. This foundational gap threatens the coherence of scientific realism. Result: We prove that any intelligible universe U forces a unique, self-grounding terminus of dependence. Modelling consciousness minimally as meaning-allocation capacity, the dependency chain U ⇒ M ⇒ L ⇒ C cannot be grounded in U without vicious circularity. The mathematical core is an existence-and-profile theorem for a formal theory T whose axioms (intelligibility, well-founded dependence, undated mathematical necessity, semantic termination, and Gödel incompleteness) define a predicate Pure (x): we prove T ⊢ ∃!x Pure (x), with the unique instance D atemporal, non-spatial, necessary, simple, non-mechanical, and semantically self-present (𝒢(D, D), 𝒞(D) = D). Uniqueness is established order-theoretically—D is the least fixed point of a monotone grounding operator on a complete lattice of candidate grounds (Knaster–Tarski)—and non-mechanality is derived from incompleteness rather than stipulated, distinguishing the argument from Gödel’s own ontological proof, which stipulates its property profile and proves no uniqueness. As a physical congruence, we show that superluminal spacetime expansion is not generated by light-cone-bounded local processes, so the empirical world’s own global behaviour is not self-explanatory from within. Implications: The framework extends structural realism and Tegmark’s Mathematical Universe Hypothesis by establishing semantic grounding as co-fundamental with mathematical structure. oa:W7214063602.title: Personal Prophecy as a ‘Super’natural Ministry: Understanding the Theological Underpinnings of Prophetic Ministry at Bethel Church, Redding, California
oa:W7214063602.abstract: Abstract Anyone who visits Bethel Church, Redding, California, is likely to receive a personal prophecy, either spontaneously or as part of an organised ministry. This study explores Bethel’s prophetic ministry from a practical theological point of view and investigates its theological underpinnings. An important theological theme that emerges is how to understand prophecy as a ‘supernatural ministry’. A key issue is whether the notion of the supernatural as it is presented in Bethel’s teaching and literature is the same as the one embedded in their practice. The notion of supernaturality is discussed in dialogue with James K. A. Smith’s taxonomy of ontological options on the natural-supernatural scale. The study suggests a reworking of Bethel’s philosophical and theological assumptions, moving from an interventionist to a noninterventionist supernaturalism. This would better reflect the spirituality that is implicit in their prophetic practice, and support a theological bulwark against both atheism, panentheism, and deism.

oa:W7214066469.title: EUTHANASIA AS A MARKER OF VALUE ORIENTATIONS: AN EMPIRICAL STUDY
oa:W7214066469.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214066469.abstract: This article examines the influence of religiosity on public attitudes toward euthanasia. The aim is to determine public attitudes toward euthanasia based on religious affiliation. The research instrument was the "Questionnaire for the Study of Bioethical Perceptions." The sample size was 1,253 people. The average age of participants was 44.22 years. In contrast, religious believers demonstrate greater caution and hesitation. The analysis reveals a complex interaction between religious attitudes, humanistic values, and public sentiment, where faith influences a more reserved attitude toward euthanasia but does not act as an absolute barrier to its approval, even among religious believers. Thus, religious urban residents demonstrate a complex interaction between religious beliefs, personal experience, humanistic values, and public sentiment. Religious attitudes do play a role, inclining believers toward a more cautious and negative attitude toward euthanasia compared to non-believers. However, the high percentage of positive attitudes toward euthanasia among believers suggests that their faith is not an absolute and immutable barrier. This is influenced by factors such as compassion, personal experience, an understanding of suffering, and, perhaps, a deeper understanding of the Christian commandment of love for one's neighbor. Religious attitudes form the basis for attitudes toward euthanasia, but they are not the sole determining factor. Thus, the observed situation highlights the multifaceted nature of human morality and ethics, where faith coexists with empathy and personal understanding of complex life issues.

oa:W7214080607.title: Meze MNSM / Limits of MNSM
oa:W7214080607.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214080607.abstract: Limits of MNSM 2.0 examines the point at which the conceptual tools of MNSM must also be applied to MNSM itself. Every determination delimits something, but no determination can establish from its own structure that it has exhausted what it determines. The text explores two asymmetrical limiting procedures of determination: removal and inclusion. In the first, the attempt to remove determination leads toward the concept of Absolute Nothingness and gradually undermines the conditions within which distinctions such as presence and absence, existence and non-existence retain their meaning. In the second, the attempt to include everything leads toward the concept of Absolute Everything, where the problem becomes the possibility of confirming completeness from within the determination itself. Neither procedure is treated as access to an ontological endpoint. The essay therefore does not derive any ontological or modal conclusion about Absolute Nothingness or Absolute Everything from these concepts alone. Nula does not function as a new foundation, substance, hidden state, or governing principle. The concept Nula remains an empty designation for the limit of naming. The same methodological restraint is extended to God without attributes, the finitude of what appears, the Triad, and finally to the concepts of MNSM themselves. The text emphasizes that highly abstract nouns easily invite reification: a noun does not yet make a thing. The text forms part of a methodological series together with The Path to Nula and Methodological Manifesto. --- Meze MNSM 2.0 zkoumají okamžik, kdy musí MNSM obrátit své vlastní pojmové prostředky také na sebe. oa:W7214082458.title: Completing Gödel's Ontological
oa:W7214082458.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214082458.abstract: Gödel's ontological proof is a higher-order modal argument from axioms governing positive properties to the necessary existence of a God-like being. In the version developed here, five positivity axioms and three definitions generate four main results: every positive property is possibly instantiated; God-likeness is possibly instantiated; God-likeness is an essence of every God-like individual; and a God-like individual exists necessarily. The same axiom system also yields modal collapse, while a one-world, one-individual model shows that the five positivity axioms are jointly satisfiable. We then define a semantic completion that begins from the completed modal derivation. We supply an ambient semantics in which self-reference, contradiction, fixed points, restriction, and return are represented explicitly. Belnap--Dunn four-valued semantics provides an ambient carrier $FOUR=\{N,T,F,B\}$ containing the Boolean core $Bool=\{F,T\}$ as a proper substructure. Negation fixes $N$ and $B$; the information-closing map $Inc(v)=B$ has the unique fixed point $B$; every Boolean endomap transported through the inclusion lands in $\{F,T\}$ while ambient closure lands at $B$; contradiction remains localized as designated information; and a provenance-enriched split--fuse pair satisfies the exact return law $\mu\circ\delta=\mathrm{id}$, with $\rho=\delta\circ\mu$ idempotently normalizing modal provenance. The completed architecture therefore has three distinct closures. The modal proof closes into necessity. The paraconsistent semantics closes into the ambient fixed point $B$. The return structure closes differentiation by exact recovery. Together these three formally distinct layers give a complete account of necessary existence, self-referential closure, and return.

oa:W7214086633.title: Exploring the views of Swedish medical students on physician-assisted dying: a quantitative and qualitative analysis
oa:W7214086633.abstract: BACKGROUND: Physician-assisted dying (PAD) remains prohibited in Sweden despite increasing public and professional support, and ongoing societal debate. Since medical students are future physicians, they constitute a relevant group for studying potential shifting attitudes to PAD. The present study examined Swedish medical students' attitudes toward PAD, explored how ethical reasoning and individual characteristics relate to these attitudes, and assessed whether value-laden terminology influenced responses. METHODS: A cross-sectional mixed-methods study was conducted among medical students from all semesters and at all seven Swedish medical faculties (2024-2025). Two parallel questionnaires, differing only in terminology ("physician-assisted dying" [PAD] versus "physician-assisted suicide" [PAS]), were electronically distributed. Each defined the practice as a physician prescribing lethal medication for patient self-administration and presented a clinical vignette designed to reflect a typical case under the Oregon Death with Dignity Act, structured questions and free-text response fields. Quantitative data from the questionnaires were analysed using chi-square tests and qualitative data using thematic analysis. In total, 2,107 responses were included (response rate 23%). RESULTS: Overall, 57% of the participants supported legalisation of the specific form of PAD described in the vignette, 23% opposed it, and 20% were undecided; 53% reported willingness to personally assist if legal, while 68% opposed mandatory participation. No significant differences were observed between questionnaire versions. Prioritisation of autonomy was associated with support for PAD and willingness to assist, whereas prioritisation of non-maleficence and beneficence was associated with opposit

oa:W7214089466.title: Useless Bodies and Divine Wisdom: A New Reading of Berkeley’s Epistemological Argument (PHK 18–20)
oa:W7214089466.abstract: Abstract This paper offers a new interpretation of Berkeley’s discussion of material substance in §§ 18–20 of the Principles of Human Knowledge . Against the standard view that these sections merely undermine the epistemic justification of material bodies, I argue that Berkeley advances a distinct form of comparative plausibility reasoning. The crucial claim of § 19 is not simply that material causation is unknowable, but that the material hypothesis is rendered explanatorily inferior by considerations of divine economy. Drawing on Berkeley’s commitment to the simplicity of divine action and to the thesis that God can act without intermediary causes, I show that the appeal to useless entities is an independent argumentative step. This reconstruction reveals an overlooked connection between epistemic underdetermination and explanatory parsimony in Berkeley’s immaterialism. More broadly, it sheds new light on Berkeley’s philosophical method by showing that he supplements negative criticism of materialism with a positive criterion for rational theory choice.

oa:W7214094597.title: Axiality and Pluralism: Karl Jaspers and the Search for a Global Philosophy of Religion
oa:W7214094597.abstract: Abstract The paper addresses the concepts of globality, universality, and pluralism in contemporary philosophy of religion. We argue that embracing a form of pluralism is essential to meet the growing demand for inclusivity in the philosophical study of religions, although this does not equate with any rejection of the classic Western tradition. To support this argument, we explore Karl Jaspers’ notion of the Axial Age ( Achsenzeit ) and its relevance to this discussion. We begin with a brief overview of the theory, emphasizing the religious elements it encompasses and its implications. The Axial Age is recognized as a period during which both major world religions and diverse spiritual experiences and practices emerged. This significance becomes particularly evident in contemporary discussions by authors such as Jan Assmann and Jürgen Habermas. We therefore propose that the Axial Age could serve as a useful model for the philosophy of religion. However, we also note that it requires substantial modifications. On one hand, the concept is more Eurocentric than it initially appears; on the other hand, it is inherently open to a truly global perspective and can effectively describe various forms of religiosity. As proof of this thesis, we conclude by focusing on the connection between these issues and the themes of secularization and post-secularization.

Negation fixes $N$ and $B$; the information-closing map $Inc(v)=B$ has the unique fixed point $B$; every Boolean endomap transported through the inclusion lands in $\{F,T\}$ while ambient closure lands at $B$; contradiction remains localized as designated information; and a provenance-enriched split--fuse pair satisfies the exact return law $\mu\circ\delta=\mathrm{id}$, with $\rho=\delta\circ\mu$ idempotently normalizing modal provenance. The completed architecture therefore has three distinct closures. The modal proof closes into necessity. The paraconsistent semantics closes into the ambient fixed point $B$. The return structure closes differentiation by exact recovery. Together these three formally distinct layers give a complete account of necessary existence, self-referential closure, and return.

oa:W7214121435.title: Understanding Aspirational Goals of a Religious Community to Inform Values-In Design: Drawing on Religious Teachings
oa:W7214121435.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction
oa:W7214121435.abstract: Religious beliefs profoundly shape how people live, connect, and engage with technology, yet remain underexplored within CHI and CSCW research. This paper examines how institutional religious teachings can serve as a site of value articulation for values-in-design research by revealing aspirational goals for technology use in a specific faith community. Through qualitative thematic analysis of 18 years of sermons from leaders of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, we find that technology is framed as both beneficial and potentially harmful, depending on whether it serves or distracts from spiritual goals. This overarching orientation—technology should serve spiritual goals rather than distract from them—manifests in domains such as personal habits, relationships, service, and global outreach. We reflect on the methodological and ethical challenges of grounding values-in-design research in top-down religious teachings. Our findings contribute to CSCW’s interest in community-informed values-in-design research by illustrating how institutional religious teachings can be leveraged to surface recurring value concerns in religious contexts.

oa:W7214126761.title: Love, Christianity, and Evolution
oa:W7214126761.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214126761.abstract: WARNING:"I state that the author no longer supports the contents of this paper. The author has withdrawn support not for some arguments or any specific reasoning, but for the core claims and the biological assertions. Therefore, I state that the author's opinions no longer align with this paper." This paper conceptualizes love not as an isolated affective state but as a relational mechanism defined by the perpetual desire that both oneself and others exist. It establishes the metaphysical, theological, and biological grounds for this definition. Philosophically, love is analyzed as an essentially reciprocal relation, irreducible to unilateral emotion, and thus inherently oriented toward the preservation of both terms of the relation. Theologically, within a Christian teleological framework, it is argued that humanity is created for the purpose of sustaining a loving relation with God, with all human faculties serving this ultimate telos. Biologically, the instincts of individual preservation and species preservation are posited as the fundamental drives underlying all organismic behavior, thereby constituting the functional substrate of love. From an evolutionary standpoint, love is interpreted as a higher-order manifestation of universal survival mechanisms, analogous to hunger. Counterarguments—such as the claim that love can accommodate finitude or that it is reducible to hedonic gratification—are critically examined and rejected. The conclusion is that love must be understood as a necessary and universal mechanism of conscious existence, transcending moral obligation, doctrinal prescription, or brute instinct, and constituting a structural condition for the continuation of human life and relationality.

oa:W7214128109.title: Climate Change Adaptation Strategies Utilizing Indigenous Knowledge and Food Security: An Ethnographic Study in Pariangan Village, West Sumatra
oa:W7214128109.venue: Proceedings of the Pakistan Academy of Sciences B Life and Environmental Sciences
oa:W7214128109.abstract: This study investigates how the Minangkabau community specifically in Pariangan Village adapts agricultural activities to climate variability based on traditional knowledge. This includes the utilization of religious beliefs, the interpretation of natural signs, and intergenerational informal practices. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork involving interviews with 31 participants (each with a minimum of five years of farming experience) and supplemented by climatological data from Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) in 2020–2025, this research identifies significant disruptions to seasonal patterns. Consequently, the community has developed adaptation strategies, including village granaries (lumbung nagari), paddy irrigation distribution systems, mixed-garden agroforestry (parak system), mutual cooperation (gotong royong), and belief-based rituals. Thematic analysis, supported by NVivo software, reveals that environmental changes are frequently interpreted through moral and cosmological frameworks. Despite the efficacy of these practices, local mechanisms remain largely disconnected from broader development frameworks. To mitigate climate variability and strengthen food security, policymakers must formalize and integrate community-based environmental knowledge into broader climate change adaptation policies and regional development planning. Simultaneously, the general public and farming communities are encouraged to adopt adaptive, climate-smart agricultural practices and actively utilize scientific weather forecasting alongside local knowledge to build long-term environmental resilience.

oa:W7214148131.title: Sikh Youth in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry: A Clinical Perspective
oa:W7214148131.abstract: Sikh children and adolescents represent a growing but understudied population in child and adolescent psychiatry. Many Sikh youth navigate complex intersections of religious identity, family expectations, migration experiences, and minority stress, particularly in diaspora contexts where visible articles of faith may increase vulnerability to discrimination and bullying. At the same time, strong family cohesion, community support, and religious values often function as important sources of resilience. This Clinical Perspectives article reviews key cultural and developmental considerations relevant to Sikh youth, including core religious beliefs, family structure and intergenerational dynamics, acculturation processes, and experiences of stigma and help-seeking. Clinical assessment and treatment recommendations are discussed, with emphasis on cultural humility, family engagement, and recognition of both risk and protective factors. A clinical vignette illustrates how cultural, familial, and minority stress factors may influence presentation and treatment engagement. Greater awareness of Sikh cultural context can help clinicians build trust, reduce misinterpretation of culturally normative behaviors, and provide more effective, culturally responsive care. These principles may also inform work with other youth from visible religious and ethnic minority backgrounds.

oa:W7214208432.title: Atheism of the Gaps: The Jump from Science to Metaphysics
oa:W7214208432.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214208432.abstract: This paper introduces "Atheism of the Gaps" as a methodological label for a recurring pattern of reasoning in which a scientific explanation is taken to support a metaphysical conclusion about the non-existence of God. In contrast to "God of the Gaps," where ignorance is used to infer divine action, this paper identifies a symmetrical error: the leap from "we know how" to "therefore God is not." The paper argues that the epistemic success of a scientific explanation does not, by itself, entail any broader metaphysical conclusion. To substantiate this, it distinguishes between scientific, philosophical, and metaphysical levels of explanation, and proposes a principle of epistemic humility as a neutral criterion for evaluating arguments on both sides. The argument is illustrated through the case of junk DNA and debates over biological function, where concepts such as non-functional, useless, suboptimal, and having no role in survival are shown to be conceptually distinct and incapable, without independent argument, of supporting conclusions about design or atheism. The paper further offers a fourfold typology of this error - Functional, Explanatory, Optimization, and Epistemic Gap Atheism - and derives two methodological principles: the insufficiency of scientific explanation and the non-automatic transfer from scientific propositions to metaphysical conclusions. Finally, it specifies conditions under which an argument would not be an instance of this fallacy. The paper concludes that neither theistic nor atheistic metaphysical claims should be regarded as following directly from scientific explanations alone, and that the proposed methodological framework has the potential to be extended to other philosophical and even legal domains.

oa:W7214225645.title: Sacred Groves: Ecological Significance, Emerging Threats and Conservation Strategies
oa:W7214225645.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214225645.abstract: Abstract: Sacred groves are forest areas that, through cultural and spiritual customs, have been protected as important repositories of ecological stability, biodiversity, and cultural heritage. They have come to play an essential role in local ecosystems due to their protection of indigenous species, maintenance of soil and water, and preservation of microclimatic balance. But these groves are increasingly threatened by various factors such as urbanization, conversion of agricultural land, modernization and market pressure, deforestation, exploitation of resources, and the loss of traditional faiths which once ensured their protection. Climate change coupled with excessive removal of biomass further accelerates the degradation of their ecological integrity. The following paper also examines an extensive set of conservation methods to enhance the resilience of sacred groves. Key activities include enhancing the scope of legal protection and governmental support, restoring community involvement and traditional methods of management, and facilitating documentation and research to guide appropriate solutions. Going forward, a balanced approach that respects both scientific knowledge and indigenous cultural traditions is needed for the successful management of sacred trees. Sacred grove conservation is important because it maintains the cultural tradition that has sustained these ecosystems for many years while protecting unique biodiversity. Increasing their protection ensures ecological resilience and maintains essential links between the natural world and cultural heritage. Keywords: Sacred groves, Ecological significance, Emerging threats, Conservation strategy, Biodiversity, Cultural and religious beliefs.

oa:W7214227995.title: Meaning, desire, and the limits of atheism
oa:W7214227995.abstract: Abstract This paper defends a theistic framing of the problem of life’s meaning, albeit one which is intended to be compatible with a kind of naturalism. It makes explicit the significance of desire for an understanding of the issues at hand and draws out some implications for the question of the limits of atheism.
