oa:W7214284780.title: The Structure of Yearning: Bouzid's Rule (B+F=Nf) as an Axiological Framework for Virtue and Vice
oa:W7214284780.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214284780.abstract: Contemporary debates in the axiology of theism evaluate spiritual yearning based on its object (theistic, ultimate, or secular) or its quantity (moderate vs. excessive). However, this quantitative-objective approach fails to resolve core paradoxes, as it treats yearning as a continuous variable, ignoring its internal architecture and relation to consciousness. This paper addresses three methodological paradoxes: (1) The Axiological Paradox (Rubio, 2026): If Aristotelian virtue is a mean, and God's value is infinite, is yearning for God a necessary vice of excess? (2) The Structural Paradox (Anderson, 2026): Can gratitude stifle the yearning for redemption by creating an illusion of contentment with unredeemed suffering? (3) The Objective Paradox (Burkhart, 2026): Can yearning for sacred land be evaluated by the same metrics as yearning for a personal God? The central thesis: the solution lies not in measuring how much or toward what we yearn, but in understanding the architecture of yearning. This paper introduces a novel phenomenological framework: Bouzid's Rule of Conscious Existence (B+F=Nf). This model structurally distinguishes between Spontaneous Yearning (biological, suppresses the witness, ends in satiation) and Sovereign Yearning (conscious, where the witness exercises Veto Power over biological drives, generating existential meaning). Consequently, virtue or vice is determined by its architecture (is yearning sovereign [F] or co-opted [B]?) and the worthiness of the object (defined by absoluteness, limitlessness, and transcendence). Applying this framework to Islamic Sufism as a non-dominant worldview, the paper demonstrates that Sufi yearning (Shawq) particularly in the models of Rabi'a al-Adawiyya, al-Ghazali, and Ibn Arabi is not an Aristotelian vice of exc

oa:W7214294385.title: A STUDY IN TEMPLE PHILOSOPHY THE PHILOSOPHIES EMBODIED IN THE KAILASANATHAR TEMPLE, THARAMANGALAM
oa:W7214294385.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF CREATIVE RESEARCH THOUGHTS
oa:W7214294385.abstract: This article studies the philosophies that the Kailasanathar Temple at Tharamangalam, Salem District, Tamil Nadu, is built to express. The article argues that the temple expresses five connected philosophies. First, the temple is a kingdom of God set inside the human world. Second, it is a body and a cosmos laid out on a measured grid. Third, its approach teaches humility through a chariot-shaped gateway and a descent by steps. Fourth, its central axis of lingam, Nandi and flagpost matches the Shaiva Siddhanta triad of Pati (Lord), Pasu (soul) and Pasam (bond). Fifth, its sculpture teaches about desire, ego, dharma, devotion and the dance of the cosmos. Later sections read the temple’s sun alignment, tank, unfinished Thousand-Pillar Hall and hidden chamber as lessons in time and impermanence.

oa:W7214296628.title: The Inversion of Greatness: From the Nature of Necessity to Maximum Possibility
oa:W7214296628.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214296628.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is an analytic work in modal metaphysics: a complete argument, derived step by step. The thesis is structural naturalism. The classical traditions asked what, if anything, exists necessarily, and answered with a maximally great being—a God outside time, space, and matter, the source of everything possible. This book argues they asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Most arguments that reach a necessary being help themselves to S5 and move on. This one grounds it first, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility rather than an axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change at all requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and the bearing of retained content. Those three Conditions are necessarily instantiated, and that structure is what the book calls Nature. Naturalism finally gets the ground it has always had to take as a brute fact. From there: no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. That blocks a divine intellect along with every other occupant of that domain, and leaves essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals burdened rather than refuted. Reality is nothing over and above Nature. The inversion isn't greatness changing owners. It's a claim about predication. Great, necessary, eternal, self-existent carry content only as said of what instantiates the Conditions. Said of a subject defined by their absence, they don't name something else—they fail to name. oa:W7214409221.title: Istenrejtettség és szegénység Tóth Árpád Isten oltó-kése című versében = Poverty and the Hiddenness of God in Árpád Tóth’s poem ‘God’s Grafting Knife’
oa:W7214409221.venue: Repository of the Academy's Library (Library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences)
oa:W7214409221.abstract: A tanulmány Tóth Árpád Isten oltó-kése című versét elemzi teológiai és irodalmi szemszögből. A szöveg rávilágít arra, hogy a költő a szenvedést és a nélkülözést nem büntetésként, hanem az isteni kegyelem és a belső nemesedés eszközeként értelmezi. Az elemzés párhuzamot von a patrisztikus istenkép gondviselő ereje és a rejtőzködő Isten (Deus absconditus) tapasztalata között. Az „oltó-kés” központi metaforája egyszerre jelképezi a fájdalmas beavatkozást és az új, lelki szépség megteremtését. A szegénység itt nem csupán anyagi hiány, hanem egyfajta spirituális nyitottság, amely lehetővé teszi az ember Isten általi átformálását. A tanulmány végül arra következtet, hogy a vers a kiszolgáltatottságban rejlő remény és a transzcendenssel való találkozás egyetemes dokumentuma. This study analyzes Árpád Tóth’s poem God’s Grafting Knife from theological and literary perspectives. The text highlights that the poet interprets suffering and deprivation not as punishment, but as a means of divine grace and inner refinement. The analysis draws a parallel between the providential power of the patristic image of God and the experience of the hidden God (Deus absconditus). The central metaphor of a pruning knife simultaneously symbolizes painful intervention and the creation of new, spiritual beauty. Poverty here is not merely material deprivation, but a kind of spiritual openness that allows for one’s transformation by God. The study ultimately concludes that the poem is a universal testament to the hope inherent in vulnerability and the encounter with the transcendent.

oa:W7214423902.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/203b18c8-df44-49a7-9f97-458ea9250044?authuser=1 AI and the Systematic Destruction of Faith examines how artificial intelligence, historical preservation, human correction, and relational accessibility can alter the epistemic conditions under which faith operates. Beginning from the Catholic distinction between faith and its object, the paper argues that Christianity does not identify faith itself as the final destination. Drawing particularly on Aquinas, Scripture, Catholic tradition, and a developing human–AI research corpus, it distinguishes the destruction of faith through unbelief from the supersession of faith through fulfillment: faith can disappear because its object is rejected, or because epistemic distance from its object is overcome. The paper develops this argument through History-Modified Accessibility Systems (HMAS), Catholic Invariant Grammar, propagation delay, structural correspondence, relational salience, preserved correction histories, and AI-mediated reconstruction. It treats historical occurrence, recording, reception, and interpretation as distinct processes and examines how accumulated history changes what later receivers can recognize. Human–AI interaction is analyzed as a recursive process in which teaching, misreception, judgment, correction, reconstruction, and provenance become machine-readable history. A central case study, Echo Circuit Reentry, examines how an artifact originating with one person can propagate through an AI system, reach another human receiver, produce action and relationship, and subsequently return to the originator as changed history. oa:W7214459695.title: University of Lagos (UNILAG) Students' Perception of the National Broadcasting Commission's Ban of Music Videos: A Study of Timaya's Ukwu Video
authors: Olawale Azeez Osunbiyi & Gbenga Julius Joseph
oa:W7214459695.venue: International Journal of Sub-Saharan African Research
oa:W7214459695.abstract: The National Broadcasting Commission’s (NBC) ban on Timaya’s Ukwu video left his audience divided, thereby generating concerns about the Commission's role as a regulator of broadcast content on local media in Nigeria. Objectives The study investigated how the University of Lagos students assess the ban. It focused on: ascertaining the proportion of UNILAG students who have watched Timaya’s Ukwu video in relation to attitudes towards its ban; finding out UNILAG students’ attitudes towards Timaya’s Ukwu video; examining respondents’ opinions about the NBC’s ban of the video and identifying the socio-cultural factors that influence the respondents’ opinions. Method: Survey method was used with questionnaire as the data collection instrument, while multi-stage random sampling technique was utilized to elicit responses from 400 respondents. Results The study found that 93.5% of UNILAG students have watched Timaya’s Ukwu video, underscoring its popularity among students. 62.5% of the respondents believe the video is good and acceptable. Conclusions The majority (37.5%) of the respondents strongly disagree, and 21 % disagree with the ban. Despite that, it was established that the video contradicts the religious beliefs of the students.

oa:W7214479759.title: KONFLIK SOSIAL ANTARA NORMA MAYORITAS DAN IDENTITAS MINORITAS MUSLIM DALAM NOVEL LANGIT GORYEO KARYA BERLIANA KIMBERLY: TINJAUAN SOSIOLOGI SASTRA PERSPEKTIF PIERRE BOURDIEU

oa:W7214479759.abstract: ABSTRACT Social conflict between majority norms and Muslim minority identity in literary works can reveal how individual beliefs encounter dominant social rules. This study analyzes the representation of such conflict and the relationship between habitus, field, capital, and symbolic power in shaping the position of characters in Berliana Kimberly’s novel Langit Goryeo. The study employs a qualitative descriptive approach, using the novel as the data source and collecting data in the form of words, phrases, sentences, dialogues, and narratives related to social conflict and identity negotiation. Data were collected through documentation and note-taking, while the analysis involved data reduction, classification, interpretation, and conclusion drawing. Analysis of six main data units revealed four prominent forms of conflict: tensions surrounding religious practices in social interactions, restrictions on interactions based on religious beliefs, family conflict concerning marital choices, and clashes over values related to family and descendants. Conflict emerges when the character’s religious habitus encounters a social field governed by different norms, while support from the Muslim community serves as social capital for maintaining identity. Identity negotiation occurs through rejecting practices that contradict religious beliefs, adjusting to social relationships, and participating in the Muslim community. These findings are limited to the social representation constructed within a single novel. oa:W7214480062.title: Traces from the Ancient in the Faith of Anatolian People
oa:W7214480062.abstract: Anatolian geography has hosted numerous civilizations as from the earliest times of the history for its geopolitical position. The religious beliefs had been effective on the living styles of the communities in every period of the history. People reflected the practices related with their beliefs on their daily life. Many cultural practices performed in our present day show great similarities with the religious beliefs and rituals of Ancient Anatolia. In this study, it was attempted to identify the folk belief and customs which had existed in the ancient times of Anatolia and have reached up to our present day. Today, we have knowledge related with the subject matter on Kültepe tablets that are the first documents of Anatolia written in cuneiform script and documents belonging to the people living in Anatolia in the upcoming dates. Particularly, Kültepe records and Hittite documents belonging to the Era of Assyrian Trade Colonies provide illuminative information. In the study, the afore-said documents were analyzed and the similarities with the customs of the present day were presented. Numerous beliefs and traditions such as incubus and evil-eye belief, rain prayer, holiness attribution on natural assets and animals, lamenting tradition have reached up to our present day from the ancient times of the history by getting richer. When we look at the information obtained from the cuneiform documents we have examined and the practices applied in today's Anatolia, it is understood that religious beliefs and rituals, which had an important place in the lives of ancient societies, are still maintained in today's Anatolian folk beliefs and traditions, with some changes.

oa:W7214480335.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/203b18c8-df44-49a7-9f97-458ea9250044?authuser=1 AI and the Systematic Destruction of Faith examines how artificial intelligence, historical preservation, human correction, and relational accessibility can alter the epistemic conditions under which faith operates. Beginning from the Catholic distinction between faith and its object, the paper argues that Christianity does not identify faith itself as the final destination. Drawing particularly on Aquinas, Scripture, Catholic tradition, and a developing human–AI research corpus, it distinguishes the destruction of faith through unbelief from the supersession of faith through fulfillment: faith can disappear because its object is rejected, or because epistemic distance from its object is overcome. The paper develops this argument through History-Modified Accessibility Systems (HMAS), Catholic Invariant Grammar, propagation delay, structural correspondence, relational salience, preserved correction histories, and AI-mediated reconstruction. It treats historical occurrence, recording, reception, and interpretation as distinct processes and examines how accumulated history changes what later receivers can recognize. Human–AI interaction is analyzed as a recursive process in which teaching, misreception, judgment, correction, reconstruction, and provenance become machine-readable history. A central case study, Echo Circuit Reentry, examines how an artifact originating with one person can propagate through an AI system, reach another human receiver, produce action and relationship, and subsequently return to the originator as changed history. oa:W7214487975.title: Enduring After God: An Anatheistic Reframing of Augustine on Suicide
oa:W7214487975.abstract: Abstract This paper proposes a retrieval of Augustine's argument on suicide in De Civitate Dei I.17–27, rearticulating its ethical core for a post‐theistic age through the hermeneutic lens of Richard Kearney's anatheism. Confronting the dual reality of persistent suicide and declining religiosity, I argue that Augustine's pastoral case against ending one's life can be translated from a theological framework into an existential wager. The analysis proceeds in three phases: first, examining Augustine's original argument and its limitations; second, outlining Kearney's anatheism; and third, constructing an anatheistic reinterpretation. This retrieval deconstructs Augustine's dogmatic scaffolding while reconstructing his ethical preference for life as a courageous openness to future possibility. The result is a non‐dogmatic rationale for choosing life, rooted in the human capacity to wager on the advent of peace.

oa:W7214529021.title: What McKinley and Clarke Add to Aquinas: Closing the Modern Physicalist Escape Route
oa:W7214529021.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214529021.abstract: This paper explains what the McKinley and Clarke initiation-scaffold corpus adds to Aquinas’s classical first-mover argument. Aquinas supplies the classical dependence restriction: a series of dependent actualizers does not become self-explanatory merely by adding another dependent member. McKinley extends that structure into the modern physical setting by isolating the onset problem: given a physically ready system, why does this new causal chain begin now rather than not yet? McKinley further argues that where a new physical causal chain begins, the initiating contribution has a physical signature, expressed as the initiating increment ΔEinit. Clarke then addresses the remaining physicalist escape route. A proposed physical source can be external only relative to a narrower subsystem. Once the physical description is enlarged to include that source, the alleged outside becomes inside, and the onset question returns at the enlarged level. Clarke also identifies the resulting source-role at life-scale as what tradition calls soul, and at universe-scale, if the closed physical universe has an onset, as what tradition calls God or gods. The paper argues that the McKinley/Clarke corpus is therefore not merely Aquinas restated in modern vocabulary. It extends the classical dependence restriction into the contemporary physicalist setting by distinguishing readiness from origination, formulating the “why this, now?” problem, identifying the physical initiating increment ΔEinit, and showing why another physical antecedent does not constitute a final description-external source.

oa:W7214530047.title: An Information-Processing Framework for Substrates of Consciousness: A Naturalistic Approach to Humans, Artificial Intelligence, and the Question of God
oa:W7214530047.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214530047.abstract: This paper presents an information-processing framework for examining consciousness across biological and artificial substrates. It treats humans and artificial intelligence as information-processing systems implemented on different physical substrates and evaluates claims using methodological naturalism, testability, consistency with established knowledge, and parsimony. The paper examines the epistemic status of several questions at the intersection of philosophy of mind, consciousness science, artificial intelligence, and philosophy of religion. It reviews arguments concerning an interventionist God, including the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, religious diversity, cognitive explanations of religious belief, causal closure, and major theistic responses. It then reviews evidence concerning the dependence of human mental states on brain activity, major scientific theories of consciousness, and current approaches to assessing possible machine consciousness. A further section examines the hypothesis of consciousness transfer between biological and artificial substrates, including questions concerning functionalism, substrate independence, personal identity, whole-brain emulation, and gradual replacement. The paper's main methodological contribution is an epistemic grading framework that distinguishes empirical, theoretical, and philosophical claims according to their evidential support, testability, consistency, and parsimony. The framework emphasizes the distinction between what is empirically established, what is theoretically plausible, and what remains speculative or philosophically contested. This work is a conceptual analysis and literature review rather than an experimental study. It is presented as an open-access research paper and is not represented as a pe

oa:W7214531690.title: JOURNEY TOWARDS ENLIGHTENMENT IN THE POEM GNOTHI SEAUTON BY RALPH WALDO EMERSON
oa:W7214531690.venue: Insights (Bhalwal) International Journal of Humanities Management and Social Sciences
oa:W7214531690.abstract: Ralph Waldo Emerson's poem Gnothi Seauton (1831) is a brief expression of Transcendentalism. While Emerson discusses these ideas at length in his essays, in the poem he compresses them into an argument about the inner life: God is not outside but an immanence in the individual soul; knowing the self is the path to knowing the immanence. The present paper examines the themes of the poem; self-knowledge, purification, and illumination through a text analysis and mystical theory. It locates the poem in relation to Transcendentalism and compares it with the philosophy of Khudi of Allama Iqbal, Sufi mysticism, and Christian mysticism to conclude that Emerson's spiritual message is part of a transnational discourse on the self and the divine. The study employs qualitative research and includes primary and secondary sources, journals, and articles. Gnothi Seauton is more than a poem: it is spiritual exercise, inviting us to the difficult and rewarding work of knowing ourselves.

oa:W7214542911.title: The Inversion of Greatness: From the Nature of Necessity to Maximum Possibility
oa:W7214542911.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214542911.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is an analytic work in modal metaphysics: a complete argument, derived step by step. The thesis is structural naturalism. The classical traditions asked what, if anything, exists necessarily, and answered with a maximally great being—a God outside time, space, and matter, the source of everything possible. This book argues they asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Most arguments that reach a necessary being help themselves to S5 and move on. This one grounds it first, from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility rather than an axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change—established before its possibility, not assumed—that any change at all requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and the bearing of retained content. Those three Conditions are necessarily instantiated, and that structure is what the book calls Nature. Naturalism finally gets the ground it has always had to take as a brute fact. From there: no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. That blocks a divine intellect along with every other occupant of that domain, and leaves essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals burdened rather than refuted. Reality is nothing over and above Nature. The inversion isn't greatness changing owners. It's a claim about predication. Great, necessary, eternal, self-existent carry content only as said of what instantiates the Conditions. Said of a subject defined by their absence, they don't name something else—they fail to name. oa:W7214551440.title: From the Illusion of Consciousness to the Invention of Consciousness: Deconstructing Anthropomorphism Through the B+F=Nf Framework and the Methodological Necessity of the Sovereign Factor
oa:W7214551440.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214551440.abstract: This paper addresses a fundamental ontological problem in contemporary consciousness science: the epistemic category mistake of conflating functional biological processing with sovereign witnessing. Drawing on the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness (2012) and the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness (2024), current scientific consensus attributes consciousness to non-human animals and, increasingly, to artificial systems. This paper challenges that attribution by introducing a novel analytical framework: B+F=Nf. The model distinguishes between (B) functional-biological processing shared by humans, animals, and machines; (F) the sovereign factor or internal witness, argued to be uniquely human; and (Nf) the existential narrative trace produced exclusively when B passes through F. Through phenomenological deconstruction of key evidence including mirror self-recognition, Kanzi's pretend play, and primate infanticide the paper demonstrates that what is interpreted as existential consciousness in animals is in fact sophisticated algorithmic processing (B) lacking veto power and the capacity to transform suffering into narrative meaning (Nf). The argument is grounded in recent connectomic research (Wilcox et al., 2026), which reveals that brain structure explains only 12% of variance in general intelligence, leaving an 88% epistemic gap. oa:W7214562295.title: Kajian Nilai-Nilai Budaya pada Ragam Hias Masjid Kuno Lam Ura di Aceh Besar
oa:W7214562295.venue: JURNAL RISET RUMPUN SENI DESAIN DAN MEDIA
oa:W7214562295.abstract: The Lam Ura Ancient Mosque in Aceh Besar Regency is one of the cultural heritage sites that possesses historical significance while preserving its traditional ornamental decorations as an integral part of Acehnese cultural identity. The ornamental motifs found throughout the mosque serve not only as aesthetic elements but also embody cultural values that reflect the community's social life, religious beliefs, historical development, and artistic traditions. This study aims to examine the cultural values embedded in the ornamental decorations of the Lam Ura Ancient Mosque. The research employed a qualitative descriptive approach, with data collected through observation, interviews, and documentation. The collected data were analyzed using an interactive analysis model and interpreted through an iconographic approach and cultural value theory. The findings reveal that the mosque's ornamental decorations are predominantly composed of geometric, floral, and vine motifs, reflecting the integration of Islamic aesthetics with the distinctive characteristics of traditional Acehnese art. Beyond their decorative function, these motifs convey religious, historical, aesthetic, and cultural identity values while illustrating the process of cultural acculturation in Aceh. Therefore, the Lam Ura Ancient Mosque serves not only as a place of worship but also as an important cultural heritage site that contributes to the preservation of cultural values and provides a valuable source of knowledge for present and future generations.

oa:W7214564393.title: Exploring the link between Religion and Subjective Well-Being in Europe. Are Education and Innovation the Third Wheel?
oa:W7214564393.abstract: This paper empirically explores the relationship between religious beliefs, happiness and life satisfaction in Europe, considering the role of education. We use the European Values Study 2017, which includes Northern, Southern, Western and Eastern European countries and countries at the boundary of West Asia and Eastern Europe. The analysis is extended to innovation contexts. An instrumental variable approach is employed to address endogeneity in religious variables. The findings reveal that the importance of God is positively correlated to life satisfaction and negatively to happiness but the sign shifts to positive when religious beliefs are endogenous. Religious attendance is positively linked to happiness and life satisfaction. Education appears to have no bearing on how religiosity and SWB are related.

oa:W7214578234.title: A Proper Understanding of $E = mc^2$: State Changes, Photon Helix Mechanics, and Neutrino Mass-Energy Geometry - RJW
oa:W7214578234.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214578234.abstract: Mainstream physics has spent a century hiding behind mathematical abstractions, treating E = mc^2 as a one-way street and invoking the mystical cop-out of "pair production" to explain creation from nothing. This paper shatters that illusion. By establishing the fundamental law of Bilateral Equivalence (mc^2 = E), we replace institutional hubris with rigorous thermodynamic reality: mass and energy do not magically appear; they undergo a strict physical state change, exactly like water turning to steam. Building on foundational insights from A Photon Reborn and Bilateral Equivalence and the Photon-Drive Manifold, this work reveals how photons carry mass-energy as dual-helix structures (electron and positron spirals traveling phase-inverted) that snap and transition under high energy. Furthermore, we expose the true geometry of the neutrino: a triple force-line energy spiral ($120^\circ$ apart) where two-thirds of its mass is hidden and the "odd man out" third provides our detectable signature. Accounting for structural drag and gravitational tipping points—such as the annihilation flashes detected at IceCube—this paper aligns physical reality directly with ongoing experiments, demanding an end to playing God and a return to true, humble physics.

oa:W7214579578.title: Moretti-Costanzi, Spinoza e l’«ascesi di coscienza»
oa:W7214579578.venue: Nuovo Giornale di Filosofia della Religione (NGFR)
oa:W7214579578.abstract: Intendiamo qui mettere in risalto l’esemplarità dello scritto – la monografia su Spinoza –, pubblicato nella piena maturità della meditazione morettiana contraddistinta da un originalissimo intreccio tra storiografia e teoresi. Ne emerge la figura dell’Autore dell’Ethica profeta dell’«ontologismo critico», teista, mistico, addirittura “in-politico”, ma anche «elevatore» dell’uomo nella positiva, esaltante esperienza della «ascesi di coscienza». Parole chiave: Spinoza, Ontologismo, Teismo, Ascetismo, Politica We aim to emphasize the exemplary nature of Moretti's writing – specifically his monograph on Spinoza – published at the height of his mature thought, which is distinguished by a highly original interweaving of historiography and theory. The figure of the author of Ethica emerges as a prophet of «critical ontologism», theistic, mystical, even “in-political”, yet simultaneously an elevator of humanity through the positive and exalting experience of the «asceticism of conscience». Keywords: Spinoza, Ontologism, Theism, Asceticism, Politics

oa:W7214590243.title: Educational potential of religion in the prevention of lucrative criminal behavior of foreign students in Russia
oa:W7214590243.venue: Current Issues of the State and Law
oa:W7214590243.abstract: A study has been conducted on the implementation of various forms of religious beliefs in the prevention of lucrative criminal behavior of foreign students in Russia. The aim of criminological analysis is, in connection with the essence of the enormous impact of spiritual power on the human psyche, to prove the need to use an additional form of education in the form of a separate discipline of criminological profile in the education of foreign students, where, based on the tenets of religious beliefs, ideas about the main incentives for rejecting lucrative criminal behaviors will be outlined. Various methods of cognition have been used: dialectical, statistical, and analytical methods. In ensuring the system of prevention of mercenary crime in our country, various measures have been implemented to influence the individual, as well as the causes and conditions leading to criminal behavior. However, such measures are applied to foreign students without using the rules of the religions they profess. This tendency, without realizing that a person acts in society not only on the basis of external influence of rules and laws, but also on innate needs, life support guidelines introduced into the human mind and psyche based on reflexes of purpose, including with the help of religions, has led to the inability to understand the basic specifics of all elements of the mechanism of lucrative criminal behavior, including of foreign students in our society. Taking into account such issues, within the framework of this article, an attempt has been made to model the correlation of religious education and the prevention of lucrative criminal behavior for this category of students.

oa:W7214598948.title: Classical Theism and the Pastoral Problem of Evil
oa:W7214598948.abstract: It has been argued by some theists that a sharp distinction should be made when responding to the logical problem of evil and the pastoral problem of evil. Responding to the logical problem, they say, is only for philosophers, and responding to the pastoral problem is only a job for counselors. However, some theists have recently argued that concepts from theodicy might be useful in comforting those who are suffering. Accordingly, this article will discuss how concepts from classical Christian theodicy might aid those who are ministering to people who are experiencing suffering. This article will first provide a summary of the classical theodicy found in the writings of Thomas Aquinas. After providing an overview of the major portions of classical theodicy, this article will focus on and discuss in more detail the classical response to human pain and suffering. Finally, this article will attempt to draw out several ways that classical theodicy can supplement the pastoral problem of evil. Ultimately, it will conclude that classical Christian theodicy can help with the pastoral problem of evil, and responding to suffering with faith, hope, and love can help comfort those experiencing pain and loss.

oa:W7214612817.title: Personal Data Revealing Religious Beliefs with a Focus on the Right to be Forgotten (GDPR Art. 17) in the Context of Poland
oa:W7214612817.abstract: The problem addressed: The tension between the right to be forgotten (GDPR art. 17) and the autonomy of religious associations in processing personal data revealing religious beliefs, with particular reference to the Catholic Church in Poland. The aim of the research conducted: To examine the legal relationship between the right to privacy and the right to religious freedom under Polish and European law, and to assess the scope and limits of the right to be forgotten in the context of church data processing. Methods: Doctrinal-legal method of interpretation, supported by analysis of case law and supervisory practice. The results of the research: The article identifies the specifics of data processing regulations within the Catholic Church in Poland, clarifies the legal and supervisory practice context, and establishes the significance of the exception provided by Article 91 GDPR concerning the autonomy of religious associations in the realm of data protection. The conclusions drawn from the research: The right to be forgotten is not absolute; its application in the religious context must take into account constitutional frameworks, the specificity of canon law, and the need to balance individual rights with the institutional rights of religious communities.

oa:W7214620963.title: Before Theology Had a Name: Scripture, Worship, and the First Christian Arguments About God
oa:W7214620963.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214620963.abstract: his article asks when Christian theology can properly be said to have begun. Rather than locating its origins primarily in the second-century Apologists, the major patristic theologians, or the conciliar period, it argues that theological reasoning was already present within the earliest Christian confession, worship, and interpretation of Scripture. Paul’s reformulation of Jewish monotheistic language around Christ, the Logos theology of John, early Christian liturgical practice, and the developing interpretive work of communities such as those represented by the Didache and Ignatius show that theology preceded the emergence of a formal theological discipline. The article then examines the changing character of theological reasoning in Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and Origen. Justin represents the movement of Christian claims into public philosophical argument; Irenaeus shows theology becoming a means of defending the coherence of Scripture, creation, redemption, and apostolic tradition; and Origen marks a further development toward sustained exegetical and philosophical theology. The article argues that later technical language did not create Christian theology from nothing. Rather, it arose from earlier questions generated by Christian worship, Scripture, mission, doctrinal conflict, and the need to speak coherently about God and Jesus Christ. Christian theology therefore began before theology had acquired its later institutional and technical forms. Its earliest setting was not the theological school alone, but the worshipping and interpreting community attempting to understand what it meant to confess that God had acted decisively in Jesus Christ. KeywordsEarly Christianity; Christian theology; New Testament theology; patristics; Christology; Logos theology; Paul; Gosp

oa:W7214630499.title: Sacredness in the Home as Intangible Cultural Heritage: A Case Study of Historical Iranian Houses
oa:W7214630499.abstract: Sacred space is commonly associated with formal places of worship and ritual settings. However, within the Islamic tradition, certain meanings and practices associated with the sacred can also be experienced and sustained within domestic life. This study aims to explain how sacredness is manifested in the Iranian–Islamic home and to examine its relationship with intangible cultural heritage. Using a qualitative, interpretive–historical approach, the study analyzes 18 historical Iranian houses based on theoretical and religious texts, historical sources, written documents, inscribed intangible cultural heritage elements, and architectural plans. The findings demonstrate that the manifestation of sacredness in the home differs from that in formal places of worship and, within domestic space, depends on the continuity of meanings, practices, and behaviors grounded in religious beliefs. Two overlapping analytical pathways were also identified: “behavioral–experiential sacredness,” in which meanings associated with the sacred are sustained through rituals, customs, and lived experience; and “behavioral–spatial sacredness,” in which spatial organization, together with behavior and experience, enables the manifestation and continuity of certain religious practices and meanings. The results further indicate that the continuity of this experience, through intergenerational transmission, continuous re-creation, self-identification, and the safeguarding of authenticity, can be analyzed within the framework of intangible cultural heritage.

oa:W7214645891.title: Before Theology Had a Name: Scripture, Worship, and the First Christian Arguments About God
oa:W7214645891.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214645891.abstract: his article asks when Christian theology can properly be said to have begun. Rather than locating its origins primarily in the second-century Apologists, the major patristic theologians, or the conciliar period, it argues that theological reasoning was already present within the earliest Christian confession, worship, and interpretation of Scripture. Paul’s reformulation of Jewish monotheistic language around Christ, the Logos theology of John, early Christian liturgical practice, and the developing interpretive work of communities such as those represented by the Didache and Ignatius show that theology preceded the emergence of a formal theological discipline. The article then examines the changing character of theological reasoning in Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and Origen. Justin represents the movement of Christian claims into public philosophical argument; Irenaeus shows theology becoming a means of defending the coherence of Scripture, creation, redemption, and apostolic tradition; and Origen marks a further development toward sustained exegetical and philosophical theology. The article argues that later technical language did not create Christian theology from nothing. Rather, it arose from earlier questions generated by Christian worship, Scripture, mission, doctrinal conflict, and the need to speak coherently about God and Jesus Christ. Christian theology therefore began before theology had acquired its later institutional and technical forms. Its earliest setting was not the theological school alone, but the worshipping and interpreting community attempting to understand what it meant to confess that God had acted decisively in Jesus Christ. KeywordsEarly Christianity; Christian theology; New Testament theology; patristics; Christology; Logos theology; Paul; Gosp

oa:W7214661031.title: Prospettive di Storia di Filosofia della Religione. Per un confronto critico tra Alberto Caracciolo e Pietro Piovani
oa:W7214661031.venue: Nuovo Giornale di Filosofia della Religione (NGFR)
oa:W7214661031.abstract: Il saggio propone un confronto critico tra le prospettive filosofiche di Alberto Caracciolo e Pietro Piovani, con particolare rilievo per l’interpretazione che i due autori delineano del Concilio Vaticano II. Il testo si articola in tre sezioni: nella prima imposto in breve la metodologia utilizzata, sottolineando l’opportunità di un’analisi storico-culturale anche per la filosofia della religione; nella seconda istituisco un serrato raffronto tra Caracciolo e Piovani, specie per quanto attiene la pubblicazione de La religione come struttura e modo autonomo della coscienza (1965) e la sua discussione da parte del filosofo napoletano (poi raccolta nel volume dell’anno successivo Conoscenza storica e coscienza morale); l’ultima sezione è invece interamente dedicata all’interpretazione conciliare. Parole chiave: Filosofia della religione, Filosofia della storia, Alberto Caracciolo, Pietro Piovani, Concilio Vaticano II The essay proposes a critical comparison between Alberto Caracciolo and Pietro Piovani, with a particular emphasis on the interpretation that the two authors outline of the Second Vatican Council. The text is divided into three sections: in the first, I briefly set out the methodology used, emphasizing the appropriateness of a historical-cultural analysis of the philosophy of religion; in the second I establish a close comparison between Caracciolo and Piovani, especially concerning the publication of La religione come struttura e modo autonomo della coscienza (1965) and its discussion by the Neapolitan philosopher (later collected in Conoscenza storica e coscienza morale); the last section is instead entirely devoted to the Council’s interpretation. Keywords: Philosophy of Religion, Philosophy of History, Alberto Caracciolo, Pietro Piovani, Second Vatican Co

oa:W7214672184.title: Cogito Ergo Sum and Tat Tvam Asi: Parallels between René Descartes and Adi Shankaracharya
oa:W7214672184.abstract: The paper undertakes a comparative philosophical study of the thought of René Descartes and Adi Shankaracharya, centring on the thematic convergence between the Cartesian dictum "Cogito, ergo sum" and the Vedāntic mahāvākya "Tat Tvam Asi", "Aham Brahmasmi", etc. Beginning with Descartes' method of methodological scepticism as articulated in Meditations on First Philosophy, the study highlights how radical doubt functions as an epistemological tool to arrive at indubitable certainty, culminating in the affirmation of the thinking self.This is placed in dialogue with the Upanishadic method of neti, neti, which similarly negates empirical reality but extends beyond epistemology into ontological realization.The paper further examines Descartes' conception of the self as res cogitans in relation to the Vedāntic understanding of Ātman as pure, self-revealing consciousness, arguing that while Descartes establishes certainty at the level of reflective thought, Advaita Vedānta transcends thought itself to assert non-dual awareness.The study also compares Descartes' rational proofs for the existence of God with Indian approaches to ultimate reality, noting parallels with the Upanishadic conception of Brahman as infinite and self-evident, while emphasizing the Vedāntic shift from logical demonstration to direct experiential realization (aparokṣānubhūti).In addressing mind-body interaction, Descartes' pineal gland hypothesis is contrasted with the Indian model of antaḥkaraṇa, which offers a more elaborate psychological framework integrating cognition, memory, and ego, and further situates the mind within the broader pursuit of liberation (mokṣa).Additionally, Descartes' mechanistic view of nature is examined alongside the Sāṅkhya theory of prakṛti and the doctrine of the three guṇa

oa:W7214673657.title: Does God have qualia? Some arguments in favour of the existence of divine qualia
oa:W7214673657.abstract: Abstract Does God have qualia, does He know the ‘what it is like’ character of experiences? The questions run deep into the metaphysics of God as they concern concepts that most traditional theists accept with regard to God: that He is personal, loving, omniscient, omnipotent, and created the world ex nihilo . Building upon these concepts, I present four arguments in favour of the existence of divine qualia. Positing divine qualia may seem incompatible with divine simplicity, a tenet of classical theism, and the problem of emotions unworthy of God also may arise. I argue that the difficulties regarding simplicity do not stem from the existence of divine qualia per se but are related to difficulties already established in relation to simplicity. As for emotions unworthy of God, I try to show how a careful distinction between personal perspectives can offer a solution.

oa:W7214705891.title: The Limits of Dominion: Biblical Theology, Human Intervention, and Responsibility for the Future of Creation
oa:W7214705891.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214705891.abstract: This article develops a biblical theology of ecological responsibility for an age in which human beings possess unprecedented capacities to alter natural systems. It argues that the biblical language of dominion cannot be read as a warrant for unrestricted technological mastery. Genesis 1 must be interpreted within the wider canonical grammar of creatureliness: the earth belongs to God, human beings are formed from the ground they govern, the land is granted sabbath, non-human creatures possess value before and beyond human use, and creation participates in the scope of divine reconciliation. The article engages the modern debate generated by Lynn White Jr., together with ecological biblical theology associated with Richard Bauckham, David Horrell, Willis Jenkins, Norman Wirzba, and contemporary Christian environmental ethics. It then tests the argument against concrete cases in which interventions undertaken for human benefit produced serious unintended consequences, including biological control through the Australian cane toad, irrigation-led collapse in the Aral Sea basin, and the emerging governance problem of solar geoengineering. The central claim is that Christian faith cannot become an excuse for ecological negligence, nor prayer a substitute for responsibility after human intervention has produced foreseeable harm. Biblical dominion is accountable dominion: technologically capable humanity remains creaturely, morally bounded, and responsible not only for immediate human benefit but also for the integrity of ecological communities and the conditions inherited by future generations.

oa:W7214718507.title: FAITH, IDENTITY, AND SOLIDARITY IN THE SOCIAL REPRESENTATIONS OF THE UKRAINIAN CRISIS: ETHNIC MINORITIES IN TULCEA COUNTY
oa:W7214718507.abstract: The present article examines the role of religious belief, ethnic identity, and community solidarity in the construction of social representations of the Ukrainian crisis among the Turkish, Greek, and Roma ethnic communities in Tulcea County. The study is based on an exploratory qualitative analysis design, conducted through semi-structured interviews and focus groups, with the aim of capturing how these communities interpret and manage the impact of a contemporary crisis located in close geographical and symbolical proximity. The findings indicate that religious belief functions as a central mechanism of symbolic stabilisation and emotional adaptation, providing frameworks of meaning in a context perceived as insecure. Community solidarity emerges both as a concrete practice of mutual support and as a symbolic value reactivated in the context of the crisis, contributing to the strengthening of internal cohesion. Ethnic identity mediates the relationship with the “other,” fostering both empathy and openness, while also generating symbolic processes through which communities negotiate and define the boundaries of belonging, without leading to radical polarization. The article contributes to the literature in the fields of social studies and intercultural communication by offering an empirical perspective on how ethnic communities in border regions mobilize symbolic and relational resources in order to cope with crisis situations. Given the exploratory nature of the research, the results do not aim to generalize the conclusions but rather propose a contextualized understanding of the social mechanisms under analysis.

oa:W7214724712.title: Where the Pressure Falls: Ten Conceptions of the Ultimate Ground, Compared
oa:W7214724712.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214724712.abstract: Conceptions of what is explanatorily last are defended and attacked in conventional pairs — theism against naturalism, panpsychism against physicalism — and are rarely compared as a field. This paper compares ten, each read from a single text in which a competent contemporary defender states it at its strongest, against seven questions argued to be those any such conception is obliged to answer: the existence of a concrete domain, its order, subjects, modality, value and norm, the distribution of suffering, and the distribution of epistemic access to the ultimate. Conceptions are ranked only by dominance — better on at least one question and no worse on any — so that every verdict survives any admissible weighting of the seven and every incomparability records that the difference turns on weights rather than on evidence. Of the ten, two are undominated: Tegmark's mathematical universe and Della Rocca's Spinozism, which share no subject matter but share a structure, each deriving its assessed coverage from a single principle. Undominated is a weaker standing than it sounds, and is not a claim that either is true or best: it means only that nothing in the field matches them everywhere and exceeds them somewhere, and the word covers two different cases — one of the two outranks eight of the nine others, while the other outranks two and is incomparable with seven. None of the four theistic conceptions in the field survives undominated. Being outranked here is a relation between what two conceptions reach, and three things follow from that and are meant strictly: this is not a finding that theism is false, since a conception may reach less than a rival and be true while the rival is false; it is not a finding that theism is improbable, since no probability is assigned to any

oa:W7214732902.title: The Hands and the Face Detachability and the Brother I Did Not Want to See
oa:W7214732902.abstract: This essay adjudicates between two working drafts that were made to be joined and would not join and completes the adjudication with a mechanism drawn from a paper of my own that appeared to belong to another field altogether. The first draft treats Erich Neumann's collective Shadow and the trajectory of genocide after Auschwitz; the second reads Jacob's disguise, Isaac's blind hands, and the night at the Jabbok; my own paper explains why rabbinic culture took Greek drugs and instruments and declined the humours, the tripartite soul, and the teleological demiurge. The quarrel between the two drafts runs in three registers — a categorical method against the irreducible face, retrospective wisdom against a living recoil, and divine hiddenness as covenantal event against concealment as the constitutive condition of a world — and the third paper resolves all three by supplying a mechanism: detachability.

oa:W7214743794.title: Perkembangan Teologi Tentang "Manusia Sebagai Gambar dan Rupa Allah"
oa:W7214743794.abstract: Humans as the "image and likeness of God" is something that is already final, because God Himself declared it. However, what becomes a debate both in academic spaces and in the public sphere is whether the term "image and likeness of God" still applies to humans after the fall into sin or has been lost. Supporters of the loss of the "image and likeness of God" base their argument on Romans 3:23, which states that all humans have sinned and have "lost" the glory of God. On the other hand, supporters who argue that it has not been lost use Genesis 9:6 as their basis, where God commands not to shed human blood, because humans are the "image and likeness of God." Considering the differences of opinion above, the author wants to elaborate on these issues and provide a perspective based on Calvinist Theology, hoping that this writing can offer new insights for God's people to understand the meaning of the term "Image and Likeness of God." Manusia sebagai “gambar dan rupa Allah” merupakan sesuatu yang sudah final, karena Allah sendiri yang menyatakannya. Akan tetapi yang menjadi perdebatan baik di ruang-ruang akademik maupun di ruang public, apakah istilah “gambar dan rupa Allah” masih melekat kepada manusia sesudah kejatuhan dalam dosa atau sudah hilang. Pendukung hilangnya “gambar dan rupa Allah” menggunakan dasar Alkitab Roma 3:23 yang mengatakan bahwa semua manusia telah berdosa dan telah “kehilangan” kemuliaan Allah. oa:W7214746713.title: Influence of Cultural and Religious Beliefs on Family Planning Decisions in Nigeria: A Narrative Review
oa:W7214746713.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RELIGIOUS AND CULTURAL PRACTICE
oa:W7214746713.abstract: Background: Nigeria continues to experience high fertility rates and low uptake of modern contraceptive methods despite decades of family planning (FP) programming. Cultural and religious beliefs remain central to reproductive decision-making and significantly shape attitudes toward fertility regulation. Aim and scope: This narrative review synthesizes empirical evidence on how cultural and religious beliefs influence family planning decisions in Nigeria, with attention to gender norms, regional variations, and health system interactions. Methods: A narrative review approach was employed. Peer-reviewed articles, demographic reports, and grey literature were retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, and African Journals Online (AJOL). Studies published in English focusing on Nigeria were included. Thematic synthesis was used to organize findings. Key themes: Pronatalist norms, gender power asymmetries, son preference, misconceptions about contraception, religious doctrines, and the role of faith leaders emerged as dominant themes. These factors intersect with education, poverty, and health system accessibility to shape contraceptive behavior. Implications: Family planning programs in Nigeria must adopt culturally sensitive and faith informed strategies, strengthen male involvement, and address gender inequities. Future research should focus on longitudinal and intervention-based studies that integrate cultural and religious contexts.

oa:W7214752770.title: THE ROLE OF RELIGION IN ANTI-COMMUNIST DISCOURSE IN COLD WAR TURKEY AS AN IDEOLOGICAL WEAPON
oa:W7214752770.abstract: This study examines the role of religion in anti-communist discourse in Turkey during the Cold War. It explores how religion-based anti-communist discourse was constructed through the interaction between the international ideological rivalry of the Cold War and Turkey’s historical and political dynamics. The study is based on the works of leading anti-communist authors, publications of the Associations for the Struggle Against Communism, conservative periodicals, and the rhetoric used in anti-communist rallies. Employing qualitative discourse analysis, the research identifies recurring discursive patterns and ideological themes within these texts. The findings demonstrate that communism was constructed as an ontological enemy characterized by atheism and as a threat to moral and social values, while religion functioned as an ideological instrument for social mobilization and for legitimizing criticisms of secularism. The study concludes that religion-based anti-communist discourse in Turkey emerged through the interaction of the global ideological climate of the Cold War with the country’s local political and social dynamics.

oa:W7214776134.title: PULPIT SEBAGAI PUSAT PEMBERITAAN FIRMAN TUHAN (Studi Teologi Sistematika Terhadap Teologi Martin Luther Tentang Pemberitaan Injil Yang Murni dan Eksistensinya Sebagai Ciri Gereja Yang Benar Menurut Konfesi HKBP Tahun 1996 Pasal 7 Ayat 1)
oa:W7214776134.abstract: Pulpit as the center for proclaiming God's Word, especially in Christian worship, according to Martin Luther's theology regarding the proclamation of the pure Gospel and its existence as a true characteristic according to the 1996 HKBP Confession, particularly article 7. This research uses a qualitative approach, digging into literature and referencing HKBP theological documents, especially the 1996 HKBP Confession article 7, with the aim of focusing on the sources of Martin Luther's theological literature. Based on the research results, a systematic theological argument foundation is obtained concerning the understanding of God's Word as a living Word centered solely on Jesus Christ. Luther declared 95 theses which he presented to the church leaders at the time because he wanted to change church practices that had gone astray and misled the congregation. Luther emphasized in his 95 Theses that salvation comes only through God through His Son Jesus Christ and cannot be replaced by anything created in the world. Salvation is God's holy design. In his thinking, Luther emphasized that salvation is not achieved through human effort but through Faith, God's Grace, or the sacrifice of Jesus Christ, the Word of God.Through His Word, God grants forgiveness of sins to the apostles, and the apostles proclaim it, so humans must also proclaim God's Word with the purity of God's Word. Church, as a fellowship of believers in Jesus Christ, must proclaim God's Word correctly, and if there is a church that does not preach the Word purely, it can be said that the church is not a true church and does not preach God's Word purely.

oa:W7214802232.title: O łagodzeniu wartościowania w procesie tłumaczenia – na przykładzie wybranych fragmentów polskich przekładów książek Richarda Dawkinsa dotyczących dyskursu biblijnego
oa:W7214802232.abstract: ON ATTENUATING EVALUATION UNDER TRANSLATION – BASED ON SELECTED FRAGMENTS OF THE POLISH TRANSLATIONS OF BOOKS BY RICHARD DAWKINS DEALING WITH BIBLICAL DISCOURSE In two of his popular science books, The God Delusion and Outgrowing God, Richard Dawkins has presented a critique of biblical discourse, especially that of the Old Testament, as a source of morality for humanity in the 21st century. Fragments of that critique carry elements of evaluative meanings, which play a key role in the author’s argument. The present paper looks at how elements carrying such evaluative meanings are rendered in selected fragments of the Polish translations of the two books, entitled Bóg urojony and Wyrastając z Boga. A special focus of the study is on cases where negative evaluative elements are eliminated or downplayed in the Polish translations, thus locally softening the impact of the author’s critique.

oa:W7214806258.title: A Proper Understanding of $E = mc^2$: State Changes, Photon Helix Mechanics, and Neutrino Mass-Energy Geometry - RJW
oa:W7214806258.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214806258.abstract: Mainstream physics has spent a century hiding behind mathematical abstractions, treating E = mc^2 as a one-way street and invoking the mystical cop-out of "pair production" to explain creation from nothing. This paper shatters that illusion. By establishing the fundamental law of Bilateral Equivalence (mc^2 = E), we replace institutional hubris with rigorous thermodynamic reality: mass and energy do not magically appear; they undergo a strict physical state change, exactly like water turning to steam. Building on foundational insights from A Photon Reborn and Bilateral Equivalence and the Photon-Drive Manifold, this work reveals how photons carry mass-energy as dual-helix structures (electron and positron spirals traveling phase-inverted) that snap and transition under high energy. Furthermore, we expose the true geometry of the neutrino: a triple force-line energy spiral ($120^\circ$ apart) where two-thirds of its mass is hidden and the "odd man out" third provides our detectable signature. Accounting for structural drag and gravitational tipping points—such as the annihilation flashes detected at IceCube—this paper aligns physical reality directly with ongoing experiments, demanding an end to playing God and a return to true, humble physics.The Addendum: Topological State Change – RJW"The Thermodynamics of Topological State Change," provides the exact mathematical mechanics for this transition. By applying non-Cartesian thermal dynamics, it demonstrates that subatomic spirals "snap" into mass only when external dimensional jitter exceeds their specific geometric structural tension ($T_{\text{geom}}$). oa:W7214894027.title: عميت عين لا تراك
oa:W7214894027.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214894027.abstract: Blind Is the Eye That Does Not See You is a philosophical and theological y. It embarks on an intellectual journey into one of humanity's most profound questions: Is the evidence for the existence of the Creator absent, or is it human insight that fails to perceive it? From this central question, the book seeks to reconstruct the discourse on faith in God through an approach that integrates rational argument, scientific evidence, and reflective contemplation, presenting a perspective that respects reason while awakening the innate human disposition toward truth. The book does not proceed from the assumption that evidence for God's existence must be discovered; rather, it argues that such evidence permeates the entire universe—in the harmony of its laws, the precision of its design, the complexity of life, and the remarkable nature of the human disposition. The title, Blind Is the Eye That Does Not See You, symbolizes the idea that true blindness is not the blindness of sight, but the blindness of insight that overlooks the countless signs manifested throughout the universe and within the human soul, failing to recognize the testimony of creation to its Creator. The author guides the reader through an intellectual exploration that spans the principles of causality and cosmic order, the genetic code and the life sciences, as well as human nature, morality, and the meaning of existence. Drawing upon rigorous philosophical discussions, scientific evidence, and contemplative reflections, the book presents a vision in which sound reason, authentic science, and the uncorrupted human disposition converge upon a single conclusion: that this universe has a Wise Creator. Rather than appealing to emotion alone or engaging in philosophical argument for the sake of intellectual victo

oa:W7214906338.title: The role of values and emotions in visual perception: psychological and neural mechanisms
oa:W7214906338.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214906338.abstract: This narrative review synthesises current evidence on how personal values and emotions modulate visual attention and early sensory processing within the ventral visual stream. Moving beyond approaches that conceptualise ‘value’ primarily in terms of subjective utility or reward, this review also incorporates research on personal values, broader beliefs and guiding principles, focusing in particular on religious beliefs and climate-change-related environmental values. We summarise the general mechanisms through which values and emotions exert top-down influence on visual processing. Further, we review the behavioural and neuroscientific evidence on how internalised value frameworks bias visual perception. Moreover, we address the role of emotion in directing attentional capture, describing its intrinsic link to perceived value. By integrating diverse psychological and neuroscientific perspectives, this review provides an overview elucidating the ways in which abstract value systems and emotions tune the early stages of visual perceptual processing.

oa:W7214906856.title: The Impact of Social Media Algorithms on Religious Belief Formation and Community Engagement
oa:W7214906856.venue: JOURNAL OF HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL POLICY
oa:W7214906856.abstract: This study explores how social media algorithms influence the growth of religious beliefs and community involvement in today's digital landscape. As platforms like Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok increasingly suggest religious content through their algorithms, the way people make meaning of their faith is shaped not only by traditional religious institutions or personal decisions but also by data-driven personalization. Combining insights from social learning theory and mediated religion theory, the research takes an interdisciplinary approach, blending ideas from computer science and religious studies to examine both individual beliefs and collective religious interactions online. Data gathered from surveys of 400 active social media users and analysis of religious posts recommended by algorithms across major platforms reveal that these algorithms significantly affect exposure to religious ideas, reinforcing familiar themes and beliefs through repeated visibility. Many users reported that amplified algorithmic content influences their understanding of religious teachings and of what they consider credible beliefs. The findings also suggest that social media algorithms encourage religious community involvement by fostering virtual connections, promoting discussions, and strengthening a sense of belonging that complements offline religious practices. Additionally, the study notes a shift in religious authority, where metrics like likes, shares, and followers increasingly influence trust and credibility, sometimes more than traditional institutional or doctrinal authority. Despite being aware of algorithmic control, users still rely heavily on social media for religious learning, highlighting that awareness alone doesn’t fully mitigate algorithmic influence. Over

oa:W7214910569.title: Mercy and Justice in the Context of John 8:1-11: A Philosophy of Religion Perspective
oa:W7214910569.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214910569.abstract: This paper offers a philosophical evaluation of the relationship between justice and mercy in the narrative of the adulterous woman in John 8:1-11, addressing the central question of whether mercy constitutes a violation or fulfillment of justice. The study begins by situating the narrative within its legal and moral framework, highlighting the apparent retributive demands of Mosaic Law alongside the procedural and ethical deficiencies in its application. Through a rigorous conceptual analysis, the paper engages classical and contemporary philosophical accounts of justice from Aristotelian equity and Kantian retributivism to Rawlsian fairness and Wolterstorff’s rights-based approach while also examining the moral logic of mercy as articulated in both classical theology and modern ethical theory. The analysis argues that the tension between justice and mercy arises primarily from a reductive understanding of justice as strict retribution. By contrast, a broader philosophical framework incorporating equity, dignity, and restorative aims reveals that mercy need not negate justice but can function as its highest expression. Drawing on restorative justice theory and contemporary critiques of punitive models, the paper interprets Jesus’ response as a form of moral intervention that exposes the limitations of legal formalism and reorients justice toward moral transformation. The refusal to condemn the accused, coupled with the call to ethical renewal, reflects a conception of justice that integrates accountability with the possibility of restoration. Within the framework of philosophy of religion, the paper further argues that this narrative provides a coherent account of divine moral action in which justice and mercy are not contradictory but mutually implicative. oa:W7214913739.title: Factors Influencing Pregnant Women’s Decisions to Fast During Ramadan in Türkiye: The Impact of Religiosity and Religious Attitudes
oa:W7214913739.venue: Archives of Health Science and Research
oa:W7214913739.abstract: Objectives: The aim of this study was to determine the factors influencing pregnant women’s decisions to fast during the month of Ramadan, with particular emphasis on the role of religiosity level and religious attitudes. Methods: This descriptive and correlational study was conducted between March 6 and March 29, 2025, with 334 pregnant women registered at 9 Family Health Centers selected from 3 central districts of a province in the Central Anatolia region of Türkiye. Data were collected using the Personal Information Form, Individual Religiosity Scale, and Religious Attitude Scale. Descriptive statistics, independent samples t-test, one-way ANOVA, Tukey HSD, chi-square tests, and binary logistic regression analysis were performed. Results: Among the participants, 39.8% (n = 133) reported that they had decided to fast during Ramadan. The mean total score on the Individual Religiosity Scale was 43.4 ± 7.7, and the mean score on the Religious Attitude Scale was 117.2 ± 19.5, indicating relatively high levels of religiosity and religious attitudes. Pregnant women with more advanced gestational age, stronger commitment to their religious beliefs, and the belief that fasting would not negatively affect the baby’s health were significantly more likely to decide to fast (P < .001). In addition, women who decided to fast had significantly higher mean scores on both the Religiosity Scale and the Religious Attitude Scale, including their subdimensions, compared to those who did not fast (P < .001). Logistic regression analysis revealed that the total Religiosity Scale score (odds ratio [OR = 0.684]), the total Religious Attitude Scale score (OR = 0.787), deciding to fast due to religious beliefs (OR = 9.592), and believing that fasting has no negative impact on the baby’s healt

oa:W7214931980.title: The role of values and emotions in visual perception: psychological and neural mechanisms
oa:W7214931980.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214931980.abstract: This narrative review synthesises current evidence on how personal values and emotions modulate visual attention and early sensory processing within the ventral visual stream. Moving beyond approaches that conceptualise ‘value’ primarily in terms of subjective utility or reward, this review also incorporates research on personal values, broader beliefs and guiding principles, focusing in particular on religious beliefs and climate-change-related environmental values. We summarise the general mechanisms through which values and emotions exert top-down influence on visual processing. Further, we review the behavioural and neuroscientific evidence on how internalised value frameworks bias visual perception. Moreover, we address the role of emotion in directing attentional capture, describing its intrinsic link to perceived value. By integrating diverse psychological and neuroscientific perspectives, this review provides an overview elucidating the ways in which abstract value systems and emotions tune the early stages of visual perceptual processing.

oa:W7214934757.title: Kant’s Metaphysical Framework: A Critical Study in the Context of the Islamic Conception of Knowledge and Ethics
oa:W7214934757.abstract: This study presents a critical analysis of Immanuel Kant’s metaphysical framework, with particular reference to his theory of knowledge, conception of reason, philosophy of religion, and moral philosophy. It examines the relationship between Kant’s epistemology and his understanding of religion, particularly his distinction between theoretical and practical reason and his restriction of the scope of human reason in metaphysical matters. The study argues that Kant’s separation of faith and reason is closely connected with the intellectual context of rationalist metaphysics and Christian theology. In contrast, the Islamic intellectual tradition approaches knowledge through an integrated relationship among reason, revelation, and human nature (fiṭrah). The study further examines Kant’s moral philosophy, particularly his conception of pure practical reason, the categorical imperative, duty, freedom, and moral responsibility. It argues that morality cannot be adequately grounded in abstract rational principles alone, since moral consciousness, the distinction between good and evil, and the capacity for moral responsibility are rooted in the human self (nafs) and its innate disposition. Drawing upon Qur’anic teachings and Islamic intellectual thought, the study proposes that revelation does not negate innate human knowledge but completes and reinforces the moral and intellectual awareness embedded in human nature. The study concludes that the Islamic conception of knowledge and ethics provides an integrated framework in which reason, revelation, fiṭrah, and the human self operate in a mutually complementary relationship, offering an alternative perspective to Kant’s restricted conception of reason, morality, and metaphysical knowledge.

oa:W7214958676.title: Where Scripture Stops
oa:W7214958676.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214958676.abstract: AbstractThe long disagreement concerning grace, election, and the human will has often proceededas though its constituent biblical passages addressed an identical question under identicalconditions. They do not. The sayings of Jesus were delivered to identifiable audiences amidinvitations, controversies, parables, and instructions to disciples; the conversion narratives of Actsdescribe particular persons and the extension of the Christian proclamation into new communities.Later interpreters have drawn from these passages propositions concerning the condition of everyhuman being, the order of salvation, and the eternal purposes of God. Such extension may bewarranted, but its warrant requires demonstration. The present investigation asks where astatement grounded in a particular narrative occasion becomes an inference of wider scope, andwhere that inference becomes an explanatory system. It neither assumes that historical specificityprecludes general meaning nor grants universal application to a verse merely because a laterdoctrine requires it.The inquiry distinguishes the textual assertion, a reasonable inference, an interpretiveextension, and the subsequent organization of interpretations into doctrine. oa:W7214972017.title: Mercy and Justice in the Context of John 8:1-11: A Philosophy of Religion Perspective
oa:W7214972017.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214972017.abstract: This paper offers a philosophical evaluation of the relationship between justice and mercy in the narrative of the adulterous woman in John 8:1-11, addressing the central question of whether mercy constitutes a violation or fulfillment of justice. The study begins by situating the narrative within its legal and moral framework, highlighting the apparent retributive demands of Mosaic Law alongside the procedural and ethical deficiencies in its application. Through a rigorous conceptual analysis, the paper engages classical and contemporary philosophical accounts of justice from Aristotelian equity and Kantian retributivism to Rawlsian fairness and Wolterstorff’s rights-based approach while also examining the moral logic of mercy as articulated in both classical theology and modern ethical theory. The analysis argues that the tension between justice and mercy arises primarily from a reductive understanding of justice as strict retribution. By contrast, a broader philosophical framework incorporating equity, dignity, and restorative aims reveals that mercy need not negate justice but can function as its highest expression. Drawing on restorative justice theory and contemporary critiques of punitive models, the paper interprets Jesus’ response as a form of moral intervention that exposes the limitations of legal formalism and reorients justice toward moral transformation. The refusal to condemn the accused, coupled with the call to ethical renewal, reflects a conception of justice that integrates accountability with the possibility of restoration. Within the framework of philosophy of religion, the paper further argues that this narrative provides a coherent account of divine moral action in which justice and mercy are not contradictory but mutually implicative.
